title: Hermione and the Secretary: how gendered task division in introductory physics labs can disrupt equitable learning
abstract: This study investigates how gendered task division in introductory physics labs can undermine equitable learning and hinder the development of students’ physics and science identities. Drawing on reflexive ethnographic observations and interviews, we identify two prevalent modes of work—Secretary-Tinkerer and Hermione-Slacker—that disproportionately disadvantage female students. In the Secretary-Tinkerer mode, women are often relegated to data recording and analysis roles, limiting their hands-on engagement with experimental apparatus. In the Hermione-Slacker mode, women assume excessive managerial responsibilities, such as organizing group work and ensuring task completion, while their partners contribute minimally. Using a physics identity framework, we analyze how these gendered divisions restrict opportunities for female students to build self-efficacy, interest, and perceived recognition as physics learners. Our findings suggest that such inequitable task allocation not only stunts the growth of physics identity among women but also perpetuates stereotypes about who belongs in physics. We propose that recognizing and addressing these patterns is essential for fostering inclusive lab environments that support the identity development of all students.

title: Biomaterials Science and Engineering
abstract: This volume presents a comprehensive collection of reviews and original research articles by leading experts in the interdisciplinary field of biomaterials science and engineering. Focusing on fundamental studies rather than immediate clinical or commercial applications, the book offers an in-depth exploration of the design, development, and characterization of innovative synthetic and engineered biomaterials. Covering a wide range of topics, including sol-gel processes, DNA-based materials, nanocomposites, peptide nanostructures, biodegradable scaffolds, and advanced coatings for biomedical devices, the contributions highlight recent advances in materials for tissue engineering, bone and dental applications, prostheses, and strategies for modulating cell-material interactions. By emphasizing methodological approaches and basic research findings, this work provides a broad perspective on the current potentials and future directions of biomaterials in biomedicine and clinical practice.

title: Highly Dynamic Ligand Binding and Light Absorption Coefficient of Cesium Lead Bromide Perovskite Nanocrystals.
abstract: Cesium lead bromide perovskite nanocrystals (CsPbBr3 NCs) exhibit remarkable photoluminescence and tunable optical properties, making them promising candidates for optoelectronic applications. However, their surface chemistry and quantitative light absorption characteristics remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we investigate the synthesis, surface ligand dynamics, and intrinsic absorption coefficient of CsPbBr3 NCs. Using elemental analysis and precise optical measurements, we determine the intrinsic absorption coefficient, enabling accurate assessment of nanocrystal concentration and purification yield. Solution 1H NMR spectroscopy reveals highly dynamic ligand binding, with ligands readily lost during purification unless both oleic acid and oleylamine are present to stabilize the surface. An increased amine content in the ligand shell enhances quantum yield by promoting stronger carboxylic acid binding. Our findings indicate that CsPbBr3 NCs are terminated by pairs of X-type ligands, such as oleylammonium bromide or oleylammonium carboxylate, consistent with an NC(X)2 binding motif. This work provides new insights into the dynamic surface chemistry of CsPbBr3 NCs and establishes a foundation for further surface modifications critical to their integration in advanced optoelectronic devices.

title: Mathematical models in the social sciences
abstract: As the need for more substantial mathematical training has increased among social science students, the lack of any adequate textbook between the very elementary and the very advanced levels has become crutial. The authors, long-time experts in this field, have answered the need with this volume, and the MIT Press has repsonded by bringing it into renewed circulation.Mathematical Models in the Social Sciences investigates and teaches the formation and analysis of mathematical models with detailed interpretations of the results. These models are self-contained, with the necessary mathematics included in each chapter. A vast range of topics in the social sciences and a wide variety of mathematical techniques are covered by the models. Ample opportunity is also provided for the students to form their own models. Republication of this book provides social science and mathematics students with a text that is the analogue of mathematical methods textbooks used in the study of the physical sciences and engineering. Prerequisites are kept to a minimum; a course in finite mathematics and a semester of calculus are all that is necessary.The chapters cover these main topics (and employ the mathematical approach parenthetically indicated): methodology; preference rankings (an axiomatic approach); ecology (two dynamic models); market stability (a dynamic model); a Markov chain model in sociology; stabilization of money flow (an application of discrete potential theory); branching processes; organization theory (applications of graph theory); and optimal scheduling (a problem in dynamic programming).

title: Aquatic Chemistry: Chemical Equilibria and Rates in Natural Waters
abstract: This paper examines the Demand-Driven Acquisition (DDA) model for academic library ebook collections, highlighting its evolution, operational mechanisms, and benefits for both libraries and users. DDA enables libraries to provide immediate access to a vast selection of ebooks, with purchases or loans triggered only by meaningful user engagement, thereby optimizing budget efficiency and ensuring collections remain relevant to current academic needs. The model offers flexible options such as traditional DDA, Short-Term Loans, and Access-to-Own, allowing libraries to tailor acquisition strategies while maintaining control over selection and spending. Integration with platforms like Ebook Central, Rialto, and OASIS streamlines management and supports data-driven decision-making. Enhanced features—including customizable alerts, DRM-free downloads, scalable access models, and real-time usage analytics—further empower libraries to adapt to evolving research trends. User-centric collection development is reinforced through direct patron input, resulting in increased usage and satisfaction. The paper concludes that DDA represents a sustainable, adaptable approach to library collection development that aligns resource allocation with demonstrated user demand.

title: Re-Imagining the Morality of Management: A Modern Virtue Ethics Approach
abstract: This paper critically examines the morality of management within business organizations operating under Anglo-American capitalism, using Alasdair MacIntyre’s critique of managerial roles as a foundation. While MacIntyre’s influential argument in After Virtue characterizes managers as embodiments of emotivism and moral neutrality, this analysis contends that his critique requires both tempering and updating in light of contemporary debates on bureaucracy and management ethics. The paper reviews responses to MacIntyre, highlighting the ongoing moral ambiguities faced by managers in complex organizational environments. It then re-engages with MacIntyre’s own virtues-goods-practice-institution schema, arguing that this framework offers a constructive means to re-imagine the morality of management by embedding ethical practices within organizational life. The implications for management practice are explored, suggesting that a modern virtue ethics approach can address persistent concerns about manipulation, compartmentalization, and moral responsibility in managerial roles, ultimately providing a more substantive and hopeful account of ethical management.

title: Handbook of Corrosion Engineering
abstract: Handbook of Corrosion Engineering: Modern Theory, Fundamentals and Practical Applications explores recent progress in metals corrosion and associated protection processes, spanning all corrosion-related characteristics utilized in natural and industrial environments, including monitoring and testing. The book combines the science and engineering of corrosion to assist readers in conducting exact corrosion evaluations in the design and plant management phases, including optimal protection methods. The book examines the basics of corrosion science, including the electrochemical mechanism, thermodynamic and kinetic aspects, different corrosion forms—such as uniform, localized, and stress corrosion phenomena—and protection systems adopted to combat corrosion, including inhibitors, coatings, and cathodic protection.

title: Beamline 10.3.2 at ALS: a hard X-ray microprobe for environmental and materials sciences.
abstract: Beamline 10.3.2 at the ALS is a bend-magnet line designed mostly for work on environmental problems involving heavy-metal speciation and location. It offers a unique combination of X-ray fluorescence mapping, X-ray microspectroscopy and micro-X-ray diffraction. The optics allow the user to trade spot size for flux in a size range of 5-17 microm in an energy range of 3-17 keV. The focusing uses a Kirkpatrick-Baez mirror pair to image a variable-size virtual source onto the sample. Thus, the user can reduce the effective size of the source, thereby reducing the spot size on the sample, at the cost of flux. This decoupling from the actual source also allows for some independence from source motion. The X-ray fluorescence mapping is performed with a continuously scanning stage which avoids the time overhead incurred by step-and-repeat mapping schemes. The special features of this beamline are described, and some scientific results shown.

title: The Learning Platform in Distance Higher Education: Student’s Perceptions
abstract: The aim of this study is to discover student’s perceptions from the School of Education about the use of the learning platform to improve educational process in distance higher education. To this end, a descriptive study with a mixed approach (quantitative and qualitative) has been applied according to the objectives of the study. An ad-hoc semi-structured questionnaire has been validated by experts, obtaining the response of 111 students of the Spanish National University of Distance Education (UNED), who are conducting social education, pedagogy, and master's degrees in education. The results showed positive values in the different dimensions analyzed: (I) Role of learning platform in distance education, (II) Instructional of the design learning platform, (III) Didactic interaction through the learning platform and (IV) The learning platform and professional practice. The analysis of the open questions, provides guidelines for improving the use of the learning platform in distance higher education regarding strengths (student’s exchange, and independent learning) and weaknesses (feedback delay, and content repository).
venue: The Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education

title: Small Business Uniqueness and the Theory of Financial Management
abstract: This paper examines the distinct characteristics of small businesses and their implications for financial management theory. Unlike large firms, small businesses typically lack access to public capital markets, have undiversified owner portfolios, face ineffective or absent limited liability, and are often managed by entrepreneurial founders with incomplete management teams. These features result in higher costs associated with market imperfections, informal relationships with stakeholders, and flexible compensation schemes. The analysis demonstrates that such uniqueness generates financial management issues that differ fundamentally from those encountered by large firms, particularly in areas such as agency problems, information asymmetry, and transaction costs. The paper argues that existing corporate finance theory does not fully address these challenges and calls for the development of a new paradigm tailored to small business financial management. Implications for future research include the need to explore alternative financial arrangements, governance structures, and decision-making processes that reflect the realities of small business operations.

title: Innovation, Dynamic Capabilities, and Leadership
abstract: This paper explores how organizations can thrive amid the volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity (VUCA) that characterize today’s business environment by leveraging innovation, dynamic capabilities, and strategic leadership. Drawing on recent research and illustrative cases, the authors distinguish between ordinary and dynamic capabilities, emphasizing that while ordinary capabilities support current operations, dynamic capabilities—such as sensing opportunities, seizing them, and transforming the organization—are essential for sustained competitive advantage in turbulent contexts. The paper argues that business model innovation is critical for adapting to disruptive change and that entrepreneurial leadership from top management teams is indispensable for building and orchestrating these higher-order capabilities. By examining the interplay between innovation processes, dynamic capabilities, and leadership approaches, the study provides a framework for understanding how organizations can navigate uncertainty and proactively shape their futures.

title: The n-of-1 clinical trial: the ultimate strategy for individualizing medicine?
abstract: N-of-1 or single subject clinical trials consider an individual patient as the sole unit of observation in a study investigating the efficacy or side-effect profiles of different interventions. The ultimate goal of an n-of-1 trial is to determine the optimal or best intervention for an individual patient using objective data-driven criteria. Such trials can leverage study design and statistical techniques associated with standard population-based clinical trials, including randomization, washout and crossover periods, as well as placebo controls. Despite their obvious appeal and wide use in educational settings, n-of-1 trials have been used sparingly in medical and general clinical settings. We briefly review the history, motivation and design of n-of-1 trials and emphasize the great utility of modern wireless medical monitoring devices in their execution. We ultimately argue that n-of-1 trials demand serious attention among the health research and clinical care communities given the contemporary focus on individualized medicine.

title: Towards a pedagogy of love: exploring pre-service teachers’ and youth’s experiences of an activist sport pedagogical model
abstract: This study explores the experiences of pre-service teachers and youth engaging in an activist sport pedagogical model within a socially vulnerable context, with a focus on the emergence of a pedagogy of love. Employing participatory action research over three semesters, data were collected through observations, group meetings, reflective diaries, artifacts, and interviews involving 10 pre-service teachers and 90 youth. Analysis revealed that a pedagogy of love was characterized by persistent challenges to inequity, the cultivation of solidarity and community, and the fostering of hope and imagination among participants. The findings suggest that activist sport pedagogy can serve as a holistic approach that centers affective relationships, commitment to humanity, and critical dialogue, offering significant implications for empowering both teachers and youth in marginalized settings.

title: LamaH-CE: LArge-SaMple DAta for Hydrology and Environmental Sciences for Central Europe
abstract: LamaH-CE is a comprehensive large-sample hydrological dataset developed for Central Europe, encompassing approximately 170,000 km² across nine countries and including 859 gauged catchments. Building on the CAMELS dataset structure, LamaH-CE provides extensive static catchment attributes—covering topography, climatology, hydrology, land cover, vegetation, soil, and geology—alongside long-term meteorological and runoff time series at daily and hourly resolutions. The dataset uniquely incorporates both independent and intermediate catchments, enabling detailed representation of river network topology and supporting analyses of local runoff generation and river routing. LamaH-CE includes over 60 catchment attributes and more than 20 runoff time series descriptors, with a focus on data quality, completeness, and human impacts. The preparation methodology, data sources, limitations, and uncertainties are thoroughly documented. Additionally, results from a conceptual hydrological baseline model are provided for input plausibility checks and benchmarking. LamaH-CE is designed as a uniform data basis to facilitate comparative hydrological research, model development, and applications in environmental sciences across diverse Central European landscapes.

title: Asymptotic formulae for likelihood-based tests of new physics
abstract: We present asymptotic formulae for likelihood-based statistical tests commonly used in searches for new physics in high energy experiments. Our approach enables efficient calculation of p-values and confidence intervals for model parameters, incorporating the effects of systematic uncertainties through nuisance parameters. By applying results from Wilks and Wald, we derive explicit expressions for the asymptotic distributions of relevant test statistics, eliminating the need for computationally intensive Monte Carlo simulations. We introduce the Asimov data set as a representative data configuration that allows straightforward estimation of median experimental sensitivity and expected statistical fluctuations. The methods are illustrated with practical examples and their implementation in the RooStats package is discussed, providing a robust framework for discovery claims and exclusion limits in particle physics analyses.

title: New advances in nanographene chemistry.
abstract: This review highlights recent advances in the bottom-up chemical synthesis of nanographenes, including both graphene molecules and graphene nanoribbons (GNRs), which offer atomically precise control over structure and properties. The paper discusses four key developments in nanographene chemistry: non-conventional synthetic methods, incorporation of non-hexagonal rings, selective heteroatom doping, and direct edge functionalization. The synthesis of GNRs with well-defined widths and edge structures is achieved by extending solution-based protocols to polymeric precursors and by employing surface-assisted cyclodehydrogenation under ultrahigh vacuum, enabling the formation and atomic-scale characterization of novel GNR architectures. These advances provide new opportunities for tailoring the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of nanographenes, paving the way for their application in nanoelectronics, optoelectronics, and spintronics.

title: Cu-free click cycloaddition reactions in chemical biology.
abstract: Bioorthogonal chemical reactions are paving the way for new innovations in biology. These reactions possess extreme selectivity and biocompatibility, such that their participating reagents can form covalent bonds within richly functionalized biological systems--in some cases, living organisms. This tutorial review will summarize the history of this emerging field, as well as recent progress in the development and application of bioorthogonal copper-free click cycloaddition reactions.

title: Evoked potentials in clinical medicine.
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive overview of the use of evoked potentials in clinical medicine, targeting medical and paramedical professionals involved in clinical diagnosis and evaluation. Organized into sections on visual, brainstem auditory, and somatosensory evoked potentials, the text emphasizes methodology and clinical findings, offering extensive references primarily from recent decades. While the methodological chapters are somewhat repetitive and less detailed than other sources, the strength of the book lies in its thorough compilation of clinical data, particularly in somatosensory evoked potentials and their application to conditions such as multiple sclerosis. The text is well-illustrated with clear figures and captions, facilitating independent understanding. However, the book is limited by an inadequate index, making topic-specific searches challenging, and by a tendency to present findings without synthesizing their implications for clinical decision-making. Despite these shortcomings, the volume serves as a valuable starting point for clinicians seeking to familiarize themselves with the field of evoked potentials and provides a solid foundation for further exploration of the literature.

title: Components of Environmental Literacy in Elementary Science Education Curriculum in Bulgaria and Turkey.
abstract: This study examines the extent to which elementary science education curricula in Bulgaria and Turkey address the six fundamental components of environmental literacy: ecological knowledge, socio-political knowledge, knowledge of environmental issues, affect, cognitive skills, and environmentally responsible behaviors. Using comparative content analysis, the research analyzes objectives from Bulgarian courses such as “The Human Being and Nature,” “Biology and Health Education,” “Chemistry and Environmental Protection,” and “Physics and Astronomy,” alongside Turkey’s “Science and Technology Education” course. Findings reveal an uneven emphasis on environmental literacy components in both countries, with the greatest focus on knowledge-related objectives, less attention to skills and affective components, and minimal emphasis on fostering environmentally responsible behaviors. The results highlight the need for a more balanced integration of all environmental literacy components in elementary science curricula to better support the development of environmentally literate citizens.

title: Building Ontologies with Basic Formal Ontology
abstract: In the era of 'big data,' science is increasingly information driven, and the potential for computers to store, manage, and integrate massive amounts of data has given rise to such new disciplinary fields as biomedical informatics. Applied ontology offers a strategy for the organization of scientific information in computer-tractable form, drawing on concepts not only from computer and information science but also from linguistics, logic, and philosophy. This book provides an introduction to the field of applied ontology that is of particular relevance to biomedicine, covering theoretical components of ontologies, best practices for ontology design, and examples of biomedical ontologies in use.After defining an ontology as a representation of the types of entities in a given domain, the book distinguishes between different kinds of ontologies and taxonomies, and shows how applied ontology draws on more traditional ideas from metaphysics. It presents the core features of the Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), now used by over one hundred ontology projects around the world, and offers examples of domain ontologies that utilize BFO. The book also describes Web Ontology Language (OWL), a common framework for Semantic Web technologies. Throughout, the book provides concrete recommendations for the design and construction of domain ontologies.

title: Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics: From Air Pollution to Climate Change
abstract: This paper examines the Demand-Driven Acquisition (DDA) model for library ebook collections, highlighting its evolution, operational mechanisms, and benefits for academic institutions. DDA enables libraries to provide users with immediate access to a vast array of ebooks, with purchases or loans triggered only by meaningful user engagement, ensuring budget efficiency and collection relevance. The model offers flexibility through various options such as traditional DDA, Short-Term Loans (STL), and Access-to-Own (ATO), allowing libraries to tailor acquisition strategies to institutional needs while maintaining control over selection and spending. Integration with platforms like Ebook Central, Rialto, and OASIS streamlines management and supports data-driven decision-making. Enhanced features such as customizable alerts, DRM-free downloads, and seamless integration with discovery services further improve user experience and collection development. Case studies and survey data indicate that DDA increases usage and aligns expenditures more closely with actual user demand, making it a sustainable and adaptive approach for modern libraries seeking to maximize resource impact and support evolving academic research needs.

title: A decade of systems biology.
abstract: Systems biology provides a framework for assembling models of biological systems from systematic measurements. Since the field was first introduced a decade ago, considerable progress has been made in technologies for global cell measurement and in computational analyses of these data to map and model cell function. It has also greatly expanded into the translational sciences, with approaches pioneered in yeast now being applied to elucidate human development and disease. Here, we review the state of the field with a focus on four emerging applications of systems biology that are likely to be of particular importance during the decade to follow: (a) pathway-based biomarkers, (b) global genetic interaction maps, (c) systems approaches to identify disease genes, and (d) stem cell systems biology. We also cover recent advances in software tools that allow biologists to explore system-wide models and to formulate new hypotheses. The applications and methods covered in this review provide a set of prime exemplars useful to cell and developmental biologists wishing to apply systems approaches to areas of interest.
venue: Annual Review of Cell and Developmental Biology

title: Topological quantum chemistry
abstract: Since the discovery of topological insulators and semimetals, there has been much research into predicting and experimentally discovering distinct classes of these materials, in which the topology of electronic states leads to robust surface states and electromagnetic responses. This apparent success, however, masks a fundamental shortcoming: topological insulators represent only a few hundred of the 200,000 stoichiometric compounds in material databases. However, it is unclear whether this low number is indicative of the esoteric nature of topological insulators or of a fundamental problem with the current approaches to finding them. Here we propose a complete electronic band theory, which builds on the conventional band theory of electrons, highlighting the link between the topology and local chemical bonding. This theory of topological quantum chemistry provides a description of the universal (across materials), global properties of all possible band structures and (weakly correlated) materials, consisting of a graph-theoretic description of momentum (reciprocal) space and a complementary group-theoretic description in real space. For all 230 crystal symmetry groups, we classify the possible band structures that arise from local atomic orbitals, and show which are topologically non-trivial. Our electronic band theory sheds new light on known topological insulators, and can be used to predict many more.

title: The Mathematical Universe
abstract: This paper investigates the consequences of the External Reality Hypothesis (ERH), which posits a physical reality entirely independent of human observers, and argues that it leads naturally to the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis (MUH), asserting that our universe is an abstract mathematical structure. By adopting a sufficiently broad definition of mathematics, the author explores how this perspective impacts foundational issues in physics, including symmetries, irreducible representations, units, free parameters, randomness, and initial conditions. The discussion extends to broader philosophical questions such as consciousness, parallel universes, and Gödel incompleteness. The hypothesis is advanced that only computable and decidable mathematical structures exist, potentially resolving the cosmological measure problem and providing insight into the apparent simplicity of physical laws. The paper also examines the relationship between mathematical structures, computation, simulation, and physical systems, advocating for a baggage-free description of reality rooted in mathematics.

title: The Past, Present, and Future of Media Literacy Education
abstract: Media literacy education in the United States is actively focused on the instructional methods and pedagogy of media literacy, integrating theoretical and critical frameworks rising from constructivist learning theory, media studies and cultural studies scholarship. This work has arisen from a legacy of media and technology use in education throughout the 20th century and the emergence of cross-disciplinary work at the intersections of scholarly work in media studies and education. Reflecting the emergence of a common ground for the field, the Core Principles of Media Literacy Education in the United States was created by a team of scholars and practitioners in 2007. This work reconciles the “protectionist” and “empowerment” wings of the media literacy education community and attempts to counter various misunderstandings among non-specialists. Two issues are identified for their potential to impact the future of the field: (1) media literacy’s relationship to the integration of educational technology into the K-12 curriculum and (2) the relationship between media literacy education and the humanities, arts, and sciences.

title: Active learning in materials science with emphasis on adaptive sampling using uncertainties for targeted design
abstract: One of the main challenges in materials discovery is efficiently exploring the vast search space for targeted properties as approaches that rely on trial-and-error are impractical. We review how methods from the information sciences enable us to accelerate the search and discovery of new materials. In particular, active learning allows us to effectively navigate the search space iteratively to identify promising candidates for guiding experiments and computations. The approach relies on the use of uncertainties and making predictions from a surrogate model together with a utility function that prioritizes the decision making process on unexplored data. We discuss several utility functions and demonstrate their use in materials science applications, impacting both experimental and computational research. We summarize by indicating generalizations to multiple properties and multifidelity data, and identify challenges, future directions and opportunities in the emerging field of materials informatics.

title: Adolescent Medicine: A Practical Guide
abstract: The clinical skills required for the primary care of adolescents encompass the domains of several specialties, but it is the precision with which these skills can be adapted to the unique requirements of adolescents that determines the quality of the clinical outcome. Several texts are now available that attempt to identify unique aspects of adolescence so that primary care clinicians may apply their skills more precisely. The authors of Adolescent Medicine: A Practical Guide use a congenial, informal prose to describe the aspects of adolescence that provide a framework for more detailed discussions of common healthrelated problems of adolescents. The book is intended to serve as an initial guide for clinicians encountering an unfamiliar adolescent problem. Chapters on physical and psychological development and a chapter on seeing adolescents in an office setting provide the framework for addressing other health problems of adolescents. The authors provide some rather uneven discussions of various clinical syndromes, from acne to chronic fatigue syndrome. Chapters dealing with aspects of sexuality—especially contraception and sexually transmitted diseases—are reasonably complete and quite readable. A chapter on adolescent sports medicine is also good and comes closest to the goal of providing a quick guide to commonly encountered health problems of adolescents. Some major problems diminish the book's quality. A continuous appeal is made to a stereotype of the adolescent patient, which, like most stereotypes, is only partially accurate. (For example, most adolescents are said to 'live in a constant state of embarrassment . . .'). This portrayal of adolescents may make them pitiable but not especially attractive as patients. There are also a few factual errors, as in the description of the click of mitral valve prolapse as diastolic. Finally, the quality of many of the figures, especially the microphotographs, is quite poor. This book only partly achieves the goals of its authors. It is difficult to envision the book as a reliable and frequently used quick reference. Other texts are available to better serve this purpose. Clinicians seeking an expanded perspective about their adolescent patients may find the book to be a useful introduction because it is both readable and relatively brief. (J. Dennis Fortenberry, MD, MS, Oklahoma University Health Sciences Center, Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, 73105)

title: Implementing the 27 PRISMA 2020 Statement items for systematic reviews in the sport and exercise medicine, musculoskeletal rehabilitation and sports science fields: the PERSiST (implementing Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and SporTs science) guidance
abstract: Poor reporting of medical and healthcare systematic reviews is a problem from which the sports and exercise medicine, musculoskeletal rehabilitation, and sports science fields are not immune. Transparent, accurate and comprehensive systematic review reporting helps researchers replicate methods, readers understand what was done and why, and clinicians and policy-makers implement results in practice. The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Statement and its accompanying Explanation and Elaboration document provide general reporting examples for systematic reviews of healthcare interventions. However, implementation guidance for sport and exercise medicine, musculoskeletal rehabilitation, and sports science does not exist. The Prisma in Exercise, Rehabilitation, Sport medicine and SporTs science (PERSiST) guidance attempts to address this problem. Nineteen content experts collaborated with three methods experts to identify examples of exemplary reporting in systematic reviews in sport and exercise medicine (including physical activity), musculoskeletal rehabilitation (including physiotherapy), and sports science, for each of the PRISMA 2020 Statement items. PERSiST aims to help: (1) systematic reviewers improve the transparency and reporting of systematic reviews and (2) journal editors and peer reviewers make informed decisions about systematic review reporting quality.

title: Risk Assessment in Geotechnical Engineering
abstract: This text presents a thorough examination of the theories and methodologies available for risk assessment in geotechnical engineering, spanning the full range from established single-variable and "first order" methods to the most recent, advanced numerical developments. In response to the growing application of LRFD methodologies in geotechnical design, coupled with increased demand for risk assessments from clients ranging from regulatory agencies to insurance companies, authors Fenton and Griffiths have introduced an innovative reliability-based risk assessment method, the Random Finite Element Method (RFEM). The authors have spent more than fifteen years developing this statistically based method for modeling the real spatial variability of soils and rocks. As demonstrated in the book, RFEM performs better in real-world applications than traditional risk assessment tools that do not properly account for the spatial variability of geomaterials.

title: Shape-controlled synthesis of metal nanocrystals: simple chemistry meets complex physics?
abstract: The shape-controlled synthesis of metal nanocrystals is a rapidly advancing field at the intersection of simple chemical methods and complex physical phenomena. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent progress in the solution-phase synthesis of metal nanocrystals with well-defined shapes, emphasizing the critical roles of nucleation, seed evolution, and growth processes. By analyzing the influence of experimental parameters such as capping agents, reaction conditions, and precursor selection, we elucidate how these factors govern the formation of diverse nanocrystal morphologies beyond equilibrium shapes predicted by classical models. The article highlights representative systems where reproducible shape control has been achieved and explores the underlying mechanisms that link seed structure and surface chemistry to final nanocrystal geometry. Applications enabled by shape-controlled nanocrystals, including catalysis, sensing, imaging, and photonics, are discussed to illustrate the technological impact of this research. The review concludes with perspectives on current challenges and future directions, underscoring the need for deeper mechanistic understanding to transform the synthesis of metal nanocrystals from an empirical art into a predictive science.

title: Stochastic Modelling for Systems Biology
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive introduction to stochastic modelling in systems biology, emphasizing the necessity of probabilistic approaches for accurately capturing the inherent randomness of biological processes. It systematically covers the representation of biochemical networks, foundational probability models, and simulation techniques including Monte Carlo methods and Markov processes. The work explores stochastic chemical kinetics with detailed discussion of the Gillespie algorithm, stochastic Petri nets, and advanced simulation strategies for both well-mixed and spatially extended systems. Case studies illustrate the application of these methods to key biological phenomena such as enzyme kinetics and genetic regulation. The paper further addresses Bayesian inference and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods for parameter estimation and model comparison in stochastic kinetic models, highlighting both exact and approximate computational techniques. Supplementary materials include software tools and SBML models to facilitate practical implementation. This resource serves as a foundational guide for researchers seeking to model, simulate, and infer the dynamics of complex biological systems under uncertainty.

title: Philosophy of Computer Science: An Introductory Course
abstract: This paper addresses the underdeveloped field of the philosophy of computer science by outlining the structure, content, and rationale of an introductory university course on the subject. Distinguishing the philosophy of computer science from the more established philosophy of artificial intelligence, the course explores foundational metaphysical, epistemological, and ethical questions unique to computer science, such as the nature of computation, algorithms, programs, and their relation to science and engineering. The syllabus is organized around key philosophical questions and incorporates critical thinking and argument analysis tailored for computer science students. The article surveys relevant literature, suggests readings, discusses assignments, and reflects on student engagement and learning outcomes. By presenting this course model, the paper advocates for broader inclusion of philosophical inquiry in computer science education to enhance analytical skills and interdisciplinary understanding.

title: Models of Wave-function Collapse, Underlying Theories, and Experimental Tests
abstract: The measurement problem in quantum mechanics, particularly the absence of macroscopic superpositions despite the linearity of the Schrödinger equation, remains unresolved within standard interpretations. This article reviews phenomenological models of spontaneous wave-function collapse, which introduce stochastic and nonlinear modifications to quantum dynamics to account for the emergence of classicality at macroscopic scales while preserving quantum predictions microscopically. Theoretical frameworks underlying these models, such as trace dynamics and gravity-induced collapse, are discussed in detail. The review also surveys recent and ongoing experimental efforts—including molecular interferometry and optomechanics—that aim to test these collapse models by probing the validity of quantum superposition in increasingly large systems. Technical challenges, current results, and future prospects for experimental falsification are summarized, highlighting the potential for decisive tests of spontaneous collapse theories in the coming decades.

title: Engineering of functional tendon.
abstract: This study addresses the limitations of current tendon repair strategies by engineering functional tendon constructs in vitro using primary rat Achilles tendon fibroblasts. Cells were cultured to confluence and induced to self-assemble into three-dimensional, scaffold-free cylindrical constructs anchored between two points. The resulting tissues exhibited morphological characteristics of embryonic tendon, including aligned, small-diameter collagen fibrils, high cellularity, and abundant noncollagenous extracellular matrix. Mechanical testing demonstrated a nonlinear stress–strain response and ultimate tensile strength comparable to embryonic chick tendon (approximately 2 MPa). These findings indicate that self-organized tendon constructs can recapitulate key structural and mechanical properties of native tendon without artificial scaffolding, representing a significant advance toward biologically compatible tendon replacements.

title: Colloquium: The physics of Maxwell's demon and information
abstract: Maxwell's demon was born in 1867 and still thrives in modern physics. He plays important roles in clarifying the connections between two theories: thermodynamics and information. Here, we present the history of the demon and a variety of interesting consequences of the second law of thermodynamics, mainly in quantum mechanics, but also in the theory of gravity. We also highlight some of the recent work that explores the role of information, illuminated by Maxwell's demon, in the arena of quantum information theory.

title: Magnetic skyrmions: advances in physics and potential applications
abstract: Magnetic skyrmions are nanoscale, topologically protected spin textures stabilized by chiral Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions in systems lacking inversion symmetry, such as non-centrosymmetric crystals and thin films with engineered interfaces. Their solitonic nature and particle-like behavior enable controlled creation, manipulation, and annihilation, making them promising candidates for future information storage, logic, and neuromorphic devices. Recent advances have focused on stabilizing individual skyrmions at room temperature in sputtered multilayers with strong interfacial DMI, overcoming earlier limitations of low-temperature operation and epitaxial growth constraints. Theoretical and experimental studies have elucidated the mechanisms of DMI at metallic and oxide interfaces, guiding material engineering for enhanced stability and tunability. These developments mark significant progress toward practical skyrmion-based spintronic technologies by leveraging their unique topology, chiral interactions, and current-driven dynamics.

title: An invitation to loop quantum gravity
abstract: This paper provides an accessible overview of loop quantum gravity (LQG), a background independent approach to quantum gravity grounded solely in the principles of general relativity and quantum mechanics. Emphasizing foundational physical concepts and their implications, the review outlines how LQG constructs a quantum theory of spacetime without assuming a fixed background geometry. Key results are summarized across canonical and path integral quantizations, matter coupling, unification attempts, extensions to supergravity and higher dimensions, and applications to black holes, cosmology, and Planck-scale phenomenology. The current experimental prospects for testing quantum gravity predictions are discussed, alongside answers to common questions and a list of open problems. The aim is to introduce the main ideas, methods, and achievements of LQG to physicists from diverse fields, providing references for further study while highlighting both the successes and ongoing challenges in the theory’s development.

title: The Impact of a Science Education Game on Students’ Learning and Perception of Inhalants as Body Pollutants
abstract: This study examined the effectiveness of the online science education game Uncommon Scents in enhancing middle school students’ understanding of the biological consequences of exposure to toxic chemicals and influencing their attitudes toward inhalant abuse. A total of 444 students in grades six through eight participated in a pre-test, three gameplay sessions, and a delayed post-test. Results showed significant gains in science content knowledge, with game usability ratings being the strongest predictor of post-test scores. Additionally, students exhibited more negative attitudes toward inhalants after the intervention, particularly among eighth graders, with knowledge gains predicting attitude shifts across all grades. These findings indicate that integrating drug education into environmental science curricula through interactive games is an effective strategy for both increasing scientific literacy and discouraging inhalant use by framing inhalants as body pollutants rather than traditional drugs.
venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology

title: Theory of neutrinos: a white paper
abstract: This white paper provides a comprehensive review of the theoretical landscape of neutrino physics in light of recent experimental advances, particularly the discovery of neutrino oscillations and the consequent evidence for nonzero neutrino masses and mixing. It systematically examines current knowledge of neutrino properties, including mass hierarchies, mixing angles, Dirac versus Majorana nature, and the implications for physics beyond the Standard Model. The report explores mechanisms for generating small neutrino masses, such as various seesaw models, and discusses their testability through phenomena like lepton flavor violation, electric dipole moments, and leptogenesis. The role of neutrinos in addressing fundamental questions such as the origin of matter-antimatter asymmetry, the existence of sterile neutrinos, and connections to grand unification, supersymmetry, extra dimensions, and other new physics scenarios is analyzed. The impact of future experiments on constraining or revealing new theoretical frameworks is highlighted, with extensive references provided to guide further study.

title: Analytical sociology and computational social science
abstract: Analytical sociology seeks to explain how individual interactions generate complex social phenomena, emphasizing the identification of underlying mechanisms responsible for emergent collective outcomes. This approach contrasts with traditional quantitative methods by prioritizing mechanism-based explanations over mere statistical associations. The recent rise of computational social science, which leverages large-scale data, simulations, and machine learning, offers powerful tools that can advance analytical sociology’s aims. While computational social scientists often focus on uncovering empirical regularities, analytical sociology insists on theory-grounded models that map realistically onto actual social processes. This article surveys the synergies and differences between the two fields, arguing that integrating computational methods with the explanatory ambitions of analytical sociology can move social science beyond description and prediction toward deeper understanding of social dynamics and mechanisms.

title: Hartree-Fock on a superconducting qubit quantum computer
abstract: Twelve-qubit quantum computing for chemistry Accurate electronic structure calculations are considered one of the most anticipated applications of quantum computing that will revolutionize theoretical chemistry and other related fields. Using the Google Sycamore quantum processor, Google AI Quantum and collaborators performed a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) simulation of two intermediate-scale chemistry problems: the binding energy of hydrogen chains (as large as H12) and the isomerization mechanism of diazene (see the Perspective by Yuan). The simulations were performed on up to 12 qubits, involving up to 72 two-qubit gates, and show that it is possible to achieve chemical accuracy when VQE is combined with error mitigation strategies. The key building blocks of the proposed VQE algorithm are potentially scalable to larger systems that cannot be simulated classically. Science, this issue p. 1084; see also p. 1054 Accurate quantum simulations of chemistry are performed using up to 12 superconducting qubits and 72 two-qubit gates. The simulation of fermionic systems is among the most anticipated applications of quantum computing. We performed several quantum simulations of chemistry with up to one dozen qubits, including modeling the isomerization mechanism of diazene. We also demonstrated error-mitigation strategies based on N-representability that dramatically improve the effective fidelity of our experiments. Our parameterized ansatz circuits realized the Givens rotation approach to noninteracting fermion evolution, which we variationally optimized to prepare the Hartree-Fock wave function. This ubiquitous algorithmic primitive is classically tractable to simulate yet still generates highly entangled states over the computational basis, which allowed us to assess the performance of our hardware and establish a foundation for scaling up correlated quantum chemistry simulations.

title: Pedagogy of the Twenty-First Century: Innovative Teaching Methods
abstract: This chapter examines the transformation of pedagogy in the twenty-first century, focusing on the adoption and impact of innovative teaching methods in response to rapid technological, social, and educational changes. It analyzes the expansion of the subject of pedagogy from traditional concepts of upbringing to broader notions of education, emphasizing competence-based and learner-centered approaches. The study explores the environmental approach to teaching, the unique characteristics and needs of the digital generation, and the integration of digital technologies into educational practice. Drawing on literature from Kazakhstani, Russian, and international sources, as well as a survey of teachers trained in advanced pedagogical methods, the chapter identifies both opportunities and challenges associated with implementing innovation in teaching. Findings highlight a dynamic interplay between traditional and innovative methods at both macro (societal) and micro (classroom) levels, revealing varying degrees of teacher readiness, systemic support, and professional development. The chapter concludes that effective modernization of pedagogy requires not only technological integration but also a cultural shift among educators toward embracing continuous innovation and reflective practice.
venue: New Pedagogical Challenges in the 21st Century - Contributions of Research in Education

title: Organizing Entrepreneurial Judgment
abstract: Entrepreneurship, long neglected by economists and management scholars, has made a dramatic comeback in the last two decades, not only among academic economists and management scholars, but also among policymakers, educators and practitioners. Likewise, the economic theory of the firm, building on Ronald Coase's (1937) seminal analysis, has become an increasingly important field in economics and management. Despite this resurgence, there is still little connection between the entrepreneurship literature and the literature on the firm, both in academia and in management practice. This book fills this gap by proposing and developing an entrepreneurial theory of the firm that focuses on the connections between entrepreneurship and management. Drawing on insights from Austrian economics, it describes entrepreneurship as judgmental decision made under uncertainty, showing how judgment is the driving force of the market economy and the key to understanding firm performance and organization.

title: The expanded biology of serotonin.
abstract: Serotonin is perhaps best known as a neurotransmitter that modulates neural activity and a wide range of neuropsychological processes, and drugs that target serotonin receptors are used widely in psychiatry and neurology. However, most serotonin is found outside the central nervous system, and virtually all of the 15 serotonin receptors are expressed outside as well as within the brain. Serotonin regulates numerous biological processes including cardiovascular function, bowel motility, ejaculatory latency, and bladder control. Additionally, new work suggests that serotonin may regulate some processes, including platelet aggregation, by receptor-independent, transglutaminase-dependent covalent linkage to cellular proteins. We review this new 'expanded serotonin biology' and discuss how drugs targeting specific serotonin receptors are beginning to help treat a wide range of diseases.

title: Authentic Assessment and Pedagogical Strategies in Higher Education
abstract: Problem statement: Researchers have noted that there is a mismatch between curriculum content and assessment practices in higher education. At the moment, the focus is still on the assessment of learning and not much on assessment for learning. Therefore, this study was conducted to examine the implementation of authentic assessment in higher education in Malaysia. Approach: The study employed a qualitative research method and involved the use of instruments such as interviews, document analysis and unobtrusive classroom observations to collect the relevant data in the classrooms of a three-credit hour course from a Masters degree programme. The total population consisted of 2 lecturers and 20 students from the two selected intact TSL 752 classes. Results: In this study, researchers identified different types of authentic assessment with the suitability to certain pedagogical strategies, their effects on students' learning and the appropriate procedures of conducting authentic assessments. The findings indicated that alternative and authentic assessment have more acceptance from students and should therefore be viewed as an alternative to traditional standardized assessment. Conclusion/Recommendations: The study identified that assessment strategies should be closely related to teaching and learning. Assessing authentic performances should become integral parts of the instructional cycle and feedback provided by the lecturer and peers should be formative in order to help the students assess their strengths and weaknesses, identifying areas of needed growth and mobilizing current capacity.

title: All-optical machine learning using diffractive deep neural networks
abstract: We present a novel all-optical machine learning framework based on Diffractive Deep Neural Networks (D2NNs), where multiple passive diffractive layers, designed through deep learning, collectively perform complex computational tasks using only optical diffraction. By physically fabricating D2NNs with 3D-printed phase-only transmission layers operating at terahertz frequencies, we experimentally demonstrate their ability to implement handwritten digit classification and imaging lens functions, achieving high accuracy and efficiency. This scalable approach leverages the inherent parallelism and speed of light propagation in optical systems, enabling power-efficient and ultrafast execution of machine learning tasks without electronic computation. The D2NN framework opens new avenues for all-optical image analysis, feature detection, object classification, and the design of adaptive optical components, offering significant potential for future advances in optical computing and intelligent imaging systems.

title: Mental Health Strategies to Combat the Psychological Impact of COVID-19 Beyond Paranoia and Panic.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has triggered widespread psychological distress, manifesting as heightened paranoia, panic, and other mental health challenges across affected populations. This commentary examines the multifaceted psychological impact of the outbreak, drawing on early experiences in Singapore and global data. It highlights how fear, uncertainty, and extensive media coverage have contributed to anxiety, depression, and stress among the general public, patients, and healthcare workers. The paper discusses the exacerbation of pre-existing mental health conditions, the emergence of new psychiatric symptoms, and the role of stigma and social disruption in intensifying psychological morbidity. It further explores the unique vulnerabilities of healthcare workers due to occupational exposure and stresses the importance of targeted mental health support. In response, the authors advocate for comprehensive mental health strategies that extend beyond crisis management to include clear communication, community engagement, psychological defense mechanisms, and accessible support services. The commentary underscores the necessity of integrating mental health considerations into public health responses to pandemics to foster resilience and mitigate long-term psychological consequences.
venue: Annals of the Academy of Medicine, Singapore

title: Black holes: complementarity or firewalls?
abstract: We argue that the following three statements cannot all be true: (i) Hawking radiation is in a pure state, (ii) the information carried by the radiation is emitted from the region near the horizon, with low energy effective field theory valid beyond some microscopic distance from the horizon, and (iii) the infalling observer encounters nothing unusual at the horizon. Perhaps the most conservative resolution is that the infalling observer burns up at the horizon. Alternatives would seem to require novel dynamics that nevertheless cause notable violations of semiclassical physics at macroscopic distances from the horizon.

title: Fluorine in medicinal chemistry and chemical biology
abstract: The extraordinary potential of fluorine-containing molecules in medicinal chemistry and chemical biology has been recognized by researchers outside of the traditional fluorine chemistry field, and thus a new wave of fluorine chemistry is rapidly expanding its biomedical frontiers. With several of the best selling drugs in the world crucially containing fluorine atoms, the incorporation of fluorine to drug leads has become an essential practice in biomedical research, especially for drug design and discovery as well as development. Focusing on the unique and significant roles that fluorine plays in medicinal chemistry and chemical biology, this book reviews recent advances and future prospects in this rapidly developing field. Topics covered include: Discovery and development of fluorine containing drugs and drug candidates. New and efficient synthetic methods for medicinal chemistry and the optimisation of fluorine-containing drug candidates. Structural and chemical biology of fluorinated amino acids and peptides. Fluorine labels as probes in metabolic study, protein engineering and clinical diagnosis. Applications of 19F NMR spectroscopy in biomedical research. An appendix presents an invaluable index of all fluorine-containing drugs that have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration, including information on structure and pharmaceutical action. Fluorine in Medicinal Chemistry and Chemical Biology will serve as an excellent reference source for graduate students as well as academic and industrial researchers who want to take advantage of fluorine in biomedical research.

title: Introducing Procedural Utility: Not Only What, But Also How Matters
abstract: This paper introduces the concept of procedural utility, arguing that individuals derive well-being not only from outcomes but also from the processes and institutions that lead to those outcomes. In contrast to the traditional economic focus on outcome utility, procedural utility encompasses the non-instrumental value people place on how they are treated and the fairness, autonomy, and respect inherent in decision-making procedures. The authors outline three building blocks of procedural utility—hedonic content, self-relatedness, and non-instrumental process value—and review evidence from psychology, law, organizational behavior, and political science to demonstrate its empirical relevance. The paper discusses the theoretical relationship between procedural and outcome utility, explores contexts in which procedural concerns are particularly salient, and highlights the policy implications of incorporating procedural utility into economic analysis. The findings suggest that recognizing procedural utility enriches our understanding of human well-being and calls for its integration into economic theory and policy design.

title: Systematic review approaches for climate change adaptation research
abstract: Recent controversy has led to calls for increased standardization and transparency in the methods used to synthesize climate change research. Though these debates have focused largely on the biophysical dimensions of climate change, human dimensions research is equally in need of improved methodological approaches for research synthesis. Systematic review approaches, and more recently realist review methods, have been used within the health sciences for decades to guide research synthesis. Despite this, penetration of these approaches into the social and environmental sciences has been limited. Here, we present an analysis of approaches for systematic review and research synthesis and examine their applicability in an adaptation context. Customized review frameworks informed by systematic approaches to research synthesis provide a conceptually appropriate and practical opportunity for increasing methodological transparency and rigor in synthesizing and tracking adaptation research. This review highlights innovative applications of systematic approaches, with a focus on the unique challenges of integrating multiple data sources and formats in reviewing climate change adaptation policy and practice. We present guidelines, key considerations, and recommendations for systematic review in the social sciences in general and adaptation research in particular. We conclude by calling for increased conceptual and methodological development of systematic review approaches to address the methodological challenges of synthesizing and tracking adaptation to climate change.

title: A Risk Society
abstract: “Risk society” is a concept that was first framed by the German sociologist Ulrich Beck in Risk Society in 1986. In Beck’s view, the modern society had deviated from (Karl Marx’s) class society or (Max Weber’s) industrial society and had developed into a social form that is highly modern, known as the “risk society.” Social theories based on unequal distribution of wealth (the functional theory, Marxism, and various kinds of postindustrial or postmodern theories that derived from it) have lost their interpretability when it comes to the crisis and inequality in the distribution of risks. Therefore, there needs to be a turn in social theories, that is to say, “risk sociology” needs to be advanced with problem awareness being “how to avoid, minimize, and direct risks or hazards systematically created as a part of modernization.”

title: A Teoria Queer e a Sociologia: o desafio de uma analítica da normalização
abstract: Originated from the American Cultural Studies, Queer Theory has gained a reputation as a critical counterpoint to the sociological studies on sexual minorities and the political identity of the social movements. Based on a creative implementation of post-structuralist philosophy for the understanding of how sexuality shapes the contemporary social order, for more than a decade its affinities and tensions, as related to the social sciences, and particularly to sociology, are in discussion. This article joins the debate, analyzes the similarities and distinctions between those two, and finally presents an overview of the current dialogue, pointing to a possible convergence in the queer project to enable an analysis of normalization.

title: Cosmology and Fundamental Physics with the Euclid Satellite
abstract: The Euclid satellite, a European Space Agency mission, is designed to investigate the origin of cosmic acceleration by mapping the geometry and large-scale structure of the universe through precise measurements of galaxy shapes and redshifts. This review presents the scientific objectives and theoretical framework guiding Euclid’s cosmological investigations, with an emphasis on probing dark energy, modified gravity, dark matter, initial conditions, and foundational assumptions in data analysis. We discuss the range of theoretical models for dark energy and gravity, the nonlinear evolution of cosmic structures, and the observational strategies Euclid will employ to test these models. The paper also examines Euclid’s potential to constrain properties of dark matter and neutrinos, as well as its synergy with other cosmological surveys. By providing forecasts for key cosmological parameters and outlining methodological challenges, this review serves as a comprehensive guide for the scientific activities of the Euclid Theory Working Group in preparation for the mission’s launch.

title: Community Structure and Crime: Testing Social-Disorganization Theory
abstract: Shaw and McKay's influential theory of community social disorganization has never been directly tested. To address this, a community-level theory that builds on Shaw and McKay's original model is formulated and tested. The general hypothesis is that low economic status, ethnic heterogeneity, residential mobility, and family disruption lead to community social disorganization, which, in turn, increases crime and delinquency rates. A community's level of social organization is measured in terms of local friendship networks, control of street-corner teenage peer groups, and prevalence of organizational participation. The model is first tested by analyzing data for 238 localities in Great Britain constructed from a 1982 national survey of 10,905 residents. The model is then replicated on an independent national sample of 11,030 residents of 300 British localities in 1984. Results from both surveys support the theory and show that between-community variations in social disorganization transmit much of the effect of community structural characteristics on rates of both criminal victimization and criminal offending.

title: The role of tissue engineering in articular cartilage repair and regeneration.
abstract: Articular cartilage repair and regeneration continue to be largely intractable because of the poor regenerative properties of this tissue. The field of articular cartilage tissue engineering, which aims to repair, regenerate, and/or improve injured or diseased articular cartilage functionality, has evoked intense interest and holds great potential for improving articular cartilage therapy. This review provides an overall description of the current state of and progress in articular cartilage repair and regeneration. Traditional therapies and related problems are introduced. More importantly, a variety of promising cell sources, biocompatible tissue engineered scaffolds, scaffoldless techniques, growth factors, and mechanical stimuli used in current articular cartilage tissue engineering are reviewed. Finally, the technical and regulatory challenges of articular cartilage tissue engineering and possible future directions are also discussed.

title: Why Does Deep and Cheap Learning Work So Well?
abstract: This paper investigates why deep learning is both highly effective and resource-efficient, despite the vast complexity of real-world data. We argue that the remarkable success of deep neural networks stems not only from mathematical universality but also from properties common in physics, such as symmetry, locality, compositionality, and polynomial log-probability, which structure the functions of practical interest. These properties allow neural networks to approximate relevant functions with exponentially fewer parameters than would be required for arbitrary functions—a phenomenon we term 'cheap learning.' We formalize these insights using information theory and draw connections to concepts like the renormalization group. Through a series of 'no-flattening' theorems, we demonstrate that certain hierarchical or compositional functions can be represented much more efficiently by deep rather than shallow networks, with significant efficiency losses incurred by attempts to approximate them in a shallow architecture. Our analysis explains why deep learning is so successful in practice: both the data encountered in natural tasks and the architectures of deep networks exploit similar simplifying structures, enabling powerful yet efficient learning.

title: Synthetic DNA Synthesis and Assembly: Putting the Synthetic in Synthetic Biology.
abstract: The chemical synthesis of DNA oligonucleotides and their assembly into synthons, genes, circuits, and even entire genomes by gene synthesis methods has become an enabling technology for modern molecular biology and enables the design, build, test, learn, and repeat cycle underpinning innovations in synthetic biology. In this perspective, we briefly review the techniques and technologies that enable the synthesis of DNA oligonucleotides and their assembly into larger DNA constructs with a focus on recent advancements that have sought to reduce synthesis cost and increase sequence fidelity. The development of lower-cost methods to produce high-quality synthetic DNA will allow for the exploration of larger biological hypotheses by lowering the cost of use and help to close the DNA read-write cost gap.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology

title: CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials
abstract: The CONSORT 2010 Statement provides updated, evidence-based guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised controlled trials, aiming to enhance the clarity, completeness, and transparency of trial reports. Building on previous versions and incorporating new methodological research and accumulated experience, CONSORT 2010 offers a 25-item checklist and flow diagram to guide authors in reporting essential aspects of trial design, conduct, analysis, and interpretation. The revision process involved extensive consultation with a diverse group of experts and led to evolutionary changes that address persistent inadequacies in trial reporting. While focused on individually randomised, two-group parallel trials, the guidelines are broadly applicable and supported by numerous journals and editorial organizations worldwide. The CONSORT initiative continues to evolve in response to emerging evidence and serves as a model for other reporting guidelines, ultimately aiming to improve the quality of published research and facilitate critical appraisal by readers, editors, and reviewers.

title: Finding communities in linear time: a physics approach
abstract: We present a method that allows for the discovery of communities within graphs of arbitrary size in times that scale linearly with their size. This method avoids edge cutting and is based on notions of voltage drops across networks that are both intuitive and easy to solve regardless of the complexity of the graph involved. We additionally show how this algorithm allows for the swift discovery of the community surrounding a given node without having to extract all the communities out of a graph.

title: Knowledge Management and Organizational Learning
abstract: This volume provides a comprehensive examination of knowledge management (KM) and organizational learning (OL), presenting current research, theoretical developments, and practical applications in the field. Through contributions from leading scholars, the book explores foundational concepts such as the distinction between knowledge management and the management of knowledge, the transformation of tacit to organizational knowledge, and the role of organizational routines in knowledge creation and storage. It addresses key issues including knowledge diffusion, the challenges of transferring tacit knowledge, the enabling role of information technology, and the integration of KM systems. The volume also investigates applications such as virtual communities of practice, open innovation, and strategies for overcoming the digital divide. Measurement and evaluation frameworks for KM effectiveness are discussed alongside approaches to valuing knowledge within virtual communities. Finally, the book examines the interplay between organizational knowledge capabilities, learning processes, performance across cultures, and sustainability. By integrating diverse perspectives and empirical findings, this collection advances understanding of how organizations can effectively manage knowledge and foster continuous learning to enhance performance and adaptability in dynamic environments.

title: High-Energy Astrophysics
abstract: During a dramatic development of the field over the last decade, German groups and institutions have played central, often decisive, roles in high-energy astrophysics. Both spatially resolved and temporal studies of gamma-ray sources are conducted with unprecedented sensitivity, deciphering the physical processes in Galactic and extragalactic sources of high-energy emission, and providing new insights into fundamental physics. Radio observations of compact objects, especially black holes and neutron stars, permit exploring physics under extreme conditions and testing for fundamental properties such as the existence of event horizons around black holes. Observations of ultra-high energy cosmic rays provide information on particle acceleration at the highest energy. The first detection in 2013 of cosmic high-energy neutrinos was named the Physics World breakthrough of the year.

title: Systems biology and genomics of breast cancer.
abstract: It is now accepted that breast cancer is not a single disease, but instead it is composed of a spectrum of tumor subtypes with distinct cellular origins, somatic changes, and etiologies. Gene expression profiling using DNA microarrays has contributed significantly to our understanding of the molecular heterogeneity of breast tumor formation, progression, and recurrence. For example, at least two clinical diagnostic assays exist (i.e., OncotypeDX RS and Mammaprint®) that are able to predict outcome in patients using patterns of gene expression and predetermined mathematical algorithms. In addition, a new molecular taxonomy based upon the inherent, or 'intrinsic,' biology of breast tumors has been developed; this taxonomy is called the 'intrinsic subtypes of breast cancer,' which now identifies five distinct tumor types and a normal breast-like group. Importantly, the intrinsic subtypes of breast cancer predict patient relapse, overall survival, and response to endocrine and chemotherapy regimens. Thus, most of the clinical behavior of a breast tumor is already written in its subtype profile. Here, we describe the discovery and basic biology of the intrinsic subtypes of breast cancer, and detail how this interacts with underlying genetic alternations, response to therapy, and the metastatic process.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology

title: Economics and the Modern Economic Historian
abstract: I reflect on the role of modern economic history in economics. I document a substantial increase in the percentage of papers devoted to economic history in the top-5 economic journals over the last few decades. I discuss how the study of the past has contributed to economics by providing ground to test economic theory, improve economic policy, understand economic mechanisms, and answer big economic questions. Recent graduates in economic history appear to have roughly similar prospects to those of other economists in the economics job market. I speculate how the increase in availability of high quality micro level historical data, the decline in costs of digitizing data, and the use of computationally intensive methods to convert large-scale qualitative information into quantitative data might transform economic history in the future.

title: Shape-controlled synthesis of metal nanocrystals: simple chemistry meets complex physics?
abstract: The shape-controlled synthesis of metal nanocrystals has emerged as a critical area at the intersection of chemistry and physics, enabling precise manipulation of nanocrystal properties for diverse applications. This review comprehensively examines recent advances in solution-phase methods for producing metal nanocrystals with well-defined shapes, highlighting the underlying principles of nucleation and growth, the influence of experimental parameters, and the role of capping agents and seed structures in dictating final morphologies. The discussion emphasizes how subtle changes in reaction conditions can lead to a wide variety of nanocrystal shapes, departing from equilibrium forms predicted by classical models such as Wulff’s theorem. By surveying reproducible and controllable synthetic protocols, the article elucidates the complex interplay between simple chemical reactions and the intricate physical mechanisms governing shape evolution. The review also explores key applications enabled by shape-controlled metal nanocrystals in catalysis, sensing, imaging, and medicine, and concludes with perspectives on current challenges and future research directions toward deeper mechanistic understanding and expanded synthetic capabilities.

title: Anomalous small-angle X-ray scattering in materials science
abstract: After the exploratory studies of the 1980s, anomalous small-angle X-ray scattering (ASAXS) is now a mature technique to disentangle complex subjects in materials science: this is illustrated through selected examples.

title: Models of Wave-function Collapse, Underlying Theories, and Experimental Tests
abstract: We describe the state of the art in preparing, manipulating and detecting coherent molecular matter. We focus on experimental methods for handling the quantum motion of compound systems from diatomic molecules to clusters or biomolecules.
