Molecular quantum optics offers many challenges and innovative prospects: already the combination of two atoms into one molecule takes several well-established methods from atomic physics, such as for instance laser cooling, to their limits. The enormous internal complexity that arises when hundreds or thousands of atoms are bound in a single organic molecule, cluster or nanocrystal provides a richness that can only be tackled by combining methods from atomic physics, chemistry, cluster physics, nanotechnology and the life sciences. We review various molecular beam sources and their suitability for matter-wave experiments. We discuss numerous molecular detection schemes and give an overview over diffraction and interference experiments that have already been performed with molecules or clusters. Applications of de Broglie studies with composite systems range from fundamental tests of physics up to quantum-enhanced metrology in physical chemistry, biophysics and the surface sciences. Nanoparticle quantum optics is a growing field, which will intrigue researchers still for many years to come. This review can, therefore, only be a snapshot of a very dynamical process.

title: All biology is computational biology
abstract: Here, I argue that computational thinking and techniques are so central to the quest of understanding life that today all biology is computational biology. Computational biology brings order into our understanding of life, it makes biological concepts rigorous and testable, and it provides a reference map that holds together individual insights. The next modern synthesis in biology will be driven by mathematical, statistical, and computational methods being absorbed into mainstream biological training, turning biology into a quantitative science.

title: Preliminary Guidelines for Empirical Research in Software Engineering
abstract: Empirical software engineering research needs research guidelines to improve the research and reporting processes. We propose a preliminary set of research guidelines aimed at stimulating discussion among software researchers. They are based on a review of research guidelines developed for medical researchers and on our own experience in doing and reviewing software engineering research. The guidelines are intended to assist researchers, reviewers, and meta-analysts in designing, conducting, and evaluating empirical studies. Editorial boards of software engineering journals may wish to use our recommendations as a basis for developing guidelines for reviewers and for framing policies for dealing with the design, data collection, and analysis and reporting of empirical studies.

title: The incidence of diagnostic error in medicine
abstract: Diagnostic errors represent a significant and underappreciated source of patient harm in medicine, with research indicating that diagnoses are incorrect or delayed in approximately 10–15% of cases. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from multiple research methodologies—including autopsy studies, patient and provider surveys, standardized patient encounters, second reviews in visual specialties, diagnostic testing audits, malpractice claim analyses, case reviews, and voluntary reporting systems—to estimate the incidence of diagnostic error. Each approach offers unique insights but also presents methodological limitations that hinder precise measurement of error rates in routine clinical practice. Autopsy studies consistently reveal major diagnostic discrepancies in 10–20% of cases, while standardized patient studies and provider surveys corroborate similar rates of diagnostic inaccuracy. Malpractice data further highlight diagnostic error as the leading cause of paid claims. The lack of a unified, robust method for measuring diagnostic errors impedes efforts to quantify their true incidence and associated harm. The review identifies promising strategies for advancing measurement—including trigger tools in electronic health records, standardized patients, and enhanced voluntary reporting—and underscores the urgent need for accurate data to drive quality improvement initiatives targeting diagnostic safety.

title: Floquet Engineering of Quantum Materials
abstract: Floquet engineering, the control of quantum systems using periodic driving, is an old concept in condensed matter physics dating back to ideas such as the inverse Faraday effect. However, there is a renewed interest in this concept owing to ( a) the rapid developments in laser and ultrafast spectroscopy techniques, ( b) discovery and understanding of various “quantum materials” hosting interesting exotic quantum properties, and ( c) communication with different areas of physics such as artificial matter and nonequilibrium quantum statistical physics. Here, starting from a nontechnical introduction with emphasis on the Floquet picture and effective Hamiltonians, we review the recent applications of Floquet engineering in ultrafast, nonlinear phenomena in the solid state. In particular, Floquet topological states and their application to ultrafast spintronics and strongly correlated electron systems are overviewed.
venue: Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics

title: The incidence of diagnostic error in medicine
abstract: A wide variety of research studies suggest that breakdowns in the diagnostic process result in a staggering toll of harm and patient deaths. These include autopsy studies, case reviews, surveys of patient and physicians, voluntary reporting systems, using standardised patients, second reviews, diagnostic testing audits and closed claims reviews. Although these different approaches provide important information and unique insights regarding diagnostic errors, each has limitations and none is well suited to establishing the incidence of diagnostic error in actual practice, or the aggregate rate of error and harm. We argue that being able to measure the incidence of diagnostic error is essential to enable research studies on diagnostic error, and to initiate quality improvement projects aimed at reducing the risk of error and harm. Three approaches appear most promising in this regard: (1) using ‘trigger tools’ to identify from electronic health records cases at high risk for diagnostic error; (2) using standardised patients (secret shoppers) to study the rate of error in practice; (3) encouraging both patients and physicians to voluntarily report errors they encounter, and facilitating this process.

title: The iPlant Collaborative: Cyberinfrastructure for Plant Biology
abstract: The iPlant Collaborative is a National Science Foundation-funded initiative designed to develop a comprehensive cyberinfrastructure that addresses the computational and data integration needs of the plant biology research community. By leveraging advances in high-performance computing, large-scale data storage, and open-source software, iPlant provides a sustainable and extensible platform that enables researchers from diverse disciplines to collaborate, integrate analytical tools, and manage complex datasets. The platform supports a wide range of users, from students to computational experts, facilitating cross-disciplinary research and training while promoting reproducibility and experimental verifiability. Through community-driven workshops and APIs for tool integration, iPlant empowers plant scientists to tackle Grand Challenges in agriculture, ecology, and bioenergy by enabling efficient analysis of genomic, phenotypic, and environmental data. This article reviews the design principles, implementation strategies, and anticipated impacts of the iPlant cyberinfrastructure on advancing plant biology research and education.

title: Flexibility and Resilience in Corporate Decision Making: A New Sustainability-Based Risk Management System in Uncertain Times
abstract: This study addresses the growing need for integrated approaches to risk management and sustainability in corporate decision-making, particularly in the context of heightened uncertainty exemplified by crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Through a hybrid analytical and empirical methodology, the research develops a novel interpretative framework that connects risk management systems with sustainability management, drawing on economic hermeneutics to enhance organizational flexibility and resilience. The paper constructs a theoretical model linking risk and sustainability, and proposes an operational multidimensional risk assessment framework applicable at business, sectoral, and systemic levels. Empirical validation using a case study from the ceramics industry demonstrates the model's utility in both retrospective and prospective scenario analysis. The findings highlight the importance of integrating technical and strategic perspectives in risk management to support sustainable development goals, offering organizations a competitive lever for sustainable growth in volatile environments.
venue: Global Journal of Flexible Systems Management

title: Strong coupling between surface plasmon polaritons and emitters: a review
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive overview of the strong coupling phenomenon between surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) and quantum emitters, such as excitons in J-aggregates, dye molecules, and quantum dots. The article introduces the fundamental physics underlying SPPs and strong coupling, using the coupled harmonic oscillator model to elucidate how hybrid light-matter states emerge when the interaction strength exceeds relevant energy scales, leading to observable effects like Rabi splitting. A historical perspective is offered alongside a detailed discussion of recent experimental advances that demonstrate strong coupling in various plasmonic systems. Theoretical approaches are critically compared across classical, semi-classical, and fully quantum mechanical frameworks, highlighting their applicability and limitations in describing strong coupling phenomena. The review concludes by outlining future directions for the field, emphasizing its potential to enable novel quantum optical systems and impact a broad range of scientific disciplines through advances in nanofabrication and photonic engineering.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: A Review on Machine Learning Algorithms
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of machine learning algorithms, highlighting their foundational principles, methodologies, and applications. Machine learning, a subset of artificial intelligence, enables computer systems to learn from data and make predictions or decisions without explicit programming. The paper discusses the essential steps in a typical machine learning process, including data collection, model training, and prediction. It categorizes machine learning algorithms into supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning approaches, detailing key techniques such as linear regression, logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, k-nearest neighbors, k-means clustering, neural networks, and principal component analysis. The review emphasizes the importance of selecting appropriate algorithms based on data characteristics and problem requirements. It also outlines the advantages of machine learning in automating complex tasks and extracting meaningful patterns from large datasets. This overview serves as a valuable resource for understanding the diversity and practical significance of machine learning algorithms in modern computational tasks.
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology

title: Fresh perspectives on TPACK: pre-service teachers’ own appraisal of their challenging and confident TPACK areas
abstract: This study extends existing research on pre-service teachers’ Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) by examining their self-identified areas of confidence and challenge through analysis of lesson plans with integrated technology. Eighty-six first-year pre-service teachers from a Finnish university outlined their confident and challenging TPACK areas within these plans, which were then analyzed quantitatively using the TPACK framework. Results reveal that pedagogical knowledge (PK) emerged as both the most confidently cited and most frequently mentioned challenging area, underscoring its centrality in early TPACK development. Other TPACK domains, such as technological knowledge (TK), pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), and technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK), were also identified as sources of both confidence and difficulty. The findings highlight the nuanced ways pre-service teachers perceive their readiness to integrate ICT in education and suggest that targeted support for specific pedagogical aspects may be critical for advancing TPACK in teacher education programs.
venue: Education and Information Technologies : Official Journal of the IFIP technical committee on Education

title: Bright ideas for chemical biology.
abstract: Small-molecule fluorescent probes are fundamental tools in chemical biology, enabling the visualization and interrogation of diverse biochemical and biological processes. Despite the vast number of available probes, most are derived from a limited set of modular core fluorophores that can be chemically tailored for specific applications. This review surveys the major classes of small-molecule fluorophores, examining their chemical structures, photophysical properties, and practical considerations for probe selection and design. Historical developments, including the origins of fluorescence and the evolution of synthetic dyes, are discussed alongside contemporary advances such as quantum dots and fluorescent proteins. The review highlights how understanding the strengths, limitations, and optimal uses of each dye class empowers researchers to leverage fluorescence-based technologies for innovative studies in chemical biology.

title: Electrostatic correlations: from plasma to biology
abstract: Electrostatic correlations are fundamental to the behavior of a wide range of systems, from classical plasmas and polar fluids to charged colloidal suspensions and biological macromolecules. This paper reviews the thermodynamic consequences of electrostatic correlations, emphasizing their role in phenomena such as phase transitions, charge renormalization, screening, charge inversion, and like-charge attraction. Through the analysis of simple models—including the Debye-Hückel theory and extensions—the review demonstrates how electrostatic correlations drive complex behaviors that are not captured by mean-field or perturbative approaches, especially in systems with strong coupling or asymmetry. The discussion encompasses electrolyte solutions, two-dimensional plasmas, colloidal systems, polyelectrolyte solutions with multivalent counterions, and biological assemblies such as DNA and cytoskeletal structures. By highlighting both the successes and limitations of various theoretical frameworks, the paper underscores the necessity of accounting for electrostatic correlations to accurately describe the structure, stability, and phase behavior of soft matter and biological systems.

title: Reducing food’s environmental impacts through producers and consumers
abstract: Food production is a major driver of global environmental degradation, yet its impacts are highly heterogeneous across producers and products. This study consolidates data from 38,700 farms and 1,600 processors, packaging types, and retailers worldwide to assess five key environmental indicators—greenhouse gas emissions, land use, freshwater withdrawals, acidification, and eutrophication—across 40 major food products. Results reveal that environmental impacts can vary more than 50-fold among producers of the same product, highlighting significant opportunities for mitigation. However, reducing impacts is complicated by trade-offs between indicators and diverse pathways to low-impact production. Notably, even the lowest-impact animal products generally exceed the environmental burdens of plant-based alternatives, underscoring the potential of dietary change to reduce food’s environmental footprint. The findings support a flexible approach in which producers monitor and manage their own impacts using multiple practices and transparently communicate these impacts to consumers to drive systemic improvements throughout the food supply chain.

title: Tumor engineering: the other face of tissue engineering.
abstract: Advances in tissue engineering have been accomplished for years by employing biomimetic strategies to provide cells with aspects of their original microenvironment necessary to reconstitute a unit of both form and function for a given tissue. We believe that the most critical hallmark of cancer is loss of integration of architecture and function; thus, it stands to reason that similar strategies could be employed to understand tumor biology. In this commentary, we discuss work contributed by Fischbach-Teschl and colleagues to this special issue of Tissue Engineering in the context of 'tumor engineering', that is, the construction of complex cell culture models that recapitulate aspects of the in vivo tumor microenvironment to study the dynamics of tumor development, progression, and therapy on multiple scales. We provide examples of fundamental questions that could be answered by developing such models, and encourage the continued collaboration between physical scientists and life scientists not only for regenerative purposes, but also to unravel the complexity that is the tumor microenvironment.

title: Quantum computational chemistry
abstract: Quantum computational chemistry is an emerging interdisciplinary field at the intersection of quantum computing and computational chemistry, aiming to leverage quantum algorithms and hardware to solve classically intractable chemical problems. This review provides a comprehensive introduction to both foundational areas, with a particular focus on the electronic structure problem, which underpins predictions of chemical reactivity, stability, and properties. The article surveys key developments in mapping chemical systems onto quantum computers using first and second quantization methods, discusses major quantum algorithms such as quantum phase estimation and variational approaches, and examines strategies for reducing quantum resource requirements and mitigating errors in near-term devices. Illustrative examples demonstrate how these methods are applied to representative molecular systems. The review concludes with a discussion of current limitations, resource estimates for future quantum simulations, and an outlook on the potential impact of quantum computational chemistry in advancing scientific discovery and industrial applications.

title: Gold nanoparticles for biology and medicine.
abstract: Gold colloids have fascinated scientists for over a century and are now heavily utilized in chemistry, biology, engineering, and medicine. Today these materials can be synthesized reproducibly, modified with seemingly limitless chemical functional groups, and, in certain cases, characterized with atomic-level precision. This Review highlights recent advances in the synthesis, bioconjugation, and cellular uses of gold nanoconjugates. There are now many examples of highly sensitive and selective assays based upon gold nanoconjugates. In recent years, focus has turned to therapeutic possibilities for such materials. Structures which behave as gene-regulating agents, drug carriers, imaging agents, and photoresponsive therapeutics have been developed and studied in the context of cells and many debilitating diseases. These structures are not simply chosen as alternatives to molecule-based systems, but rather for their new physical and chemical properties, which confer substantive advantages in cellular and medical applications.

title: International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering
abstract: This paper presents novel algorithms for automated meshing and unit cell analysis of periodic composites using hierarchical tri-quadratic tetrahedral elements. Addressing the challenges of accurately modeling complex material arrangements and ensuring compatibility at matrix-reinforcement interfaces, the proposed methods begin with a hierarchical quad-tree (2D) or oc-tree (3D) mesh of pixel or voxel elements. Through successive element splitting and nodal shifting, these algorithms generate final meshes that precisely capture constituent volume fractions and material-scale stress and strain fields under various loading conditions. The approach effectively resolves both the two-way meshing problem—achieving full displacement compatibility between phases—and the external face-matching problem required for periodic boundary conditions. Performance and convergence behavior are demonstrated on densely packed fiber, particulate, and 3D textile-reinforced composites, showing that the techniques enable efficient, accurate finite element modeling for computational homogenization of complex heterogeneous materials.

title: Internationalization of traditional Chinese medicine: current international market, internationalization challenges and prospective suggestions
abstract: Through reviewing the current international market for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), this paper identified the internationalization challenges for TCM, including unclear therapeutic material basis and mechanism, difficulty of quality control, low preparation level, registration/policy barriers, and shortage of intellectual property. To deal with these challenges, suggestions were given including: (1) product innovation of TCM (study the TCM by using the methods and means of western medicine; innovate the basic theory of TCM; develop TCM health product); (2) standard innovation of TCM; (3) building big data platform of Chinese medicine (big data platform of TCM preparation; big data platform on the quality of TCM).

title: On the Economics and Biology of Trust
abstract: In recent years, many social scientists have claimed that trust plays an important role in economic and social transactions. Despite its proposed importance, the measurement and the definition of trust seem to be not fully settled, and the identification of the exact role of trust in economic interactions has proven to be elusive. It is still not clear whether trust is just an epiphenomenon of good institutions or whether it plays an independent causal role capable of shaping important aggregate economic outcomes. In this paper, I rely on a behavioral definition of trust that enables us to relate it to economic primitives such as preferences and beliefs. I review strong biological and behavioral evidence indicating that trusting is not just a special case of risk-taking, but based on important forms of social preferences such as betrayal aversion. Behaviorally defined trust also opens the door for understanding national and ethnic trust differences in terms of differences in preferences and beliefs, and it suggests ways to examine and interpret a causal role of trust.

title: Self-organization and the physics of glassy networks
abstract: Network glasses are the physical prototype for many self-organized systems, ranging from proteins to computer science. Conventional theories of gases, liquids and crystals do not account for the strongly material-selective character of the glass-forming tendency, the phase diagrams of glasses or their optimizable properties. A new topological theory, only 25 years old, has succeeded where conventional theories have failed. It shows that (probably all slowly quenched) glasses, including network glasses, are the result of the combined effects of a few simple mechanisms. These glass-forming mechanisms are topological in nature and have already been identified for several important glasses, including chalcogenide alloys, silicates (window glass and computer chips) and proteins.

title: Quantum chemistry structures and properties of 134 kilo molecules
abstract: We present a comprehensive quantum chemistry dataset comprising computed geometric, electronic, energetic, and thermodynamic properties for 134,000 stable small organic molecules containing C, H, O, N, and F atoms, selected from the GDB-17 chemical universe as the GDB-9 subset (molecules with up to nine heavy atoms). Properties including equilibrium geometries, harmonic frequencies, dipole moments, polarizabilities, and atomization energies, enthalpies, and free energies were calculated at the B3LYP/6-31G(2df,p) level of theory. For the 6,095 constitutional isomers of the predominant stoichiometry C7H10O2, higher-accuracy G4MP2 energetics are also provided. The dataset, validated against more accurate quantum chemical methods and encompassing diverse molecular structures such as amino acids and nucleobases, offers an unprecedented resource for benchmarking computational methods, developing machine learning models, and exploring structure-property relationships within small organic molecules. All data are publicly available in an extended XYZ format to facilitate data-driven research in computational chemistry and materials design.

title: Helicobacter pylori persistence: biology and disease.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori are bacteria that have coevolved with humans to be transmitted from person to person and to persistently colonize the stomach. Their population structure is a model for the ecology of the indigenous microbiota. A well-choreographed equilibrium between bacterial effectors and host responses permits microbial persistence and health of the host but confers risk of serious diseases, including peptic ulceration and gastric neoplasia.

title: Social sustainability: a catchword between political pragmatism and social theory
abstract: This paper critically examines the concept of social sustainability, highlighting its evolution from a politically pragmatic catchword to a subject of social theory. By analyzing sustainability models and selected indicator frameworks, the authors reveal that social sustainability is often ambiguously defined and theoretically underdeveloped compared to its ecological and economic counterparts. The paper argues that current operationalizations frequently reflect political agendas rather than robust sociological foundations, resulting in inconsistent priorities and unclear integration among the three pillars of sustainability. To address these gaps, the authors propose a concept of social sustainability grounded in the notions of human needs and work, emphasizing their role as central processes linking society and nature. The paper concludes that social sustainability should be recognized as both an analytical and normative concept, necessitating clearer theoretical articulation to inform policy and practice.

title: Inclusive Pedagogy and Universal Design Approaches for Diverse Learning Environments
abstract: This chapter explores the integration of inclusive pedagogy and Universal Design for Learning (UDL) as frameworks to enhance equity and belonging in diverse educational environments. Recognizing the challenges faculty face when teaching students with varied backgrounds, abilities, and experiences, the chapter outlines eight evidence-based strategies drawn from educational research, psychology, neuroscience, and practical teaching experience. Inclusive pedagogy is presented as a shift from deficit-based approaches toward embedding equitable access and opportunities within classroom practices, emphasizing transparency, representation, and student engagement. UDL is introduced as a complementary framework that anticipates diversity by providing multiple means of engagement, representation, and expression, thereby benefiting all learners rather than offering individualized accommodations. The chapter argues for flexible instructional design that proactively addresses the needs of a heterogeneous student body, ultimately fostering deeper learning and a stronger sense of belonging for all students.
venue: Diversity and Inclusion in Global Higher Education

title: Deep learning for computational chemistry
abstract: Deep learning, a class of machine learning algorithms based on multilayer neural networks, has recently experienced a resurgence and is transforming computational chemistry. This review introduces the fundamental theory of deep neural networks, emphasizing their ability to learn hierarchical representations from raw data, which distinguishes them from traditional machine learning approaches reliant on expert-driven feature engineering. We survey the broad applicability of deep learning across key areas in computational chemistry, including quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, virtual screening, protein structure prediction, quantum chemistry, and materials property prediction. Empirical evidence demonstrates that deep neural network models consistently outperform state-of-the-art non-neural network methods across diverse tasks, often surpassing previous performance expectations. The convergence of mature GPU-accelerated computing and the exponential growth of chemical data further enhances the potential of deep learning in this field. We conclude that deep learning represents a powerful and versatile tool poised to address complex challenges in computational chemistry and anticipate its continued integration and impact within the discipline.

title: PEG Hydrogels for the Controlled Release of Biomolecules in Regenerative Medicine
abstract: Polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels are widely used in a variety of biomedical applications, including matrices for controlled release of biomolecules and scaffolds for regenerative medicine. The design, fabrication, and characterization of PEG hydrogels rely on the understanding of fundamental gelation kinetics as well as the purpose of the application. This review article will focus on different polymerization mechanisms of PEG-based hydrogels and the importance of these biocompatible hydrogels in regenerative medicine applications. Furthermore, the design criteria that are important in maintaining the availability and stability of the biomolecules as well as the mechanisms for loading of biomolecules within PEG hydrogels will also be discussed. Finally, we overview and provide a perspective on some of the emerging novel design and applications of PEG hydrogel systems, including the spatiotemporal-controlled delivery of biomolecules, hybrid hydrogels, and PEG hydrogels designed for controlled stem cell differentiation.

title: Challenges of unculturable bacteria: environmental perspectives
abstract: Unculturable bacteria represent a significant challenge in environmental microbiology due to their vast diversity and the limitations of traditional culture-dependent techniques, which capture only a small fraction of microbial life. This review examines the prevalence and ecological roles of viable but nonculturable (VBNC) bacteria in natural environments, emphasizing their adaptive strategies for survival under adverse conditions and their potential for awakening in response to specific environmental signals. The paper discusses recent advances in culture-independent molecular methods, such as metagenomics and other omics technologies, which have expanded our understanding of unculturable microbial communities and their metabolic capabilities. Furthermore, it highlights the implications of unculturable bacteria for bioremediation, noting that the effectiveness of environmental rehabilitation often depends on the activity of these hidden microbial players. The review also addresses current trends in isolating previously uncultured bacteria and explores their potential applications in environmental biotechnology, particularly for pollutant degradation and ecosystem restoration. Overall, the paper underscores the need for continued research into the physiology, genetics, and ecological functions of unculturable bacteria to fully exploit their potential in sustainable environmental management.
venue: Reviews in Environmental Science and Bio\/technology

title: Philosophy of Computer Science: An Introductory Course
abstract: There are many branches of philosophy called 'the philosophy of X,' where X = disciplines ranging from history to physics. The philosophy of artificial intelligence has a long history, and there are many courses and texts with that title. Surprisingly, the philosophy of computer science is not nearly as well-developed. This article proposes topics that might constitute the philosophy of computer science and describes a course covering those topics, along with suggested readings and assignments.

title: Human-Computer Interaction
abstract: Beginning Fall 2020, Carnegie Mellon students within the School of Computer Science (SCS) can declare a primary major in HCI. (Non-SCS students at Carnegie Mellon can continue to couple one of our other highly popular undergraduate options -the Additional Major in Interdisciplinary HCI (https://hcii.cmu.edu/academics/hci-undergraduate/major/) or the Minor in Interdisciplinary HCI (https://hcii.cmu.edu/academics/hci-undergraduate/ minor/) -with their primary University major.)

title: A materials-science perspective on tackling COVID-19
abstract: The ongoing SARS-CoV-2 pandemic highlights the importance of materials science in providing tools and technologies for antiviral research and treatment development. In this Review, we discuss previous efforts in materials science in developing imaging systems and microfluidic devices for the in-depth and real-time investigation of viral structures and transmission, as well as material platforms for the detection of viruses and the delivery of antiviral drugs and vaccines. We highlight the contribution of materials science to the manufacturing of personal protective equipment and to the design of simple, accurate and low-cost virus-detection devices. We then investigate future possibilities of materials science in antiviral research and treatment development, examining the role of materials in antiviral-drug design, including the importance of synthetic material platforms for organoids and organs-on-a-chip, in drug delivery and vaccination, and for the production of medical equipment. Materials-science-based technologies not only contribute to the ongoing SARS-CoV-2 research efforts but can also provide platforms and tools for the understanding, protection, detection and treatment of future viral diseases. Materials science provides tools and technologies for the protection against viral infections, as well as for the understanding, diagnosis, treatment and prevention of viral diseases. This Review discusses present and future directions in antiviral materials-science research, with a focus on COVID-19.

title: Auctions: Theory and Practice
abstract: This book is a non-technical introduction to auction theory; its practical application in auction design (including many examples); and its uses in other parts of economics. It can be used for a graduate course on auction theory, or – by picking selectively – an advanced undergraduate or MBA course on auctions and auction design. Part A introduces the basic theory. Part B shows how modern auction-theoretic tools illuminate a range of mainstream economic questions that are superficially unconnected with auctions. Part C discusses practical auction design. Part D describes the one-hundred-billion dollar 3G mobile-phone license auctions. None of the writing is technical, except in the Appendices. The material was presented as the inaugural (2003) Toulouse Lectures in Economics and is forthcoming at Princeton University Press. This document contains the Contents, Preface and Introduction to the book. A draft of the FULL BOOK is available at http://www.paulklemperer.org.

title: Topic Modeling in Management Research: Rendering New Theory from Textual Data
abstract: Increasingly, management researchers are using topic modeling, a new method borrowed from computer science, to reveal phenomenon-based constructs and grounded conceptual relationships in textual da...

title: A White Paper on keV sterile neutrino Dark Matter
abstract: We present a comprehensive review of keV-scale sterile neutrino Dark Matter, collecting views and insights from all disciplines involved—cosmology, astrophysics, nuclear, and particle physics—in each case viewed from both theoretical and experimental/observational perspectives. After reviewing the role of active neutrinos in particle physics, astrophysics, and cosmology, we focus on sterile neutrinos in the context of the Dark Matter puzzle. Here, we first review the physics motivation for sterile neutrino Dark Matter, based on challenges and tensions in purely cold Dark Matter scenarios. We then round out the discussion by critically summarizing all known constraints on sterile neutrino Dark Matter arising from astrophysical observations, laboratory experiments, and theoretical considerations. In this context, we provide a balanced discourse on the possibly positive signal from X-ray observations. Another focus of the paper concerns the construction of particle physics models, aiming to explain how sterile neutrinos of keV-scale masses could arise in concrete settings beyond the Standard Model of elementary particle physics. The paper ends with an extensive review of current and future astrophysical and laboratory searches, highlighting new ideas and their experimental challenges, as well as future perspectives for the discovery of sterile neutrinos.

title: Simulating chemistry using quantum computers.
abstract: The difficulty of simulating quantum systems, well known to quantum chemists, prompted the idea of quantum computation. One can avoid the steep scaling associated with the exact simulation of increasingly large quantum systems on conventional computers, by mapping the quantum system to another, more controllable one. In this review, we discuss to what extent the ideas in quantum computation, now a well-established field, have been applied to chemical problems. We describe algorithms that achieve significant advantages for the electronic-structure problem, the simulation of chemical dynamics, protein folding, and other tasks. Although theory is still ahead of experiment, we outline recent advances that have led to the first chemical calculations on small quantum information processors.

title: Definition of Health 2.0 and Medicine 2.0: A Systematic Review
abstract: This systematic review aimed to identify unique definitions and recurrent topics associated with the terms Health 2.0 and Medicine 2.0, which describe the application of Web 2.0 technologies in health care. A comprehensive search of scientific databases (PubMed, Scopus, CINAHL) and gray literature using major search engines yielded 1937 articles, from which 46 unique definitions were extracted and analyzed using the constant comparison method. Seven main topics emerged from these definitions, reflecting the evolving nature of Health 2.0 and Medicine 2.0 concepts. The findings reveal significant variability and lack of consensus in definitions, highlighting the need for further conceptual development to support research and practice in this area. This review contributes to clarifying the terminology and encourages ongoing discussion about the scope and meaning of Health 2.0 and Medicine 2.0.

title: Serious Games for education and training
abstract: Serious Games (SGs) are gaining an ever increasing interest for education and traning. Exploiting the latest simulation and visualization technologies, SGs are able to contextualize the player’s experience in challenging, realistic environments, supporting situated cognition. However, we still miss methods and tools for effectively and deeply infusing pedagogy and instruction inside digital games. After presenting an overview of the state of the art of the SG taxonomies, the paper introduces the pedagogical theories and models most relevant to SGs and their implications on SG design. We also present a schema for a proper integration of games in education, supporting different goals in different steps of a formal education process. By analyzing a set of well-established SGs and formats, the paper presents the main mechanics and models that are being used in SG designs, with a particular focus on assessment, feedback and learning analytics. An overview of tools and models for SG design is also presented. Finally, based on the performed analysis, indications for future research in the field are provided.

title: Auctions: Theory and Practice
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive, non-technical introduction to auction theory, its practical applications in auction design, and its broader relevance across economics. It is structured to serve as a resource for graduate, advanced undergraduate, or MBA courses, as well as for general readers. The text begins by outlining fundamental auction theory and surveying key literature, then demonstrates how auction-theoretic tools can illuminate diverse economic phenomena beyond traditional auction settings. Subsequent sections focus on practical aspects of auction design, highlighting the importance of addressing issues such as collusion and entry deterrence, and drawing lessons from real-world examples. The book culminates in an in-depth case study of the record-setting 3G mobile-phone license auctions, analyzing their design, execution, bidder strategies, and outcomes. Throughout, the material emphasizes the critical role of thoughtful auction design in achieving successful outcomes and illustrates how insights from auction theory can inform both policy and practice in economics.

title: Magnetite and Green Rust: Synthesis, Properties, and Environmental Applications of Mixed-Valent Iron Minerals.
abstract: Mixed-valent iron [Fe(II)-Fe(III)] minerals such as magnetite and green rust have received a significant amount of attention over recent decades, especially in the environmental sciences. These mineral phases are intrinsic and essential parts of biogeochemical cycling of metals and organic carbon and play an important role regarding the mobility, toxicity, and redox transformation of organic and inorganic pollutants. The formation pathways, mineral properties, and applications of magnetite and green rust are currently active areas of research in geochemistry, environmental mineralogy, geomicrobiology, material sciences, environmental engineering, and environmental remediation. These aspects ultimately dictate the reactivity of magnetite and green rust in the environment, which has important consequences for the application of these mineral phases, for example in remediation strategies. In this review we discuss the properties, occurrence, formation by biotic as well as abiotic pathways, characterization techniques, and environmental applications of magnetite and green rust in the environment. The aim is to present a detailed overview of the key aspects related to these mineral phases which can be used as an important resource for researchers working in a diverse range of fields dealing with mixed-valent iron minerals.

title: Discovering indigenous science: Implications for science education†
abstract: This paper examines the significance of indigenous science, particularly traditional ecological knowledge (TEK), and its implications for science education. By analyzing the epistemological and pedagogical dimensions of multicultural science, the authors highlight how TEK—rooted in the long-standing practices and worldviews of oral cultures—offers time-tested, context-specific, and sustainable approaches to understanding nature. The paper discusses challenges in integrating TEK into mainstream science curricula, including differing knowledge systems, cultural assumptions, and historical marginalization of indigenous perspectives. It argues that the dominance of Western modern science in education often excludes valuable local knowledge, which is increasingly recognized by scientists and policymakers for its relevance to contemporary environmental crises. The authors advocate for a more inclusive science education that bridges cultural borders, enabling students to engage with both Western and indigenous sciences. Through an extensive review of TEK literature and concrete examples, the paper provides recommendations for curriculum development that respects cultural diversity and supports sustainability, ultimately calling for a reconceptualization of science education to better serve diverse learners and address global ecological challenges.

title: Flexibility and Resilience in Corporate Decision Making: A New Sustainability-Based Risk Management System in Uncertain Times
abstract: Risk management plays a key role in uncertain times, preventing corporations from acting rashly and incorrectly, allowing them to become flexible and resilient. A global turbulence such as the COVID-19 pandemic has had a strong impact on individual companies and entire economic sectors, raising the question of whether a paradigm shift is necessary, in order to enable a new cycle of development that is much environmentally, socially and economically sustainable. This environmental and socio-economic context of profound uncertainty forces organizations to consider more carefully the risk factors affecting their business continuity, as well as how these factors relate to sustainability issues. However, there is a gap in knowledge about how risk management systems relate to sustainability management systems, and how both of them exert influence on business performance, especially from a theoretical point of view. The aim of this study is to address this gap, by developing a new interpretative framework for the analysis of risk management strategies in organizations. This approach has been identified in economic hermeneutics as an innovative methodological tool to improve the knowledge of risk and design the most appropriate management strategies. The paper provides two main results: the first one is the construction of a theoretical model that relates risk management to sustainability management; the second one is an operational framework of multidimensional risk assessment useful for analysis at different levels (business, competitive scenario and system). Finally, the model also makes it possible to carry out a sustainability assessment through risk evaluation in the perspective of the sustainable development goals.
venue: Global Journal of Flexible Systems Management

title: Human-Computer Interaction
abstract: This volume presents selected papers from the 5th International Conference on Human-Computer Interaction (EWHCI '95), held in Moscow, Russia, in July 1995. The conference aimed to foster collaboration and knowledge exchange between researchers from the former Soviet Union and the international HCI community. The collection covers a range of topics including industrial design, activity theory, toolkits for interface development, educational software, information retrieval, hypertext theory, object-oriented hypermedia databases, distributed environments, and knowledge-based user interface design. Special emphasis is placed on multidisciplinary approaches and the integration of activity theory into HCI research. The volume also includes a summary of a tutorial on activity theory, highlighting its relevance to the field. These contributions reflect ongoing advances in human-computer interaction and underscore the importance of international cooperation in shaping future research directions.

title: Mitigating bias in machine learning for medicine
abstract: Machine learning (ML) systems hold significant promise for improving medical care but are vulnerable to bias at multiple stages of development, potentially leading to systematic errors and health disparities. This paper examines sources of bias arising during data collection, model development, evaluation, and deployment in clinical practice. It highlights how non-representative training data, algorithmic design choices, and domain shifts can disproportionately impact underrepresented patient groups. The authors propose a range of mitigation strategies, including assembling diverse datasets, applying mathematical de-biasing techniques, employing interpretability and explainability tools during model evaluation, and implementing ongoing monitoring after deployment. Regulatory frameworks such as FDA guidelines and reporting checklists like PROBAST are discussed as mechanisms to support transparency and accountability. The paper emphasizes the need for continuous vigilance and adaptation to ensure ML-based medical systems deliver equitable and reliable outcomes across diverse patient populations.

title: The Materials Science beamline upgrade at the Swiss Light Source
abstract: The wiggler X-ray source of the Materials Science beamline at the Swiss Light Source has been replaced with a 14 mm-period cryogenically cooled in-vacuum undulator. In order to best exploit the increased brilliance of this new source, the entire front-end and optics have been redesigned.

title: Deep Learning and Its Application to LHC Physics
abstract: Deep learning has rapidly advanced the analysis capabilities in high-energy physics, particularly at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), by enabling the extraction of complex patterns from high-dimensional data that traditional methods struggle to address. This review introduces the foundational concepts of neural networks and deep learning for physicists, surveys their transformative applications in LHC data analysis—including event selection, jet classification, tracking, and fast simulation—and highlights key breakthroughs where deep learning has surpassed previous approaches. The paper also discusses ongoing challenges such as optimization objectives, interpretability, reliance on simulations, and software infrastructure. Finally, it outlines future prospects for integrating deep learning more deeply into particle physics research, emphasizing its potential to enhance discovery and understanding in the field.
venue: Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science

title: Digital twins to personalize medicine
abstract: Personalized medicine faces significant challenges in integrating and interpreting the vast, complex data required to tailor treatments for individual patients. This paper proposes the use of digital twins—computational models that replicate the molecular, phenotypic, and environmental characteristics of individual patients—as a scalable solution to this challenge. By constructing high-resolution network models that incorporate multi-omics, clinical, and environmental data, digital twins can be computationally treated with thousands of drugs to identify optimal therapies. Network analysis tools enable the prioritization of key genes, cell types, and tissues involved in disease mechanisms, while machine learning approaches can further enhance model accuracy and predictive power. The integration of diverse data types into multilayer modules allows for comprehensive disease modeling and facilitates the translation of in silico findings to patient care. Although significant technical, ethical, and logistical challenges remain, the implementation of digital twins has the potential to revolutionize personalized medicine by improving diagnostics, guiding targeted therapies, and inspiring new research directions.

title: Scientific collaboration networks. II. Shortest paths, weighted networks, and centrality.
abstract: Using computer databases of scientific papers in physics, biomedical research, and computer science, we have constructed networks of collaboration between scientists in each of these disciplines. In these networks two scientists are considered connected if they have coauthored one or more papers together. Here we study a variety of nonlocal statistics for these networks, such as typical distances between scientists through the network, and measures of centrality such as closeness and betweenness. We further argue that simple networks such as these cannot capture variation in the strength of collaborative ties and propose a measure of collaboration strength based on the number of papers coauthored by pairs of scientists, and the number of other scientists with whom they coauthored those papers.
venue: Physical review. E, Statistical, nonlinear, and soft matter physics

title: Heart Valve Tissue Engineering: Concepts, Approaches, Progress, and Challenges
abstract: Potential applications of tissue engineering in regenerative medicine range from structural tissues to organs with complex function. This review focuses on the engineering of heart valve tissue, a goal which involves a unique combination of biological, engineering, and technological hurdles. We emphasize basic concepts, approaches and methods, progress made, and remaining challenges. To provide a framework for understanding the enabling scientific principles, we first examine the elements and features of normal heart valve functional structure, biomechanics, development, maturation, remodeling, and response to injury. Following a discussion of the fundamental principles of tissue engineering applicable to heart valves, we examine three approaches to achieving the goal of an engineered tissue heart valve: (1) cell seeding of biodegradable synthetic scaffolds, (2) cell seeding of processed tissue scaffolds, and (3) in-vivo repopulation by circulating endogenous cells of implanted substrates without prior in-vitro cell seeding. Lastly, we analyze challenges to the field and suggest future directions for both preclinical and translational (clinical) studies that will be needed to address key regulatory issues for safety and efficacy of the application of tissue engineering and regenerative approaches to heart valves. Although modest progress has been made toward the goal of a clinically useful tissue engineered heart valve, further success and ultimate human benefit will be dependent upon advances in biodegradable polymers and other scaffolds, cellular manipulation, strategies for rebuilding the extracellular matrix, and techniques to characterize and potentially non-invasively assess the speed and quality of tissue healing and remodeling.

title: Outlier Detection in High Dimensional Data
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the science that allows computers to replicate human intelligence in areas such as decision-making, text processing, visual perception. Artificial Intelligence is the broader field that contains several subfields such as machine learning, robotics, and computer vision. Machine Learning is a branch of Artificial Intelligence that allows a machine to learn and improve at a task over time. Deep Learning is a subset of machine learning that makes use of deep artificial neural networks for training. The paper proposed on outlier detection for multivariate high dimensional data for Autoencoder unsupervised model.

title: Behavioral economics: reunifying psychology and economics.
abstract: Behavioral economics seeks to reunify psychology and economics by integrating more realistic psychological assumptions into economic theory, thereby improving predictions of economic behavior and informing policy. Historically, the disciplines diverged due to differing scientific approaches—economists favoring mathematical formalism and psychologists emphasizing experimental methods—and the adoption of rationality assumptions that ignored psychological evidence. Recent advances in behavioral economics incorporate psychological insights into core economic principles, offering alternatives to traditional models such as prospect theory for risky decision-making, hyperbolic discounting for intertemporal choice, social utility models for altruism and fairness, and empirically grounded learning rules for equilibrium processes. These developments demonstrate that psychologically informed models can be mathematically tractable, parsimonious, and predictive, supporting a productive reunification of the two fields and promising richer understanding and application of economic behavior.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Quantum Chemistry in the Age of Quantum Computing.
abstract: Quantum chemistry faces significant challenges due to the exponential complexity of simulating quantum systems on classical computers, limiting the accuracy and scalability of electronic structure calculations for molecules and materials. The emergence of quantum computing offers a transformative approach by leveraging quantum mechanical phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to efficiently represent and manipulate complex wave functions. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the intersection between quantum chemistry and quantum computing, detailing the limitations of classical methods, the computational complexity of quantum chemical problems, and the development of quantum algorithms tailored for both fault-tolerant and near-term noisy quantum devices. Key topics include phase estimation, variational quantum eigensolvers, Hamiltonian simulation, hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, and mappings from chemical problems to qubit representations. By bridging concepts from chemistry, physics, and computer science, this work aims to inform both chemists seeking to harness quantum computational tools and quantum information scientists interested in chemical applications. The article concludes with a discussion of current progress, ongoing challenges, and future directions for realizing practical quantum advantage in chemical simulations.

title: Statistical physics of social dynamics
abstract: This paper reviews the application of statistical physics to the study of social dynamics, highlighting how collective phenomena such as consensus formation, cultural dissemination, language evolution, crowd behavior, hierarchy emergence, human activity patterns, and social spreading can be understood as macroscopic outcomes of interactions among individuals. The authors discuss key modeling approaches—including agent-based models and dynamical systems—while emphasizing the importance of network topology and universality in capturing large-scale regularities despite the complexity of individual behavior. By systematically surveying models for opinion dynamics, cultural and language change, crowd phenomena, and the coevolution of social states and network structure, the review demonstrates the value of statistical physics in revealing order-disorder transitions and scaling laws in social systems. The paper also stresses the critical role of empirical validation and identifies open challenges at the intersection of physics and social science.

title: An Introduction to Optimization on Smooth Manifolds
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive introduction to optimization on smooth manifolds, extending classical unconstrained optimization methods from linear spaces to more general curved spaces. Beginning with foundational concepts such as the search space, cost function, and the distinction between unconstrained and constrained optimization, the work motivates the need for geometric structure in algorithm design. The central focus is on smooth manifolds—spaces locally resembling Euclidean space but potentially possessing complex global geometry—and the development of Riemannian structures that enable the definition of gradients and Hessians in this broader context. The text systematically introduces key geometric tools, including tangent spaces, retractions, Riemannian connections, and advanced notions like geodesics and parallel transport, illustrating their roles in generalizing algorithms such as gradient descent and Newton’s method. Applications and examples are used throughout to demonstrate how manifold optimization arises naturally in practice. The treatment balances intuition via embedded manifolds with intrinsic definitions, culminating in a discussion of quotient manifolds and convexity on Riemannian manifolds. Overall, the paper aims to bridge geometry and algorithmic design, equipping readers with both theoretical foundations and practical tools for optimization beyond Euclidean settings.

title: Path Dependence, its Critics, and the Quest for ‘Historical Economics’
abstract: It is now widely acknowledged that institutions are a crucial factor in economic performance. Major developments have been made in our understanding of the nature and evolution of economic institutions in the last few years. This book brings together some key contributions in this area by leading internationally renowned scholars including Paul A. David, Christopher Freeman, Alan P. Kirman, Jan Kregel, Brian J. Loasby, J. Stanley Metcalfe, Bart Nooteboom and Ugo Pagano. This essential reader covers topics such as the relationship between institutions and individuals, institutions and economic development, the nature and role of markets, and the theory of institutional evolution. The book not only outlines cutting-edge developments in the field but also indicates key directions of future research for institutional and evolutionary economics.

title: Engineering hydrogels as extracellular matrix mimics.
abstract: Extracellular matrix (ECM) is a complex cellular environment consisting of proteins, proteoglycans, and other soluble molecules. ECM provides structural support to mammalian cells and a regulatory milieu with a variety of important cell functions, including assembling cells into various tissues and organs, regulating growth and cell-cell communication. Developing a tailored in vitro cell culture environment that mimics the intricate and organized nanoscale meshwork of native ECM is desirable. Recent studies have shown the potential of hydrogels to mimic native ECM. Such an engineered native-like ECM is more likely to provide cells with rational cues for diagnostic and therapeutic studies. The research for novel biomaterials has led to an extension of the scope and techniques used to fabricate biomimetic hydrogel scaffolds for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine applications. In this article, we detail the progress of the current state-of-the-art engineering methods to create cell-encapsulating hydrogel tissue constructs as well as their applications in in vitro models in biomedicine.

title: The Sociology of the European Union
abstract: This article sets out an agenda for integrating sociological approaches into the study of the European Union (EU), arguing that mainstream EU studies have largely neglected the social foundations and consequences of European integration. The authors critique the tendency to equate sociological analysis with constructivist, discursive, or meta-theoretical methods, and instead advocate for an empirical sociology that foregrounds issues of class, inequality, networks, and mobility. Drawing on comparative historical sociology and political economy, the paper calls for a deeper examination of the structural processes underpinning Europeanization and highlights the need to reconnect EU studies with broader debates about varieties of capitalism and models of society. By reviewing exemplary empirical works, the article demonstrates how a sociological perspective can enrich understanding of both the drivers and effects of European integration, ultimately proposing a more comprehensive research agenda that situates EU politics within its wider societal context.

title: Copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) and beyond: new reactivity of copper(I) acetylides.
abstract: Copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) has emerged as a highly reliable and versatile method for covalently linking diverse molecular building blocks, profoundly impacting fields such as organic synthesis, medicinal chemistry, materials science, and bioconjugation. This review traces the development of CuAAC, emphasizing its mechanistic intricacies involving copper(I) acetylide intermediates and the dynamic equilibria that govern catalytic efficiency and selectivity. The unique ability of copper(I) to activate terminal alkynes and organic azides under mild conditions enables rapid, regioselective formation of 1,4-disubstituted 1,2,3-triazoles with broad functional group tolerance and minimal byproducts. The discussion extends to the influence of catalyst sources, ligands, and reaction media on performance, as well as the limitations of other transition metals in catalyzing this transformation. By highlighting both fundamental mechanistic insights and practical considerations, this review underscores the continued evolution of copper(I) acetylide reactivity and its expanding utility in modern chemical science.

title: Some applications of the Lambert W function to physics
abstract: Two standard physics problems are solved in terms of the Lambert W function, to show the applicability of this recently defined function to physics. Other applications of the function are cited, but not described. The problems solved concern Wien's displacement law and the fringing fields of a capacitor, the latter problem being representative of some problems solved using conformal transformations. The physical content of the solutions remains unchanged, but they gain a new elegance and convenience. PACS No.: 41.10F

title: Why we need to focus on developing ethical, responsible, and trustworthy artificial intelligence approaches for environmental science
abstract: Given the growing use of Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods across all aspects of environmental sciences, it is imperative that we initiate a discussion about the ethical and responsible use of AI. In fact, much can be learned from other domains where AI was introduced, often with the best of intentions, yet often led to unintended societal consequences, such as hard coding racial bias in the criminal justice system or increasing economic inequality through the financial system. A common misconception is that the environmental sciences are immune to such unintended consequences when AI is being used, as most data come from observations, and AI algorithms are based on mathematical formulas, which are often seen as objective. In this article, we argue the opposite can be the case. Using specific examples, we demonstrate many ways in which the use of AI can introduce similar consequences in the environmental sciences. This article will stimulate discussion and research efforts in this direction. As a community, we should avoid repeating any foreseeable mistakes made in other domains through the introduction of AI. In fact, with proper precautions, AI can be a great tool to help reduce climate and environmental injustice. We primarily focus on weather and climate examples but the conclusions apply broadly across the environmental sciences.

title: “Fundamental Causes” of Social Inequalities in Mortality: A Test of the Theory∗
abstract: This study tests the theory that socioeconomic status (SES) is a “fundamental cause” of social inequalities in mortality, maintaining its association with health outcomes despite changing mechanisms and risk factors over time. Drawing on data from the National Longitudinal Mortality Study, which tracked over 370,000 individuals for nine years, the authors examine whether SES is more strongly associated with mortality from preventable causes than from less preventable ones. The findings confirm that SES disparities are greater for deaths from causes amenable to prevention or treatment, supporting the theory that SES operates through flexible resources—such as money, knowledge, power, and social connections—that can be used to avoid risks and adopt protective strategies as new health threats and interventions emerge. These results underscore the enduring impact of social conditions on health and highlight the necessity of sociological perspectives in understanding and addressing persistent health inequalities.
venue: Journal of Health and Social Behavior

title: American Medical Society for Sports Medicine position statement: concussion in sport
abstract: Sport-related concussion (SRC) is a common injury in recreational and organised sport. Over the past 30 years, there has been significant progress in our scientific understanding of SRC, which in turn has driven the development of clinical guidelines for diagnosis, assessment and management of SRC. In addition to a growing need for knowledgeable healthcare professionals to provide evidence-based care for athletes with SRC, media attention and legislation have created awareness and, in some cases, fear about many issues and unknowns surrounding SRC. The American Medical Society for Sports Medicine (AMSSM) formed a writing group to review the existing literature on SRC, update its previous position statement, and to address current evidence and knowledge gaps regarding SRC. The absence of definitive outcomes-based data is challenging and requires relying on the best available evidence integrated with clinical experience and patient values. This statement reviews the definition, pathophysiology and epidemiology of SRC, the diagnosis and management of both acute and persistent concussion symptoms, the short-term and long-term risks of SRC and repetitive head impact exposure, SRC prevention strategies, and potential future directions for SRC research. The AMSSM is committed to best clinical practices, evidence-based research and educational initiatives that positively impact the health and safety of athletes.

title: Bioconductor: open software development for computational biology and bioinformatics
abstract: The Bioconductor project is a collaborative, open-source initiative aimed at developing extensible software tools for computational biology and bioinformatics. Motivated by the increasing computational demands of high-throughput biological data and the need for transparent, reproducible research, Bioconductor provides a flexible environment that lowers barriers to interdisciplinary collaboration and facilitates the adoption of advanced statistical methods by biologists. The project emphasizes open development practices, modular design, comprehensive documentation, and community engagement to ensure efficient software evolution and widespread usability. This paper details the project's organizational strategies, technical infrastructure, and development methodologies, compares Bioconductor to other open bioinformatics platforms, discusses ongoing challenges such as data integration and scalability, and illustrates its utility through practical examples in genomic data analysis.

title: Toxicity and Safety Implications of Herbal Medicines Used in Africa
abstract: The use of herbal medicines has seen a great upsurge globally. In developing countries, many patronize them largely due to cultural acceptability, availability and cost. In devel-oped countries, they are used because they are natural and therefore assumed to be safer than allopathic medicines. In recent times, however, there has been a growing concern about their safety. This has created a situation of ambivalence in discussions regarding their use. Some medicinal plants are intrinsically toxic by virtue of their constituents and can cause adverse reactions if inappropriately used. Other factors such as herb-drug interactions, lack of adherence to good manufacturing practice (GMP), poor regulatory measures and adulteration may also lead to adverse events in their use. Many in vivo tests on aqueous extracts largely support the safety of herbal medicines, whereas most in vitro tests on isolated single cells mostly with extracts other than aqueous ones show contrary results and thus continue the debate on herbal medicine safety. It is expected that toxicity studies concerning herbal medicine should reflect their traditional use to allow for rational discussions regarding their safety for their beneficial use. While various attempts continue to establish the safety of vari ous herbal medicines in man, their cautious and responsible use is required.

title: Coupled Cluster Theory in Materials Science
abstract: Coupled cluster (CC) theory, a quantum chemical wavefunction-based approach, offers a systematically improvable and highly accurate alternative to density functional theory (DFT) for electronic structure calculations in materials science. While DFT remains the standard due to its balance of accuracy and computational efficiency, its limitations in treating strong correlation and non-local interactions motivate the exploration of CC methods. This review introduces the fundamental concepts of CC theory, recent algorithmic advances that enhance its computational feasibility for molecules and periodic solids, and its connection to the random-phase approximation. We discuss strategies for improving computational performance, including parallelization and reduced scaling techniques, as well as challenges related to achieving convergence to the thermodynamic limit. The implementation of periodic CC methods in different numerical frameworks, such as plane-wave projector-augmented-wave and numeric atom-centered orbital bases, is examined alongside their respective advantages. Applications of CC theory to cohesive energies, phase diagrams, defect formation, surface reactions, and excited-state properties demonstrate its potential for benchmark-quality predictions in materials simulations. The review highlights how ongoing developments are expanding the practical scope of CC theory, enabling more reliable and user-friendly high-accuracy electronic structure calculations for complex materials systems.

title: Anion receptor chemistry.
abstract: This article looks back at advances made in anion complexation since the turn of the millennium and ahead to the application of receptors in areas such as organocatalysis and nanotechnology.

title: Direct detection of WIMP dark matter: concepts and status
abstract: The direct detection of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) as candidates for dark matter is a central challenge in contemporary physics, motivated by extensive astrophysical and cosmological evidence for non-luminous, non-baryonic matter that shapes the structure and evolution of the Universe. This review outlines the theoretical foundations and experimental strategies for WIMP detection, focusing on the operation of ultra-sensitive detectors in underground laboratories designed to observe rare WIMP-nucleus scattering events. Key aspects discussed include the expected interaction signatures, the necessity of stringent background suppression, and the modeling of local dark matter distributions that inform signal predictions. The current status of leading experiments is summarized, highlighting recent results and ongoing advancements in detector technology and analysis techniques. The outlook emphasizes future prospects for improving sensitivity and exploring new parameter spaces, with the ultimate goal of achieving a definitive direct detection of WIMP dark matter.
venue: Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics

title: Clinical epigenetics settings for cancer and cardiovascular diseases: real-life applications of network medicine at the bedside
abstract: Despite impressive efforts invested in epigenetic research in the last 50 years, clinical applications are still lacking. Only a few university hospital centers currently use epigenetic biomarkers at the bedside. Moreover, the overall concept of precision medicine is not widely recognized in routine medical practice and the reductionist approach remains predominant in treating patients affected by major diseases such as cancer and cardiovascular diseases. By its’ very nature, epigenetics is integrative of genetic networks. The study of epigenetic biomarkers has led to the identification of numerous drugs with an increasingly significant role in clinical therapy especially of cancer patients. Here, we provide an overview of clinical epigenetics within the context of network analysis. We illustrate achievements to date and discuss how we can move from traditional medicine into the era of network medicine (NM), where pathway-informed molecular diagnostics will allow treatment selection following the paradigm of precision medicine.

title: Property-Based Software Engineering Measurement
abstract: This paper addresses the lack of theoretical foundations in software engineering measurement by proposing a property-based mathematical framework for defining and distinguishing key measurement concepts such as size, length, complexity, cohesion, and coupling. The authors argue that ambiguities and inconsistencies in the literature stem from imprecise definitions and overlapping use of terminology, which hinder both academic progress and practical application. The proposed framework is generic, applying to a wide range of software artifacts beyond code, and is grounded in precise mathematical properties that characterize each concept independently. By formalizing these properties, the framework enables more rigorous validation of software measures, facilitates clearer communication among researchers, and provides practical guidance for analysts and practitioners evaluating or developing measurement tools. The paper reviews existing literature, compares alternative approaches, and illustrates the application of the framework with well-known measures, ultimately contributing to a more robust theoretical basis for software measurement and supporting more objective assessment of software quality attributes.

title: Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics: From Air Pollution to Climate Change
abstract: This paper examines the Demand-Driven Acquisition (DDA) model for academic libraries, highlighting its evolution, operational flexibility, and impact on collection development. DDA enables libraries to provide users with immediate access to a vast selection of ebooks, triggering purchases or loans only after meaningful user engagement, thereby ensuring budget efficiency and relevance. The model supports customizable acquisition strategies through platforms such as Ebook Central, Rialto, and OASIS, offering options like Short-Term Loans and Access-to-Own to accommodate diverse institutional needs. Enhanced by data-driven insights and integration with discovery services, DDA empowers libraries to build user-centric collections that adapt to emerging research trends while maintaining control over expenditures and title selection. User feedback and case studies demonstrate increased usage and satisfaction, affirming DDA’s role as a sustainable and scalable solution for modern library resource management.

title: Variational autoencoders for new physics mining at the Large Hadron Collider
abstract: We present a novel approach for model-independent searches of physics beyond the Standard Model at the Large Hadron Collider by deploying variational autoencoders (VAEs) trained on known Standard Model processes. Our method leverages the VAE’s ability to learn the underlying distribution of standard events and identifies anomalies as outliers based on reconstruction loss, without assumptions about specific new physics signatures. Using simulated LHC data streams, we demonstrate that a one-sided threshold test on the VAE output can effectively isolate rare or previously unseen event topologies, enabling the selection and cataloging of anomalous events for further scrutiny.
