Other glassy systems are briefly discussed, as well as recently developed synthesis techniques that will keep these systems rich with interesting physics for years to come.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Lateral flow assays
abstract: Lateral flow assays (LFAs) are the technology behind low-cost, simple, rapid and portable detection devices popular in biomedicine, agriculture, food and environmental sciences. This review presents an overview of the principle of the method and the critical components of the assay, focusing on lateral flow immunoassays. This type of assay has recently attracted considerable interest because of its potential to provide instantaneous diagnosis directly to patients. The range and interpretation of results and parameters used for evaluation of the assay will also be discussed. The main advantages and disadvantages of LFAs will be summarized and relevant future improvements to testing devices and strategies will be proposed. Finally, the major recent advances and future diagnostic applications in the LFA field will be explored.

title: Herwig++ physics and manual
abstract: In this paper we describe $\mathsf{Herwig++}$ version 2.2, a general-purpose Monte Carlo event generator for the simulation of hard lepton-lepton and hadron-hadron collisions. A number of important hard scattering processes are available, together with an interface via the Les Houches Accord to specialized matrix element generators for additional processes. The simulation of Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) physics includes a range of models and allows new models to be added by encoding the Feynman rules of the model. The parton-shower approach is used to simulate initial- and final-state QCD radiation, including colour coherence effects, with special emphasis on the correct description of radiation from heavy particles. The underlying event is simulated using an eikonal multiple parton-parton scattering model. The formation of hadrons from the quarks and gluons produced in the parton shower is described using the cluster hadronization model. Hadron decays are simulated using matrix elements, where possible including spin correlations and off-shell effects.

title: A procedure for evaluating environmental impact
abstract: This paper presents a systematic procedure for evaluating the environmental impact of proposed actions, developed in response to the requirements of the Environmental Policy Act of 1969. The core of the method is a generalized matrix that serves as both a comprehensive checklist and an analytical tool for assessing the magnitude and importance of potential impacts across various environmental factors. The procedure guides users through a sequence of steps, including defining project objectives, analyzing technological alternatives, characterizing the existing environment, detailing proposed actions, and evaluating impacts for each alternative. Emphasis is placed on interdisciplinary collaboration, objective analysis of impact magnitude, and value-based judgments regarding significance. The approach facilitates transparent and consistent preparation of environmental impact statements and supports informed decision-making by providing a structured framework for comparing alternatives and justifying recommendations. This matrix-based system is intended as a practical interim guide for agencies and practitioners tasked with environmental assessments, pending further refinement through broader application and feedback.

title: Systems biology of the structural proteome
abstract: Background: The success of genome-scale models (GEMs) can be attributed to the high-quality, bottom-up reconstructions of metabolic, protein synthesis, and transcriptional regulatory networks on an organism-specific basis. Such reconstructions are biochemically, genetically, and genomically structured knowledge bases that can be converted into a mathematical format to enable a myriad of computational biological studies. In recent years, genome-scale reconstructions have been extended to include protein structural information, which has opened up new vistas in systems biology research and empowered applications in structural systems biology and systems pharmacology.ResultsHere, we present the generation, application, and dissemination of genome-scale models with protein structures (GEM-PRO) for Escherichia coli and Thermotoga maritima. We show the utility of integrating molecular scale analyses with systems biology approaches by discussing several comparative analyses on the temperature dependence of growth, the distribution of protein fold families, substrate specificity, and characteristic features of whole cell proteomes. Finally, to aid in the grand challenge of big data to knowledge, we provide several explicit tutorials of how protein-related information can be linked to genome-scale models in a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/SBRG/GEMPro/tree/master/GEMPro_recon/). Conclusions: Translating genome-scale, protein-related information to structured data in the format of a GEM provides a direct mapping of gene to gene-product to protein structure to biochemical reaction to network states to phenotypic function. Integration of molecular-level details of individual proteins, such as their physical, chemical, and structural properties, further expands the description of biochemical network-level properties, and can ultimately influence how to model and predict whole cell phenotypes as well as perform comparative systems biology approaches to study differences between organisms. GEM-PRO offers insight into the physical embodiment of an organism’s genotype, and its use in this comparative framework enables exploration of adaptive strategies for these organisms, opening the door to many new lines of research. With these provided tools, tutorials, and background, the reader will be in a position to run GEM-PRO for their own purposes.

title: Pedagogical content knowledge in science education: perspectives and potential for progress
abstract: This paper reviews the development, interpretation, and significance of pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) in science education, highlighting its potential to improve science teaching quality. Despite extensive research since the 1980s, PCK remains largely unfamiliar to many practicing science teachers, who often conflate subject matter expertise with effective teaching. The review examines how PCK—defined as the integration of subject knowledge and pedagogy to make content accessible to learners—has been conceptualized and researched within science education. It addresses ongoing debates about the relationship between subject matter knowledge (SMK) and PCK, the challenges of making PCK explicit in teacher education, and the difficulties in assessing and developing PCK among novice and experienced teachers. By synthesizing existing research, the paper argues that a deeper understanding of PCK’s nature, development, and role in classroom practice is essential for preparing high-quality science teachers. The review concludes by suggesting that focusing on PCK can inform teacher education programs, bridge gaps between research and practice, and ultimately enhance student learning in science.

title: Double Beta Decay, Majorana Neutrinos, and Neutrino Mass
abstract: The theoretical and experimental issues relevant to neutrinoless double beta decay are reviewed. The impact that a direct observation of this exotic process would have on elementary particle physics, nuclear physics, astrophysics, and cosmology is profound. Now that neutrinos are known to have mass and experiments are becoming more sensitive, even the nonobservation of neutrinoless double beta decay will be useful. If the process is actually observed, we will immediately learn much about the neutrino. The status and discovery potential of proposed experiments are reviewed in this context, with significant emphasis on proposals favored by recent panel reviews. The importance of and challenges in the calculation of nuclear matrix elements that govern the decay are considered in detail. The increasing sensitivity of experiments and improvements in nuclear theory make the future exciting for this field at the interface of nuclear and particle physics.

title: Applying educational theory to develop a framework to support the delivery of experiential entrepreneurship education
abstract: Experiential approaches have become increasingly common in entrepreneurship education in response to calls for different approaches to the traditional didactic process-driven approach. Experiential approaches offer the potential to develop the skills and mindset that are required in entrepreneurship. Research has highlighted the critical importance of educator pedagogical competence in the delivery and quality of teaching and learning in further and higher education. Nevertheless, educator narratives and practices are often based on foundations that suggest a lack in the depth of knowledge and understanding of the underlying pedagogic learning theories and practice. This paper brings educational theory and pedagogic practice together in a three-stage framework of the experiential entrepreneurship learning process to support entrepreneurship educators within further and higher education.,This paper reviews and brings together the seminal educational theories and philosophies of constructivism, objectivism, Kolb's (1984) theory of experiential learning, Schon's (1983) reflection-in-action and Mezirow's (1997) theory of transformative learning, to develop a framework which underpins the experiential entrepreneurship learning process.,This paper develops a three-stage framework which informs the roles of an educator and a learner in experiential entrepreneurship education within further and higher education, based on educational theories and philosophies that inform the learning process.,The developed framework supports the pedagogic competence of educators in the delivery of experiential entrepreneurship education through a deeper understanding of the supporting theory that informs the pedagogic practice. This will provide consolidation to enable educators to maximise the effectiveness of their educational practice (Kaynardag, 2019) and can increase the legitimacy of entrepreneurship education (Foliard et al., 2018).,This paper meets calls in the literature to provide a closer engagement between educational theory and pedagogic practice to afford guidance as to how educators can navigate some of the different educational theories and philosophies to consolidate the effective delivery of quality experiential entrepreneurship education. Applying seminal educational theories and philosophies to ensure the quality of experiential education can support the legitimacy of experiential entrepreneurship education.

title: Collider Physics
abstract: These lectures are intended as a pedagogical introduction to physics at $e^+e^-$ and hadron colliders. A selection of processes is used to illustrate the strengths and capabilities of the different machines. The discussion includes $W$ pair production and chargino searches at $e^+e^-$ colliders, Drell-Yan events and the top quark search at the Tevatron, and Higgs searches at the LHC.

title: Lange's Handbook of Chemistry
abstract: Lange’s Handbook of Chemistry, now in its sixteenth edition, serves as a comprehensive one-volume reference for chemists and chemical engineers, providing an extensive compilation of reliable numerical data and factual information essential for both professionals and students. The handbook is organized into four major sections: Inorganic Chemistry, Organic Chemistry, Spectroscopy, and General Information with Conversion Tables. Each section offers detailed tables on the physical and chemical properties of thousands of compounds, including critical constants, thermodynamic values, and spectroscopic data. The new edition features expanded coverage of recently discovered elements and compounds, updated tables on laboratory methods, and improved organization for easier access to information. Emphasis is placed on accuracy, completeness, and utility, with the aim of meeting the general needs of users without recourse to other sources. This edition continues the tradition of previous versions by incorporating user feedback and advances in chemical knowledge to maintain its status as an indispensable resource for chemical data.

title: The physics of heavy Z' gauge bosons
abstract: The $\mathrm{U}{(1)}^{\ensuremath{'}}$ symmetry associated with a possible heavy ${Z}^{\ensuremath{'}}$ would have profound implications for particle physics and cosmology. The motivations for such particles in various extensions of the standard model, possible ranges for their masses and couplings, and classes of anomaly-free models are discussed. Present limits from electroweak and collider experiments are briefly surveyed, as are prospects for discovery and diagnostic study at future colliders. Implications of a ${Z}^{\ensuremath{'}}$ are discussed, including an extended Higgs sector, extended neutralino sector, and solution to the $\ensuremath{\mu}$ problem in supersymmetry; exotic fermions needed for anomaly cancellation; possible flavor changing neutral current effects; neutrino mass; possible ${Z}^{\ensuremath{'}}$ mediation of supersymmetry breaking; and cosmological implications for cold dark matter and electroweak baryogenesis.

title: Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work
abstract: This paper argues that developing evaluative judgement—the ability to assess the quality of one's own and others' work—should be a central aim of higher education, as it underpins lifelong learning and professional competence. The authors trace the conceptual evolution of evaluative judgement, distinguishing it from related constructs such as self-assessment and sustainable assessment, and propose a concise definition. They critique current assessment practices for often positioning students as passive recipients of feedback, which may inhibit the development of independent evaluative skills. The paper examines five pedagogical approaches—self-assessment, peer assessment, feedback, rubrics, and exemplars—and recommends refinements to better foster evaluative judgement. By reframing assessment within a broader pedagogical discourse, the authors highlight how integrating these practices can cultivate students’ capacity to make informed quality judgements. The paper concludes that prioritizing evaluative judgement is essential for preparing graduates who can adapt to future learning needs and professional challenges, and calls for further research and innovation in educational practice to support its development.

title: Physics and financial economics (1776–2014): puzzles, Ising and agent-based models
abstract: This short review presents a selected history of the mutual fertilization between physics and economics—from Isaac Newton and Adam Smith to the present. The fundamentally different perspectives embraced in theories developed in financial economics compared with physics are dissected with the examples of the volatility smile and of the excess volatility puzzle. The role of the Ising model of phase transitions to model social and financial systems is reviewed, with the concepts of random utilities and the logit model as the analog of the Boltzmann factor in statistical physics. Recent extensions in terms of quantum decision theory are also covered. A wealth of models are discussed briefly that build on the Ising model and generalize it to account for the many stylized facts of financial markets. A summary of the relevance of the Ising model and its extensions is provided to account for financial bubbles and crashes. The review would be incomplete if it did not cover the dynamical field of agent-based models (ABMs), also known as computational economic models, of which the Ising-type models are just special ABM implementations. We formulate the ‘Emerging Intelligence Market Hypothesis’ to reconcile the pervasive presence of ‘noise traders’ with the near efficiency of financial markets. Finally, we note that evolutionary biology, more than physics, is now playing a growing role to inspire models of financial markets.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: The Economics Approach to Cities
abstract: The economic approach to cities relies on a spatial equilibrium for workers, employers and builders. The worker's equilibrium implies that positive attributes in one location, like access to downtown or high wages, are offset by negative attributes, like high housing prices. The employer's equilibrium requires that high wages be offset by a high level of productivity, perhaps due to easy access to customers or suppliers. The search for the sources of productivity differences that can justify high wages is the basis for the study of agglomeration economies which has been a significant branch of urban economics in the past 20 years. The builder's equilibrium condition pushes us to understand the causes of supply differences across space that can explain why some places have abundant construction and low prices while others have little construction and high prices. Since the economic theory of cities emphasizes a search for exogenous causes of endogenous outcomes like local wages, housing prices and city growth, it is unsurprising that the economic empirics on cities have increasingly focused on the quest for exogenous sources of variation. The economic approach to urban policy emphasizes the need to focus on people, rather than places, as the ultimate objects of policy concern and the need for policy to anticipate the mobility of people and firms.

title: Quantum Simulation
abstract: Simulating quantum mechanics is known to be a difficult computational problem, especially when dealing with large systems. However, this difficulty may be overcome by using some controllable quantum system to study another less controllable or accessible quantum system, i.e., quantum simulation. Quantum simulation promises to have applications in the study of many problems in, e.g., condensed-matter physics, high-energy physics, atomic physics, quantum chemistry and cosmology. Quantum simulation could be implemented using quantum computers, but also with simpler, analog devices that would require less control, and therefore, would be easier to construct. A number of quantum systems such as neutral atoms, ions, polar molecules, electrons in semiconductors, superconducting circuits, nuclear spins and photons have been proposed as quantum simulators. This review outlines the main theoretical and experimental aspects of quantum simulation and emphasizes some of the challenges and promises of this fast-growing field.

title: Physics potential and experimental challenges of the LHC luminosity upgrade
abstract: Abstract.We discuss the physics potential and the experimental challenges of an upgraded LHC running at an instantaneous luminosity of 1035 cm-2s-1. The detector R&D needed to operate ATLAS and CMS in a very high radiation environment and the expected detector performance are discussed. A few examples of the increased physics potential are given, ranging from precise measurements within the Standard Model (in particular in the Higgs sector) to the discovery reach for several New Physics processes.

title: The use of herbal medicines during breastfeeding: a population-based survey in Western Australia
abstract: Main concerns for lactating women about medications include the safety of their breastfed infants and the potential effects of medication on quantity and quality of breast milk. While medicine treatments include conventional and complementary medicines, most studies to date have focused on evaluating the safety aspect of conventional medicines. Despite increasing popularity of herbal medicines, there are currently limited data available on the pattern of use and safety of these medicines during breastfeeding. This study aimed to identify the pattern of use of herbal medicines during breastfeeding in Perth, Western Australia, and to identify aspects which require further clinical research.MethodsThis study was conducted using a self-administered questionnaire validated through two pilot studies. Participants were 18 years or older, breastfeeding or had breastfed in the past 12 months. Participants were recruited from various community and health centres, and through advertising in newspapers. Simple descriptive statistics were used to summarise the demographic profile and attitudes of respondents, using the SPSS statistical software.ResultsA total of 304 questionnaires from eligible participants were returned (27.2% response rate) and analysed. Amongst the respondents, 59.9% took at least one herb for medicinal purposes during breastfeeding, whilst 24.3% reported the use of at least one herb to increase breast milk supply. Most commonly used herbs were fenugreek (18.4%), ginger (11.8%), dong quai (7.9%), chamomile (7.2%), garlic (6.6%) and blessed thistle (5.9%). The majority of participants (70.1%) believed that there was a lack of information resources, whilst 43.4% perceived herbal medicines to be safer than conventional medicines. Only 28.6% of users notified their doctor of their decision to use herbal medicine(s) during breastfeeding; 71.6% had previously refused or avoided conventional medicine treatments due to concerns regarding safety of their breastfed infants.ConclusionsThe use of herbal medicines is common amongst breastfeeding women, while information supporting their safety and efficacy is lacking. This study has demonstrated the need for further research into commonly used herbal medicines. Evidence-based information should be available to breastfeeding women who wish to consider use of all medicines, including complementary medicines, to avoid unnecessary cessation of breastfeeding or compromising of pharmacotherapy.

title: Boundary crossing pedagogy in STEM education
abstract: This commentary explores a boundary crossing framework for conceptualizing integrated STEM pedagogy, emphasizing the need to address epistemic and pedagogical boundaries between STEM disciplines. The paper identifies four dialogical learning processes as central to boundary crossing and proposes an interactive pedagogical framework that highlights situated learning, communities of practice, problem solving, dialogical processes, and boundary objects as key connective factors. Drawing on theoretical perspectives and a Hong Kong school case study, the commentary illustrates how boundary crossing can facilitate authentic integration of disciplinary knowledge while maintaining disciplinary rigor. The discussion underscores the importance of designing learning environments that support dynamic interactions among STEM domains and concludes with reflective insights on advancing boundary crossing pedagogy in STEM education.

title: The Evolution of the Corporate Social Performance Model
abstract: This paper traces the evolution of the corporate social performance model by focusing on three challenges to the concept of corporate social responsibility: economic responsibility, public responsibility, and social responsiveness, it also examines social issues management as a dimension of corporate social performance. It concludes that the corporate social performance model is valuable for business and society study and that it provides the beginnings of a paradigm for the field.

title: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials as Emerging Tools for Materials Science
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are rapidly transforming atomistic modeling in materials science by bridging the gap between the accuracy of quantum-mechanical methods and the efficiency of classical force fields. This progress report reviews the principles underpinning MLIPs, including the construction of reference databases, atomic structure representations, and regression techniques for learning potential energy surfaces from electronic-structure data. The report highlights recent advances and key applications of MLIPs in simulating complex materials systems, such as phase-change materials for memory devices, nanoparticle catalysts, and carbon-based electrodes for energy storage and sensing. By enabling large-scale molecular dynamics simulations with near first-principles accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost, MLIPs are poised to become indispensable tools for exploring structure-property relationships and guiding materials discovery. The report also discusses current challenges and future directions, emphasizing the need for robust datasets, transferable models, and integration with existing computational frameworks. Overall, MLIPs represent a significant step forward in predictive materials modeling, with broad implications for both fundamental research and technological innovation.

title: The Effectiveness of Business Codes: A Critical Examination of Existing Studies and the Development of an Integrated Research Model
abstract: This paper critically examines the existing body of research on the effectiveness of business codes, highlighting significant inconsistencies in findings due to divergent definitions, methodological limitations, and a lack of theoretical grounding. Through a comprehensive review of conceptual and empirical studies, the authors identify key sources of confusion, such as varying interpretations of what constitutes a business code and differences in research design. To address these challenges, the paper offers a clarified definition of business codes and proposes an integrated research model to better assess their impact on organizational behavior and outcomes. The study concludes by outlining directions for future research that emphasize the need for greater conceptual clarity, improved empirical methodologies, and a more robust theoretical framework to advance understanding of how business codes influence ethical conduct within organizations.

title: 'Translanguaging' as a socially just pedagogy
abstract: South African higher education relies primarily on English as the medium of education. This is a result of the colonial history of the country, yet it disadvantages a large section of South African students who undertake their education in a language that is not their first language. It also reproduces the monolingual norm and anglonormativity. This can be read as a social justice issue, since students are impacted negatively by discrimination through language. Indeed, recent protest movements, particularly Rhodes Must Fall, have highlighted language as a critical issue in the “decolonisation” of the university curriculum. This article presents translanguaging pedagogy as a way to address this issue; it analyses the implementation of translanguaging pedagogies in an introductory course at the University of Cape Town in 2015 and 2016. Through an analysis of lecturer reflections, classroom practice and assessments, it highlights how translanguaging pedagogies can empower students who are disempowered by English monolingualism and it demonstrates how students respond positively to these pedagogies. The article makes the argument that multilingual pedagogies are a necessary response to the current crisis in South African higher education.

title: 2D and 3D cell cultures – a comparison of different types of cancer cell cultures
abstract: This state-of-the-art review examines the differences between two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) cancer cell culture systems, highlighting their respective advantages and limitations in modeling tumor biology. While 2D cultures are widely used due to their simplicity and cost-effectiveness, they fail to accurately replicate the complex cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions, morphology, and microenvironment found in vivo, leading to altered gene expression and cellular behavior. In contrast, 3D culture models—including suspension cultures, gel-based systems, and scaffold-based approaches—better mimic the architecture and physiological conditions of tumors, preserving cellular polarity, morphology, and heterogeneity. These models facilitate more accurate studies of cancer-initiating cells, invasion, metastasis, drug response, and biomarker discovery. The review underscores the importance of selecting appropriate culture systems for cancer research to enhance the relevance of experimental findings and support the development of effective therapeutic strategies.

title: On the role of traditional ecological knowledge as a collaborative concept: a philosophical study
abstract: This philosophical study examines the concept of traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) and its role in environmental governance, focusing on its function as a collaborative rather than a strictly defined term. Through an analysis of science and policy literatures, the paper identifies significant variation and controversy in definitions of TEK, stemming from differing assumptions about knowledge mobilization and the relationship between TEK and scientific disciplines. These definitional disputes often reflect deeper tensions regarding authority, expertise, and the integration of indigenous and non-indigenous perspectives in environmental management. The paper argues that efforts to establish a single, universally accepted definition of TEK are less productive than recognizing TEK as a collaborative concept that fosters ongoing learning and mutual respect among diverse stakeholders. The study concludes that environmental professionals should prioritize the development of long-term processes for dialogue and cooperation over attempts to standardize the meaning of TEK, thereby enhancing cross-cultural collaboration in natural resource stewardship and adaptation to environmental change.

title: Formação de professores no Brasil: características e problemas
abstract: This paper examines teachers' education in Brazil considering four aspects: the legislation on teacher training; the socio-educational characteristics of the students; the main features of the teacher training courses; the curriculum and programs of Pedagogy, Portuguese, Mathematics and Biology teacher training. The last three aspects are treated according to research produced between 2008 and 2009. The interaction of these different aspects points out a worrisome scenario as for the results of such education. The ambiguities of existing norms, the fragmentation between and within teacher training courses and the part of curriculum devoted to building specific skills and knowledge for teaching practice deserve more attention from universities providing teachers' education.

title: Constructivism: reflections on twenty five years teaching the constructivist approach in medical education
abstract: There is no single overarching theoretical framework that accounts for how we learn in all situations. There are many theories of how we learn from our experiences and there are many theories of what experiences are. We know that we do learn and that we have knowledge but there is no consensus on the relationship between the mechanism by which our brains learn and the optimal way in which we should be taught. In other words there is no necessary connection between epistemology and pedagogy. We seem capable of learning from a wide variety of pedagogical processes and although there is empirical evidence that some ways of learning are more effective than others in specific situations no one pedagogical method dominates. However, reflecting on twenty five years as a medical educationalist I have come to the conclusion that there is one framework that makes more connections between different epistemological and pedagogical theories than others and that could have support from neuroscience. I wish to explore the connections between a variety of educational, communication and psychotherapeutic processes and try to show that constructivism holds the promise of providing some unity to the practice of education and learning. The constructivist model The constructivist theory of learning, whose philosophical origins are frequently ascribed to Kant and whose educational origins to Piaget, is based on the premise that the act of learning is based on a process which connects new knowledge to pre-existing knowledge. I do not intend to go into all the arguments surrounding this theory and to describe the variety of constructivist models that have been created. The reader is referred to the extensive literature on the subject.1-6 For the purposes of my argument it is simply necessary to acknowledge some basic assumptions underpinning the theory from which important connections to other educational theories can be made as well as to therapeutic practices, neuroscience and even the nature of scientific knowledge. Possibly the most well-known articulation of the underlying assumption of constructivism is the famous quotation of Ausubel: “The most important factor influencing learning is what the learner already knows”.7 In many years of teaching teachers how to teach I have found many people have an intuitive grasp of this fact and tailor their teaching to take account of the background knowledge of their students. Piaget expressed it differently by stressing that experience is constantly being ‘assimilated’ or filtered through pre-existing concepts.8 New knowledge is therefore interpreted by existing knowledge and then connected to existing knowledge. The implications of this conception are manifold and spread beyond conventional education into interpersonal communication and psychotherapy. In addition this phenomenon begs the question of how the process is conducted and manifested in the brains of individuals. The statement of Ausubel7 automatically leads to a pedagogical intervention even if it is merely ascertaining the prior knowledge of a learner by asking questions. Piaget avoided suggesting detailed pedagogy but certain ways of teaching flow from his assumptions. He stressed that learning was fundamentally about interacting with the world in order to explore the ‘rules of the game’ and to discover the causal relationships between events. This leads to an active pedagogy involving exploration, experience and experimentation. Dewey aptly summarized this idea by saying that learners should be actors rather than spectators.9 Others have extended this concept to suggest that individals interact with the world in order to extract meaning from it and to construct a coherent and consistent cognitive model. Another way of saying this is that our brains are programmed to support our survival. From an evolutionary perspective organisms have evolved brains which create and internalize an increasingly complex and accurate model of the world. Based on our experience of interacting with the world we have each created our own unique model of reality. Nevertheless we are social beings and we cannot ignore the power of social interactivity that has influenced this process, a concept emphasised by the Russian psychologist Vygotsky.10 Other human beings influence the way in which we construct our models giving rise to the teacher and to the various social processes of pedagogy. Model building in the individual, based on interactivity with the world, is the result of a cognitive process which involves the experience of the world being assimilated and filtered through prior knowledge as previously described. If sense or meaning can be attached to the experience then the experience fits with existing cognitive structures (Piaget’s ‘schemas’). However, if the experience does not make sense then a feeling of dissatisfaction or cognitive dissonance can ensue in which the individual will seek to reach some sort of mental equilibrium by exploration or questioning. At this point the individual may make use of the faculty of imagination to suggest or hypothesise why the experience is problematic. It is the existence of human imagination, the ability of each of us to interrogate our mental model, to speculate and to ask questions that is one of the hallmarks of our intelligence and our capacity to survive. Albert Einstein famously stated that ‘imagination is more important than knowledge’ since he realized that ultimately all knowledge is derived from an initial process of imagination that is subsequently tested against the world. As individuals we can simulate reality by asking ourselves ‘what if?’ questions. We can perform acts in our imagination before doing them in reality and risking having our genes deleted from the gene pool.11 Our imagined conjectures can be tested by seeking other experiences and by so doing we can resolve the dissonance and elaborate our learning and our mental model.

title: Physics for neuromorphic computing
abstract: Neuromorphic computing seeks to emulate the brain’s remarkable energy efficiency and computational capabilities by leveraging novel physics and materials to create artificial neurons and synapses. This paper argues that realizing neuromorphic hardware requires a fundamental reinvention of electronics, moving beyond conventional CMOS technology, which is limited by its two-dimensional architecture, separation of memory and processing, and high energy consumption. We review how advances in physics and material science are enabling the development of nanoscale devices that can mimic key neuronal and synaptic functions, offering high connectivity, low power operation, and in-situ memory. The field is advancing along two main trajectories: mapping established artificial intelligence algorithms onto physical substrates for improved efficiency, and drawing deeper inspiration from neuroscience to incorporate complex dynamics and learning mechanisms. We highlight recent breakthroughs in both approaches, including memristive crossbars and optical neural networks. Finally, we discuss ongoing challenges such as integrating algorithms with hardware design, scaling up from small prototypes to large networks, and achieving the multifunctionality and adaptability inherent in biological brains. These efforts underscore the essential role of physics in shaping the future of neuromorphic computing.

title: The structure of scientific collaboration networks.
abstract: The structure of scientific collaboration networks is investigated. Two scientists are considered connected if they have authored a paper together and explicit networks of such connections are constructed by using data drawn from a number of databases, including MEDLINE (biomedical research), the Los Alamos e-Print Archive (physics), and NCSTRL (computer science). I show that these collaboration networks form 'small worlds,' in which randomly chosen pairs of scientists are typically separated by only a short path of intermediate acquaintances. I further give results for mean and distribution of numbers of collaborators of authors, demonstrate the presence of clustering in the networks, and highlight a number of apparent differences in the patterns of collaboration between the fields studied.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: The Role of Teachers in Task-Based Language Education
abstract: This article critically examines the often-overlooked role of teachers in task-based language teaching (TBLT), arguing that teachers are central to the effectiveness, implementation, and ongoing development of TBLT. Drawing on empirical research and pedagogical literature, the paper explores three key perspectives: teachers as mediators of students’ language development, as change agents in the adoption and adaptation of TBLT, and as researchers contributing to its refinement. The analysis highlights the limitations of viewing TBLT as solely learner-centered and emphasizes the necessity of teacher involvement for overcoming learning obstacles, providing scaffolding, and ensuring meaningful engagement with tasks. The article also reviews frameworks describing effective teacher behaviors—such as the “7 C’s”—and discusses how these can enhance student learning outcomes within TBLT. Finally, it underscores the importance of involving teachers in classroom-based research to bridge gaps between theory and practice, ultimately advocating for a more nuanced understanding of teachers’ multifaceted roles in task-based language education.

title: The challenges and opportunities of a global health crisis: the management and business implications of COVID-19 from an Asian perspective
abstract: On March 11, 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the coronavirus (COVID-19) outbreak a pandemic. As the evolution and implications of the COVID-19 crisis are still unfolding, we posit that exploring the experiences and strategic responses of Asian countries may shed light on ways to combat COVID-19 for the rest of the world. In this paper, we first articulate the importance of resilience, strategic agility, and entrepreneurship in the context of the fight against COVID-19. Then, with the focus on China, South Korea, and Singapore, we discuss the impact COVID-19 is having on economies and businesses, governmental support for businesses and societies, and implications for global supply chain disruptions. We hope that the global health system will recover quickly, and that the world economy will be revitalized with the contributions and collaboration of science (including social science), industry, and governments.

title: Critical Pedagogy in Uncertain Times: Hope and Possibilities
abstract: This edited volume, now in its second edition, brings together the some of the most important figures in the evolution of Critical Pedagogy and a number of up-and-coming scholars. Together they provide comprehensive analyses related to the struggles against the triangulation of Neoliberalism, Conservatism, and Nationalism, not just in education but in all of social life, through the democratizing forces of critical pedagogy. Its re-release coincides with the 50th anniversary of the publication of Paulo Freire’s landmark publication, Pedagogy of the Oppressed. The second edition has been updated with a majority of new chapters to address the current political shifts that have hastened erosion of the public sphere and public education today.  These critical pedagogues show how neoliberal attacks can be collectively resisted, challenged, and eradicated especially by those of us teaching in schools and universities.

title: Teachers’ roles and identities in student-centered classrooms
abstract: This study investigates the evolving roles and identities of teachers in student-centered STEM classrooms, focusing on how educators adapt to and are impacted by the shift from traditional, teacher-directed instruction to student-centered, peer-mediated learning environments. Drawing on qualitative data from 13 STEM teachers across four urban secondary schools implementing an innovative student-centered program, the research explores teachers’ self-perceptions, challenges encountered during the transition, and their professional growth or resistance. Findings reveal that while all teachers recognized benefits and distinctions from traditional teaching, their adaptation processes varied: some embraced student-centered pedagogy as congruent with their existing identities, others struggled to reconcile new expectations with established beliefs, and a few underwent significant identity shifts or chose to exit the program. The study concludes that transforming classroom environments fundamentally influences teachers’ professional identities and approaches, highlighting the need for targeted support in teacher education and professional development to facilitate successful adoption of student-centered practices in STEM education.

title: Guidelines for Field Surveys of the Quality of Medicines: A Proposal
abstract: Poor-quality medicines, including counterfeit, substandard, and degraded products, pose significant threats to public health, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where regulatory oversight is limited. Despite the global importance of this issue, reliable data on the prevalence and distribution of poor-quality medicines are scarce, largely due to methodological shortcomings in field surveys. This paper reviews existing literature and expert opinion to propose guidelines for conducting statistically valid field surveys of medicine quality. It highlights the limitations of convenience sampling, which is prone to bias and lacks representativeness, and advocates for standardized random sampling strategies that enable accurate estimation of the prevalence of poor-quality medicines and outlets selling them. The authors also introduce a draft checklist—the Medicine Quality Assessment Reporting Guidelines (MEDQUARG)—to improve transparency and consistency in reporting survey methodologies and findings. By providing practical recommendations for sampling design, data collection, and reporting, this proposal aims to facilitate robust surveillance of medicine quality and inform policy interventions to safeguard public health.

title: Keldysh field theory for driven open quantum systems
abstract: Recent experimental developments in diverse areas—ranging from cold atomic gases to light-driven semiconductors to microcavity arrays—move systems into the focus which are located on the interface of quantum optics, many-body physics and statistical mechanics. They share in common that coherent and driven–dissipative quantum dynamics occur on an equal footing, creating genuine non-equilibrium scenarios without immediate counterpart in equilibrium condensed matter physics. This concerns both their non-thermal stationary states and their many-body time evolution. It is a challenge to theory to identify novel instances of universal emergent macroscopic phenomena, which are tied unambiguously and in an observable way to the microscopic drive conditions. In this review, we discuss some recent results in this direction. Moreover, we provide a systematic introduction to the open system Keldysh functional integral approach, which is the proper technical tool to accomplish a merger of quantum optics and many-body physics, and leverages the power of modern quantum field theory to driven open quantum systems.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Science of Science
abstract: The science of science (SciSci) is an emerging interdisciplinary field that leverages the vast availability of digital data on scholarly activity to quantitatively examine the structure, evolution, and dynamics of scientific discovery. By integrating methodologies from network science, scientometrics, sociology, and computational modeling, SciSci reveals how scientific knowledge develops through complex networks of scholars, institutions, ideas, and artifacts. Recent advances have uncovered patterns in collaboration and citation networks that illuminate the emergence of new fields, the dynamics of impactful discoveries, and the trade-offs scientists face between risk-taking and career advancement. Notably, SciSci finds that while most researchers pursue topics close to their expertise—constraining innovation—those who venture into novel areas are more likely to achieve breakthroughs. The field also distinguishes the roles of small and large teams in driving disruptive versus developmental research. As science becomes increasingly collaborative and data-rich, SciSci provides critical insights for designing tools and policies to accelerate scientific progress. However, future challenges include accounting for disciplinary and cultural differences across fields and regions, suggesting that domain-specific approaches will be essential for maximizing the impact of SciSci on research policy and practice.

title: Assessing data quality in citizen science (preprint)
abstract: Citizen science projects in ecology and environmental science have the potential to generate large, valuable datasets that can inform research, policy, and resource management, but concerns about data quality—particularly accuracy and bias—have limited their acceptance. This paper reviews evidence from a range of citizen science initiatives, demonstrating that volunteer-collected data can match or exceed the quality of professional datasets when appropriate project design and quality assurance measures are implemented. Effective strategies include iterative project development, comprehensive volunteer training and testing, expert validation, replication across volunteers, and statistical modeling to address systematic error and bias. The variability in individual volunteer performance is comparable to that observed among professionals, and most biases present in citizen science data are also found in professionally collected datasets and can be mitigated using established statistical tools. The authors argue that citizen science data should be evaluated on the basis of methodological rigor and data stewardship rather than the involvement of volunteers alone, encouraging a shift toward more nuanced assessments of data quality in citizen science.

title: Participatory medicine: a driving force for revolutionizing healthcare
abstract: Participatory medicine, as a core component of predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory (P4) medicine, is revolutionizing healthcare by integrating systems medicine, big data, and active patient involvement. This editorial explores how systems biology approaches and the aggregation of vast personal data clouds are enabling individualized models for health optimization and disease prevention. The transition to participatory medicine presents significant technical and societal challenges, including the development of advanced analytical tools, addressing ethical and privacy concerns, redefining the roles of patients and healthcare professionals, and fostering educational initiatives for all stakeholders. Patient-activated social networks and robust information technology infrastructures are highlighted as key drivers for empowering individuals and decentralizing care. The authors propose pilot programs focused on wellness and advocate for new professional roles, such as healthcare and wellness coaches, to interpret complex data for patients. Ultimately, participatory medicine promises to transform healthcare into a more collaborative, data-driven, and patient-centered system.

title: A Note on inflation and transPlanckian physics
abstract: This paper investigates the potential impact of trans-Planckian physics on the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) anisotropies generated during inflation. By employing a simple toy model that permits analytic treatment, the study focuses on ambiguities in the choice of vacuum state at the onset of inflation, particularly when quantum fluctuations originate at scales comparable to or smaller than the Planck length. The analysis demonstrates that reasonable variations in the initial vacuum, such as those motivated by minimum uncertainty or adiabatic arguments, can lead to corrections in the predicted fluctuation spectrum of order H/Λ, where H is the Hubble parameter during inflation and Λ denotes the scale of new physics (e.g., the Planck scale). These findings suggest that trans-Planckian effects could be more significant than previously estimated by some effective field theory approaches, highlighting the sensitivity of inflationary predictions to unknown high-energy physics and underscoring the need for careful consideration of initial state choices in cosmological models.

title: Use of herbal medicine during pregnancy among women with access to public healthcare in Nairobi, Kenya: a cross-sectional survey
abstract: This cross-sectional survey investigated the prevalence and patterns of herbal medicine use during pregnancy among 333 women attending a public childcare clinic in Nairobi, Kenya, an urban setting with high access to public healthcare. Data were collected through interviewer-administered questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. The study found that 12% of respondents used herbal medicine during their most recent pregnancy, with use significantly associated with lower educational attainment and prior experience with herbal remedies. Only a minority disclosed herbal medicine use to healthcare professionals, and approximately 20% reported concomitant use with Western medicine for the same condition. Herbal medicines were primarily used for ailments such as back pain, toothache, indigestion, respiratory infections, and malaria, as well as for general health maintenance. Self-prescribing and sourcing from family or friends were common, and both users and non-users expressed uncertainty regarding the safety of Western versus herbal medicines during pregnancy. The findings highlight the need for healthcare providers to engage in open discussions about herbal medicine use and potential drug-herb interactions with pregnant women. Further research is recommended to explore the health outcomes associated with herbal medicine use during pregnancy in diverse settings.

title: Coupled Cluster Theory in Materials Science
abstract: In this tutorial-style review we discuss basic concepts of coupled cluster theory and recent developments that increase its computational efficiency for calculations of molecules, solids and materials in general. We will touch upon the connection between coupled cluster theory and the random-phase approximation that is widely used in the field of solid-state physics. We will discuss various approaches to improve the computational performance without compromising on accuracy. These approaches include large-scale parallel design as well as techniques that reduce the pre-factor of the computational complexity. A central part of this article discusses the convergence of calculated properties to the thermodynamic limit, which is of significant importance for reliable predictions of materials properties and constitutes an additional challenge compared to calculations of large molecules. We mention technical aspects of computer code implementations of periodic coupled cluster theories in different numerical frameworks of the one-electron orbital basis; the projector-augmented-wave formalism using a plane wave basis set and the numeric atom-centered-orbital (NAO) with resolution-of-identity. We will discuss results and the possible scope of these implementations and how they can help advance the current state of the art in electronic structure theory calculations of materials.

title: A Reconsideration of Environmental Federalism
abstract: This paper provides a review and assessment of the debate over environmental federalism-the issue of the roles of different levels of government in environmental management. The paper begins with the presentation of three benchmark cases that provide a framework for thinking about the issue. It then offers a review, first of the theoretical literature and second of some new, provocative empirical literature on the race to the bottom. The paper contends that there remains, under certain circumstances, an important role for decentralized government in the setting of environmental standards and the design of regulatory programs. The central government, in addition to setting standards for 'national' pollutants, has a fundamental contribution to make in supporting research in environmental science and pollution control technology and in providing needed information and guidance to state and local governments.

title: Graph theory and networks in Biology.
abstract: A survey of the use of graph theoretical techniques in Biology is presented. In particular, recent work on identifying and modelling the structure of bio-molecular networks is discussed, as well as the application of centrality measures to interaction networks and research on the hierarchical structure of such networks and network motifs. Work on the link between structural network properties and dynamics is also described, with emphasis on synchronisation and disease propagation.

title: Avogadro: an advanced semantic chemical editor, visualization, and analysis platform
abstract: Avogadro is an advanced, open-source semantic chemical editor and visualization platform designed to address the limitations of existing molecular graphics and builder tools in computational chemistry, materials science, and related fields. It provides a flexible, extensible framework with high-quality three-dimensional rendering, a robust plugin architecture supporting both C++ and Python, and native support for the Chemical Markup Language (CML) file format to enhance semantic accessibility and interoperability. Avogadro enables users to build and manipulate molecular structures, prepare input files, analyze computational chemistry outputs, and interface with external programs for tasks such as crystal structure prediction and molecular dynamics simulation setup. The platform features integrated access to chemical databases, supports a wide range of chemical data formats, and is easily extendable for specialized applications in organic, inorganic, biological, and materials chemistry. Freely available under an open-source license, Avogadro serves both researchers and developers as a powerful tool for molecular modeling, visualization, and analysis across multiple operating systems.

title: Handbook of Corrosion Engineering
abstract: The Handbook of Corrosion Engineering provides a comprehensive and practical reference for understanding, assessing, and mitigating corrosion in engineering materials. Organized into twelve chapters across three thematic sections, the handbook covers fundamental corrosion principles, environmental factors, and high-temperature effects; advanced techniques for modeling, life prediction, inspection, monitoring, and failure analysis; and strategies for prevention and control including materials selection, protective coatings, inhibitors, and cathodic and anodic protection. Emphasizing both theoretical foundations and real-world applications, this second edition integrates recent advances in materials science, computer-aided analysis, and corrosion management. Designed for practicing engineers and professionals, it offers detailed guidance on detection, maintenance, testing methodologies, and design considerations to enhance the durability and reliability of structures exposed to corrosive environments.

title: Computational Modeling, Formal Analysis, and Tools for Systems Biology
abstract: As the amount of biological data in the public domain grows, so does the range of modeling and analysis techniques employed in systems biology. In recent years, a number of theoretical computer science developments have enabled modeling methodology to keep pace. The growing interest in systems biology in executable models and their analysis has necessitated the borrowing of terms and methods from computer science, such as formal analysis, model checking, static analysis, and runtime verification. Here, we discuss the most important and exciting computational methods and tools currently available to systems biologists. We believe that a deeper understanding of the concepts and theory highlighted in this review will produce better software practice, improved investigation of complex biological processes, and even new ideas and better feedback into computer science.

title: Theoretical Nuclear Physics
abstract: A semi-empirical basis is used to describe and correlate the known nuclear properties including the theoretical concepts, methods, and considerations which have been devised in order to interpret the experimentsl material and to advance the ability to predict and control nuclear phenomena. General properties, two-body problems at low energies, nuclear forces, two-body problems at high energies, three- and four-body problems, nuclear spectroscopy, nuclear reactions, spontaneous decay of nuclei, interaction of nuclei with electromagnetic radiation, and beta decay are treated. 1200 references. (JFP)

title: A Teoria Queer e a Sociologia: o desafio de uma analítica da normalização
abstract: Este artigo examina o surgimento e desenvolvimento da Teoria Queer como contraponto crítico à tradição sociológica no estudo das sexualidades e das minorias sexuais, destacando suas origens nos Estudos Culturais norte-americanos e sua fundamentação no pós-estruturalismo francês, especialmente nas obras de Michel Foucault e Jacques Derrida. Analisa as tensões e afinidades entre a Teoria Queer e a Sociologia, enfatizando o desafio de construir uma analítica da normalização que vá além da lógica identitária e minorizante predominante nos estudos sociológicos clássicos. O texto argumenta que a Teoria Queer propõe uma abordagem inovadora ao tratar a sexualidade como dispositivo histórico do poder, questionando as categorias binárias e os processos de naturalização das identidades sociais. Ao mapear o diálogo entre essas correntes, o artigo aponta para possibilidades de convergência teórica e metodológica orientadas à crítica dos regimes de normalização que estruturam a ordem social contemporânea.

title: Deep materials informatics: Applications of deep learning in materials science
abstract: The rapid expansion of data-driven approaches in materials science has given rise to materials informatics, with deep learning emerging as a transformative tool for extracting knowledge from complex, high-volume materials data. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of deep learning fundamentals, highlighting its advantages—such as automated feature extraction, improved accuracy with large datasets, and fast predictions—as well as challenges including data and computational requirements, network architecture selection, and model interpretability. Recent advances in deep materials informatics are discussed through illustrative applications such as property prediction from composition, crystal structure determination, multiscale modeling in composites, microstructure characterization and reconstruction, and materials design. The increasing availability of large-scale materials datasets, coupled with ongoing developments in deep learning methodologies, holds significant promise for accelerating the discovery, design, and deployment of next-generation materials. The paper concludes with a perspective on the future impact of deep learning in advancing materials science.

title: Pharmaceutical Particle Engineering via Spray Drying
abstract: This review examines recent advances in pharmaceutical particle engineering through spray drying, highlighting the transition from empirical formulation to a more systematic, engineering-based approach grounded in an improved understanding of particle formation mechanisms. The paper introduces a theoretical framework and practical equations for predicting particle properties based on material characteristics and process parameters, with a focus on the use of dimensionless numbers to classify and estimate the impact of excipient and process variables on particle morphology. Key concepts in structured microparticle terminology, particle size analysis, and the relevance of various equivalent diameters—particularly aerodynamic diameter for respiratory delivery—are discussed. The review also surveys experimental research on factors influencing particle formation and presents a range of pharmaceutical applications, including low-density particles, composite structures, microencapsulation, and glass stabilization. Emphasis is placed on how engineered microparticles with tailored nanoscale substructures enhance stability and efficacy in drug delivery systems, underscoring the central role of rational particle design in meeting complex therapeutic requirements.

title: Establishing a baseline of science communication skills in an undergraduate environmental science course
abstract: Seminal reports, based on recommendations by educators, scientists, and in collaboration with students, have called for undergraduate curricula to engage students in some of the same practices as scientists—one of which is communicating science with a general, non-scientific audience (SciComm). Unfortunately, very little research has focused on helping students develop these skills. An important early step in creating effective and efficient curricula is understanding what baseline skills students have prior to instruction. Here, we used the Essential Elements for Effective Science Communication (EEES) framework to survey the SciComm skills of students in an environmental science course in which they had little SciComm training. Results Our analyses revealed that, despite not being given the framework, students included several of the 13 elements, especially those which were explicitly asked for in the assignment instructions. Students commonly targeted broad audiences composed of interested adults, aimed to increase the knowledge and awareness of their audience, and planned and executed remote projects using print on social media. Additionally, students demonstrated flexibility in their skills by slightly differing their choices depending on the context of the assignment, such as creating more engaging content than they had planned for. Conclusions The students exhibited several key baseline skills, even though they had minimal training on the best practices of SciComm; however, more support is required to help students become better communicators, and more work in different contexts may be beneficial to acquire additional perspectives on SciComm skills among a variety of science students. The few elements that were not well highlighted in the students’ projects may not have been as intuitive to novice communicators. Thus, we provide recommendations for how educators can help their undergraduate science students develop valuable, prescribed SciComm skills. Some of these recommendations include helping students determine the right audience for their communication project, providing opportunities for students to try multiple media types, determining the type of language that is appropriate for the audience, and encouraging students to aim for a mix of communication objectives. With this guidance, educators can better prepare their students to become a more open and communicative generation of scientists and citizens.

title: Coupled-cluster computations of atomic nuclei
abstract: Coupled-cluster theory has emerged as a powerful and efficient ab initio method for the computation of atomic nuclei, particularly those with closed-shell or subshell configurations. This review summarizes recent conceptual and technical advances in the application of coupled-cluster methods to nuclear physics, including developments in model spaces, treatment of weakly bound and unbound systems, and the incorporation of three-nucleon forces. We discuss computational strategies for ground and excited states, observables beyond energies, extensions beyond the CCSD approximation, and time-dependent formulations. The method’s flexibility is illustrated through results for nucleonic matter and a range of exotic isotopes, including helium, oxygen, and calcium. Comparisons with other ab initio approaches highlight the strengths and limitations of coupled-cluster theory in addressing the nuclear many-body problem. The review concludes with an outlook on open challenges and future directions in the field.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Using critical consciousness to inform health professions education
abstract: This literature review examines how critical consciousness is defined and discussed within health professions education (HPE) and explores the practical application of critical pedagogy in this context. Through a systematic search and thematic analysis of 30 relevant articles, the review identifies five core themes: appreciating educational and practice contexts, illuminating power structures, moving beyond procedural learning, enacting reflection, and promoting equity and social justice. The findings suggest that integrating critical consciousness into HPE can support the development of compassionate, socially responsible health professionals who are equipped to act as agents of change. The review highlights the importance of considering the philosophical foundations of both critical pedagogy and prevailing competency-based models to ensure authentic implementation. Practical strategies for educators are discussed, emphasizing the need for careful adaptation within existing HPE structures to foster humanistic and equitable healthcare practice.

title: The anomaly of silicon in plant biology.
abstract: Silicon is the second most abundant element in soils and is present in plant tissues at concentrations comparable to or exceeding those of essential macronutrients, yet it is not generally recognized as essential for higher plants except for certain groups such as the Equisitaceae. This review examines the paradoxical status of silicon in plant biology, highlighting its ubiquity in soils and nutrient solutions, its ready uptake by plants, and its significant but variable accumulation in plant tissues. Despite the lack of consensus on its essentiality—stemming from difficulties in creating silicon-free environments and ambiguous experimental results—ample evidence indicates that silicon availability can enhance plant growth, mineral nutrition, mechanical strength, and resistance to biotic and abiotic stresses. The omission of silicon from conventional nutrient solutions may lead to experimental artifacts and misinterpretations in studies of plant nutrition and stress physiology. The review concludes that while silicon cannot currently be classified as an essential element for most higher plants, its prominent role in plant biology warrants greater consideration in both research and agricultural practice.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Medicine sellers and malaria treatment in sub-Saharan Africa: what do they do and how can their practice be improved?
abstract: Medicine sellers are widely used for fever and malaria treatment in sub-Saharan Africa, but concerns surround the appropriateness of drugs and information provided. Because there is increasing interest in improving their services, we reviewed the literature on their characteristics and interventions to improve their malaria-related practices. Sixteen interventions were identified, involving a mixture of training/capacity building, demand generation, quality assurance, and creating an enabling environment. Although evidence is insufficient to prove which approaches are superior, tentative conclusions were possible. Interventions increased rates of appropriate treatment, and medicine sellers were willing to participate. Features of successful interventions included a comprehensive situation analysis of the legal and market environment; buy-in from medicine sellers, community members and government; use of a combination of approaches; and maintenance of training and supervision. Interventions must be adapted to include artemisinin-based combination therapies, and their sustainability and potential to operate at a national level should be further explored.
venue: American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene

title: The quest for modernisation of traditional Chinese medicine
abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) has evolved from an ancient, experience-based system into a globally significant component of healthcare, prompting increasing efforts toward its modernisation. This review synthesises the historical trajectory and recent advancements in TCM, with particular emphasis on the outcomes of the European Union’s FP7 GP-TCM project, which fostered international collaboration and set new standards for TCM research. The modernisation process is delineated into three phases: foundational development of education and infrastructure in China (1950s–1970s), establishment of legal, scientific, and international frameworks (1980s–2000s), and current consolidation of scientific evidence and clinical practice through interdisciplinary and cross-sectoral partnerships (2011 onwards). Key milestones include the integration of TCM into mainstream healthcare, landmark drug discoveries such as artemisinin, and the expansion of research networks worldwide. The review highlights ongoing challenges related to quality control, safety, and scientific validation in a globalised context. It proposes integrity, integration, and innovation as guiding principles for future research and development, aiming to further bridge traditional practices with modern medical science and facilitate the integration of TCM into contemporary healthcare systems.

title: Advances in Economics and Econometrics: Theory and Applications: Theory and experiment in the analysis of strategic interaction
abstract: Much of economics has to do with the coordination of independent decisions, and such questions with some well-known exceptions are inherently game theoretic. Yet when the Econometric Society held its First World Congress in 1965, economic theory was still almost entirely non-strategic and game theory remained largely a branch of mathematics, whose applications in economics were the work of a few pioneers. As recently as the early 1970s, the profession's view of game-theoretic modeling was typified by Paul Samuelson's customarily vivid phrase, 'the swamp of n-person game theory'; and even students to whom the swamp seemed a fascinating place thought carefully before descending from the high ground of perfect competition and monopoly. The game-theoretic revolution that ensued altered the landscape in ways that would have been difficult to imagine in 1965, adding so much to our understanding that many questions whose strategic aspects once made them seem intractable are now considered fit for textbook treatment. This process was driven by a fruitful dialogue between game theory and economics, in which game theory supplied a rich language for describing strategic interactions and a set of tools for predicting their outcomes, and economics contributed questions and intuitions about strategic behavior

title: THE EMERGENCE OF MULTISPECIES ETHNOGRAPHY
abstract: Anthropologists have been committed, at least since Franz Boas, to investigating relationships between nature and culture. At the dawn of the 21st century, this enduring interest was inflected with some new twists. An emergent cohort of “multispecies ethnographers” began to place a fresh emphasis on the subjectivity and agency of organisms whose lives are entangled with humans. Multispecies ethnography emerged at the intersection of three interdisciplinary strands of inquiry: environmental studies, science and technology studies (STS), and animal studies. Departing from classically ethnobiological subjects, useful plants and charismatic animals, multispecies ethnographers also brought understudied organisms—such as insects, fungi, and microbes—into anthropological conversations. Anthropologists gathered together at the Multispecies Salon, an art exhibit, where the boundaries of an emerging interdiscipline were probed amidst a collection of living organisms, artifacts from the biological sciences, and surprising biopolitical interventions.

title: The statistical physics of cities
abstract: Rapid urbanization presents complex challenges related to energy use, pollution, inequality, and sustainability, necessitating robust theoretical frameworks for understanding and managing city dynamics. This paper explores how statistical physics provides powerful tools and concepts to model urban systems, leveraging the increasing availability of large-scale urban data. By treating cities as complex systems characterized by emergent collective behaviors, the study examines key urban phenomena including population distribution, segregation dynamics, polycentric transitions in activity organization, mobility patterns, energy consumption, and scaling laws governing socio-economic and infrastructural growth. The analysis highlights the interplay between empirical data and theoretical models, such as those explaining Zipf’s law for city size distributions and diffusion-based approaches that account for migration and internal growth. The paper underscores the interdisciplinary nature of urban science and demonstrates how statistical physics can bridge theory with observation, identify critical parameters, and inform strategies to mitigate urban challenges in a rapidly changing world.

title: Human and Financial Capital for Microenterprise Development: Evidence from a Field and Lab Experiment
abstract: Microenterprises constitute an important source of employment, and developing such enterprises is a key policy concern in most countries. But what is the most efficient tool for microenterprise development? We study this question in a developing country context Tanzania, where microenterprises are the source of employment for more than half of the labor force, and we report from a field experiment that jointly investigated the importance of a human capital intervention business training and a financial capital intervention business grant. Using data from three survey rounds, a lab experiment, and administrative records of the microfinance institution, we present evidence on business performance, management practices, happiness, business knowledge, and noncognitive abilities. Our study demonstrates strong effects of the combination of the two interventions on male entrepreneurs, while the effects on female entrepreneurs are much more muted. The results suggest that long-term finance is an important constraint for microfinance entrepreneurs, but that business training is essential to transform financial capital into productive investments. Our study also points to the need for more comprehensive measures to promote the businesses of female entrepreneurs. Data, as supplemental material, are available at http://dx.doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2014.1933 . This paper was accepted by John List, behavioral economics.

title: Developing employability in engineering education: a systematic review of the literature
abstract: This systematic review examines research from 2007 to 2017 on curricular and pedagogical strategies that promote employability in engineering education, with a particular focus on the integration and prioritization of engineering knowledge and professional skills. Drawing on a social realist theoretical framework, the review analyzes how engineering programs globally address the gap between academic preparation and industry expectations. Findings reveal an interdependent relationship between technical expertise and professional competencies such as communication, teamwork, and ethical awareness. The review highlights that both domains are essential for preparing graduates to tackle complex real-world problems and adapt to evolving professional demands. Recommendations emphasize the need for holistic curricular reforms that balance disciplinary knowledge with the development of soft skills, offering guidance for educators seeking to enhance graduate employability in the 21st century.

title: Transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis (TRIPOD): the TRIPOD Statement
