Key benefits of using ChatGPT in business management are improved customer service, business process automation, and more data-driven decision-making.

title: Genetics and biology of prostate cancer
abstract: Here, Wang et al. review available prostate cancer model systems, the prostate cancer genome atlas, cellular and functional heterogeneity in the tumor microenvironment, tumor-intrinsic and tumor-extrinsic mechanisms underlying therapeutic resistance, and technological advances focused on disease detection and management

title: Scaffolds based bone tissue engineering: the role of chitosan.
abstract: As life expectancy increases, malfunction or loss of tissue caused by injury or disease leads to reduced quality of life in many patients at significant socioeconomic cost. Even though major progress has been made in the field of bone tissue engineering, present therapies, such as bone grafts, still have limitations. Current research on biodegradable polymers is emerging, combining these structures with osteogenic cells, as an alternative to autologous bone grafts. Different types of biodegradable materials have been proposed for the preparation of three-dimensional porous scaffolds for bone tissue engineering. Among them, natural polymers are one of the most attractive options, mainly due to their similarities with extracellular matrix, chemical versatility, good biological performance, and inherent cellular interactions. In this review, special attention is given to chitosan as a biomaterial for bone tissue engineering applications. An extensive literature survey was performed on the preparation of chitosan scaffolds and their in vitro biological performance as well as their potential to facilitate in vivo bone regeneration. The present review also aims to offer the reader a general overview of all components needed to engineer new bone tissue. It gives a brief background on bone biology, followed by an explanation of all components in bone tissue engineering, as well as describing different tissue engineering strategies. Moreover, also discussed are the typical models used to evaluate in vitro functionality of a tissue-engineered construct and in vivo models to assess the potential to regenerate bone tissue are discussed.

title: Nanofluidics: A New Arena for Materials Science
abstract: Nanofluidics, the study of fluid behavior in nanoscale environments, has rapidly advanced in the past decade, revealing unique physical phenomena and offering new opportunities for materials science. This progress report highlights how nanofluidic systems—characterized by ultra-high surface-to-volume ratios and confined geometries—enable novel mechanisms for manipulating and synthesizing nanoscale materials. The article reviews recent developments in five key areas: fabrication methods for nanofluidic devices, integration of functionalized surfaces and material components, manipulation of biological and nanoscale objects, and the synthesis of new nanomaterials within nanofluidic environments. While significant challenges remain, particularly in device fabrication, measurement, and functional integration, these hurdles also present exciting opportunities for materials scientists to drive the field toward application-oriented research. The convergence of nanofluidics and materials science promises to unlock unprecedented control over matter at the nanoscale, paving the way for innovative technologies and multidisciplinary applications.

title: How to measure the impact of citizen science on environmental attitudes, behaviour and knowledge? A review of state-of-the-art approaches
abstract: The effects of citizen science are wide ranging, influencing science, society, the economy, the environment, as well as individual participants. However, in many citizen science projects, impact evaluation is still overly simplistic. This is particularly the case when assessing the impact of participation in citizen science on the environmental attitudes, behaviour and knowledge of citizen scientists. In an attempt to bridge the gap between the state of the art in relevant scientific fields and citizen science, this systematic literature review identified best practices and approaches in the field of environmental psychology for measuring environmental attitudes, behaviour and knowledge. From the literature, five relevant and validated approaches were identified that can be used to measure changes in attitudes, behaviour and knowledge in citizen science projects. This would allow for improved understanding of the impacts of citizen science, as well as for improved project evaluation as a whole.

title: Machine learning in medicine: a practical introduction
abstract: Machine learning techniques are increasingly being adopted in medicine due to their success in predictive tasks and the growing availability of large datasets. This paper provides a conceptual and practical introduction to machine learning for medical researchers and clinicians, demonstrating the development and evaluation of predictive algorithms using open-source software and public domain data. Using a breast cancer dataset, we developed and compared three classification models—regularized General Linear Model regression, Support Vector Machines with a radial basis function kernel, and single-layer Artificial Neural Networks—achieving high accuracy (0.94–0.96), sensitivity (0.97–0.99), and specificity (0.85–0.94). The best performance was observed with the SVM model, and further improvement was achieved through a voting ensemble approach. We offer a step-by-step guide to implementing these methods in the R programming environment, emphasizing their applicability to other complex medical tasks such as natural language processing and image recognition. This work aims to build capacity in the medical community for applying machine learning techniques to enhance diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision-making.

title: Acid rain and air pollution: 50 years of progress in environmental science and policy
abstract: Over the past fifty years, acid rain has evolved from a largely unrecognized phenomenon to a central focus of international environmental science and policy. This review traces the historical development of acid rain research, beginning with early observations in Europe and North America, and highlights the pivotal role of scientific discoveries in driving policy responses such as the UNECE Convention on Long-range Transboundary Air Pollution. The integration of long-term monitoring, critical loads concepts, and integrated assessment modeling provided a robust foundation for international agreements that have led to significant reductions in emissions of sulphur dioxide and other pollutants, resulting in measurable ecosystem recovery. The paper examines key milestones in science-policy interactions, underscores the importance of sustained scientific infrastructure, and situates acid rain within broader environmental challenges including climate change and the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Lessons learned from five decades of coordinated action offer valuable insights for addressing current and future transboundary air pollution issues.

title: What Kind of Pedagogies for the 21st Century?
abstract: This paper examines the urgent need to transform educational pedagogies to equip learners with the competencies and skills required for the 21st century. Despite widespread recognition of the limitations of traditional lecture-based models, these approaches remain prevalent, often failing to foster critical thinking, creativity, collaboration, and effective communication. Drawing on current literature and global discussions, the paper outlines a comprehensive vision for 21st-century pedagogy that emphasizes learner-centered approaches, project and problem-based learning, personalization, meaningful use of technology, and the cultivation of metacognitive skills. It highlights the importance of designing relevant, real-world learning experiences, promoting lifelong learning, and redefining teacher roles to support innovative practices. The paper concludes that adapting curricula and pedagogical strategies is essential for preparing learners to navigate complex societal, economic, and environmental challenges, ensuring they are equipped for productive work, active citizenship, and continuous personal development in a rapidly changing world.

title: Higgs boson mass and new physics
abstract: A bstractWe discuss the lower Higgs boson mass bounds which come from the absolute stability of the Standard Model (SM) vacuum and from the Higgs inflation, as well as the prediction of the Higgs boson mass coming from the asymptotic safety of the SM. We account for the three-loop renormalization group evolution of the couplings of the SM and for a part of the two-loop corrections that involve the QCD coupling αs to the initial conditions for their running. This is one step beyond the current state-of-the-art procedure (“one-loop matching-two-loop running”). This results in a reduction of the theoretical uncertainties in the Higgs boson mass bounds and predictions, associated with the SM physics, to 1–2 GeV. We find that with the account of existing experimental uncertainties in the mass of the top quark and αs (taken at the 2σ level) the bound reads MH ≥ Mmin (equality corresponds to the asymptotic-safety prediction), where $ {{M}_{{\min }}}=\left( {129\pm 6} \right) $ GeV. We argue that the discovery of the SM Higgs boson in this range would be in agreement with the hypothesis of the absence of new energy scales between the Fermi and Planck scales, whereas the coincidence of MH with Mmin would suggest that the electroweak scale is determined by Planck physics. In order to clarify the relation between the Fermi and Planck scales a construction of an electron-positron or muon collider with a center-of-mass energy ~ (200 + 200 GeV) (Higgs and t-quark factory) would be needed.

title: The genetic transformation of bone biology.
abstract: Recent advances in genetic research have profoundly transformed our understanding of bone biology, particularly in elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying bone development, physiology, and pathology. This review focuses on the genetic regulation of bone cell differentiation beyond embryonic patterning, emphasizing the pivotal roles of osteoclasts and osteoblasts in bone remodeling and disease. Genetic studies in mice and humans have identified key transcription factors such as Pu.1, c-Fos, and NF-κB as central regulators of osteoclast differentiation, with loss-of-function mutations resulting in distinct skeletal phenotypes like osteopetrosis. The interplay between genetic pathways and extracellular signals orchestrates the balance between bone formation and resorption, a process disrupted in conditions such as osteoporosis. Despite significant progress in understanding osteoclast biology, the molecular control of osteoblast function remains less defined, highlighting critical gaps and emerging questions in the field. Overall, genetic approaches continue to drive conceptual advances in bone biology, offering new insights into skeletal diseases and potential therapeutic targets.

title: Establishing a baseline of science communication skills in an undergraduate environmental science course
abstract: This study investigates the baseline science communication (SciComm) skills of undergraduate students enrolled in an environmental science course with minimal prior SciComm training. Using the Essential Elements for Effective Science Communication (EEES) framework, we analyzed student projects to assess their ability to communicate scientific concepts to non-expert audiences. Results indicate that, without explicit instruction in the framework, students incorporated several key elements of effective SciComm, particularly those emphasized in assignment guidelines. Students typically targeted broad, interested adult audiences, aimed to increase knowledge and awareness, and utilized remote communication methods such as social media. They also demonstrated adaptability by modifying their approaches based on assignment context. However, some elements of effective SciComm were less intuitive for novice communicators and were underrepresented in student work. Our findings suggest that while students possess foundational SciComm skills, additional support and targeted instruction are needed to develop more comprehensive communication abilities. We provide recommendations for educators to enhance SciComm training, including audience identification, exposure to diverse media types, appropriate language selection, and balancing communication objectives. These strategies can better prepare undergraduates to become effective science communicators and informed citizens.

title: The CompTox Chemistry Dashboard: a community data resource for environmental chemistry
abstract: Despite an abundance of online databases providing access to chemical data, there is increasing demand for high-quality, structure-curated, open data to meet the various needs of the environmental sciences and computational toxicology communities. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) web-based CompTox Chemistry Dashboard is addressing these needs by integrating diverse types of relevant domain data through a cheminformatics layer, built upon a database of curated substances linked to chemical structures. These data include physicochemical, environmental fate and transport, exposure, usage, in vivo toxicity, and in vitro bioassay data, surfaced through an integration hub with link-outs to additional EPA data and public domain online resources. Batch searching allows for direct chemical identifier (ID) mapping and downloading of multiple data streams in several different formats. This facilitates fast access to available structure, property, toxicity, and bioassay data for collections of chemicals (hundreds to thousands at a time). Advanced search capabilities are available to support, for example, non-targeted analysis and identification of chemicals using mass spectrometry. The contents of the chemistry database, presently containing ~ 760,000 substances, are available as public domain data for download. The chemistry content underpinning the Dashboard has been aggregated over the past 15 years by both manual and auto-curation techniques within EPA’s DSSTox project. DSSTox chemical content is subject to strict quality controls to enforce consistency among chemical substance-structure identifiers, as well as list curation review to ensure accurate linkages of DSSTox substances to chemical lists and associated data. The Dashboard, publicly launched in April 2016, has expanded considerably in content and user traffic over the past year. It is continuously evolving with the growth of DSSTox into high-interest or data-rich domains of interest to EPA, such as chemicals on the Toxic Substances Control Act listing, while providing the user community with a flexible and dynamic web-based platform for integration, processing, visualization and delivery of data and resources. The Dashboard provides support for a broad array of research and regulatory programs across the worldwide community of toxicologists and environmental scientists.

title: Universities in a competitive global marketplace
abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this systematic review was to explore the nature of the marketing of higher education (HE) and universities in an international context. The objectives of the review were to: systematically collect, document, scrutinise and critically analyse the current research literature on supply‐side higher education marketing; establish the scope of higher education marketing; identify gaps in the research literature; and make recommendations for further research in this field.Design/methodology/approach – The approach for this study entailed extensive searches of relevant business management and education databases. The intention was to ensure that, as far as possible, all literature in the field was identified – while keeping the focus on literature of greatest pertinence to the research questions.Findings – The paper finds that potential benefits of applying marketing theories and concepts that have been effective in the business world are gradually being recognised by researchers in the ...

title: Dipolar physics: a review of experiments with magnetic quantum gases
abstract: Since the achievement of quantum degeneracy in gases of chromium atoms in 2004, the experimental investigation of ultracold gases made of highly magnetic atoms has blossomed. The field has yielded the observation of many unprecedented phenomena, in particular those in which long-range and anisotropic dipole–dipole interactions (DDIs) play a crucial role. In this review, we aim to present the aspects of the magnetic quantum-gas platform that make it unique for exploring ultracold and quantum physics as well as to give a thorough overview of experimental achievements. Highly magnetic atoms distinguish themselves by the fact that their electronic ground-state configuration possesses a large electronic total angular momentum. This results in a large magnetic moment and a rich electronic transition spectrum. Such transitions are useful for cooling, trapping, and manipulating these atoms. The complex atomic structure and large dipolar moments of these atoms also lead to a dense spectrum of resonances in their two-body scattering behaviour. These resonances can be used to control the interatomic interactions and, in particular, the relative importance of contact over dipolar interactions. These features provide exquisite control knobs for exploring the few- and many-body physics of dipolar quantum gases. The study of dipolar effects in magnetic quantum gases has covered various few-body phenomena that are based on elastic and inelastic anisotropic scattering. Various many-body effects have also been demonstrated. These affect both the shape, stability, dynamics, and excitations of fully polarised repulsive Bose or Fermi gases. Beyond the mean-field instability, strong dipolar interactions competing with slightly weaker contact interactions between magnetic bosons yield new quantum-stabilised states, among which are self-bound droplets, droplet assemblies, and supersolids. Dipolar interactions also deeply affect the physics of atomic gases with an internal degree of freedom as these interactions intrinsically couple spin and atomic motion. Finally, long-range dipolar interactions can stabilise strongly correlated excited states of 1D gases and also impact the physics of lattice-confined systems, both at the spin-polarised level (Hubbard models with off-site interactions) and at the spinful level (XYZ models). In the present manuscript, we aim to provide an extensive overview of the various related experimental achievements up to the present.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Business Practices in Small Firms in Developing Countries
abstract: Management has a large effect on the productivity of medium and large firms. But does management matter in micro and small firms, where the majority of the labor force in developing countries works? We develop 26 questions that measure business practices in marketing, stock-keeping, record-keeping, and financial planning. These questions have been administered in surveys in Bangladesh, Chile, Ghana, Kenya, Mexico, Nigeria, and Sri Lanka. We show that variation in business practices explains as much of the variation in outcomes-sales, profits, and labor productivity and total factor productivity-in microenterprises as in larger enterprises. Panel data from three countries indicate that better business practices predict higher survival rates and faster sales growth. The association of business practices with firm outcomes is robust to including numerous measures of the owner's human capital. We find that owners with higher human capital, children of entrepreneurs, and firms with employees employ better business practices. Data, as supplemental material, are available at http://dx.doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2016.2492 . This paper was accepted by Toby Stuart, entrepreneurship and innovation.

title: Evolution of DOHaD: the impact of environmental health sciences.
abstract: This paper traces the evolution of the Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD) paradigm, highlighting the increasing integration of environmental health sciences over the past two decades. Initially centered on nutrition, DOHaD research has expanded to encompass the effects of chemical exposures during critical developmental windows and their role in the etiology of non-communicable diseases across the lifespan. Through portfolio analyses of National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS)-funded grants from 1991, 2001, and 2011, the study documents a shift in research focus from metals and air pollutants to a broader array of chemicals including endocrine disruptors and persistent organic pollutants. The analysis reveals a growing emphasis on brain health, reproductive outcomes, cancer, and emerging endpoints such as obesity. Advances in genomics and epigenetics have enabled deeper investigation into mechanisms underlying disease susceptibility, particularly regarding gene-environment interactions and epigenetic modifications. The findings underscore the necessity of broadening the DOHaD framework to fully incorporate environmental chemical exposures and advocate for continued research to define sensitive periods of vulnerability and elucidate disease mechanisms.
venue: Journal of Developmental Origins of Health and Disease

title: Wnt signaling in cancer.
abstract: Aberrant regulation of the Wnt signaling pathway is a prevalent theme in cancer biology. From the earliest observation that Wnt overexpression could lead to malignant transformation of mouse mammary tissue to the most recent genetic discoveries gleaned from tumor genome sequencing, the Wnt pathway continues to evolve as a central mechanism in cancer biology. This article summarizes the evidence supporting a role for Wnt signaling in human cancer. This includes a review of the genetic mutations affecting Wnt pathway components, as well as some of epigenetic mechanisms that alter expression of genes relevant to Wnt. I also highlight some research on the cooperativity of Wnt with other signaling pathways in cancer. Finally, some emphasis is placed on laboratory research that provides a proof of concept for the therapeutic inhibition of Wnt signaling in cancer.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology

title: Topological quantum chemistry
abstract: We present a unified theory of topological quantum chemistry that bridges the local real-space perspective of chemical bonding with the global momentum-space description of electronic band structures. By systematically classifying all possible band connectivities in the 230 crystallographic space groups using graph-theoretic and group-theoretic methods, we establish a comprehensive framework that links the symmetry properties of atomic orbitals to the topological character of energy bands. Our approach introduces elementary band representations (EBRs) as the fundamental building blocks for understanding band topology, enabling the identification of both trivial and topologically nontrivial phases, including previously unrecognized classes of topological insulators and semimetals. This theory not only explains the scarcity of known topological materials within conventional band theory but also provides predictive tools to discover many more, offering a complete and practical methodology for classifying and designing topological materials based on their crystal symmetry and orbital content.

title: Machine Learning in Medicine
abstract: Machine learning has emerged as a transformative approach in medicine, driven by advances in computational power and the availability of large-scale data. This review examines the potential applications of machine learning in healthcare, distinguishing between tasks where computers approximate physician performance and those where they may uncover novel insights beyond human capability. Key concepts such as supervised and unsupervised learning are introduced, with examples including automated electrocardiogram interpretation, risk prediction models, and the identification of disease subtypes through pattern recognition. Despite the proliferation of research applying machine learning to medical data, few algorithms have meaningfully impacted clinical practice, highlighting significant barriers to implementation. The paper explores technical challenges such as feature selection, model choice, and parameter optimization, and discusses why these obstacles have limited the integration of machine learning into routine care. Strategies to overcome these challenges are considered, emphasizing the need for robust validation and careful translation of computational advances into clinical benefit.
venue: Mach. Learn. under Resour. Constraints Vol. 3

title: Discovering indigenous science: Implications for science education†
abstract: Indigenous science relates to both the science knowledge of long-resident, usually oral culture peoples, as well as the science knowledge of all peoples who as participants in culture are affected by the worldview and relativist interests of their home communities. This article explores aspects of multicultural science and pedagogy and describes a rich and well-documented branch of indigenous science known to biologists and ecologists as traditional ecological knowledge (TEK). Although TEK has been generally inaccessible, educators can now use a burgeoning science-based TEK literature that documents numerous examples of time-proven, ecologically relevant, and cost effective indigenous science. Disputes regarding the universality of the standard scientific account are of critical importance for science educators because the definition of science is a de facto “gatekeeping” device for determining what can be included in a school science curriculum and what cannot. When Western modern science (WMS) is defined as universal it does displace revelation-based knowledge (i.e., creation science); however, it also displaces pragmatic local indigenous knowledge that does not conform with formal aspects of the “standard account.” Thus, in most science classrooms around the globe, Western modern science has been taught at the expense of indigenous knowledge. However, because WMS has been implicated in many of the world's ecological disasters, and because the traditional wisdom component of TEK is particularly rich in time-tested approaches that foster sustainability and environmental integrity, it is possible that the universalist “gatekeeper” can be seen as increasingly problematic and even counter productive. This paper describes many examples from Canada and around the world of indigenous people's contributions to science, environmental understanding, and sustainability. The authors argue the view that Western or modern science is just one of many sciences that need to be addressed in the science classroom. We conclude by presenting instructional strategies that can help all science learners negotiate border crossings between Western modern science and indigenous science. © 2000 John Wiley & Sons, Inc. Sci Ed85:6–34, 2001.

title: Quantum Chemistry in the Age of Quantum Computing.
abstract: Practical challenges in simulating quantum systems on classical computers have been widely recognized in the quantum physics and quantum chemistry communities over the past century. Although many approximation methods have been introduced, the complexity of quantum mechanics remains hard to appease. The advent of quantum computation brings new pathways to navigate this challenging and complex landscape. By manipulating quantum states of matter and taking advantage of their unique features such as superposition and entanglement, quantum computers promise to efficiently deliver accurate results for many important problems in quantum chemistry, such as the electronic structure of molecules. In the past two decades, significant advances have been made in developing algorithms and physical hardware for quantum computing, heralding a revolution in simulation of quantum systems. This Review provides an overview of the algorithms and results that are relevant for quantum chemistry. The intended audience is both quantum chemists who seek to learn more about quantum computing and quantum computing researchers who would like to explore applications in quantum chemistry.

title: Polydopamine Surface Chemistry: A Decade of Discovery.
abstract: Polydopamine is one of the simplest and most versatile approaches to functionalizing material surfaces, having been inspired by the adhesive nature of catechols and amines in mussel adhesive proteins. Since its first report in 2007, a decade of studies on polydopamine molecular structure, deposition conditions, and physicochemical properties have ensued. During this time, potential uses of polydopamine coatings have expanded in many unforeseen directions, seemingly only limited by the creativity of researchers seeking simple solutions to manipulating surface chemistry. In this review, we describe the current state of the art in polydopamine coating methods, describe efforts underway to uncover and tailor the complex structure and chemical properties of polydopamine, and identify emerging trends and needs in polydopamine research, including the use of dopamine analogs, nitrogen-free polyphenolic precursors, and improvement of coating mechanical properties.

title: Diagnosis and treatment of diabetic foot infections.
abstract: Diabetic foot infections are a significant cause of morbidity and lower-extremity amputations, necessitating prompt and coordinated management. This guideline, developed by the Infectious Diseases Society of America, outlines evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of these infections. Key risk factors include peripheral neuropathy, vascular insufficiency, and poor glycemic control, with foot ulceration serving as the primary predisposing condition. Diagnosis relies on clinical assessment, supported by appropriate microbiological cultures and imaging studies, particularly MRI for deep tissue involvement. Empirical antibiotic therapy should be guided by infection severity and likely pathogens, with definitive regimens tailored to culture results and clinical response. Surgical intervention is indicated for deep abscesses, extensive necrosis, or osteomyelitis. Optimal wound care—including debridement and off-loading—is essential alongside antimicrobial therapy. The guideline emphasizes the importance of multidisciplinary care, early follow-up, and individualized treatment duration based on infection resolution rather than wound healing. Adjunctive therapies such as granulocyte colony-stimulating factors or hyperbaric oxygen may be considered in refractory cases. Further research is needed to refine classification systems, diagnostic strategies, and therapeutic approaches for diabetic foot infections.

title: Facilitators and barriers of herbal medicine use in Accra, Ghana: an inductive exploratory study
abstract: The use of complementary and alternative medicine including herbal medicine is increasing in many countries including Ghana. However, there is paucity of research on the perspectives of patrons of herbal medicine regarding the facilitators and barriers of herbal medicine use. This study sought to investigate the facilitators and barriers of herbal medicine among Ghanaian adults who use one form of herbal medicine or the other.MethodsThe study employed an inductive exploratory qualitative approach. It was conducted at a private herbal clinic in Accra. Purposive sampling was employed to recruit 16 participants. Data collection was through individual face-to-face interviews and these were transcribed and analysed using content analysis procedures.ResultsIt was realized that the factors that enhanced the use of herbal medicine included use of convincing information to enhance the initiation of herbal medicine use, effectiveness of herbal medicine, personal preference for herbal medicine, perceived ineffectiveness of western medicine and integration of spirituality in herbal medicine. The factors that hindered herbal medicine use included negative perceptions and attitudes about herbal medicine, poor vending environment, poor knowledge of vendors, high cost of herbal products at credible herbal clinics and inconsistent effectiveness of some herbal products. Participants desired that the national health insurance scheme will cover the cost of herbal medicine to alleviate the financial burden associated with herbal medicine use.ConclusionAlthough some Ghanaians patronize herbal medicine, the negative perceptions about herbal medicine resulting from deceitful producers and vendors call for enhanced education and monitoring to ensure that effective herbal products are used.

title: Untangling the origins of competitive advantage
abstract: This paper examines the foundational question of what drives the emergence and persistence of competitive advantage among firms, contrasting the perspectives of strategy research and population ecology. While strategy scholars emphasize the role of managerial foresight and the dynamic development of firm capabilities, population ecologists attribute performance heterogeneity primarily to initial conditions and organizational inertia. We argue that a deeper understanding of the origins and dynamics of competitive advantage is essential for advancing strategy research beyond documenting performance differentials. To this end, we propose an empirical framework that distinguishes between the effects of initial conditions and the rate of adoption of performance-enhancing practices, allowing for a systematic comparison between strategic choice and ecological explanations. Applying this framework to the diffusion of science-driven drug discovery in the pharmaceutical industry, we illustrate how both initial resource endowments and adaptive strategic responses to environmental cues shape competitive advantage. Our analysis highlights the importance of integrating insights from both traditions to better untangle the complex processes underlying firm-level performance differences.

title: What Is Citizen Science? – A Scientometric Meta-Analysis
abstract: This study presents a scientometric meta-analysis of the concept of citizen science (CS), examining its evolution, disciplinary adoption, and scientific output using two datasets from the Web of Science. By combining quantitative scientometric methods with qualitative analysis to refine search terms, the research identifies three primary strands of CS: biology and conservation, where CS is predominantly used for data collection and classification; geographic information research, involving citizen participation in spatial data gathering; and social sciences and epidemiology, focusing on public engagement in environmental and health issues. The analysis reveals that while the overall volume of CS-related publications remains modest, there has been significant growth in recent years, particularly driven by digital platforms facilitating large-scale data collection. The findings highlight both the diversity of interpretations and applications of CS across disciplines and the methodological challenges in mapping its full scope due to varying terminology and publication practices. This study contributes a more nuanced understanding of what constitutes citizen science and underscores the need for clearer definitions to enhance recognition and analysis of volunteer contributions in scientific research.

title: Analysing teacher knowledge for technology education in primary schools
abstract: This study investigates the interrelationships among primary school teachers’ subject matter knowledge (SMK), pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), attitude, and self-efficacy in the context of technology education. Recognizing that teacher knowledge significantly influences classroom practice and pupil learning, the research addresses a gap in empirical evidence regarding how these domains interact. Using tests and questionnaires administered to Dutch primary school teachers, the study employs path analysis to examine hypothesized relationships between knowledge domains. Results indicate that SMK is a crucial foundation for both PCK and self-efficacy, while self-efficacy strongly shapes teachers’ attitudes toward technology. The findings suggest that teacher training should prioritize the development of SMK and PCK, as these enhance confidence and foster more positive attitudes toward technology teaching. This positive cycle is expected to increase the frequency and quality of technology instruction, thereby supporting ongoing professional growth and improved technology education in primary schools.
venue: International Journal of Technology and Design Education

title: Helicobacter pylori persistence: biology and disease.
abstract: Helicobacter pylori is a human-adapted bacterium that persistently colonizes the stomach, establishing a dynamic equilibrium with its host through complex interactions shaped by coevolution. This review explores the biological mechanisms underlying H. pylori persistence, emphasizing the bacterium’s remarkable genetic diversity generated by high mutation and recombination rates, which enable adaptation to host-specific selective pressures. The resulting population structure resembles a quasispecies, with closely related variants occupying distinct gastric microniches and responding to local environmental cues. Host-microbial cross-signaling mediates both microbial persistence and host responses, balancing health and disease risk. While H. pylori colonization increases susceptibility to peptic ulceration and gastric cancer, emerging evidence suggests protective roles against certain esophageal diseases and broader impacts on human physiology. The principles governing H. pylori’s long-term colonization provide a paradigm for understanding persistent host-microbe relationships, with implications for chronic inflammation, oncogenesis, and modern metabolic disorders.

title: The physics of exceptional points
abstract: A short résumé is given about the nature of exceptional points (EPs) followed by discussions about their ubiquitous occurrence in a great variety of physical problems. EPs feature in classical as well as in quantum mechanical problems. They are associated with symmetry breaking for -symmetric Hamiltonians, where a great number of experiments has been performed, in particular in optics, and to an increasing extent in atomic and molecular physics. EPs are involved in quantum phase transition and quantum chaos; they produce dramatic effects in multichannel scattering, specific time dependence and more. In nuclear physics, they are associated with instabilities and continuum problems. Being spectral singularities they also affect approximation schemes. This article is part of a special issue of Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical devoted to ‘Quantum physics with non-Hermitian operators’.

title: Role of Social Software Tools in Education: A Literature Review.
abstract: This literature review examines the role of social software tools, such as blogs, wikis, social networking sites, and virtual environments, in educational contexts from the perspective of educators. Drawing on a comprehensive analysis of academic publications, recent reports, and online commentaries up to January 2009, the paper addresses key questions regarding the characteristics, theoretical foundations, benefits, challenges, and practical considerations associated with integrating social software into learning and teaching. Findings highlight how these tools support learner-centric approaches, foster communication, creativity, collaboration, and informal learning, while also presenting issues related to privacy, digital literacy, and quality assurance. The review offers insights into aligning social software with established learning theories and provides guidance for educators and policymakers considering their adoption. By synthesizing diverse literature sources and practitioner experiences, the paper contributes to understanding the pedagogical potential and practical implications of social software initiatives in higher and further education.

title: Machine learning in the search for new fundamental physics
abstract: Machine learning has become an essential tool in the search for new fundamental physics, particularly in high energy physics experiments such as those at the Large Hadron Collider, rare event searches, and neutrino experiments. This review surveys the recent advances in machine learning, with a focus on deep learning techniques that enable the analysis of large, high-dimensional datasets to identify subtle signatures of physics beyond the Standard Model. We discuss how modern machine learning methods are being integrated into all stages of the experimental data pipeline, from data acquisition and reconstruction to final analysis, and highlight their role in both supervised and unsupervised searches for new particles and interactions. The review also addresses challenges related to data representation, simulation accuracy, computational efficiency, and model robustness, emphasizing the need for tailored solutions that leverage domain-specific knowledge. By showcasing frontier applications and ongoing developments, we illustrate how machine learning is expanding the discovery potential of terrestrial experiments in the quest to uncover new fundamental laws of nature.

title: Citizen Science and Biological Invasions: A Review
abstract: Biological invasions are among the most challenging ecological and conservation riddles of our times. Fortunately, citizen science projects became a valuable tool to detect non-indigenous species (NIS), document their spread, prevent dispersion, and eradicate localized populations. We evaluated the most undisputed definitions of citizen science and proposed that a combination of two of them is a better reflection of what citizen science has become. Thus, citizen science is any environmental and/or biological data collection and analysis, including data quality control, undertaken by members of the general public, as individuals or as organized groups of citizens, with the guidance and/or assistance of scientists toward solving environmental and/or community questions. With this review, we also assessed how citizen science has been advancing biological invasions research and its focus, by analyzing 126 peer-reviewed articles that used citizen science methods or data concerning NIS. Most of the articles studied terrestrial species (68%) and terrestrial plants were the most studied group (22.7%). Surprisingly, most first detection reports were of non-indigenous marine fish probably due to the constraints in accessing aquatic ecosystems which delays the detection of new NIS. Citizen science projects running over broad geographical areas are very cost-effective for the early detection of NIS, regardless of the studied environment. We also discuss the applicability and need to adapt the methods and approaches toward the studied ecosystem and species, but also the profile of the participating citizens, their motivations, level of engagement, or social status. We recommend authors to better acknowledge the work done by contributing citizens, and the putative limitations of data generated by citizen science projects. The outreach planning of citizen science projects is also evaluated, including the use of dedicated web platforms vs. pre-existent and disseminated web platforms, while discussing how such outreach actions can be maximized. Lastly, we present a framework that contextualizes the contributions of citizen science, scientific research, and regional and national stakeholders toward the integrated management of biological invasions.

title: Towards quantum chemistry on a quantum computer.
abstract: Quantum chemistry calculations, essential for understanding molecular properties, are limited by the exponential scaling of computational resources required by classical algorithms. Recent advances propose that quantum computers can efficiently solve these problems with only polynomial resource scaling. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a key step towards this goal by implementing the iterative phase estimation algorithm (IPEA) on a photonic quantum computing platform to calculate the energy spectrum of molecular hydrogen (H₂) in a minimal basis. Our approach achieves high precision and robustness, reconstructing potential energy surfaces with chemical accuracy. We discuss the integration of classical computation for certain algorithmic steps and outline strategies for overcoming scalability challenges, including efficient state preparation and operator decomposition. Theoretical analysis confirms that simulating general molecular systems on quantum computers requires resources scaling polynomially with system size. This work represents a significant step toward practical quantum simulation of complex chemical systems and lays the foundation for future scalable quantum chemistry applications.

title: Nursing students’ experiences of a pedagogical transition from campus learning to distance learning using digital tools
abstract: This study explores nursing students’ experiences during the rapid pedagogical transition from traditional campus-based learning to distance learning using digital tools, prompted by the COVID-19 pandemic. Employing a mixed-methods approach, researchers conducted focus group interviews to identify key themes and developed a web-based questionnaire completed by 96 out of 132 students. Qualitative analysis revealed three main dimensions affecting students’ experiences: didactic aspects of digital teaching, the study environment, and students’ personal resources, with social interaction emerging as a central theme across all dimensions. Quantitative findings indicated that most students preferred campus-based education and perceived a decline in motivation and learning quality following the transition to distance learning, largely due to reduced opportunities for social interaction. Nevertheless, approximately one-third of students favored distance learning with digital tools. The study concludes that diminished social interaction negatively impacted the overall learning experience but suggests that a blended learning approach could balance pedagogical effectiveness with the benefits of interpersonal engagement in nursing education.

title: New materials physics
abstract: This review presents a survey of, and guide to, new materials physics (NMP) research. It begins with an overview of the goals of NMP and then presents important ideas and techniques for the design and growth of new materials. An emphasis is placed on the use of compositional phase diagrams to inform and motivate solution growth of single crystals. The second half of this review focuses on the vital process of generating actionable ideas for the growth and discovery of new materials and ground states. Motivations ranging from (1) wanting a specific compound, to (2) wanting a specific ground state to (3) wanting to explore for known and unknown unknowns, will be discussed and illustrated with abundant examples. The goal of this review is to inform, inspire, an even entertain, as many practitioners of this field as possible.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: TCMSP: a database of systems pharmacology for drug discovery from herbal medicines
abstract: BackgroundModern medicine often clashes with traditional medicine such as Chinese herbal medicine because of the little understanding of the underlying mechanisms of action of the herbs. In an effort to promote integration of both sides and to accelerate the drug discovery from herbal medicines, an efficient systems pharmacology platform that represents ideal information convergence of pharmacochemistry, ADME properties, drug-likeness, drug targets, associated diseases and interaction networks, are urgently needed.DescriptionThe traditional Chinese medicine systems pharmacology database and analysis platform (TCMSP) was built based on the framework of systems pharmacology for herbal medicines. It consists of all the 499 Chinese herbs registered in the Chinese pharmacopoeia with 29,384 ingredients, 3,311 targets and 837 associated diseases. Twelve important ADME-related properties like human oral bioavailability, half-life, drug-likeness, Caco-2 permeability, blood-brain barrier and Lipinski’s rule of five are provided for drug screening and evaluation. TCMSP also provides drug targets and diseases of each active compound, which can automatically establish the compound-target and target-disease networks that let users view and analyze the drug action mechanisms. It is designed to fuel the development of herbal medicines and to promote integration of modern medicine and traditional medicine for drug discovery and development.ConclusionsThe particular strengths of TCMSP are the composition of the large number of herbal entries, and the ability to identify drug-target networks and drug-disease networks, which will help revealing the mechanisms of action of Chinese herbs, uncovering the nature of TCM theory and developing new herb-oriented drugs. TCMSP is freely available at http://sm.nwsuaf.edu.cn/lsp/tcmsp.php.

title: A BIBLIOMETRIC ANALYSIS OF NATURAL DISASTERS AND BUSINESS MANAGEMENT IN TOURISM
abstract: Natural disasters are a critical factor for the development of business management in the tourism industry, leading to an increasing number of publications on the relationship between natural disasters and tourism business management (ND&T). In order to identify the research status of ND&T and explore the direction for future research, this paper collects 335 publications related to ND&T and develops a bibliometric analysis of the existing publications. First, we map the leading countries/regions, institutions, authors, and journals of ND&T to visualize the general analysis. Then the cooperation network is provided to show the collaboration relationship between countries/regions, institutions, and authors. Third, we introduce the keyword analysis to obtain research hotspots of ND&T. And finally, we explore the research theme analysis through literature review and conclude four topics. The findings of the topic analysis suggest that research on ND&T is receiving increasing attention, and more cooperation is required in the future to deepen the theoretical and empirical focus on tourists.
venue: Journal of Business and Economic Management

title: Chalcone: A Privileged Structure in Medicinal Chemistry.
abstract: Privileged structures have been widely used as an effective template in medicinal chemistry for drug discovery. Chalcone is a common simple scaffold found in many naturally occurring compounds. Many chalcone derivatives have also been prepared due to their convenient synthesis. These natural products and synthetic compounds have shown numerous interesting biological activities with clinical potentials against various diseases. This review aims to highlight the recent evidence of chalcone as a privileged scaffold in medicinal chemistry. Multiple aspects of chalcone will be summarized herein, including the isolation of novel chalcone derivatives, the development of new synthetic methodologies, the evaluation of their biological properties, and the exploration of the mechanisms of action as well as target identification. This review is expected to be a comprehensive, authoritative, and critical review of the chalcone template to the chemistry community.

title: Medicine sellers and malaria treatment in sub-Saharan Africa: what do they do and how can their practice be improved?
abstract: Medicine sellers are a primary source of malaria treatment in sub-Saharan Africa, offering accessible and affordable care but often providing inappropriate drugs and advice. This review synthesizes literature on the characteristics and operations of medicine sellers and evaluates interventions aimed at improving their malaria-related practices. Sixteen interventions were identified, employing strategies such as training, demand generation, quality assurance, and environmental support. Evidence suggests these interventions can enhance appropriate treatment rates and that medicine sellers are receptive to participation. Key factors for success include thorough situation analysis, stakeholder engagement, multifaceted approaches, and ongoing training and supervision. However, evidence remains insufficient to determine the most effective strategies, and interventions must adapt to incorporate artemisinin-based combination therapies. Further research is needed to assess sustainability and scalability at the national level.
venue: American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene

title: Energy band-gap engineering of graphene nanoribbons.
abstract: We report experimental evidence of energy band-gap engineering in graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) fabricated via lithographic patterning of single-layer graphene. By systematically varying the width and crystallographic orientation of over two dozen GNRs, we observe that lateral confinement induces an energy gap near the charge neutrality point, with narrower ribbons exhibiting larger gaps. Temperature-dependent conductance measurements reveal strong suppression of conductance at low temperatures for narrow GNRs, indicating the opening of a band gap. Nonlinear transport measurements allow direct extraction of the energy gap, which scales inversely with ribbon width, consistent with theoretical predictions. No systematic dependence on crystallographic orientation is observed. Our findings demonstrate that lithographic techniques enable precise control over the electronic properties of graphene nanostructures through width modulation, providing a viable route for band-gap engineering in graphene-based nanoelectronic devices.

title: Engineering of functional tendon.
abstract: Surgical tendon repair is limited by the availability of viable tissue for transplantation. Because of its relatively avascular nature, tendon is a prime candidate for engineered tissue replacement. To address this problem, cells isolated from rat Achilles tendon were grown to confluence in culture and allowed to self-assemble into a cylinder between two anchor points. The resulting scaffold-free tissue was composed of aligned, small-diameter collagen fibrils, a large number of cells, and an excess of noncollagenous extracellular matrix; all characteristics of embryonic tendon. The stress-strain response of the constructs also resembles the nonlinear behavior of immature tendons, and the ultimate tensile strength is approximately equal to that of embryonic chick tendon, roughly 2 MPa. These physical and mechanical properties indicate that these constructs are the first viable tendons engineered in vitro, without the aid of artificial scaffolding.

title: Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age
abstract: This paper reviews the development of network science, focusing on the emergence of random graph theory and its application to real-world networks as explored in Duncan J. Watts’s Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age and Albert-László Barabási’s Linked. It traces the origins of the field from the foundational work of Erdős and Rényi on random graphs, through Milgram’s small-world experiments, to the formulation of the Watts-Strogatz small-world model and Barabási-Albert preferential attachment model. The review highlights how these models explain key properties observed in diverse networks, such as short average path lengths, high clustering, and power-law degree distributions. It also discusses the limitations and misinterpretations of these models when applied to empirical data, emphasizing that while preferential attachment produces power laws, not all power laws arise from this mechanism. The paper concludes by noting the profound impact of network science on understanding complex systems in social, biological, and technological domains, while cautioning against overgeneralization of its results.

title: Global Community of Disaster Risk Reduction Scientists and Decision Makers Endorse a Science and Technology Partnership to Support the Implementation of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030
abstract: At the inaugural UNISDR Science and Technology Conference on the Implementation of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030, over 750 global stakeholders—including scientists, policymakers, practitioners, and business leaders—convened to endorse a new Science and Technology Partnership and Road Map aimed at supporting the Framework’s goals. The conference facilitated multidisciplinary collaboration across four key work streams: leveraging networks to integrate science, policy, and practice; improving disaster risk understanding and early warning systems; advancing data standards and innovative practices for risk measurement; and identifying research and capacity gaps in disaster risk reduction (DRR). Side events addressed critical issues such as gender inequality, youth engagement, ethics, and research funding in DRR science. Notable outcomes included commitments to launch platforms for Women in DRR Science and Young Scientists in DRR. The conference set a clear agenda for the scientific community’s role in implementing the Sendai Framework, emphasizing knowledge transfer, innovation, and ongoing collaboration through the Science and Technology Partnership. Progress will be monitored biennially at Global Platforms on Disaster Risk Reduction, with all stakeholders invited to contribute to the Road Map’s delivery.
venue: International Journal of Disaster Risk Science

title: Chemical markers for the quality control of herbal medicines: an overview
abstract: The quality control of herbal medicines is challenged by their complex and variable chemical compositions, necessitating reliable analytical approaches to ensure consistency, safety, and efficacy. Chemical markers serve as critical tools for the authentication of species, evaluation of raw materials and finished products, and detection of adulterants or toxic substances. This review provides an overview of the selection criteria and classification systems for chemical markers, highlighting their roles in quality assessment. Eight categories of chemical markers are proposed: therapeutic, bioactive, synergistic, characteristic, main, correlative, toxic, and general components used with fingerprint spectra. The article discusses the advantages and limitations of each category, emphasizing the importance of selecting appropriate markers based on therapeutic relevance, specificity, detectability, and physicochemical properties. Case studies illustrate the practical application of chemical markers in quality control protocols for widely used herbal medicines. The review concludes that systematic selection and utilization of chemical markers are essential for standardizing herbal medicines and advancing their research and clinical use.

title: Open Babel: An open chemical toolbox
abstract: A frequent problem in computational modeling is the interconversion of chemical structures between different formats. While standard interchange formats exist (for example, Chemical Markup Language) and de facto standards have arisen (for example, SMILES format), the need to interconvert formats is a continuing problem due to the multitude of different application areas for chemistry data, differences in the data stored by different formats (0D versus 3D, for example), and competition between software along with a lack of vendor-neutral formats.ResultsWe discuss, for the first time, Open Babel, an open-source chemical toolbox that speaks the many languages of chemical data. Open Babel version 2.3 interconverts over 110 formats. The need to represent such a wide variety of chemical and molecular data requires a library that implements a wide range of cheminformatics algorithms, from partial charge assignment and aromaticity detection, to bond order perception and canonicalization. We detail the implementation of Open Babel, describe key advances in the 2.3 release, and outline a variety of uses both in terms of software products and scientific research, including applications far beyond simple format interconversion.ConclusionsOpen Babel presents a solution to the proliferation of multiple chemical file formats. In addition, it provides a variety of useful utilities from conformer searching and 2D depiction, to filtering, batch conversion, and substructure and similarity searching. For developers, it can be used as a programming library to handle chemical data in areas such as organic chemistry, drug design, materials science, and computational chemistry. It is freely available under an open-source license from http://openbabel.org.

title: The Physical Implementation of Quantum Computation
abstract: After a brief introduction to the principles and promise of quantum information processing, the requirements for the physical implementation of quantum computation are discussed. These five requirements, plus two relating to the communication of quantum information, are extensively ex- plored and related to the many schemes in atomic physics, quantum optics, nuclear and electron magnetic resonance spectroscopy, superconducting electronics, and quantum-dot physics, for achiev- ing quantum computing. I. INTRODUCTION � The advent of quantum information processing, as an abstract concept, has given birth to a great deal of new thinking, of a very concrete form, about how to create physical computing devices that operate in the hitherto unexplored quantum mechanical regime. The efforts now underway to produce working laboratory devices that perform this profoundly new form of information pro- cessing are the subject of this book. In this chapter I provide an overview of the common objectives of the investigations reported in the remain- der of this special issue. The scope of the approaches, proposed and underway, to the implementation of quan- tum hardware is remarkable, emerging from specialties in atomic physics (1), in quantum optics (2), in nuclear (3) and electron (4) magnetic resonance spectroscopy, in su- perconducting device physics (5), in electron physics (6), and in mesoscopic and quantum dot research (7). This amazing variety of approaches has arisen because, as we will see, the principles of quantum computing are posed using the most fundamental ideas of quantum mechanics, ones whose embodiment can be contemplated in virtually every branch of quantum physics. The interdisciplinary spirit which has been fostered as a result is one of the most pleasant and remarkable fea- tures of this field. The excitement and freshness that has been produced bodes well for the prospect for discovery, invention, and innovation in this endeavor.

title: Emotion, rationality, and decision-making: how to link affective and social neuroscience with social theory
abstract: In this paper, we argue for a stronger engagement between concepts in affective and social neuroscience on the one hand, and theories from the fields of anthropology, economics, political science, and sociology on the other. Affective and social neuroscience could provide an additional assessment of social theories. We argue that some of the most influential social theories of the last four decades—rational choice theory, behavioral economics, and post-structuralism—contain assumptions that are inconsistent with key findings in affective and social neuroscience. We also show that another approach from the social sciences—plural rationality theory—shows greater compatibility with these findings. We further claim that, in their turn, social theories can strengthen affective and social neuroscience. The former can provide more precise formulations of the social phenomena that neuroscientific models have targeted, can help neuroscientists who build these models become more aware of their social and cultural biases, and can even improve the models themselves. To illustrate, we show how plural rationality theory can be used to further specify and test the somatic marker hypothesis. Thus, we aim to accelerate the much-needed merger of social theories with affective and social neuroscience.

title: Requirements for Traffic Engineering Over MPLS
abstract: This paper defines the functional requirements for implementing effective traffic engineering within Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) networks. It analyzes the limitations of existing interior gateway protocols (IGPs) in managing traffic and resources, motivating the need for enhanced capabilities in MPLS domains. The document details key performance objectives—both traffic-oriented, such as minimizing packet loss and delay, and resource-oriented, such as optimizing bandwidth utilization and minimizing congestion. It specifies necessary attributes for traffic trunks and network resources, including support for constraint-based routing, explicit path selection, load distribution, resilience, and performance monitoring. The requirements outlined aim to enable efficient, reliable, and scalable network operations in both large Internet backbones and enterprise environments by leveraging MPLS mechanisms to achieve advanced traffic engineering goals.

title: The Antitrust Analysis of Multi-Sided Platform Businesses
abstract: This paper surveys the economics literature on multi-sided platform businesses with a focus on competition policy issues such as market definition, mergers, monopolization, and coordinated behavior. It reviews the industrial organization theory underlying multi-sided platforms and examines how antitrust analysis must be adapted to account for the presence of multiple interdependent customer groups. The paper demonstrates that standard economic models used in antitrust analysis for single-sided firms often do not apply directly to multi-sided platforms, highlighting the need for explicit consideration of cross-group interactions and indirect network effects. The survey synthesizes theoretical and empirical findings, showing that multi-sided platforms require distinct analytical approaches in antitrust contexts due to their unique economic characteristics, and discusses the implications for competition authorities and policy makers as these platforms play increasingly significant roles in modern industries.

title: Non-Hermitian physics
abstract: A review is given on the foundations and applications of non-Hermitian classical and quantum physics. First, key theorems and central concepts in non-Hermitian linear algebra, including Jordan normal form, biorthogonality, exceptional points, pseudo-Hermiticity, and parity-time symmetry, are delineated in a pedagogical and mathematically coherent manner. Building on these, we provide an overview of how diverse classical systems, ranging from photonics, mechanics, electrical circuits, and acoustics to active matter, can be used to simulate non-Hermitian wave physics. In particular, we discuss rich and unique phenomena found therein, such as unidirectional invisibility, enhanced sensitivity, topological energy transfer, coherent perfect absorption, single-mode lasing, and robust biological transport. We then explain in detail how non-Hermitian operators emerge as an effective description of open quantum systems on the basis of the Feshbach projection approach and the quantum trajectory approach. We discuss their applications to physical systems relevant to a variety of fields, including atomic, molecular and optical physics, mesoscopic physics, and nuclear physics with emphasis on prominent phenomena and subjects in quantum regimes, such as quantum resonances, superradiance, the continuous quantum Zeno effect, quantum critical phenomena, Dirac spectra in quantum chromodynamics, and nonunitary conformal field theories. Finally, we introduce the notion of band topology in complex spectra of non-Hermitian systems and present their classifications by providing the proof, first given by this review in a complete manner, as well as a number of instructive examples. Other topics related to non-Hermitian physics, including nonreciprocal transport, speed limits, nonunitary quantum walk, are also reviewed.

title: Revealing noncovalent interactions.
abstract: Non-covalent interactions play a critical role in diverse chemical and biological processes, yet their identification and characterization remain challenging due to their subtle nature and the limitations of traditional molecular structure analysis. In this work, we introduce a real-space method for revealing non-covalent interactions based on the electron density and its derivatives, particularly the reduced density gradient and the second derivative (Hessian) of the electron density. By analyzing regions of low electron density and low reduced gradient, our approach isolates non-covalent interactions such as van der Waals forces, hydrogen bonds, and steric repulsion in a wide range of systems from small molecules to large biomolecular assemblies. Further discrimination between interaction types is achieved through examination of the sign of the second eigenvalue of the density Hessian, enabling distinction between stabilizing and destabilizing interactions. This method requires only atomic coordinates, making it efficient and broadly applicable to complex systems including proteins and nucleic acids. The resulting visualization as continuous surfaces provides new insights into non-bonded interactions beyond simple atom pair contacts, offering valuable guidance for rational design in chemistry and biology.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Polyphenols: chemistry, dietary sources, metabolism, and nutritional significance.
abstract: Polyphenols are a diverse group of naturally occurring compounds found abundantly in plant-based foods, recognized for their complex chemical structures and significant roles in human health. This review examines the chemistry of polyphenols, detailing their classification into flavonoids, phenolic acids, stilbenes, and lignans, and explores their primary dietary sources such as fruits, vegetables, tea, wine, and whole grains. The paper discusses the metabolic pathways polyphenols undergo in the human body, including absorption, biotransformation by gut microbiota, and bioavailability factors that influence their physiological effects. Emphasis is placed on the nutritional significance of polyphenols, highlighting their antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and potential disease-preventive properties. The review also addresses current challenges in polyphenol research and suggests directions for future studies to better understand their impact on nutrition and health.

title: Handbook of Qualitative Research
abstract: The third edition of the Handbook of Qualitative Research, edited by Denzin and Lincoln, serves as a foundational reference for qualitative researchers, offering comprehensive updates and new topics that reflect the evolving landscape of the field. This edition expands its scope to include indigenous research, critical and performance ethnography, arts-based inquiry, narrative research, Foucault’s influence, ethics, online research strategies, and evaluation policies. The handbook is organized into an introduction and six parts: an overview of the discipline’s current state; a call for socially and morally engaged science; epistemological foundations; research methods; data collection and analysis techniques; interpretation, evaluation, and presentation of results; and future directions for qualitative inquiry. Each section integrates updated chapters from previous editions alongside new contributions, making this volume an essential resource for understanding both the theoretical and practical dimensions of qualitative research.

title: Cosmic rays and particle physics
abstract: The study of high energy cosmic rays is a diversified field of observational and phenomenological physics addressing questions ranging from shock acceleration of charged particles in various astrophysical objects, via transport properties through galactic and extragalactic space, to questions of dark matter, and even to those of particle physics beyond the Standard Model including processes taking place in the earliest moments of our Universe. After decades of mostly independent evolution of nuclear, particle and high energy cosmic ray physics we find ourselves entering a symbiotic era of these fields of research. Some examples of interrelations will be given from the perspective of modern Particle-Astrophysics and new major experiments will briefly be sketched.

title: Nanobubble Technology in Environmental Engineering: Revolutionization Potential and Challenges.
abstract: Nanobubble technology, characterized by bubbles less than 1000 nm in diameter, has emerged as a promising tool in environmental engineering due to its unique properties, including high gas transfer efficiency, longevity, negative surface charge, and the ability to generate reactive oxygen species. These features enable nanobubbles to enhance processes such as aeration, pollutant degradation, pathogen disinfection, and sediment remediation, potentially revolutionizing water treatment by improving contaminant removal efficiency, reducing operational costs, and downsizing treatment facilities. However, significant challenges remain regarding the stable and cost-effective generation of nanobubbles in complex wastewater matrices, the scalability of current production methods, and the limited understanding of nanobubble interactions with microbial communities and pollutants under real-world conditions. Additionally, the practical benefits of nanobubbles compared to microbubbles require further evaluation to justify their exclusive use. Addressing these challenges through continued research is essential for realizing the full potential of nanobubble technology as a sustainable and transformative approach in environmental engineering.

title: Osteoarthritis: a disease of the joint as an organ.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent and disabling joint disorder traditionally mischaracterized as mere degenerative wear and tear, but is now recognized as a complex disease involving the entire joint as an organ. This review synthesizes current understanding of OA pathogenesis, highlighting how pathological changes extend beyond articular cartilage to include subchondral bone thickening, osteophyte formation, synovial inflammation, ligament and meniscal degeneration, and alterations in periarticular tissues. Central to OA progression are activated chondrocytes that drive matrix remodeling and degradation through upregulation of matrix metalloproteinases and inflammatory mediators, influenced by mechanical stress, cytokine signaling, and epigenetic modifications. Inflammatory pathways, including NF-κB and MAPK cascades, Toll-like receptor activation by damage-associated molecular patterns, and complement system involvement, further amplify tissue catabolism. Age-related changes such as cellular senescence, oxidative stress, impaired autophagy, and increased cell death exacerbate joint degeneration. The interplay of these mechanisms underscores OA as a multifactorial disease process resulting in joint failure, emphasizing the need for therapeutic strategies targeting the whole joint environment rather than isolated tissues.

title: Floquet Engineering of Quantum Materials
abstract: Floquet engineering, the control of quantum systems using periodic driving, is an old concept in condensed matter physics dating back to ideas such as the inverse Faraday effect. However, there is a renewed interest in this concept owing to ( a) the rapid developments in laser and ultrafast spectroscopy techniques, ( b) discovery and understanding of various “quantum materials” hosting interesting exotic quantum properties, and ( c) communication with different areas of physics such as artificial matter and nonequilibrium quantum statistical physics. Here, starting from a nontechnical introduction with emphasis on the Floquet picture and effective Hamiltonians, we review the recent applications of Floquet engineering in ultrafast, nonlinear phenomena in the solid state. In particular, Floquet topological states and their application to ultrafast spintronics and strongly correlated electron systems are overviewed.
venue: Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics

title: The biology of extracellular vesicles: The known unknowns
abstract: For many years, double-layer phospholipid membrane vesicles, released by most cells, were not considered to be of biological significance. This stance has dramatically changed with the recognition of extracellular vesicles (EVs) as carriers of biologically active molecules that can traffic to local or distant targets and execute defined biological functions. The dimensionality of the field has expanded with the appreciation of diverse types of EVs and the complexity of vesicle biogenesis, cargo loading, release pathways, targeting mechanisms, and vesicle processing. With the expanded interest in the field and the accelerated rate of publications on EV structure and function in diverse biomedical fields, it has become difficult to distinguish between well-established biological features of EV and the untested hypotheses or speculative assumptions that await experimental proof. With the growing interest despite the limited evidence, we sought in this essay to formulate a set of unsolved mysteries in the field, sort out established data from fascinating hypotheses, and formulate several challenging questions that must be answered for the field to advance.

title: Algorithms on Strings, Trees, and Sequences: Computer Science and Computational Biology
abstract: Traditionally an area of study in computer science, string algorithms have, in recent years, become an increasingly important part of biology, particularly genetics. This volume is a comprehensive look at computer algorithms for string processing. In addition to pure computer science, Gusfield adds extensive discussions on biological problems that are cast as string problems and on methods developed to solve them. This text emphasizes the fundamental ideas and techniques central to today's applications. New approaches to this complex material simplify methods that up to now have been for the specialist alone. With over 400 exercises to reinforce the material and develop additional topics, the book is suitable as a text for graduate or advanced undergraduate students in computer science, computational biology, or bio-informatics.

title: Effects of abiotic stress on plants: a systems biology perspective
abstract: The natural environment for plants is composed of a complex set of abiotic stresses and biotic stresses. Plant responses to these stresses are equally complex. Systems biology approaches facilitate a multi-targeted approach by allowing one to identify regulatory hubs in complex networks.
