title: Sedimentation engineering : processes, measurements, modeling, and practice
abstract: Sedimentation Engineering: Theories, Measurements, Modeling, and Practice (ASCE Manuals and Reports on Engineering Practice No. 110) is intended to supplement ''Sedimentation Engineering: Classic Edition'' (ASCE Manuals and Reports on Engineering Practice No. 54), a seminal text on the nature and scope of sedimentation problems, methods for their investigation, and practical approaches to their solution.''Sedimentation Engineering: Theories, Measurements, Modeling, and Practice'' updates selected topics in the original manual and addresses new topics, such as the hydraulic action of flowing water in the context of rivers and inland water bodies.

title: Modeling meets science and technology: an introduction to a special issue on negative emissions
abstract: This introductory article presents the rationale and scope of a special issue on negative emissions technologies, or carbon dioxide removal (CDR), highlighting their unique role in reducing atmospheric carbon stocks and enabling stringent climate stabilization targets. The issue brings together nine papers that examine CDR through integrated assessment modeling, technology optimization, environmental science, and political science, fostering interdisciplinary dialogue. Five papers employ economic models to assess the deployment and implications of various CDR strategies—biological and geological—including afforestation, BECCS, and direct air capture, while four address ecological, engineering, and governance dimensions. The introduction underscores the importance of understanding both the opportunities and limitations of CDR in climate policy, particularly regarding overshoot scenarios and the feasibility of achieving long-term temperature goals. By synthesizing insights from diverse disciplines, this special issue aims to advance knowledge on the integration of CDR into climate models and inform future research and policy development.

title: Bell Nonlocality
abstract: This monograph provides a comprehensive and conceptually focused exploration of Bell nonlocality, treating it as an observable phenomenon independent of theoretical interpretation. Eschewing historical and expository treatments, the book emphasizes the mathematical structure and conceptual foundations of nonlocality, both in general and within quantum theory. The core material is presented in Part I, while Part II addresses the practical implications of nonlocality through device-independent certification in quantum technologies. Part III extends to foundational issues, highlighting connections to broader questions in physics. Experimental aspects are briefly addressed, with references to key milestones, but the primary aim is to clarify the phenomenon’s theoretical landscape. The work is intended as a resource for readers seeking a clear, modern understanding of Bell nonlocality and its significance in contemporary quantum science.

title: Big data and machine learning for materials science
abstract: Herein, we review aspects of leading-edge research and innovation in materials science that exploit big data and machine learning (ML), two computer science concepts that combine to yield computational intelligence. ML can accelerate the solution of intricate chemical problems and even solve problems that otherwise would not be tractable. However, the potential benefits of ML come at the cost of big data production; that is, the algorithms demand large volumes of data of various natures and from different sources, from material properties to sensor data. In the survey, we propose a roadmap for future developments with emphasis on computer-aided discovery of new materials and analysis of chemical sensing compounds, both prominent research fields for ML in the context of materials science. In addition to providing an overview of recent advances, we elaborate upon the conceptual and practical limitations of big data and ML applied to materials science, outlining processes, discussing pitfalls, and reviewing cases of success and failure.

title: Hygiene, Sanitation, and Water: Forgotten Foundations of Health
abstract: As the first article in a four-part PLoS Medicine series on water and sanitation, Jamie Bartram and Sandy Cairncross argue that the massive burden of ill health associated with poor hygiene, sanitation, and water supply demands more attention from health professionals and policymakers.

title: The Limits of Reductionism in Medicine: Could Systems Biology Offer an Alternative?
abstract: In the first of a two part series, Ahn and colleagues discuss the reductionist approach pervading medicine and explain how a systems approach (as advocated by systems biology) may complement reductionism.

title: Do Doctors Practice Defensive Medicine?
abstract: `Defensive medicine' is a potentially serious social problem: if fear of liability drives health care providers to administer treatments that do not have worthwhile medical benefits, then the current liability system may generate inefficiencies many times greater than the costs of compensating malpractice claimants. To obtain direct empirical evidence on this question, we analyze the effects of malpractice liability reforms using data on all elderly Medicare beneficiaries treated for serious heart disease in 1984, 1987, and 1990. We find that malpractice reforms that directly reduce provider liability pressure lead to reductions of 5 to 9 percent in medical expenditures without substantial effects on mortality or medical complications. We conclude that liability reforms can reduce defensive medical practices.

title: Sanitation and Health
abstract: As one article in a four-part PLoS Medicine series on water and sanitation, David Trouba and colleagues discuss the importance of improved sanitation to health and the role that the health sector can play in its advocacy.

title: Recent advances in quantitative LA-ICP-MS analysis: challenges and solutions in the life sciences and environmental chemistry
abstract: Laser ablation–inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (LA-ICP-MS) is a widely accepted method for direct sampling of solid materials for trace elemental analysis. The number of reported applications is high and the application range is broad; besides geochemistry, LA-ICP-MS is mostly used in environmental chemistry and the life sciences. This review focuses on the application of LA-ICP-MS for quantification of trace elements in environmental, biological, and medical samples. The fundamental problems of LA-ICP-MS, such as sample-dependent ablation behavior and elemental fractionation, can be even more pronounced in environmental and life science applications as a result of the large variety of sample types and conditions. Besides variations in composition, the range of available sample states is highly diverse, including powders (e.g., soil samples, fly ash), hard tissues (e.g., bones, teeth), soft tissues (e.g., plants, tissue thin-cuts), or liquid samples (e.g., whole blood). Within this article, quantification approaches that have been proposed in the past are critically discussed and compared regarding the results obtained in the applications described. Although a large variety of sample types is discussed within this article, the quantification approaches used are similar for many analytical questions and have only been adapted to the specific questions. Nevertheless, none of them has proven to be a universally applicable method.

title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
abstract: An innovator in contemporary thought on economic and political development looks here at decline rather than growth. Albert O. Hirschman makes a basic distinction between alternative ways of reacting to deterioration in business firms and, in general, to dissatisfaction with organizations: one, “exit,” is for the member to quit the organization or for the customer to switch to the competing product, and the other, “voice,” is for members or customers to agitate and exert influence for change “from within.” The efficiency of the competitive mechanism, with its total reliance on exit, is questioned for certain important situations. As exit often undercuts voice while being unable to counteract decline, loyalty is seen in the function of retarding exit and of permitting voice to play its proper role.  The interplay of the three concepts turns out to illuminate a wide range of economic, social, and political phenomena. As the author states in the preface, “having found my own unifying way of looking at issues as diverse as competition and the two-party system, divorce and the American character, black power and the failure of ‘unhappy’ top officials to resign over Vietnam, I decided to let myself go a little.”

title: The Physical Implementation of Quantum Computation
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the physical requirements for implementing quantum computation, beginning with an introduction to the foundational principles and potential advantages of quantum information processing. It identifies and elaborates on five essential criteria for realizing practical quantum computers: scalable systems with well-characterized qubits, the ability to initialize qubits to a known state, long relevant decoherence times, a universal set of quantum gates, and qubit-specific measurement capability. Additionally, two further requirements related to quantum communication are discussed. The analysis connects these criteria to a broad spectrum of proposed physical implementations, including systems based on atomic physics, quantum optics, nuclear and electron magnetic resonance spectroscopy, superconducting electronics, and quantum dots. By examining the challenges and prospects associated with each approach, the paper highlights the interdisciplinary nature of the field and underscores the ongoing innovation driving progress toward viable quantum computing technologies.

title: The Reservoir model and architecture for open federated cloud computing
abstract: Cloud computing promises scalable, on-demand IT services but faces significant limitations in scalability, interoperability, and business service management (BSM) support. This paper introduces the Reservoir model and architecture, designed to enable open federated cloud computing that addresses these deficiencies. The Reservoir approach proposes a modular, extensible architecture supporting dynamic federation among autonomous cloud providers, allowing seamless resource pooling and service provisioning across organizational boundaries while preserving provider autonomy. By embedding automated BSM and SLA management into the infrastructure, Reservoir facilitates reliable, cost-effective delivery of enterprise-grade services and democratizes cloud participation for small and medium-sized providers. The paper delineates motivations and use cases for federated clouds, defines a reference model and open architecture for interoperability, and presents a loosely coupled cloud stack with standardized interfaces. The Reservoir model establishes a foundation for next-generation cloud computing as a global utility, enabling competitive, flexible, and high-quality IT service delivery.
venue: IBM Journal of Research and Development

title: Does the Hubble constant tension call for new physics?
abstract: The Λ Cold Dark Matter model (ΛCDM) represents the current standard model in cosmology. Within this, there is a tension between the value of the Hubble constant, H0, inferred from local distance indicators and the angular scale of fluctuations in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). In terms of Bayseian evidence, we investigate whether the tension is significant enough to warrant new physics in the form of modifying or adding energy components to the standard cosmological model. We find that late time dark energy explanations are not favoured by data whereas a pre-CMB decoupling extra dark energy component has a positive, although not substantial, Bayesian evidence. A constant equation of state of the additional early energy density is constrained to 0.086+0.04−0.03. Although this value deviates significantly from 1/3, valid for dark radiation, the latter is favoured based on the Bayesian evidence. If the tension persists, future estimates of H0 at the 1% level will be able to decisively determine which of the proposed explanations is favoured.
venue: Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics

title: The Search for R&D Spillovers
abstract: R&D spillovers are, potentially, a major source of endogenous growth in various recent 'new growth theory' models. This paper reviews the basic model of R&D spillovers and then focuses on the empirical evidence for their existence and magnitude. It surveys the older empirical literature with special attention to the economic difficulties of actually coming up with convincing evidence on this topic. Taken individually, many of the studies are flawed and subject to a variety of reservations, but the overall impression remains that R&D spillovers are both prevalent and important. Copyright 1992 by The editors of the Scandinavian Journal of Economics.

title: Silkworm: A Promising Model Organism in Life Science
abstract: Abstract As an important economic insect, silkworm Bombyx mori (L.) (Lepidoptera: Bombycidae) has numerous advantages in life science, such as low breeding cost, large progeny size, short generation time, and clear genetic background. Additionally, there are rich genetic resources associated with silkworms. The completion of the silkworm genome has further accelerated it to be a modern model organism in life science. Genomic studies showed that some silkworm genes are highly homologous to certain genes related to human hereditary disease and, therefore, are a candidate model for studying human disease. In this article, we provided a review of silkworm as an important model in various research areas, including human disease, screening of antimicrobial agents, environmental safety monitoring, and antitumor studies. In addition, the application potentiality of silkworm model in life sciences was discussed.

title: The biology of extracellular vesicles: The known unknowns
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are membrane-bound particles released by cells that play crucial roles in intercellular communication, physiological regulation, and disease processes. Despite significant advances in characterizing their biogenesis, cargo, and functional diversity, many aspects of EV biology remain incompletely understood. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the molecular mechanisms governing EV formation, release, and uptake, highlighting the heterogeneity of vesicle subtypes such as exosomes and microvesicles. It discusses the challenges in distinguishing EV populations, standardizing isolation techniques, and interpreting functional assays due to overlapping markers and methodological limitations. The paper also explores emerging evidence for EV involvement in immune modulation, cancer progression, and tissue regeneration while emphasizing unresolved questions regarding their in vivo dynamics, specificity of cargo selection, and physiological relevance. By outlining these “known unknowns,” the review underscores the need for rigorous experimental approaches and novel technologies to unravel the complexities of EV biology and harness their potential as diagnostic and therapeutic tools.

title: Personalisation in educational technology: the absence of underlying pedagogies
abstract: Personalization is one of the recurring themes in education and has occupied a large amount of specialised literature, since its appearance in the 1960s. A systematic exploration of the literature of the last 55 years (1960–2015) is presented and is intended to analyse which educational perspective underlies the customized environments or experiences proposed in the educational technology that is addressed in the literature. It is important to understand that this analysis is a very relevant challenge, if we want to understand what pedagogical approaches have been continuously developed and how and why we should consider their future. The results show a complete centralisation of experiences in technological developments, the majority of them focussed in Higher Education, as well as a lack of an explicit pedagogical perspective in the experiences analysed, especially those with greater impact. It also shows a shortage of in-house pedagogical material – developed in the light of this research, that evolves and makes an impact on the educational landscape.
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title: Gas-grain chemistry in cold interstellar cloud cores with a microscopic Monte Carlo approach to surface chemistry
abstract: Aims. We have recently developed a microscopic Monte Carlo approach to study surface chemistry on interstellar grains and the morphology of ice mantles. The method is designed to eliminate the problems inherent in the rate-equation formalism to surface chemistry. Here we report the first use of this method in a chemical model of cold interstellar cloud cores that includes both gas-phase and surface chemistry. The surface chemical network consists of a small number of diffusive reactions that can produce molecular oxygen, water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol and assorted radicals. Methods. The simulation is started by running a gas-phase model including accretion onto grains but no surface chemistry or evaporation. The starting surface consists of either flat or rough olivine. We introduce the surface chemistry of the three species H, O and CO in an iterative manner using our stochastic technique. Under the conditions of the simulation, only atomic hydrogen can evaporate to a significant extent. Although it has little effect on other gas-phase species, the evaporation of atomic hydrogen changes its gas-phase abundance, which in turn changes the flux of atomic hydrogen onto grains. The effect on the surface chemistry is treated until convergence occurs. We neglect all non-thermal desorptive processes. Results. We determine the mantle abundances of assorted molecules as a function of time through 2 $\times$ 10 5 yr. Our method also allows determination of the abundance of each molecule in specific monolayers. The mantle results can be compared with observations of water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and methanol ices in the sources W33A and Elias 16. Other than a slight underproduction of mantle CO, our results are in very good agreement with observations.

title: SwissADME: a free web tool to evaluate pharmacokinetics, drug-likeness and medicinal chemistry friendliness of small molecules
abstract: SwissADME is a freely accessible web-based tool designed to facilitate the early-stage evaluation of small molecules for drug discovery by predicting key pharmacokinetic properties, drug-likeness, and medicinal chemistry friendliness. Integrating a suite of robust and rapid computational models—including proprietary methods such as the BOILED-Egg, iLOGP, and Bioavailability Radar—SwissADME enables users to assess absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion (ADME), physicochemical parameters, and structural alerts relevant to drug development. The platform offers a user-friendly interface that accommodates both cheminformatics specialists and non-experts, supporting input via SMILES strings or molecular sketches and delivering intuitive, molecule-specific output panels with interactive visualizations. By providing consensus predictions from multiple algorithms and facilitating seamless integration with other SwissDrugDesign tools, SwissADME streamlines the prioritization of compounds with optimal pharmacokinetic profiles and synthetic accessibility, thereby accelerating the identification of promising drug candidates in silico.

title: Cu-free click cycloaddition reactions in chemical biology.
abstract: Copper-free click cycloaddition reactions have emerged as powerful tools in chemical biology, enabling highly selective and biocompatible covalent labeling of biomolecules within complex biological environments, including living systems. This review traces the evolution of bioorthogonal chemistry, focusing on the development and mechanistic underpinnings of copper-free cycloaddition strategies designed to overcome the limitations posed by cellular environments, such as cytotoxicity, competing nucleophiles, and redox sensitivity. Key advances discussed include the design of strained cyclooctynes and their derivatives for rapid azide-alkyne cycloadditions, as well as alternative approaches utilizing oxanorbornadienes and tetrazine-based inverse-electron-demand Diels–Alder reactions. The review highlights how these innovations have expanded the toolkit for probing dynamic biological processes with minimal perturbation, facilitating applications ranging from biomolecular imaging to targeted therapeutics. The continued refinement of copper-free click reagents promises to further enhance the precision and versatility of chemical biology research.

title: Why we need to focus on developing ethical, responsible, and trustworthy artificial intelligence approaches for environmental science
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) into environmental science offers significant opportunities for improved prediction and decision-making but also raises critical concerns about ethical, responsible, and trustworthy deployment. This position paper argues that environmental sciences are not immune to the unintended societal consequences observed in other domains where AI has perpetuated bias and injustice. Through specific examples, the authors illustrate how issues such as biased training data, lack of geo-diversity, inappropriate model use, and insufficient transparency can undermine the reliability and fairness of AI applications in weather, climate, and broader environmental contexts. The paper emphasizes the need for the environmental science community to proactively address these challenges by adopting ethical frameworks, ensuring diverse and representative data, and fostering inclusive practices. By learning from past mistakes in other fields and prioritizing environmental justice, AI can become a powerful tool for advancing sustainability and equity. The discussion aims to stimulate further research and community engagement to guide the responsible development and application of AI across environmental sciences.

title: Magnetars: the physics behind observations. A review
abstract: Magnetars are neutron stars characterized by ultra-strong magnetic fields, whose unique observational properties—such as persistent and variable X-ray emission, long spin periods, rapid spin-down rates, and diverse bursting activity—are best explained within the magnetar model, where magnetic field decay and dissipation power their emission. This review synthesizes recent advances in both observational and theoretical studies of magnetars, including the discovery of transient and low-field sources, developments in modeling persistent and burst emissions, and insights from neutron star asteroseismology. The review also discusses the implications of magnetic field evolution for magnetar activity and its connections to other isolated neutron star populations. By integrating multiwavelength observations with state-of-the-art theoretical frameworks, this work highlights how magnetars serve as natural laboratories for testing physical theories under extreme conditions, thereby advancing our understanding of fundamental physics in strong magnetic fields.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: New directions in environmental justice studies: examining the state and violence
abstract: The field of environmental justice studies has blossomed into a multidisciplinary body of scholarship in the last few decades with contributions across the social sciences, humanities, law, and the sciences. Our framing of environmental justice scholarship centers on the necessity of examining the role of state and institutional violence in producing environmental injustice through interlocking systems of racial capitalism, settler colonialism, and enslavement. We link themes of violence and the role of the state in the expansion of environmental justice studies to the major topics of land and resource conflicts, prisons and incarceration, and emotions. We draw on this scholarship to explore how theories and politics of environmental justice are inflected by the constraints and leverage points within racial capitalism, settler colonialism, and the afterlives of enslavement. This paper offers an assessment of theoretical advances, and charts a course for next possible stages of the literature’s development and EJ activism.

title: Density of states prediction for materials discovery via contrastive learning from probabilistic embeddings
abstract: Machine learning for materials discovery has largely focused on predicting an individual scalar rather than multiple related properties, where spectral properties are an important example. Fundamental spectral properties include the phonon density of states (phDOS) and the electronic density of states (eDOS), which individually or collectively are the origins of a breadth of materials observables and functions. Building upon the success of graph attention networks for encoding crystalline materials, we introduce a probabilistic embedding generator specifically tailored to the prediction of spectral properties. Coupled with supervised contrastive learning, our materials-to-spectrum (Mat2Spec) model outperforms state-of-the-art methods for predicting ab initio phDOS and eDOS for crystalline materials. We demonstrate Mat2Spec’s ability to identify eDOS gaps below the Fermi energy, validating predictions with ab initio calculations and thereby discovering candidate thermoelectrics and transparent conductors. Mat2Spec is an exemplar framework for predicting spectral properties of materials via strategically incorporated machine learning techniques. Electrons and phonons give rise to important properties of materials. The machine learning framework Mat2Spec vastly accelerates their computational characterization, enabling discovery of materials for thermoelectrics and solar energy technologies.

title: Challenges in cardiac tissue engineering.
abstract: Cardiac tissue engineering holds significant promise for regenerating damaged myocardium and developing advanced models for cardiac research, yet faces substantial scientific and translational challenges. Key requirements include the identification of suitable human cell sources, recreation of the complex cardiac tissue matrix, achievement of electromechanical coupling, establishment of robust contractile function, and development of functional vascularization. The selection of autologous or immunotolerant, phenotypically stable cardiac cell populations is critical, with ongoing exploration of adult stem cells, embryonic stem cells, and induced pluripotent stem cells. Additional obstacles involve engineering clinically relevant tissue size with adequate vascular supply, ensuring synchronous electrical and mechanical integration with host myocardium, and achieving reproducible manufacturing standards. Regulatory and policy considerations further complicate clinical translation. Addressing these multifaceted challenges is essential for realizing the therapeutic potential of engineered cardiac tissues to prevent or reverse heart failure.

title: The art of co-production of knowledge in environmental sciences and management: lessons from international practice
abstract: This review paper addresses the challenging question of “how to” design and implement co-production of knowledge in climate science and other environmental and agricultural sciences. Based on a grounded theory review of nine (9) published case studies of transdisciplinary and collaborative research projects, the paper offers a set of common themes regarding specific components and processes for the design, implementation, and achievement of co-production of knowledge work, which represent the “Modus Operandi” of knowledge co-production. The analysis focuses on practical methodological guidance based on lessons from how different research teams have approached the challenges of complex collaborative research. We begin by identifying broad factors or actions that inhibit or facilitate the process, then highlight specific practices associated with co-production of knowledge and necessary competencies for undertaking co-production. We provide insights on issues such as the integration of social and professional cultures, gender and social equity, and power dynamics, and illustrate the different ways in which researchers have addressed these issues. By exploring the specific practices involved in knowledge co-production, this paper provides guidance to researchers on how to navigate different possibilities of the process of conducting transdisciplinary and co-production of knowledge research projects that best fit their research context, stakeholder needs, and research team capacities.

title: Bayesian reasoning and machine learning
abstract: This work provides a comprehensive introduction to Bayesian reasoning and its central role in modern machine learning, emphasizing probabilistic approaches for modeling, inference, and data-driven decision making. Addressing the challenges posed by the rapid growth of complex, high-dimensional data across scientific and commercial domains, the text unifies foundational concepts through the framework of graphical models, which combine graph theory and probability to facilitate efficient representation and computation. Designed for readers with modest mathematical backgrounds, the book prioritizes conceptual understanding supported by worked examples, practical exercises, and an accompanying MATLAB toolbox that bridges theory and implementation. The material is structured to support a range of courses, from introductory graphical models to advanced topics in approximate inference and dynamical systems, enabling students from diverse fields to develop the skills necessary to construct novel algorithms and engage with contemporary research in probabilistic machine learning.

title: Molecular Biology of the Cell
abstract: Molecular Biology of the Cell, 2nd edition, provides a comprehensive and lucid overview of contemporary cell and molecular biology, reflecting the rapid advancements in the field since its first edition. The text is organized into three main sections covering cellular biochemistry, molecular organization, and the transition from single cells to multicellular organisms, with clear explanations and extensively revised illustrations. Topics include genetic mechanisms, membrane and cytoplasmic organization, cell signaling, growth control, cell adhesion, development, immune and nervous systems, plant cell organization, and cancer biology. The book is notable for its clarity, up-to-date content with references through late 1988, and practical approach that integrates clinical relevance. It serves as an essential resource for pathologists and biologists seeking to remain current with modern cellular biology and is highly recommended for both trainees and established professionals.

title: Hydrogels for Regenerative Medicine
abstract: Regenerative medicine requires materials that are biodegradable, biocompatible, struc‐ turally and chemically stable, and that can mimic the properties of the native extracellular matrix (ECM). Hydrogels are hydrophilic three-dimensional networks that have long re‐ ceived attention in the field of regenerative medicine due to their unique properties. Hy‐ drogels have a potential to be the future of regenerative medicine due to their desirable mechanical and chemical properties, ease of their synthesis, and their multiple applicabil‐ ity as drug delivery vehicles, scaffolds, and constructs for cell culture. In this chapter, we have described hydrogels in terms of their cross-linking and then discussed the most re‐ cent developments in the use of hydrogels for peripheral nerve regeneration, tooth regen‐ eration, and 3D bioprinting.

title: Malignant astrocytic glioma: genetics, biology, and paths to treatment.
abstract: Malignant astrocytic gliomas, particularly glioblastoma (GBM), represent the most common and aggressive primary brain tumors, characterized by rapid progression, extensive invasion, resistance to conventional and targeted therapies, and poor prognosis. Recent advances in stem cell biology, genomics, and molecular modeling have significantly enhanced our understanding of the genetic and biological mechanisms underlying GBM pathogenesis, revealing substantial intratumoral heterogeneity and distinct molecular subtypes with unique genetic alterations. Classification of gliomas now integrates histopathological, immunohistochemical, and molecular features, with markers such as GFAP, OLIG2, and emerging stem cell-associated proteins aiding in diagnosis and prognostication. The identification of cancer stem cell populations and key genetic lesions driving hallmark features of malignancy has informed the development of refined model systems and novel therapeutic strategies targeting critical pathways. Although challenges remain in overcoming therapeutic resistance and disease recurrence, these scientific advances provide a foundation for more precise classification, improved understanding of disease origins, and the rational design of targeted treatments that hold promise for meaningful clinical benefit in this otherwise intractable disease.

title: A Holistic Approach to Marine Eco-Systems Biology
abstract: The structure, robustness, and dynamics of ocean plankton ecosystems remain poorly understood due to sampling, analysis, and computational limitations. The Tara Oceans consortium organizes expeditions to help fill this gap at the global level.

title: Nickel-catalyzed cross-couplings involving carbon-oxygen bonds.
abstract: Nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions involving carbon-oxygen bonds have emerged as powerful tools for constructing complex molecular architectures, offering an attractive alternative to traditional palladium-catalyzed processes that typically rely on aryl halides. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the historical development, mechanistic insights, and recent advances in nickel-catalyzed homocoupling, cross-coupling, and functionalization of C–O bonds, with a particular focus on phenol- and enol-derived electrophiles such as sulfonates, sulfates, esters, and carbamates. The advantages of using nickel catalysts include lower cost, greater abundance, and unique reactivity that enables the activation of less reactive C–O bonds under milder conditions and with broader substrate scope. The review highlights the synthetic value of phenol-derived electrophiles due to their natural abundance and functional group compatibility, discusses strategies for overcoming the inherent strength of C–O bonds, and compares nickel catalysis to other transition metal systems. By organizing the literature according to electrophile class and coupling type, this work underscores the versatility and practical significance of nickel catalysis in sustainable organic synthesis and sets the stage for future developments in C–O bond activation chemistry.

title: Discovery of a Weyl fermion state with Fermi arcs in niobium arsenide
abstract: Weyl semimetals represent a novel class of topological quantum materials, distinguished by the presence of Weyl fermions as low-energy quasiparticle excitations and unique surface states known as Fermi arcs. Here, we report the experimental discovery of a Weyl semimetal state in niobium arsenide (NbAs) through comprehensive angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) studies utilizing both soft X-ray and ultraviolet photons. Our measurements reveal the existence of bulk Weyl cones and nodes, as well as surface Fermi arc states that connect the projected Weyl nodes, in excellent agreement with theoretical predictions and first-principles calculations. The crystal structure of NbAs, lacking inversion symmetry, is shown to be essential for realizing the Weyl semimetal phase. The observation of these topological features establishes NbAs as a robust platform for investigating exotic quantum phenomena associated with Weyl fermions and Fermi arcs, bridging concepts between high-energy and condensed matter physics, and opening new avenues for research into topological quantum materials.

title: INNOVATIVE APPROACHES IN COACH EDUCATION PEDAGOGY
abstract: This paper examines the limitations of traditional, didactic coach education programs and explores innovative pedagogical approaches designed to better address the complex realities of coaching practice. Drawing on recent research and practical experiences, the authors discuss problem-based learning, action research, and ethno-drama as methods that move beyond competency-based frameworks to foster critical thinking and holistic understanding among student coaches. The study highlights the pivotal role of coach educators in facilitating these learner-centered approaches and emphasizes the increased responsibility required to support meaningful student engagement and reflection. Findings suggest that such pedagogies enhance students’ appreciation for the interdisciplinary and dynamic nature of coaching, promote transferable knowledge, and encourage critical reflection on practice. The paper concludes by proposing future research directions focused on the training and support needs of coach educators in implementing innovative pedagogical strategies within coach education.

title: Exposure Science: A View of the Past and Milestones for the Future
abstract: The study of human exposure to environmental toxicants has evolved as a scientific field over the past 30 years. Objectives This review provides a historical perspective on the growth of exposure science as a field, with some emphasis on the results from initial observational studies in obtaining information needed for generating hypotheses on significant human contact with environmental agents, testing the performance of models, and reducing exposures to protect public health. Discussion Advances in activity pattern and behavioral research that established a suite of variables needed to accurately define contact and factors that influence contact are also discussed. The identification and characterization of these factors have played a pivotal role in the growth of the field and in developing exposure reduction strategies. Answers to two key questions on the relevance and fundamental value of exposure science to the fields of environmental health and risk management are presented as a path forward: a) What does one do with such exposure information? b) What roles does exposure science play in situations beyond observational analyses and interpretation? Conclusions The discussion identifies the need for more focused use of observational studies of exposure for epidemiologic analyses. Further, the introduction and use of new tools and approaches for hypothesis testing that can improve the use of exposure science in prevention research for risk management is needed to affect the source-to-effect continuum. A major restructuring of the field is not required to achieve innovation. However, additional resources for training and education are required to ensure that the potential for exposure science to play a central role in reducing and preventing excess risk within environmental/occupational health is achieved.

title: Multivariate Techniques for Specifying Tree-Growth and Climate Relationships and for Reconstructing Anomalies in Paleoclimate
abstract: This study applies advanced multivariate statistical techniques to analyze the complex relationships between tree-ring growth and climatic variables across western North America, enabling the reconstruction of paleoclimatic anomalies. By developing response functions from extensive, precisely dated tree-ring chronologies, the research objectively quantifies the climatic information embedded in tree growth records from diverse sites and species. Transfer functions calibrated with regional climate data allow for the estimation of past anomalous climate variations, including atmospheric circulation patterns, extending reconstructions back to A.D. 1700 where instrumental records are lacking. The findings demonstrate that multivariate approaches can effectively disentangle the influences of multiple environmental factors on tree growth, thereby enhancing the use of dendrochronological data for understanding long-term climate variability and improving paleoclimate reconstructions.

title: Sisvar: a computer statistical analysis system
abstract: Sisvar is a free, user-friendly statistical analysis software developed to address the specific needs of Brazilian researchers and educators, particularly in experimental statistics. Initially created in Pascal and later updated for Windows, Sisvar offers robust modules for analysis of variance (ANOVA), multiple comparisons, regression, and hypothesis testing, with a focus on balanced data and fixed Gauss-Markov linear models. Its interactive interface and detailed output have contributed to its widespread adoption in academic and research institutions across Brazil. Key advantages include the ability to efficiently slice interaction effects in linear models and perform advanced procedures such as the Scott-Knott test, which are not available in most competing software. While Sisvar is limited to balanced designs and fixed effects, its reliability, accessibility, and tailored features make it a valuable tool for statistical analysis in the Brazilian scientific community. Ongoing development aims to further expand its capabilities with a new Java-based version.

title: A Critical Look at the Use of SEM in International Business Research
abstract: This paper critically examines the application of structural equation modeling (SEM) in international business research, focusing on the relative use and justification of covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM) and partial least squares SEM (PLS-SEM). Through a systematic review of six leading international business and marketing journals from 1990 to 2013, the study finds that CB-SEM overwhelmingly dominates, with PLS-SEM underutilized despite its advantages for exploratory and predictive research in dynamic and complex environments. The analysis reveals that researchers often select PLS-SEM primarily due to data or sampling constraints rather than leveraging its methodological strengths for theory development. The paper identifies a lack of adherence to best practices in PLS-SEM application and highlights missed opportunities for advancing theory building in the field. By offering practical guidelines and recommendations, this study contributes to improving methodological rigor and encourages more informed choices between SEM approaches to better align with research objectives in international business and marketing.

title: Scientific collaboration networks. II. Shortest paths, weighted networks, and centrality.
abstract: This paper presents a quantitative analysis of scientific collaboration networks constructed from large-scale bibliographic databases in physics, biomedical research, and computer science. By representing scientists as nodes and coauthorships as links, we examine statistical properties such as the distribution of collaborators, shortest paths between scientists, and centrality measures including closeness and betweenness. Recognizing that simple unweighted networks do not capture the strength of collaborative ties, we introduce a weighted approach based on the number of coauthored papers and shared collaborators. Our results reveal that scientific collaboration networks are highly connected, with short average path lengths and significant variation in individual centrality. We discuss how these findings inform the identification of well-connected scientists and provide insights into the structure and dynamics of professional scientific communities.
venue: Physical review. E, Statistical, nonlinear, and soft matter physics

title: Explaining Underrepresentation: A Theory of Precluded Interest
abstract: What processes best explain women’s underrepresentation in science, math, and engineering fields in the U.S.? Do they also explain men’s underrepresentation in the humanities? Two survey studies across two U.S. West Coast universities (N = 62; N = 614) addressed these questions in the context of two fields: one male-dominated (computer science) and the other female-dominated (English). Among a set of social predictors—including perceived similarity to the people in the field, social identity threats, and expectations of success—the best mediator of women’s lower interest in computer science and men’s lower interest in English was perceived similarity. Thus, changing students’ social perceptions of how they relate to those in the field may help to diversify academic fields.

title: The Physics of Musical Instruments
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive exploration of the physical principles underlying the operation and sound production of Western musical instruments. Emphasizing a quantitative approach, it systematically examines vibrating systems, including strings, bars, membranes, plates, and shells, and analyzes how their mechanical properties and modes of vibration contribute to musical tone and timbre. The authors integrate historical context and cultural considerations with detailed mathematical and physical explanations, highlighting the interplay between tradition, craftsmanship, and acoustical science. By synthesizing decades of research and incorporating recent advances in the field, the text serves as both an authoritative reference for researchers and an accessible resource for readers with a background in physics who seek to understand the scientific foundations of musical instrument design and performance.

title: Scaffolds based bone tissue engineering: the role of chitosan.
abstract: As the demand for effective bone regeneration therapies rises with an aging population, limitations of current clinical approaches such as autologous and allogeneic bone grafts have driven the development of bone tissue engineering strategies. This review provides a comprehensive overview of scaffold-based bone tissue engineering, emphasizing the critical role of chitosan as a biomaterial. Chitosan’s structural similarity to extracellular matrix, biocompatibility, biodegradability, and ability to support cellular interactions make it an attractive candidate for scaffold fabrication. The article discusses key concepts in bone biology, requirements for scaffold design, and the integration of osteogenic cells with three-dimensional scaffolds to promote bone regeneration. An extensive literature survey highlights various methods for preparing chitosan-based scaffolds, their in vitro biological performance, and their potential to facilitate in vivo bone repair. The review also examines current in vitro and in vivo models used to evaluate the functionality and regenerative capacity of tissue-engineered constructs. Overall, chitosan-based scaffolds demonstrate significant promise as substrates for supporting osteogenic differentiation and advancing the field of bone tissue engineering.

title: Longevity, senescence, and the genome
abstract: This comprehensive volume by Caleb E. Finch offers an in-depth exploration of the biological and genetic mechanisms underlying longevity and senescence across a wide range of plant and animal species. Integrating advances in molecular genetics with comparative biology, the book examines fundamental questions regarding the measurement, onset, and variability of senescence, as well as the influence of genes at multiple organizational levels. Finch critically evaluates the roles of selective versus random changes in gene expression, the impact of developmental and environmental factors, and the universality of age-related degeneration. The analysis highlights that genetic mechanisms affecting lifespan and certain aspects of senescence are identifiable in specific organisms, suggesting that senescence may be modifiable through genetic interventions. While evolutionary perspectives and broad taxonomic coverage occasionally overshadow human-specific pathology, the work stands as a masterful synthesis that provides essential insights for researchers and students in the rapidly expanding field of aging biology.

title: Environmental Policy Attitudes: Issues, Geographical Scale, and Political Trust
abstract: This study investigates how public attitudes toward environmental policy vary by issue type, geographical scale, and political trust. Using data from the 2007 Cooperative Congressional Election Study, we analyze support for government action across pollution and resource preservation issues at local, national, and global levels. Our findings reveal that Americans express stronger support for government intervention on pollution issues, particularly at local and national scales, than for resource preservation or global environmental challenges. Political ideology and party affiliation consistently predict environmental policy preferences, with Republicans and conservatives less supportive of increased government action regardless of their trust in government. Higher trust in government is associated with greater support for addressing pollution and global issues. These results highlight the importance of distinguishing between specific environmental issues and scales when assessing public opinion and underscore the persistent influence of political orientation on environmental policy attitudes.

title: Balancing Technology, Pedagogy and the New Normal: Post-pandemic Challenges for Higher Education
abstract: The Covid-19 pandemic has presented an opportunity for rethinking assumptions about education in general and higher education in particular. In the light of the general crisis the pandemic caused, especially when it comes to the so-called emergency remote teaching (ERT), educators from all grades and contexts experienced the necessity of rethinking their roles, the ways of supporting the students’ learning tasks and the image of students as self-organising learners, active citizens and autonomous social agents. In our first Postdigital Science and Education paper, we sought to distil and share some expert advice for campus-based university teachers to adapt to online teaching and learning. In this sequel paper, we ask ourselves: Now that campus-based university teachers have experienced the unplanned and forced version of Online Learning and Teaching (OLT), how can this experience help bridge the gap between online and in-person teaching in the following years? The four experts, also co-authors of this paper, interviewed aligning towards an emphasis on pedagogisation rather than digitalisation of higher education, with strategic decision-making being in the heart of post-pandemic practices. Our literature review of papers published in the last year and analysis of the expert answers reveal that the ‘forced’ experience of teaching with digital technologies as part of ERT can gradually give place to a harmonious integration of physical and digital tools and methods for the sake of more active, flexible and meaningful learning.

title: Behavioral economics: reunifying psychology and economics.
abstract: 'Behavioral economics' improves the realism of the psychological assumptions underlying economic theory, promising to reunify psychology and economics in the process. Reunification should lead to better predictions about economic behavior and better policy prescriptions.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Information Production and Capital Allocation: Decentralized vs. Hierarchical Firms
abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework to compare decentralized and hierarchical organizational structures in their effectiveness at producing information and allocating capital among investment projects. The analysis highlights that decentralized firms, characterized by single managers with local authority, are better suited for environments where project evaluation relies on “soft” information—information that is difficult to verify or transmit credibly within a hierarchy. In such settings, decentralization enhances research incentives and leads to more efficient capital allocation within units, though it may limit flexibility in reallocating resources across units. Conversely, hierarchical firms with multiple management layers have a comparative advantage when information can be “hardened” and easily communicated up the chain, enabling both efficient cross-unit capital reallocation and stronger research incentives through advocacy for resources. The model also predicts that, when soft information predominates but firm size must remain large, flatter organizational structures are preferable. As an application, the paper examines bank consolidation and its impact on small-business lending, arguing that the observed decline in such lending following mergers is consistent with the theory: large hierarchical banks are less effective at utilizing soft information critical for small-business credit decisions. The findings provide insight into the trade-offs between organizational design, information production, and capital allocation efficiency.

title: The art of co-production of knowledge in environmental sciences and management: lessons from international practice
abstract: This paper examines the practical implementation of knowledge co-production in environmental sciences and management by analyzing nine international case studies using a grounded theory literature review approach. The study identifies key components, processes, and competencies that facilitate or hinder effective co-production, emphasizing the importance of integrating diverse social and professional cultures, addressing gender and social equity, and navigating power dynamics. Findings highlight that successful co-production requires deliberate project design, inclusive stakeholder engagement throughout all research stages, and adaptive strategies to overcome challenges such as time constraints, mismatched expectations, and insufficient organizational support. The paper offers methodological guidance for researchers seeking to enhance the relevance and usability of scientific knowledge in environmental decision-making, contributing to a more nuanced understanding of transdisciplinary collaboration and providing actionable lessons for future projects in climate science and environmental management.

title: Employability attributes and personality preferences of postgraduate business management students
abstract: Orientation: The demand for sustained employability and a proactive career agency has led to a renewed interest in the dispositional and psychological attributes of students and employees – like their employability attributes and personality preferences – because these relate to the proactive management of their career development in a changing employment world. Research purpose: The purpose of the study was to determine the relationship between employees’ employability attributes (as the Employability Attributes Scale measures them) and their personality preferences (as the Myers-Briggs Type indicator, Form M, measures them). Motivation for the study: There seems to be a paucity of information about how employees’ personality preferences relate to their employability attributes in South Africa’s multicultural organisational context. Research design, approach and method: The authors conducted a quantitative survey. It involved a non-probability sample of 304 early career adults enrolled for an Honour’s degree in business management in an open distance learning higher education institution. They used correlational statistics and multiple regression analyses to analyse the data. Main findings: The authors observed a number of significant relationships between the participants’ personality preferences and their employability attributes. Practical/managerial implications: Career counsellors and human resource practitioners need to recognise how employees’ personality preferences influence their employability attributes in the management of their career development and employability. Contribution/value add: The findings add to the existing career literature on the career metacompetencies that influence employees’ employability. They also provide valuable information that organisations can use for career development support and counselling practices in the contemporary world of work.

title: A review of imaging techniques for systems biology
abstract: This paper presents a review of imaging techniques and of their utility in system biology. During the last decade systems biology has matured into a distinct field and imaging has been increasingly used to enable the interplay of experimental and theoretical biology. In this review, we describe and compare the roles of microscopy, ultrasound, CT (Computed Tomography), MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging), PET (Positron Emission Tomography), and molecular probes such as quantum dots and nanoshells in systems biology. As a unified application area among these different imaging techniques, examples in cancer targeting are highlighted.

title: European Respiratory Society
abstract: The mission of the European Respiratory Society (ERS) is to advance respiratory medicine by stimulating and coordinating the actions of its members, in order to achieve the highest possible medical, paramedical and social standards in the treatment of respiratory disease in Europe. The society’s 2005 congress had approximately 16 000 registered participants from 100 countries and with over 110 scientific and clinical sessions, the congress was Europe’s largest annual scientific gathering in respiratory medicine.

title: The physics of fast radio bursts
abstract: In 2007, a very bright radio pulse was identified in the archival data of the Parkes Telescope in Australia, marking the beginning of a new research branch in astrophysics. In 2013, this kind of millisecond bursts with extremely high brightness temperature takes a unified name, fast radio burst (FRB). Over the first few years, FRBs seemed very mysterious because the sample of known events was limited. With the improvement of instruments over the last five years, hundreds of new FRBs have been discovered. The field is now undergoing a revolution and understanding of FRB has rapidly increased as new observational data increasingly accumulate. In this review, we will summarize the basic physics of FRBs and discuss the current research progress in this area. We have tried to cover a wide range of FRB topics, including the observational property, propagation effect, population study, radiation mechanism, source model, and application in cosmology. A framework based on the latest observational facts is now under construction. In the near future, this exciting field is expected to make significant breakthroughs.
venue: Science China Physics Mechanics and Astronomy

title: Formulas and Theorems for the Special Functions of Mathematical Physics
abstract: This comprehensive reference presents an extensive compilation of formulas and theorems for the special functions central to mathematical physics, systematically covering the gamma function, hypergeometric and Bessel functions, Legendre functions, orthogonal polynomials, Kummer and Whittaker functions, parabolic cylinder functions, incomplete gamma functions, elliptic integrals and functions, as well as integral transforms and coordinate transformations. Each chapter provides definitions, key properties, recurrence relations, differential equations, integral representations, asymptotic expansions, and interrelations among functions, with formulas organized by increasing complexity to facilitate ease of use. The work incorporates updated material and expanded references to books and monographs, making it an indispensable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking precise results and methodologies in the theory and application of special functions.

title: Factors related to the choice of family medicine: a reassessment and literature review.
abstract: This literature review reassesses factors influencing medical students’ choice of family medicine as a specialty by analyzing 36 articles published since 1993. The findings indicate that a rural background and lower parental socioeconomic status are positively associated with selecting family medicine, while higher parental socioeconomic status has a negative association. Early career intentions toward primary care, valuing the importance of primary care, lower income expectations, and lack of interest in research careers also predict a greater likelihood of choosing family medicine. Publicly owned medical schools and required family medicine clinical experiences increase the number of students entering the field, and comprehensive primary care programs are effective in boosting interest. Faculty role models can exert both positive and negative influences. Students who do not choose family medicine often cite concerns about prestige, income, and the broad knowledge base required. Those intending to practice in rural or underserved areas are more likely to select family medicine. The review concludes that multiple, consistent factors—including student background, values, school characteristics, and educational experiences—shape specialty choice, highlighting areas for targeted interventions to address declining interest in family medicine.
venue: The Journal of the American Board of Family Practice

title: Engineering BioBrick vectors from BioBrick parts
abstract: Synthetic biology seeks to streamline the engineering of biological systems through standardized biological parts, with the BioBrick standard emerging as a widely adopted framework for genetic part assembly. However, plasmid vectors used to propagate BioBrick parts have remained ad hoc and non-standardized, limiting modularity and reuse. In this work, we present a methodology for engineering BioBrick vectors from BioBrick parts by designing a new set of standardized vector components and introducing a BioBrick base vector that facilitates rapid construction of diverse vectors. Using this approach, we assembled seven new BioBrick vectors and demonstrated their effectiveness in propagating and assembling BioBrick standard biological parts. Our process extends the principles of standardization and part reuse to vector design, enabling the synthetic biology community to efficiently generate, share, and improve an expanded repertoire of BioBrick-compatible vectors. This advancement supports more robust, scalable, and collaborative genetic engineering efforts.

title: Modeling meets science and technology: an introduction to a special issue on negative emissions
abstract: This article introduces the Climatic Change special issue dedicated to negative emissions technologies, also known as carbon dioxide removal (CDR) from the atmosphere. CDR is the only class of mitigation options able to reduce the carbon stock in the atmosphere significantly. In this special issue CDR is explored from the perspectives of integrated assessment, technology optimization, environmental science, and political science.

title: Chemistry and biology of multicomponent reactions.
abstract: Multicomponent reactions (MCRs) are one-pot reactions employing more than two starting materials, for example, 3, 4, ..., 7, where most of the atoms of the starting materials are incorporated in the final product. (1) Several descriptive tags are regularly attached to MCRs (Figure 1): they are atom economic, for example, the majority if not all of the atoms of the starting materials are incorporated in the product; they are efficient, for example, they efficiently yield the product since the product is formed in one-step instead of multiple sequential steps; they are convergent, for example, several starting materials combine in one reaction to form the product; they exhibit a very high bond-forming-index (BFI), for example, several non-hydrogen atom bonds are formed in one synthetic transformation. (2) Therefore MCRs are often a useful alternative to sequential multistep synthesis.

title: Longevity, senescence, and the genome
abstract: Featuring extensive references, updated for this paperback edition, 'Longevity, Senescence, and the Genome' constitutes a contribution to biomedicine and the evolutionary biology of ageing. To enhance gerontology's focus on human age-related dysfunctions, Caleb E. Finch provides a comparative review of all the phyla of organisms, broadening gerontology to intersect with behavioral, developmental, evolutionary, and molecular biology. By comparing species that have different developmental and life spans, Finch proposes a typology of senescence from rapid to gradual to negligible, and he provides the first multiphyletic calculations of mortality rate constants.

title: Modularity and community structure in networks.
abstract: Many networks of interest in the sciences, including social networks, computer networks, and metabolic and regulatory networks, are found to divide naturally into communities or modules. The problem of detecting and characterizing this community structure is one of the outstanding issues in the study of networked systems. One highly effective approach is the optimization of the quality function known as 'modularity' over the possible divisions of a network. Here I show that the modularity can be expressed in terms of the eigenvectors of a characteristic matrix for the network, which I call the modularity matrix, and that this expression leads to a spectral algorithm for community detection that returns results of demonstrably higher quality than competing methods in shorter running times. I illustrate the method with applications to several published network data sets.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Enablers and Inhibitors of Business-IT Alignment
abstract: This paper provides insight into identifying areas that help or hinder business-IT alignment. Alignment focuses on the activities that management performs to achieve cohesive goals across the organization. The aim of this paper is to determine the most important enablers and inhibitors to alignment. The paper presents and analyzes the results of a multi-year study of strategic alignment. Data were obtained from business and information technology executives from over 500 firms representing 15 industries who attended classes addressing alignment at IBM’s Advanced Business Institute. The executives were asked to describe those activities that assist in achieving alignment and those which seem to hinder it. These enablers and inhibitors to alignment were then analyzed with respect to industry, to time, and executive position. The results indicate that certain activities can assist in the achievement of this state of alignment while others are clearly barriers. Achieving alignment is evolutionary and dynamic.
