venue: Communications of the Association for Information Systems

title: Annual Review Of Nuclear And Particle Science
abstract: The contents of this review reflect some of the shifts of emphasis that are occurring among the fields of astrophysics, nuclear physics, and elementary particle physics. Particle physics has made great advances in the unification of the fundamental forces of nature. Discussions and planning for a next big step in accelerator-colliders are presented. The technology of superconducting magnet systems as well as the fundamental physical principles of particle accelerators are discussed. Also presented are: high-resolution electronic particle detectors; nuclear physics changes such as pion interactions within nuclei; discussion of future relativistic heavy-ion colliders; the role of rotational degrees of freedom in heavy-ion collisions at low and moderate energies; hyperon beta decays; and the analysis of materials via nuclear reaction techniques. Neutrinos, their interactions and possible masses, have an important bearing on cosmology and the matter density of the universe in addition to their inherent interest in the microscopic world and this is also examined.

title: Personalized Medicine and the Practice of Medicine in the 21st Century
abstract: Personalized medicine, driven by advances in genomics and pharmacogenomics, is transforming the practice of medicine in the 21st century by enabling more precise, individualized therapeutic strategies. This review examines the historical development and current applications of personalized medicine, highlighting how genetic variability among individuals influences drug response and disease progression. Key examples such as HER-2/neu testing for trastuzumab in breast cancer, genotyping for warfarin dosing, and CYP450 enzyme testing illustrate the clinical integration of pharmacogenomic information. The article discusses the impact of these innovations on drug development, regulatory practices, and patient care, while also addressing ongoing challenges related to implementation, cost, and clinical utility. Ultimately, personalized medicine holds promise for improving treatment efficacy, reducing adverse drug reactions, and optimizing healthcare delivery, but its widespread adoption will require overcoming scientific, logistical, and ethical barriers.

title: Advancing environmental exposure assessment science to benefit society
abstract: Growing evidence links air pollution exposure to significant adverse health outcomes, particularly among disadvantaged populations who often experience higher pollutant levels and greater susceptibility. This review examines recent advances in environmental exposure assessment, highlighting the shift from coarse, community-level monitoring to granular, individual-level measurements that capture personal exposures and contextual factors. These technological developments have enabled more targeted policy interventions, such as urban traffic restrictions and cleaner fuel mandates, which are increasingly informed by detailed exposure data. The paper also presents an illustrative study in New York City that integrates individual exposure monitoring with economic, behavioral, biological, familial, and environmental variables to better understand health impacts and inform policy. While challenges remain in translating personal exposure data into regulatory action, the integration of advanced assessment methods with policy initiatives holds promise for reducing health disparities and improving public health outcomes on both local and global scales.

title: New frontiers for the materials genome initiative
abstract: The Materials Genome Initiative (MGI) has transformed materials discovery by integrating theory, computation, and experiment to accelerate the development and deployment of new materials. This review summarizes insights from a 2017 National Science Foundation workshop that assessed MGI’s achievements and identified emerging challenges and opportunities. Key advances enabled by MGI include high-throughput screening, data-driven modeling, and collaborative infrastructure that have led to breakthroughs in areas such as polymeric self-assembly, polar metals, and organic light-emitting diodes. The workshop highlighted six priority domains—health and consumer applications, information technologies, new functional materials, efficient separation processes, energy and catalysis, and multicomponent materials with additive manufacturing—as critical for future progress. The article discusses technical successes, infrastructural needs, and cultural shifts required to fully realize MGI’s vision, emphasizing the importance of open data sharing, interdisciplinary collaboration, and new incentive structures. By outlining unifying themes and aspirational perspectives, this review charts a course for advancing the MGI paradigm to address societal needs through accelerated materials innovation.

title: Floquet Engineering of Quantum Materials
abstract: Floquet engineering leverages periodic driving fields to dynamically control and induce novel quantum states in materials, offering a powerful framework for manipulating electronic, magnetic, and topological properties on ultrafast timescales. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the theoretical foundations and recent advances in Floquet engineering applied to quantum materials, with emphasis on the Floquet theorem, effective Hamiltonians, and many-body methods. Key phenomena such as Floquet-induced topological states, Thouless pumping, high-frequency expansions, and laser-assisted hopping are discussed alongside their implications for ultrafast spintronics, nonlinear transport, and strongly correlated electron systems. The interplay between periodic driving and material-specific properties enables the realization of exotic phases—including Floquet Chern insulators and dynamically controlled Mott insulators—while also presenting challenges related to heating and thermalization. The review highlights both fundamental insights and potential applications in next-generation electronic devices, demonstrating how Floquet engineering serves as a versatile tool for exploring and harnessing emergent behaviors in quantum materials.
venue: Annual Review of Condensed Matter Physics

title: Consequences of Realism for Sociological Theory‐Building
abstract: This paper examines the implications of adopting a realist philosophy of science—specifically, causal realism—for sociological theory-building in response to the discipline’s current fragmentation and theoretical stagnation. Arguing that both positivism and epistemological relativism have led to degenerative effects on sociology by constraining methodological innovation and undermining explanatory ambitions, the author contends that a new meta-theoretical foundation is needed. Causal realism is proposed as an alternative that emphasizes the delineation and definition of sociology’s object of study, enabling the development of robust, explanatory theories grounded in a shared understanding of social reality. The paper outlines how this approach can provide a common platform for sociological inquiry, reinvigorate theoretical progress, and restore coherence to the discipline by moving beyond externally derived philosophies and focusing on sociology’s own epistemic needs.

title: The Economics Approach to Cities
abstract: This paper outlines the economic approach to understanding cities, emphasizing the centrality of spatial equilibrium among workers, firms, and builders. It explains how positive attributes in one location, such as higher wages or better amenities, are typically offset by negatives like higher housing costs or disamenities, resulting in a no-arbitrage condition across space. The analysis highlights the importance of agglomeration economies in explaining productivity differences that justify wage disparities between cities, and investigates how variations in construction costs and regulatory environments shape housing supply and prices. The paper also discusses empirical methods in urban economics, focusing on the search for exogenous variation to identify causal relationships. Finally, it argues that urban policy should prioritize improving individual welfare over place-based interventions, taking into account the mobility of people and firms and the incentives created by policy choices.

title: Discipline and Bounding: The History and Sociology of Science as Seen through the Externalism-Internalism Debate
abstract: From the beginning of the Second World War to the ending of the Cold War no problematic so deeply shaped the academic history and sociology of science than that inscribed in talk of 'internalism' and 'externalism'. Insofar as empirical work was deemed relevant to developing an overall appreciation of the nature of science, its dynamics and its relations with social and cultural environments, that relevance was locally achieved by gestures at opposed 'internalist' and 'externalist' theories, orientations, domains, and accompanying historiographic baggage. Students were initiated into the history and sociology of science by being told about these genres and the present state of play. Graduates' early orientation to their fields was achieved through affiliation with one or other genre and camp of practitioners. Reviews of the state of the history and sociology of science were seemingly obligated to use 'internalism' and 'externalism' as expository structures. Nowadays, however, historians of science commonly tell each other and their students that their discipline has transcended, outgrown or resolved those debates, and that it is a sign of the maturity of the field that references to the 'internal' and the 'external' have become less common or at least less unselfconscious. When uttered at all, the terms are likely to be surrounded by quotes, air-quotes or tones of voice. If in the 1960s the central problematic of the academic discipline known as the history of science was pointed to by reference to the 'internal' and the 'external', by the late 1980s such usages increasingly betrayed the amateur, the neophyte, the outsider, or the out of touch. Within a generation the discourse of 'internalism' and 'externalism' seems to have passed from the commonplace to the gauche. I want to suggest that this trajectory never transmitted the appropriate intermediate stages. I do not think that the theories indicated by 'externalism' and 'internalism' were ever properly defined or described. I do not think that the virtues of any defensible and coherent construals of these theories were ever properly considered and assessed. I do not think that talk of external and internal (hereafter eli) 'factors' was ever properly associated with the respective theories, nor that such talk was adequately defended in terms of relevant

title: PEtab—Interoperable specification of parameter estimation problems in systems biology
abstract: Parameter estimation is a critical task in systems biology, requiring the integration of experimental data with mathematical models to infer unknown parameters. However, the diversity of modeling tools and formats has led to challenges in reproducibility, interoperability, and transparency of parameter estimation workflows. Here, we present PEtab, a standardized and interoperable specification for parameter estimation problems in systems biology. PEtab defines a set of tabular and YAML-based formats to describe models, experimental conditions, measurements, observables, and parameter constraints in a tool-agnostic manner. By providing a clear and extensible structure, PEtab enables seamless exchange of parameter estimation problems between different software tools and facilitates reproducible research. We demonstrate the utility of PEtab through integration with multiple modeling environments and showcase its application to a range of published models. Our results highlight that PEtab fosters transparency, comparability, and reusability in parameter estimation tasks, thereby accelerating model-driven discovery in systems biology.

title: Lecture Notes in Economics and Mathematical Systems
abstract: This series reports on new developments in mathematical economics, economic theory, econometrics, operations research and mathematical systems. The series welcomes proposals for: 1. Research monographs 2. Lectures on a new field or presentations of a new angle in a classical field 3. Seminars on topics of current research 4. Reports of meetings provided they are of exceptional interest and devoted to a single topic. In the case of a research monograph, or of seminar notes, the timeliness of a manuscript may be more important than its form, which may be preliminary or tentative. Manuscripts should be no less than 150 and preferably no more than 500 pages in length. The series and the volumes published in it are indexed by Scopus and ISI (selected volumes).

title: Sampling in software engineering research: a critical review and guidelines
abstract: This paper critically examines the state of sampling practices in empirical software engineering research, revealing that representative and random sampling are infrequently employed and often misunderstood, leading to concerns about the generalizability of research findings. Through a comprehensive review of recent high-quality studies, the authors identify a widespread reliance on convenience and non-probability sampling strategies, with limited use of more sophisticated or probabilistic methods. The paper synthesizes existing knowledge into an accessible primer on sampling concepts and techniques tailored to software engineering, highlighting the importance of appropriate sampling for both positivist and interpretivist research paradigms. Extensive guidelines are proposed to improve the design, reporting, and evaluation of sampling in future studies, emphasizing that while striving for representativeness is important, non-probability sampling remains valuable—especially in qualitative contexts—and should not be dismissed outright. The work aims to foster methodological rigor and consensus in the field by clarifying common misconceptions and offering practical recommendations for researchers.

title: The Finnish miracle of PISA: historical and sociological remarks on teaching and teacher education
abstract: This paper critically examines the so-called Finnish miracle in education as highlighted by the PISA 2000 results, moving beyond commonly cited pedagogical explanations such as excellent teachers and high-quality teacher education. Drawing on historical and sociological perspectives, the study explores the broader social, cultural, and historical factors that underpin Finland’s educational success. It interrogates the limitations and problematic nature of international comparative assessments like PISA, questioning whether such measures genuinely enhance understanding of educational systems or merely contribute to a global spectacle of accountability. The analysis also uncovers paradoxes and dilemmas often obscured by narratives of success, ultimately presenting two significant paradoxes that are crucial for comprehending the current state and future trajectory of Finnish secondary education.

title: Physics of microswimmers—single particle motion and collective behavior: a review
abstract: Microswimmers, encompassing both biological entities such as bacteria and spermatozoa and synthetic analogs, exhibit unique locomotion strategies at low Reynolds numbers where viscous forces dominate. This review synthesizes current understanding of the physical principles underlying single particle motion and collective behavior in microswimmers. We discuss the diverse propulsion mechanisms evolved by microorganisms, including rotating helical flagella and undulating cilia, as well as innovative approaches in artificial microswimmer design that harness chemical or thermal energy for directed movement. The hydrodynamics of swimming, synchronization phenomena among flagella and cilia, and interactions with surfaces are examined in detail. Furthermore, we explore emergent collective behaviors such as swarming, flocking, and vortex formation arising from hydrodynamic and steric interactions among large assemblies of microswimmers. Theoretical models and experimental findings are integrated to elucidate the interplay between individual motility and collective dynamics. Finally, we highlight the relevance of these insights for the development of synthetic active matter and potential applications in medicine, environmental science, and material engineering.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Lectures on holographic methods for condensed matter physics
abstract: These notes are loosely based on lectures given at the CERN Winter School on Supergravity, Strings and Gauge theories, February 2009, and at the IPM String School in Tehran, April 2009. I have focused on a few concrete topics and also on addressing questions that have arisen repeatedly. Background condensed matter physics material is included as motivation and easy reference for the high energy physics community. The discussion of holographic techniques progresses from equilibrium, to transport and to superconductivity.

title: From Big Data to Precision Medicine
abstract: For over a decade the term “Big data” has been used to describe the rapid increase in volume, variety and velocity of information available, not just in medical research but in almost every aspect of our lives. As scientists, we now have the capacity to rapidly generate, store and analyse data that, only a few years ago, would have taken many years to compile. However, “Big data” no longer means what it once did. The term has expanded and now refers not to just large data volume, but to our increasing ability to analyse and interpret those data. Tautologies such as “data analytics” and “data science” have emerged to describe approaches to the volume of available information as it grows ever larger. New methods dedicated to improving data collection, storage, cleaning, processing and interpretation continue to be developed, although not always by, or for, medical researchers. Exploiting new tools to extract meaning from large volume information has the potential to drive real change in clinical practice, from personalized therapy and intelligent drug design to population screening and electronic health record mining. As ever, where new technology promises “Big Advances,” significant challenges remain. Here we discuss both the opportunities and challenges posed to biomedical research by our increasing ability to tackle large datasets. Important challenges include the need for standardization of data content, format, and clinical definitions, a heightened need for collaborative networks with sharing of both data and expertise and, perhaps most importantly, a need to reconsider how and when analytic methodology is taught to medical researchers. We also set “Big data” analytics in context: recent advances may appear to promise a revolution, sweeping away conventional approaches to medical science. However, their real promise lies in their synergy with, not replacement of, classical hypothesis-driven methods. The generation of novel, data-driven hypotheses based on interpretable models will always require stringent validation and experimental testing. Thus, hypothesis-generating research founded on large datasets adds to, rather than replaces, traditional hypothesis driven science. Each can benefit from the other and it is through using both that we can improve clinical practice.

title: Use of herbal medicine during pregnancy among women with access to public healthcare in Nairobi, Kenya: a cross-sectional survey
abstract: Maternal health is a public health priority in many African countries, but little is known about herbal medicine use in pregnancy. This study aimed to determine the pattern of use of herbal medicine in an urban setting, where women have relatively high access to public healthcare.MethodsThis cross-sectional study included 333 women attending a childcare clinic in a district public health hospital in Nairobi, Kenya, during January and February, 2012, and who had delivered a baby within the past 9 months. Qualitative and quantitative data on herbal medicine use during their latest pregnancy were collected through an interviewer-administered questionnaire. Data was analysed descriptively and the Chi square test and Fishers’ exact test used to analyse relationships among variables.ResultsAbout 12% of women used herbal medicine during their most recent pregnancy. The use of herbal medicine was associated with a lower level of education (p = 0.007) and use before the index pregnancy (p <0.001). Only 12.5% of users disclosed such use to healthcare professionals, and about 20% used herbal medicine concomitantly with Western medicine for the same illness/condition. Women used herbal medicine for back pain, toothache, indigestion and infectious diseases, such as respiratory tract infections and malaria. A proportion of users took herbal medicine only to boost or maintain health. There were high rates of self-prescribing, as well as sourcing from family and friends. Beliefs about safety and efficacy were consistent with patterns of use or non-use, although both users and non-users were unsure about the safety and contraindications of Western medicine during pregnancy compared with that of herbal medicine.ConclusionHerbal medicine is used by 12% of pregnant women with access to healthcare in an urban context in Kenya, and often occurs without the knowledge of healthcare practitioners. Healthcare professionals should play a role in rational use of both herbal and Western medicine, by discussing contraindications and the potential for drug-herb interactions with patients. More studies are needed into the use of herbal medicines during pregnancy, labour and the postpartum period in different geographical areas, and into the health outcomes associated with their use.

title: Strain engineering of graphene's electronic structure.
abstract: We demonstrate that strain engineering offers a versatile and non-destructive approach to modulate the electronic properties of graphene, enabling the realization of all-graphene integrated circuits. By inducing controlled strain profiles via substrate patterning rather than direct modification of the graphene sheet, we show that key device functionalities—such as electron beam collimation, one-dimensional channels, surface states, and quantum confinement—can be achieved within a continuous graphene layer. Using a tight-binding framework, we analyze how strain-induced changes in hopping amplitudes manifest as effective gauge fields, leading to direction-dependent tunneling, transport gaps, and confined electronic modes analogous to those in nanoribbons. Our results highlight the potential of substrate-mediated strain engineering as a scalable platform for graphene-based electronics, circumventing the limitations associated with edge patterning and preserving the intrinsic quality of graphene.

title: Surface chemistry influences implant biocompatibility.
abstract: The biocompatibility of implantable medical devices is critically influenced by their surface chemistry, which governs protein adsorption and subsequent cellular responses that can lead to adverse reactions such as inflammation, fibrosis, thrombosis, and infection. This review summarizes current understanding of how specific surface properties, including hydrophilicity, charge, and chemical functionalities, modulate protein conformation and immune activation at the biomaterial interface. Advances in surface modification techniques—such as self-assembled monolayers, chemical grafting, and plasma treatments—have enabled the creation of well-defined surfaces to systematically study these interactions. While in vitro studies demonstrate that tailored surface chemistries can reduce undesirable protein adsorption and cell activation, translation to improved in vivo biocompatibility remains challenging. A deeper mechanistic understanding of protein:cell:biomaterial interactions at the molecular level is essential for the rational design of next-generation implants with enhanced tissue integration and reduced foreign body responses.

title: CMS Physics Technical Design Report, Volume II: Physics Performance
abstract: This report presents a comprehensive assessment of the expected physics performance of the CMS experiment at the CERN Large Hadron Collider, based on extensive Monte Carlo simulations and advanced reconstruction and analysis software developed by the CMS Collaboration. It details the capabilities of CMS for a broad range of physics processes, including Standard Model measurements, Higgs boson searches, and exploration of physics beyond the Standard Model. The document describes the methodologies for event reconstruction, particle identification, and selection criteria, evaluating detector response and systematic uncertainties. The results demonstrate the experiment’s sensitivity to key signatures such as high-mass resonances, supersymmetry, and rare decays, and outline strategies for early data analysis and discovery potential. This technical design report thus provides a foundational reference for future physics analyses with CMS, supporting both precision measurements and new physics searches at the energy frontier.

title: Recent advances and applications of deep learning methods in materials science
abstract: Deep learning (DL) has rapidly emerged as a transformative approach in materials science, enabling automated analysis and feature extraction from diverse data modalities including atomistic, image-based, spectral, and textual datasets. This review provides a comprehensive overview of fundamental DL concepts and highlights recent advances in applying DL methods to atomistic simulations, materials imaging, spectral analysis, and natural language processing within materials research. We examine the integration of large-scale materials databases, the use of synthetic data and generative models, and the adoption of advanced modeling techniques such as transfer learning and active learning to address challenges posed by limited data. The strengths and limitations of DL approaches are discussed for both theoretical and experimental applications, alongside an assessment of available software tools and datasets. The review concludes with insights into ongoing efforts in uncertainty quantification, interpretability, and the future potential for DL to accelerate discovery and innovation in materials science.

title: Personal Knowledge: Towards a post-critical philosophy
abstract: This paper advances a post-critical philosophy of knowledge by challenging the prevailing ideals of objectivity and impersonal detachment in epistemology. Through an exploration of the tacit dimension of knowing, the role of personal commitment, and the interplay between skills, passions, and conviviality, it argues that all acts of knowing are inherently personal and shaped by the knower’s participation. The work critiques the logic of doubt and affirms a logic of achievement rooted in intellectual passions and responsible judgment. By articulating the justification of personal knowledge, it proposes a new framework that integrates subjective experience with rigorous inquiry, ultimately redefining objectivity and emphasizing the creative, communal, and evolutionary aspects of human understanding.

title: Tropospheric chemistry: A global perspective
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive model of global tropospheric photochemistry, constrained by observed concentrations of key trace gases including H2O, O3, CO, CH4, NO, NO2, and HNO3. The analysis highlights significant uncertainties in the distribution and sources of nitrogen oxides, yet uses available data to limit model parameters. Calculated concentrations of reactive species such as OH, HO2, H2O2, and various nitrogen and hydrocarbon intermediates are examined as functions of altitude, latitude, and season. Results indicate that nitrogen oxide sources in the remote troposphere are geographically dispersed and smaller than previously estimated, while global CO and CH4 sources are quantified with contributions from fossil fuel combustion, methane oxidation, biomass burning, and biospheric hydrocarbons. The model finds that industrial and agricultural activities account for about half of global CO emissions and that northern hemisphere production exceeds that in the southern hemisphere by a factor of two. Tropospheric ozone production from CO and CH4 oxidation is found to be balanced by photochemical loss. The study also demonstrates that atmospheric methylchloroform (CH3CCl3) measurements can serve as an important test for model predictions of OH concentrations, which are estimated to be accurate within a factor of two. Improved constraints on source strengths and better observational data are identified as critical needs for refining global tropospheric chemical models.

title: Why digital medicine depends on interoperability
abstract: Digital medicine holds significant promise for transforming healthcare through innovations such as artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and mobile health technologies. However, the lack of interoperability among current medical data systems—characterized by isolated databases, incompatible formats, and proprietary software—hampers the effective exchange, analysis, and interpretation of health information. This perspective article argues that interoperability is a foundational requirement for realizing the full potential of digital medicine. The authors provide an overview of interoperability at technical, syntactic, semantic, and organizational levels and highlight its critical role in four key areas: artificial intelligence and big data, medical communication, research, and international cooperation. By enabling seamless data integration and standardized communication across diverse healthcare systems, interoperability facilitates digital transformation and supports improved patient care globally. The article emphasizes the need for international standards, clear medical terminologies, and supportive policies to overcome current barriers and advance digital health innovation.

title: Advances in Bioconjugation.
abstract: Bioconjugation, the covalent modification of biomolecules, has emerged as a critical tool in chemical biology, enabling advances in ligand discovery, biochemical assays, diagnostics, imaging, and industrial catalysis. Recent progress in chemoselective reactions has facilitated the development of mild and site-specific bioconjugation methods applicable to proteins, nucleic acids, and carbohydrates under physiological conditions. These innovations have expanded the utility of bioconjugates in high-throughput screening, biosensor design, and in vivo imaging, while also supporting the creation of more stable and functional biomolecule conjugates for therapeutic and industrial use. This review highlights key advances in bioconjugation chemistry, with particular emphasis on the stability of linkages—a crucial yet often underappreciated factor influencing bioconjugate performance. By summarizing current methodologies and their limitations, we aim to guide researchers in selecting optimal strategies for their applications and to inspire further innovation in the field.

title: Advancing environmental risk assessment for transgenic biofeedstock crops
abstract: Transgenic modification of plants is a key enabling technology for developing sustainable biofeedstocks for biofuels production. Regulatory decisions and the wider acceptance and development of transgenic biofeedstock crops are considered from the context of science-based risk assessment. The risk assessment paradigm for transgenic biofeedstock crops is fundamentally no different from that of current generation transgenic crops, except that the focus of the assessment must consider the unique attributes of a given biofeedstock crop and its environmental release. For currently envisioned biofeedstock crops, particular emphasis in risk assessment will be given to characterization of altered metabolic profiles and their implications relative to non-target environmental effects and food safety; weediness and invasiveness when plants are modified for abiotic stress tolerance or are domesticated; and aggregate risk when plants are platforms for multi-product production. Robust risk assessments for transgenic biofeedstock crops are case-specific, initiated through problem formulation, and use tiered approaches for risk characterization.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Medicine: Today and Tomorrow
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the landscape of medicine, offering innovative solutions for clinical practice through advanced data analysis and decision support. This perspective paper reviews current applications of AI-powered technologies across various medical specialties, including cardiology, pulmonology, endocrinology, nephrology, gastroenterology, neurology, and histopathology. Notable examples include AI-driven detection of atrial fibrillation and epilepsy seizures, continuous glucose monitoring for diabetes management, risk prediction in cardiovascular and renal diseases, image analysis in gastroenterology and cancer diagnostics, and wearable sensors for neurological assessment. While patients increasingly embrace these tools for personalized and participatory care, healthcare professionals face challenges related to education gaps, increased administrative burdens, concerns about professional roles, and unresolved legal and ethical issues. The implementation of augmented medicine necessitates rigorous validation through clinical trials and integration of digital health literacy into medical education. This paper discusses the benefits, opportunities, and risks associated with established AI applications in clinical practice, highlighting the need for collaborative efforts among clinicians, educators, institutions, and policymakers to ensure responsible adoption and maximize patient outcomes.

title: Phase-Field Methods in Materials Science and Engineering
abstract: This comprehensive and self-contained, one-stop source discusses phase-field methodology in a fundamental way, explaining complex mathematical and numerical techniques for solving phase-field and related continuum-field models. It also presents techniques used to model various phenomena in a detailed, step-by-step way, such that readers can carry out their own code developments.Features many examples of how the methods explained can be used in materials science and engineering applications.Visit the following page and click on 'Examples' to find a file with codes: http://www.wiley-vch.de/publish/en/books/bySubjectEE00/ISBN3-527-40747-2/?sID=82ekfegtfqadsjnpdnh0rpvkh3

title: Reported Subjective Well-Being: A Challenge for Economic Theory and Economic Policy
abstract: This paper examines the growing integration of subjective well-being measures into economic research, arguing that self-reported life satisfaction provides a credible empirical proxy for individual utility. Utilizing data from the German Socio-Economic Panel, the study investigates two key areas: the influence of income aspirations on the relationship between income and happiness, and the significant negative impact of unemployment on life satisfaction, independent of income effects. The findings challenge traditional economic assumptions that rely solely on observable choices and objective utility, highlighting the value of incorporating subjective well-being data to better understand individual welfare. The paper discusses the implications of these insights for both economic theory and policy, suggesting that a focus on reported well-being can inform more effective and human-centered economic policies.
venue: Journal of Contextual Economics – Schmollers Jahrbuch

title: The Oxford handbook of sociology, social theory, and organization studies : contemporary currents
abstract: This chapter examines the evolving relationship between social movement theory and organization studies, tracing their distinct historical origins and the gradual convergence of their analytical frameworks. Initially, social movement research focused on spontaneous, emotional collective action, often viewed as irrational and disruptive, while organization theory centered on rational, bureaucratic structures promoting stability and order. Over time, scholars in both fields began to recognize the interplay between movements and organizations, with social movement theorists incorporating concepts of formal organization, resources, and strategy, and organizational scholars drawing on movement theory to understand contestation and change within institutions. The chapter reviews key theoretical developments, highlights influential contributions that bridge the two traditions, and identifies emerging directions for research at their intersection, emphasizing how activism and grassroots mobilization inform our understanding of organizational dynamics and institutional transformation.

title: Black holes: complementarity or firewalls?
abstract: We demonstrate that the three widely held assumptions about black holes—purity of Hawking radiation, validity of low-energy effective field theory outside a microscopic distance from the horizon, and the absence of drama for infalling observers—are mutually inconsistent. Through thought experiments involving Hawking radiation and the experience of infalling observers, we show that if information is preserved and emitted in the Hawking radiation as required by unitarity, then an infalling observer must encounter high-energy quanta at the horizon, contradicting the expectation of a smooth passage. This suggests that either the equivalence principle fails at the horizon, resulting in a 'firewall' that destroys infalling observers, or that novel, possibly nonlocal dynamics must operate at macroscopic distances from the horizon, violating semiclassical physics. Our analysis challenges black hole complementarity and indicates that resolving the information paradox may require significant departures from conventional quantum field theory or general relativity near black hole horizons.

title: Manufacturing Engineering
abstract: Manufacturing Engineering is concerned with designing, building, planning, operating, and managing economical production systems for discrete manufacturing. Manufacturing engineers need to have a thorough knowledge of materials and manufacturing processes. They should also be able to design, operate and manage integrated systems that include people, materials, machine tools, material handling equipment, robots, quality measuring equipment, controls and computers.
venue: Lecture Notes on Multidisciplinary Industrial Engineering

title: The future landscape of large language models in medicine
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have rapidly emerged as transformative artificial intelligence tools capable of generating human-like text and engaging in complex language tasks. Their integration into medicine offers significant opportunities to enhance patient care, medical research, and education by facilitating communication, democratizing access to knowledge, and streamlining documentation. However, the adoption of LLMs also presents challenges, including risks of misinformation, privacy concerns, algorithmic biases, and the potential for misuse due to limited transparency and accountability. This perspective provides a comprehensive overview of the development and current capabilities of LLMs, examines their potential applications across clinical practice, research, and education, and discusses critical limitations that must be addressed to ensure their safe and effective use in healthcare. The future landscape of LLMs in medicine will depend on balancing innovation with robust safeguards to maximize benefits while mitigating risks.

title: Applications of social constructivist learning theories in knowledge translation for healthcare professionals: a scoping review
abstract: This scoping review examines the application of social constructivist learning theories in knowledge translation (KT) for healthcare professionals. Despite the recognized importance of theory in designing effective KT interventions to bridge research-practice gaps, the use of social constructivist theory in KT literature remains limited and inconsistently justified. A systematic search across six databases identified 35 relevant papers published between 1992 and 2011. Analysis revealed that while social constructivist theory has potential to inform KT by emphasizing active, contextually situated knowledge construction among clinicians, its explicit integration and rationale in KT studies are often lacking. The review highlights the need for more deliberate application of social constructivist principles in KT intervention design and evaluation, suggesting that frameworks such as Knowledge to Action may benefit from stronger constructivist underpinnings to enhance evidence uptake and practice change among healthcare professionals.

title: Role of platelet-derived growth factors in physiology and medicine.
abstract: Platelet-derived growth factors (PDGFs) and their receptors (PDGFRs) have served as prototypes for growth factor and receptor tyrosine kinase function for more than 25 years. Studies of PDGFs and PDGFRs in animal development have revealed roles for PDGFR-alpha signaling in gastrulation and in the development of the cranial and cardiac neural crest, gonads, lung, intestine, skin, CNS, and skeleton. Similarly, roles for PDGFR-beta signaling have been established in blood vessel formation and early hematopoiesis. PDGF signaling is implicated in a range of diseases. Autocrine activation of PDGF signaling pathways is involved in certain gliomas, sarcomas, and leukemias. Paracrine PDGF signaling is commonly observed in epithelial cancers, where it triggers stromal recruitment and may be involved in epithelial-mesenchymal transition, thereby affecting tumor growth, angiogenesis, invasion, and metastasis. PDGFs drive pathological mesenchymal responses in vascular disorders such as atherosclerosis, restenosis, pulmonary hypertension, and retinal diseases, as well as in fibrotic diseases, including pulmonary fibrosis, liver cirrhosis, scleroderma, glomerulosclerosis, and cardiac fibrosis. We review basic aspects of the PDGF ligands and receptors, their developmental and pathological functions, principles of their pharmacological inhibition, and results using PDGF pathway-inhibitory or stimulatory drugs in preclinical and clinical contexts.

title: Rhetorical Variation across Research Article Abstracts in Environmental Science and Applied Linguistics
abstract: This study investigates rhetorical variation in research article abstracts from environmental science and applied linguistics by analyzing 200 abstracts published between 2010 and 2013 using Hyland’s five-move analytical framework. The analysis identifies typical move structures and associated linguistic features in each discipline, revealing that environmental science abstracts most commonly follow the I-P-M-Pr-C (Introduction, Purpose, Method, Product, Conclusion) structure, while applied linguistics abstracts predominantly use the P-M-Pr-C (Purpose, Method, Product, Conclusion) pattern. All moves except the Introduction were conventional across both disciplines. The findings highlight both shared and distinct rhetorical conventions shaped by disciplinary norms, offering practical implications for academic writing instruction and supporting non-native English speakers in producing effective abstracts for scholarly publication.

title: Theory and methods of economic evaluation of health care.
abstract: Most economic evaluations of health care programmes at the moment are cost­ effectiveness and cost-utility analyses. The problem with these methods is that their theoretical foundations are unclear. This has led to confusion about how to define the costs and health effects and how to interpret the results of these studies. In the environmental and traffic safety fields it is instead common to carry out traditional cost-bene:fit analyses of health improving programmes. This striking difference in how health programmes are assessed in different fields was the original motivation for writing this book. The aim of the book is to tty and provide a coherent framework within cost-bene:fit analysis and welfare economics for the different methods of economic evaluation in the health care field. The book is written in an easily accessible manner and several examples of applications of the different methods are provided. It is my hope that it will be useful both for teaching purposes and as a guide for practitioners in the field. Glenn C. Blomquist, John D. Graham, Rich O'Conor and four anonymous referees provided helpful comments on previous versions of the manuscript. I would also like to express my gratitude to the following persons for helping me to prepare the manuscript: Carl-Magnus Berglund, Carin Blanksvard, Ann Brown, and Ziad Obeid.
venue: Developments in health economics and public policy

title: Microscale technologies for tissue engineering and biology.
abstract: Microscale technologies are emerging as powerful tools for tissue engineering and biological studies. In this review, we present an overview of these technologies in various tissue engineering applications, such as for fabricating 3D microfabricated scaffolds, as templates for cell aggregate formation, or for fabricating materials in a spatially regulated manner. In addition, we give examples of the use of microscale technologies for controlling the cellular microenvironment in vitro and for performing high-throughput assays. The use of microfluidics, surface patterning, and patterned cocultures in regulating various aspects of cellular microenvironment is discussed, as well as the application of these technologies in directing cell fate and elucidating the underlying biology. Throughout this review, we will use specific examples where available and will provide trends and future directions in the field.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Metalloproteinases in biology and pathology of the nervous system
abstract: Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) have been implicated in several diseases of the nervous system. Here we review the evidence that supports this idea and discuss the possible mechanisms of MMP action. We then consider some of the beneficial functions of MMPs during neural development and speculate on their roles in repair after brain injury. We also introduce a family of proteins known as ADAMs (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase), as some of the properties previously ascribed to MMPs are possibly the result of ADAM activity.

title: Environmental DNA for biomonitoring
abstract: This special issue addresses some of these challenges by present- ing the latest advances in eDNA field and discussing their strengths and limitations when applied to routine biomonitoring.

title: Measurement of Business Economic Performance: An Examination of Method Convergence
abstract: This study investigates the convergence among alternative methods used to measure business economic performance, addressing concerns about the comparability and validity of different approaches. Using a sample of business units, the research examines the extent to which commonly employed financial and composite performance measures yield consistent results. The analysis reveals significant, but not complete, convergence among various measurement methods, highlighting both overlaps and discrepancies in performance assessments. The findings underscore the importance of method selection in empirical research and suggest that reliance on a single measure may lead to incomplete or biased conclusions. Implications for future research and managerial practice are discussed, emphasizing the need for multi-method approaches in evaluating business economic performance.

title: Structural Design Elements in Biological Materials: Application to Bioinspiration
abstract: Eight structural elements in biological materials are identified as the most common amongst a variety of animal taxa. These are proposed as a new paradigm in the field of biological materials science as they can serve as a toolbox for rationalizing the complex mechanical behavior of structural biological materials and for systematizing the development of bioinspired designs for structural applications. They are employed to improve the mechanical properties, namely strength, wear resistance, stiffness, flexibility, fracture toughness, and energy absorption of different biological materials for a variety of functions (e.g., body support, joint movement, impact protection, weight reduction). The structural elements identified are: fibrous, helical, gradient, layered, tubular, cellular, suture, and overlapping. For each of the structural design elements, critical design parameters are presented along with constitutive equations with a focus on mechanical properties. Additionally, example organisms from varying biological classes are presented for each case to display the wide variety of environments where each of these elements is present. Examples of current bioinspired materials are also introduced for each element.

title: Clinical epigenetics settings for cancer and cardiovascular diseases: real-life applications of network medicine at the bedside
abstract: Despite significant advances in epigenetic research, the integration of epigenetic biomarkers and therapies into routine clinical practice for cancer and cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remains limited. This review examines the current landscape of clinical epigenetics, highlighting the potential of network medicine (NM) to address the complexity of these diseases by leveraging multi-omics data, systems biology, and artificial intelligence. We discuss the mechanisms and clinical relevance of epigenetic modifications, including DNA methylation and histone modifications, and summarize the development and approval of epi-drugs for hematologic malignancies, with ongoing trials exploring their use in solid tumors and CVDs. The limitations of reductionist approaches underscore the need for NM to enable precision medicine by integrating molecular interaction networks for improved diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy selection. By bridging basic science and clinical application, this review provides insights into how NM can facilitate the translation of epigenetic discoveries to bedside care, ultimately advancing personalized treatment strategies for cancer and CVD patients.

title: Data Science of the Natural Environment: A Research Roadmap
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive research roadmap for the emerging field of environmental data science, emphasizing its potential to transform our understanding and management of the natural environment. Drawing on interdisciplinary expertise and a strategic partnership between Lancaster University’s Data Science Institute and the Centre for Ecology and Hydrology, the authors define environmental data science, systematically analyze its unique challenges—including complexity, spatial and temporal reasoning, and uncertainty—and highlight the need for integrative, collaborative approaches. The paper includes a case study on modeling extreme melt events on the Greenland Ice Sheet to illustrate the promise of data-driven methods in addressing pressing environmental issues. Concluding with a prioritized list of ten key research challenges, the authors call for the creation of an international, cross-disciplinary community to advance environmental data science and address global challenges such as climate change through innovative data-centric solutions.

title: Coupled spin and valley physics in monolayers of MoS2 and other group-VI dichalcogenides.
abstract: We show that inversion symmetry breaking together with spin-orbit coupling leads to coupled spin and valley physics in monolayers of MoS2 and other group-VI dichalcogenides, making possible controls of spin and valley in these 2D materials. The spin-valley coupling at the valence-band edges suppresses spin and valley relaxation, as flip of each index alone is forbidden by the valley-contrasting spin splitting. Valley Hall and spin Hall effects coexist in both electron-doped and hole-doped systems. Optical interband transitions have frequency-dependent polarization selection rules which allow selective photoexcitation of carriers with various combination of valley and spin indices. Photoinduced spin Hall and valley Hall effects can generate long lived spin and valley accumulations on sample boundaries. The physics discussed here provides a route towards the integration of valleytronics and spintronics in multivalley materials with strong spin-orbit coupling and inversion symmetry breaking.

title: What is Systems Biology?
abstract: This perspective article addresses the ongoing ambiguity surrounding the definition of systems biology, a field characterized by its interdisciplinary nature and rapid growth. The author explores the aesthetic motivations that drive systems biologists, emphasizing the interplay of diversity, simplicity, and complexity as central qualities that distinguish the discipline. By examining what systems biology is not, the article clarifies its boundaries and distinguishes it from related research activities. The discussion highlights the importance of computational modeling and integrative analysis of large-scale biological data, while also underscoring the field’s foundational role in enabling synthetic biology. Ultimately, the article proposes that systems biology should be defined as the scientific endeavor aimed at providing a comprehensive framework for understanding and engineering biological systems, thus laying the groundwork for advances in synthetic biology.

title: Arbitrage Theory in Continuous Time
abstract: The fourth edition of this textbook on pricing and hedging of financial derivatives, now also including dynamic equilibrium theory, continues to combine sound mathematical principles with economic applications. Concentrating on the probabilistic theory of continuous time arbitrage pricing of financial derivatives, including stochastic optimal control theory and optimal stopping theory, the book is designed for graduate students in economics and mathematics, and combines the necessary mathematical background with a solid economic focus. It includes a solved example for every new technique presented, contains numerous exercises, and suggests further reading in each chapter. All concepts and ideas are discussed, not only from a mathematics point of view, but the mathematical theory is also always supplemented with lots of intuitive economic arguments. In the substantially extended fourth edition Tomas Björk has added completely new chapters on incomplete markets, treating such topics as the Esscher transform, the minimal martingale measure, f-divergences, optimal investment theory for incomplete markets, and good deal bounds. There is also an entirely new part of the book presenting dynamic equilibrium theory. This includes several chapters on unit net supply endowments models, and the Cox–Ingersoll–Ross equilibrium factor model (including the CIR equilibrium interest rate model). Providing two full treatments of arbitrage theory—the classical delta hedging approach and the modern martingale approach—the book is written in such a way that these approaches can be studied independently of each other, thus providing the less mathematically oriented reader with a self-contained introduction to arbitrage theory and equilibrium theory, while at the same time allowing the more advanced student to see the full theory in action.

title: The cost of defensive medicine on 3 hospital medicine services.
abstract: This study assessed the cost of defensive medicine on three hospital medicine services by having physicians rate the defensiveness of their own orders. Hospitalists at one tertiary and two community hospitals evaluated 4,215 orders for 769 patients, indicating the degree to which each order was motivated by concerns about malpractice liability. Results showed that 28% of orders were at least partially defensive, accounting for 13% of total hospital costs, while only 2.9% of costs were due to completely defensive orders, primarily from additional hospital days. Physician characteristics and attitudes toward litigation were not associated with defensive ordering or costs. The findings suggest that although a significant proportion of hospital orders have some defensive component, only a small fraction of overall costs are attributable to fully defensive practices, indicating limited potential for cost savings through tort reform.

title: “Fundamental Causes” of Social Inequalities in Mortality: A Test of the Theory∗
abstract: Medicine and epidemiology currently dominate the study of the strong association between socioeconomic status and mortality. Socioeconomic status typically is viewed as a causally irrelevant “confounding variable” or as a less critical variable marking only the beginning of a causal chain in which intervening risk factors are given prominence. Yet the association between socioeconomic status and mortality has persisted despite radical changes in the diseases and risk factors that are presumed to explain it. This suggests that the effect of socioeconomic status on mortality essentially cannot be understood by reductive explanations that focus on current mechanisms. Accordingly, Link and Phelan (1995) proposed that socioeconomic status is a “fundamental cause” of mortality disparities—that socioeconomic disparities endure despite changing mechanisms because socioeconomic status embodies an array of resources, such as money, knowledge, prestige, power, and beneficial social connections, that protect health no matter what mechanisms are relevant at any given time. We identified a situation in which resources should be less helpful in prolonging life, and derived the following prediction from the theory: For less preventable causes of death (for which we know little about prevention or treatment), socioeconomic status will be less strongly associated with mortality than for more preventable causes. We tested this hypothesis with the National Longitudinal Mortality Study, which followed Current Population Survey respondents (N = 370,930) for mortality for nine years. Our hypothesis was supported, lending support to the theory of fundamental causes and more generally to the importance of a sociological approach to the study of socio-economic disparities in mortality.
venue: Journal of Health and Social Behavior

title: Contribution of microreactor technology and flow chemistry to the development of green and sustainable synthesis
abstract: Microreactor technology and flow chemistry have emerged as transformative tools in advancing green and sustainable synthesis by enabling safer, more efficient, and environmentally benign chemical processes. This review highlights recent developments demonstrating how flow microreactors facilitate flash chemistry, catalysis, hazardous transformations, and continuous processing, often surpassing the limitations of traditional batch methods. Key advantages include enhanced mixing, precise temperature and residence time control, improved safety, reduced waste, and lower energy consumption. Notable examples illustrate the successful generation and trapping of highly reactive intermediates, protecting-group-free synthesis, and the use of greener solvents and milder conditions. Collectively, these advances underscore the pivotal role of microreactor technology and flow chemistry in meeting the principles of green chemistry and driving the sustainable evolution of chemical manufacturing.

title: On the role of traditional ecological knowledge as a collaborative concept: a philosophical study
abstract: The concept of traditional ecological knowledge (TEK), along with synonymous or closely related terms like indigenous knowledge and native science, has some of its origins in literatures on international development and adaptive management. There is a tendency to want to determine one definition for TEK that can satisfy every stakeholder in every situation. Yet a scan of environmental science and policy literatures reveals there to be differences in definitions that make it difficult to form a consensus. What should be explored instead is the role that the concept of TEK plays in facilitating or discouraging cross-cultural and cross-situational collaboration among actors working for indigenous and non-indigenous institutions of environmental governance, such as tribal natural resources departments, federal agencies working with tribes, and co-management boards.MethodsThis is a philosophical paper that explores how the concept of TEK is defined in science and policy literatures and what purpose it serves for improving cooperative environmental and natural resources stewardship and management between indigenous and non-indigenous institutions. The philosophical method applied here is one that outlines numerous possible meanings of a concept (TEK, in this paper) and the implications of each meaning for science and policy.ResultsIn science and policy literatures, there are different definitions of TEK. Controversy can brew over TEK when people hold definitions that are based on different assumptions. There are two kinds of assumptions about the meaning of TEK. The first kind refers to assumptions about the mobilization of TEK, or what I call knowledge mobilization. The second kind involves assumptions about how to understand the relationship between TEK and disciplines like ecology or biology, or, in other words, the relation between TEK and science. Different positions that fall under the two kinds of assumptions (knowledge mobilization; TEK and science) can generate disagreements because they imply differences about “whose” definition of TEK gets privileged, who is counted as having expert authority over environmental governance issues, and how TEK should be factored into policy processes that already have a role for disciplines like forestry or toxicology in them.ConclusionsIn light such disagreements, I argue that the concept of TEK should be understood as a collaborative concept. It serves to invite diverse populations to continually learn from one another about how each approaches the very question of “knowledge” in the first place, and how these different approaches can be blended to better steward natural resources and adapt to climate change. The implication is that environmental scientists and policy professionals, indigenous and non-indigenous, should not be in the business of creating definitions of TEK. Instead, they should focus more on creating long term processes that allow the different implications of approaches to knowledge in relation to stewardship goals to be responsibly thought through.

title: Knowledge Management and Organizational Learning
abstract: This series is introduced by the International Association for Knowledge Management (www.IAKM.net) with an aim to offer advanced peer-reviewed reference books to researchers, practitioners and students in the field of knowledge management in organizations. Both discussions of new theories and advances in the field, as well as reviews of the state-of-the art will be featured regularly. Particularly, the books will be open to these contributions: Reviews of the state-of-the art (i.e. syntheses of recent studies on a topic, classifications and discussions of theories, approaches and methods, etc.) that can both serve as a reference and allow opening new horizons Discussions on new theories and methods of scientific research in organisational knowledge management Critical reviews of empirical evidence and empirical validations of theories Contributions that build a bridge between the various disciplines and fields that converge towards knowledge management (i.e.: computer science, cognitive sciences, economics, other management fields, etc.) and propose the development of a common background of notions, concepts and scientific methods Surveys of new practical methods that can inspire practitioners and researchers in their applications of knowledge management methods in companies and public services

title: History of cannabis as a medicine: a review.
abstract: Cannabis as a medicine was used before the Christian era in Asia, mainly in India. The introduction of cannabis in the Western medicine occurred in the midst of the 19th century, reaching the climax in the last decade of that century, with the availability and usage of cannabis extracts or tinctures. In the first decades of the 20th century, the Western medical use of cannabis significantly decreased largely due to difficulties to obtain consistent results from batches of plant material of different potencies. The identification of the chemical structure of cannabis components and the possibility of obtaining its pure constituents were related to a significant increase in scientific interest in such plant, since 1965. This interest was renewed in the 1990's with the description of cannabinoid receptors and the identification of an endogenous cannabinoid system in the brain. A new and more consistent cycle of the use of cannabis derivatives as medication begins, since treatment effectiveness and safety started to be scientifically proven.

title: Coupled-cluster computations of atomic nuclei
abstract: In the past decade, coupled-cluster theory has seen a renaissance in nuclear physics, with computations of neutron-rich and medium-mass nuclei. The method is efficient for nuclei with product-state references, and it describes many aspects of weakly bound and unbound nuclei. This report reviews the technical and conceptual developments of this method in nuclear physics, and the results of coupled-cluster calculations for nucleonic matter, and for exotic isotopes of helium, oxygen, calcium, and some of their neighbors.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: On the Unification Problem in Physics
abstract: Revised translation of Kaluza's historic 1921 paper, 'Zum Unit\'atsproblem der Physik,' on 5-dimensional spacetime, used to unify gravity and electromagnetism. This version is based, in part, on a 1984 translation provided by T. Muta, but revised and formatted using LaTeX to closely match the original paper in appearance and pagination. Kaluza's original notation is restored.
venue: International Journal of Modern Physics D

title: Evolutionary biology of aging
abstract: This book provides a comprehensive and accessible introduction to the evolutionary biology of aging, focusing on the theoretical foundations and empirical evidence supporting evolutionary explanations for senescence. Rose presents historical context and mathematical models, notably antagonistic pleiotropy and mutation accumulation (reframed as age-specificity of gene action), and reviews experimental tests of these theories, primarily drawing on his own research. The text argues that aging is genetically and evolutionarily distinct from fitness, though the empirical scope is somewhat narrow and alternative data are sometimes too readily dismissed. Later chapters critique non-evolutionary theories of aging and propose an evolutionary paradigm for gerontology, emphasizing the lack of conserved senescence mechanisms and advocating for physiological over molecular studies. While the book succeeds in clarifying evolutionary perspectives and minimizing mathematical complexity for non-specialists, it is less comprehensive in experimental coverage and offers limited guidance on mechanistic research directions. Overall, it is a valuable resource for researchers interested in the genetic and evolutionary aspects of aging but leaves open questions regarding underlying physiological and molecular processes.

title: Revolutionizing medicine in the 21st century through systems approaches.
abstract: This paper explores the transformative potential of systems approaches in 21st-century medicine, arguing that the integration of high-dimensional data and holistic network analysis will drive a shift from reactive, disease-focused care to proactive, predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory (P4) medicine. By conceptualizing biology as an information science and leveraging advances in digitalization, systems medicine enables the comprehensive mapping of biological parts, their interactions, and dynamic behaviors across multiple scales. Case studies in neurodegeneration and chronic respiratory disease illustrate how systems biology can unravel complex disease mechanisms, improve signal-to-noise ratios in large datasets, and identify novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. The authors envision a future where each patient’s health is characterized by a vast, multi-layered data cloud distilled into actionable insights through advanced information technologies. This paradigm promises not only to enhance clinical outcomes and patient engagement but also to reduce healthcare costs and deliver significant societal benefits.

title: Opportunities and Challenges for Machine Learning in Materials Science
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is rapidly transforming materials science by enabling accelerated materials discovery, improved property prediction, and enhanced design capabilities. This review surveys recent advances in the integration of ML within materials science and engineering (MS&E), highlighting key application areas such as materials informatics, molecular simulations, and the development of new computational tools. The paper discusses both supervised and unsupervised learning approaches, emphasizing their respective roles in handling complex datasets and extracting meaningful patterns without explicit programming. It also addresses best practices for model development, including assessment of model accuracy, applicability domains, and error estimation. The review identifies significant opportunities arising from increased computational power, data availability, and open-source software, while also outlining persistent challenges such as data quality, model interpretability, and the need for robust benchmarking. By providing practical guidance and curated resources for researchers at all levels, this work aims to support the effective adoption of ML in MS&E and foster continued innovation in the field.

title: Fundamentals of computer graphics
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the fundamental concepts, mathematical foundations, and practical techniques in computer graphics. It covers key areas including graphics APIs, the graphics pipeline, numerical methods, and efficiency considerations in program design. Essential mathematical tools such as vectors, matrices, linear algebra, probability, integration, and signal processing are introduced to support understanding of graphics algorithms. The text explores core topics like rasterization, ray tracing, shading models, texture mapping, and data structures for scene representation. Advanced subjects include Monte Carlo integration, physics-based rendering, animation principles, and hardware programming with shaders and buffers. The paper also addresses color science, visual perception, tone reproduction, implicit modeling techniques, and their applications in games and visualization. Through a structured presentation of theory and practice, this work serves as a foundational resource for students and practitioners seeking to master the principles and applications of computer graphics.

title: Pretreatment data is highly predictive of liver chemistry signals in clinical trials
abstract: Purpose The goal of this retrospective analysis was to assess how well predictive models could determine which patients would develop liver chemistry signals during clinical trials based on their pretreatment (baseline) information. Patients and methods Based on data from 24 late-stage clinical trials, classification models were developed to predict liver chemistry outcomes using baseline information, which included demographics, medical history, concomitant medications, and baseline laboratory results. Results Predictive models using baseline data predicted which patients would develop liver signals during the trials with average validation accuracy around 80%. Baseline levels of individual liver chemistry tests were most important for predicting their own elevations during the trials. High bilirubin levels at baseline were not uncommon and were associated with a high risk of developing biochemical Hy’s law cases. Baseline γ-glutamyltransferase (GGT) level appeared to have some predictive value, but did not increase predictability beyond using established liver chemistry tests. Conclusion It is possible to predict which patients are at a higher risk of developing liver chemistry signals using pretreatment (baseline) data. Derived knowledge from such predictions may allow proactive and targeted risk management, and the type of analysis described here could help determine whether new biomarkers offer improved performance over established ones.

title: Mitigating bias in machine learning for medicine
abstract: Several sources of bias can affect the performance of machine learning systems used in medicine and potentially impact clinical care. Here, we discuss solutions to mitigate bias across the different development steps of machine learning-based systems for medical applications. Vokinger et al. discuss potential sources of bias in machine learning systems used in medicine. The authors propose solutions to mitigate bias across the different stages of model development, from data collection and preparation to model evaluation and application.

title: Accelerating materials discovery using artificial intelligence, high performance computing and robotics
abstract: The accelerating demands for rapid materials discovery, driven by global challenges such as pandemics and climate change, necessitate a transformation in scientific workflows. This perspective explores how the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), high performance computing (HPC), and robotics is reshaping the materials discovery cycle by enabling automated, parallel, and iterative processes that augment traditional human-intensive approaches. We discuss enabling technologies for extracting and structuring unstructured technical data, such as the IBM DeepSearch platform, which leverages advanced natural language processing and knowledge graph construction to facilitate large-scale data ingestion and querying. Additionally, we examine the role of AI-driven simulations in overcoming limitations of sparse experimental data and computational bottlenecks, highlighting advances in machine-learned potentials and predictive modeling. Through a case study on the development of sustainable photoacid generators for photoresists, we demonstrate how these heterogeneous technologies, when orchestrated in concert, create powerful closed-loop workflows that accelerate hypothesis generation, experimentation, and knowledge extraction. The paper concludes by identifying ongoing challenges in data access, entity resolution, and complex querying, underscoring the need for continued innovation to fully realize the potential of AI, HPC, and robotics in materials science.

title: A data ecosystem to support machine learning in materials science
abstract: The integration of machine learning into materials science is hindered by challenges in accessing, sharing, and utilizing diverse and complex datasets and tools. This paper presents a data ecosystem comprising the Materials Data Facility (MDF) and the Data and Learning Hub for Science (DLHub), designed to address these challenges by enabling seamless data discovery, automated metadata extraction, and linking of materials data with machine learning models. Through detailed examples, we demonstrate how MDF and DLHub facilitate data publication, search, and model deployment via user-friendly web and programmatic interfaces, thereby accelerating materials research and supporting the broader adoption of machine learning in the field.

title: Two-dimensional gas of massless Dirac fermions in graphene
abstract: Quantum electrodynamics (resulting from the merger of quantum mechanics and relativity theory) has provided a clear understanding of phenomena ranging from particle physics to cosmology and from astrophysics to quantum chemistry. The ideas underlying quantum electrodynamics also influence the theory of condensed matter, but quantum relativistic effects are usually minute in the known experimental systems that can be described accurately by the non-relativistic Schrödinger equation. Here we report an experimental study of a condensed-matter system (graphene, a single atomic layer of carbon) in which electron transport is essentially governed by Dirac's (relativistic) equation. The charge carriers in graphene mimic relativistic particles with zero rest mass and have an effective ‘speed of light’ c* ≈ 106 m s-1. Our study reveals a variety of unusual phenomena that are characteristic of two-dimensional Dirac fermions. In particular we have observed the following: first, graphene's conductivity never falls below a minimum value corresponding to the quantum unit of conductance, even when concentrations of charge carriers tend to zero; second, the integer quantum Hall effect in graphene is anomalous in that it occurs at half-integer filling factors; and third, the cyclotron mass mc of massless carriers in graphene is described by E = mcc*2. This two-dimensional system is not only interesting in itself but also allows access to the subtle and rich physics of quantum electrodynamics in a bench-top experiment.

title: The Social Lens: An Invitation to Social and Sociological Theory
abstract: This fully updated Third Edition of Kenneth Allan’s acclaimed The Social Lens emphasizes the diversity of classical and contemporary theory, critical thinking, and the importance of historical context. Chosen for the diversity of their perspectives and their suitability for introducing students to contemporary social thought, a wide variety of theorists appear in the text with their individual voices vividly intact. The author engages students in the historic and contemporary changes that have spawned diverse social theories and invites them to see theory as an element within a broader range of critical thinking skills that can be applied to current social problems.

title: Colloquium: Aligning molecules with strong laser pulses
abstract: We review the theoretical and experimental status of intense laser alignment---a field at the interface between intense laser physics and chemical dynamics with potential applications ranging from high harmonic generation and nanoscale processing to stereodynamics and control of chemical reactions. After placing the intense laser approach in context with other alignment techniques, we proceed with a discussion of the physics underlying this technique and a description of methods of observing it in the laboratory.
