abstract: This literature review examines empirical research on pedagogies of embodiment in physical education, aiming to identify key characteristics and implications for teaching and learning. Through a systematic search and thematic analysis of 42 peer-reviewed studies, two main themes emerged: enabling critical reflection and exploring new movements. The first theme highlights how pedagogies of embodiment foster critical thinking by providing students with opportunities to question and discuss prevailing norms related to gender, health, and body ideals within physical education. The second theme demonstrates how engaging with new movement experiences enhances body awareness and supports meaningful, empowering learning. The review finds that pedagogies of embodiment are characterized by pupil-centered and inductive teaching approaches, which encourage student participation in activity selection and content creation, as well as ongoing reflection before, during, and after activities. These approaches expand the range of activities in physical education and promote embodied learning, empowerment, and positive movement experiences. The review concludes by calling for further research into how pedagogies of embodiment can challenge traditional practices in physical education and support both teachers and learners in developing transformative educational experiences.

title: Transition pedagogy: A third generation approach to FYE - A case study of policy and practice for the higher education sector
abstract: This paper examines the evolution of first year experience (FYE) policy and practice at a large Australian university, highlighting the limitations of piecemeal approaches and the ongoing challenge of achieving institution-wide integration. Drawing on a decade of research and institutional evidence, the authors present a case study of how Queensland University of Technology moved towards a holistic, coordinated strategy by conceptualizing FYE as “everybody’s business.” The paper introduces “transition pedagogy” as a third generation approach that integrates co-curricular and curricular initiatives through intentionally designed curriculum and seamless partnerships between academic and professional staff. This model is proposed as an effective means to address the diverse needs of commencing students, fostering engagement, support, and belonging. The case study offers practical insights into the implementation of transition pedagogy and its potential to inform policy and practice across the higher education sector.

title: Simulation Modeling and Analysis
abstract: This second edition of Simulation Modeling and Analysis includes a chapter on 'Simulation in Manufacturing Systems' and examples. The text is designed for a one-term or two-quarter course in simulation offered in departments of industrial engineering,business,computer science and operations research.

title: Partial Differential Equations of Physics
abstract: Apparently, all partial differential equations that describe physical phenomena in space-time can be cast into a universal quasilinear, first-order form. In this paper, we do two things. First, we describe some broad features of systems of differential equations so formulated. Examples of such features include hyperbolicity of the equations, constraints and their roles (e.g., in connection with the initial-value formulation), how diffeomorphism freedom is manifest, and how interactions between systems arise and operate. Second, we give a number of examples that illustrate how the equations for physical systems are cast into this form. These examples suggest that the first-order, quasilinear form for a system is often not only the simplest mathematically, but also the most transparent physically.

title: Paradigm Shifts - E-Business and Business/Systems Integration
abstract: The last decade or so spawned a host of business and technology innovations. On the business side, we saw business process reengineering, the management philosophies of customer relationship management and supply chain management, virtual organizations, electronic commerce, and business-tobusiness trading exchanges. On the technology side, we saw client-server computing, enterprise resource planning systems, the widespread adoption of Internet protocols, intranets and enterprise information portals, software package support for customer relationship management, supply chain management and other activities related to electronic business, and applications service providers. This tutorial puts put these business and technology innovations into historical context and relates them to one another through the unifying concepts of business integration and systems integration. One theme of the tutorial is the incomplete linkage between business integration and systems integration. Another is the imperfect relationship between the management philosophies of customer relationship management, supply chain management and electronic
venue: Communications of the Association for Information Systems

title: Seeking the Roots of Entrepreneurship: Insights from Behavioral Economics
abstract: This paper investigates the persistent puzzle of why individuals choose to enter and remain in entrepreneurship despite empirical evidence showing low average, risk-adjusted returns and high rates of failure. Drawing on Frank Knight’s distinction between risk and uncertainty, the authors review research on the individual determinants of entrepreneurial activity, focusing on how standard economic models based on expected utility fall short in explaining observed entrepreneurial behavior. The paper critically evaluates three main behavioral economic explanations—differences in risk aversion, overconfidence, and nonpecuniary motivations—and finds that while each offers some explanatory power, none fully accounts for the empirical patterns. The authors argue that a comprehensive understanding of entrepreneurship likely requires integrating multiple perspectives and highlight the importance of distinguishing between behavioral biases and preferences for informing effective entrepreneurship policy. The paper concludes by outlining promising directions for future research aimed at unraveling the complex roots of entrepreneurial decision-making.

title: The physics of fast radio bursts
abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration, highly luminous radio transients first discovered in 2007, which have since become a major focus in astrophysics due to their mysterious origins and extreme physical properties. This review synthesizes recent advances in the understanding of FRBs, drawing on hundreds of new detections enabled by improved instrumentation and large-scale surveys. We summarize the basic observational characteristics of FRBs, including their dispersion, scattering, scintillation, and polarization properties, and discuss how propagation effects through intervening plasma provide insights into both the sources and the cosmic medium. The review further explores statistical studies and population analyses that reveal the diversity and event rates of FRBs, as well as the discovery of repeating sources and periodic activity. We examine leading models for FRB radiation mechanisms and progenitors, with particular attention to neutron stars and magnetars, especially in light of recent associations with Galactic magnetar activity. Finally, we highlight the emerging role of FRBs as powerful cosmological probes for measuring baryonic content and testing fundamental physics. Ongoing observational campaigns and theoretical developments promise significant breakthroughs in unraveling the physics of FRBs in the near future.
venue: Science China Physics Mechanics and Astronomy

title: Bladder cancer, a review of the environmental risk factors
abstract: BackgroundMany epidemiological studies and reviews have been performed to identify the causes of bladder cancer. The aim of this review is to investigate the links between various environmental risk factors and cancer of the bladder.MethodsA systematic literature search was performed using PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, Scholar Google and Russian Google databases to identify reviews and epidemiological studies on bladder cancer risk factors associated with the environment published between 1998 and 2010. Only literature discussing human studies was considered.ResultsSmoking, mainly cigarette smoking, is a well known risk factor for various diseases, including bladder cancer. Another factor strongly associated with bladder cancer is exposure to arsenic in drinking water at concentrations higher than 300 µg/l. The most notable risk factor for development of bladder cancer is occupational exposure to aromatic amines (2-naphthylamine, 4-aminobiphenyl and benzidine) and 4,4'-methylenebis(2-chloroaniline), which can be found in the products of the chemical, dye and rubber industries as well as in hair dyes, paints, fungicides, cigarette smoke, plastics, metals and motor vehicle exhaust. There are also data suggesting an effect from of other types of smoking besides cigarettes (cigar, pipe, Egyptian waterpipe, smokeless tobacco and environmental tobacco smoking), and other sources of arsenic exposure such as air, food, occupational hazards, and tobacco. Other studies show that hairdressers and barbers with occupational exposure to hair dyes experience enhanced risk of bladder cancer. For example, a study related to personal use of hair dyes demonstrates an elevated bladder cancer risk for people who used permanent hair dyes at least once a month, for one year or longer.ConclusionSmoking, in particular from cigarettes, exposure to arsenic in drinking water, and occupational exposure to aromatic amines and 4,4'-methylenebis(2-chloroaniline) are well known risk factors for various diseases including bladder cancer. Although the number of chemicals related to occupational exposure is still growing, it is worth noting that it may take several years or decades between exposure and the subsequent cancer.

title: Adverse drug reactions and off-label and unlicensed medicines in children: a nested case?control study of inpatients in a pediatric hospital
abstract: Off-label and unlicensed (OLUL) prescribing has been prevalent in pediatric practice. Using data from a prospective cohort study of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) among pediatric inpatients, we aimed to test the hypothesis that OLUL status is a risk factor for ADRs.MethodsA nested case?control study was conducted within a prospective cohort study. Details of all medicines administered were recorded, including information about OLUL status. The odds ratio for OLUL medicines being implicated in a probable or definite ADR was calculated. A multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression model was fitted to the data to assess the influence that OLUL medicine use had on the hazard of an ADR occurring.ResultsA total of 10,699 medicine courses were administered to 1,388 patients. The odds ratio (OR) of an OLUL medicine being implicated in an ADR compared with an authorized medicine was 2.25 (95% confidence interval (CI) 1.95 to 2.59). Medicines licensed in children but given to a child below the minimum age or weight had the greatest odds of being implicated in an ADR (19% of courses in this category were implicated, OR 3.54 (95% CI 2.82 to 4.44). Each additional OLUL medicine given significantly increased the hazard of an ADR (hazard ratio (HR) 1.3 95% CI 1.2 to 1.3, P <0.001). Each additional authorized medicine given also significantly increased the hazard (HR 1.2 95% CI 1.2 to 1.3, P <0.001).ConclusionsOLUL medicines are more likely to be implicated in an ADR than authorized medicines. The number of medicines administered is a risk factor for ADRs highlighting the need to use the lowest number of medicines, at the lowest dose for the shortest period, with continual vigilance by prescribers, in order to reduce the risk of ADRs.

title: Synthetic Organic Electrochemical Methods Since 2000: On the Verge of a Renaissance.
abstract: Electrochemistry represents one of the most intimate ways of interacting with molecules. This review discusses advances in synthetic organic electrochemistry since 2000. Enabling methods and synthetic applications are analyzed alongside innate advantages as well as future challenges of electroorganic chemistry.

title: Chapter 5: Physics of energetic ions
abstract: This chapter reviews the progress accomplished since the redaction of the first ITER Physics Basis (1999 Nucl. Fusion 39 2137–664) in the field of energetic ion physics and its possible impact on burning plasma regimes. New schemes to create energetic ions simulating the fusion-produced alphas are introduced, accessing experimental conditions of direct relevance for burning plasmas, in terms of the Alfvénic Mach number and of the normalised pressure gradient of the energetic ions, though orbit characteristics and size cannot always match those of ITER. Based on the experimental and theoretical knowledge of the effects of the toroidal magnetic field ripple on direct fast ion losses, ferritic inserts in ITER are expected to provide a significant reduction of ripple alpha losses in reversed shear configurations. The nonlinear fast ion interaction with kink and tearing modes is qualitatively understood, but quantitative predictions are missing, particularly for the stabilisation of sawteeth by fast particles that can trigger neoclassical tearing modes. A large database on the linear stability properties of the modes interacting with energetic ions, such as the Alfvén eigenmode has been constructed. Comparisons between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements of mode structures and drive/damping rates approach a satisfactory degree of consistency, though systematic measurements and theory comparisons of damping and drive of intermediate and high mode numbers, the most relevant for ITER, still need to be performed. The nonlinear behaviour of Alfvén eigenmodes close to marginal stability is well characterized theoretically and experimentally, which gives the opportunity to extract some information on the particle phase space distribution from the measured instability spectral features. Much less data exists for strongly unstable scenarios, characterised by nonlinear dynamical processes leading to energetic ion redistribution and losses, and identified in nonlinear numerical simulations of Alfvén eigenmodes and energetic particle modes. Comparisons with theoretical and numerical analyses are needed to assess the potential implications of these regimes on burning plasma scenarios, including in the presence of a large number of modes simultaneously driven unstable by the fast ions.

title: The anomaly of silicon in plant biology.
abstract: Silicon is the second most abundant element in soils, the mineral substrate for most of the world's plant life. The soil water, or the 'soil solution,' contains silicon, mainly as silicic acid, H4SiO4, at 0.1-0.6 mM--concentrations on the order of those of potassium, calcium, and other major plant nutrients, and well in excess of those of phosphate. Silicon is readily absorbed so that terrestrial plants contain it in appreciable concentrations, ranging from a fraction of 1% of the dry matter to several percent, and in some plants to 10% or even higher. In spite of this prominence of silicon as a mineral constituent of plants, it is not counted among the elements defined as 'essential,' or nutrients, for any terrestrial higher plants except members of the Equisitaceae. For that reason it is not included in the formulation of any of the commonly used nutrient solutions. The plant physiologist's solution-cultured plants are thus anomalous, containing only what silicon is derived as a contaminant of their environment. Ample evidence is presented that silicon, when readily available to plants, plays a large role in their growth, mineral nutrition, mechanical strength, and resistance to fungal diseases, herbivory, and adverse chemical conditions of the medium. Plants grown in conventional nutrient solutions are thus to an extent experimental artifacts. Omission of silicon from solution cultures may lead to distorted results in experiments on inorganic plant nutrition, growth and development, and responses to environmental stress.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Handbook of Computational Social Choice
abstract: Computational social choice is an interdisciplinary field at the intersection of social choice theory and computer science, focused on the algorithmic and complexity-theoretic aspects of collective decision making. Building upon a rich tradition in mathematics, economics, and political science, computational social choice emerged in the early 2000s as researchers began to apply computational paradigms to analyze and design aggregation mechanisms such as voting rules. This introductory chapter traces the historical development of social choice theory, highlighting key milestones from antiquity through the classical period to the recent computational turn. It illustrates how early problems and paradoxes in voting inspired both foundational concepts and modern algorithmic investigations, including the computational complexity of manipulation and control. The chapter outlines the dual thrusts of contemporary research: leveraging computational techniques to better understand and innovate social choice mechanisms, and applying social choice theory to computational environments such as multiagent systems, recommendation platforms, and crowdsourcing. The handbook aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the field's structure, key concepts, and active research areas for scholars from computer science, economics, mathematics, and related disciplines, while acknowledging the ongoing expansion and dynamism of computational social choice.

title: Hartree-Fock on a superconducting qubit quantum computer
abstract: We report quantum simulations of molecular systems using the Hartree-Fock method on the Google Sycamore superconducting qubit processor, achieving simulations with up to twelve qubits—doubling the scale of previous experiments—and circuits with over ten times more gates. Employing a variational quantum eigensolver and a Givens rotation-based ansatz, we model binding energies for hydrogen chains (H6, H8, H10, H12) and the isomerization of diazene, demonstrating substantial improvements in experimental fidelity through N-representability-based error mitigation. Our approach prepares Hartree-Fock wavefunctions via variational relaxation, benchmarking hardware performance with highly entangled but classically tractable noninteracting fermion dynamics. These results validate key algorithmic primitives for quantum chemistry on near-term devices and establish a scalable foundation for more complex correlated quantum simulations.

title: Quality assessment tools for evidence from environmental science
abstract: Assessing the quality of studies is essential for reliable evidence syntheses in environmental science, particularly when informing policy decisions. While formal quality assessment tools are recommended to reduce reviewer bias and enhance transparency and reproducibility, the existence of approximately 300 such tools complicates tool selection and can lead to inconsistent quality estimates and potentially conflicting systematic review conclusions. This paper examines best practices in healthcare quality assessment and evaluates their applicability to environmental science, emphasizing that effective tools should demonstrate construct validity, facilitate inter-reviewer agreement, be applicable across study designs, and remain user-friendly. The feasibility of adapting healthcare-derived tools for environmental studies is demonstrated through existing systematic reviews, and pilot versions of modified assessment tools are provided. The authors advocate for environmental practitioners to revise, test, and adopt these best practice tools to improve the reliability and policy relevance of evidence syntheses in environmental science.

title: Brain-Computer Interface in Stroke Rehabilitation
abstract: This paper reviews recent developments in the application of brain-computer interface (BCI) technology for stroke rehabilitation, emphasizing studies involving stroke patients and clinical trials reporting motor improvements. The review highlights the limitations of traditional active motor training (AMT) and constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT), particularly for patients with severe motor deficits, and explores the potential of motor imagery (MI)-based BCIs as an alternative that does not depend on residual motor function. The paper discusses various BCI modalities, such as EEG, MEG, and NIRS, and feedback mechanisms including visual, robotic, orthotic, and functional electrical stimulation. Advances in signal processing and machine learning have enabled more effective detection of MI-related brain activity, facilitating objective assessment and rehabilitation. A comprehensive summary of recent clinical studies is presented, demonstrating both technological progress and evidence of clinical efficacy. The review concludes by addressing current challenges and future directions for integrating BCI into stroke rehabilitation protocols.
venue: Journal of Computing Science and Engineering

title: Machine learning and artificial neural network accelerated computational discoveries in materials science
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been referred to as the “fourth paradigm of science,” and as part of a coherent toolbox of data‐driven approaches, machine learning (ML) dramatically accelerates the computational discoveries. As the machinery for ML algorithms matures, significant advances have been made not only by the mainstream AI researchers, but also those work in computational materials science. The number of ML and artificial neural network (ANN) applications in the computational materials science is growing at an astounding rate. This perspective briefly reviews the state‐of‐the‐art progress in some supervised and unsupervised methods with their respective applications. The characteristics of primary ML and ANN algorithms are first described. Then, the most critical applications of AI in computational materials science such as empirical interatomic potential development, ML‐based potential, property predictions, and molecular discoveries using generative adversarial networks (GAN) are comprehensively reviewed. The central ideas underlying these ML applications are discussed, and future directions for integrating ML with computational materials science are given. Finally, a discussion on the applicability and limitations of current ML techniques and the remaining challenges are summarized.

title: Factors of Safety and Reliability in Geotechnical Engineering
abstract: This paper examines the factors of safety and reliability in geotechnical engineering through the analysis of a real case involving the collapse of a diaphragm wall during construction. The study details the sequence of events leading up to the failure, highlighting deficiencies in the original geotechnical investigation, such as insufficient sampling and optimistic parameter selection. The methodology involves a chronological assessment of design and construction parameters, emphasizing the impact of using average rather than characteristic geotechnical values in structural calculations. The findings demonstrate that inadequate consideration of soil variability and insufficient safety factors contributed to the collapse, and that adherence to more rigorous geotechnical characterization and conservative design approaches could have prevented the incident. The paper underscores the complexity and high cost of technical solutions following structural failures, as well as the importance of robust geotechnical studies and appropriate safety margins in ensuring reliability in geotechnical engineering projects.

title: Complexity Thinking and Evolutionary Economic Geography
abstract: Thus far, most of the work towards the construction of an evolutionary economic geography has drawn upon a particular version of evolutionary economics, namely the Nelson-Winter framework, which blends Darwinian concepts and metaphors (especially variety, selection, novelty and inheritance) and elements of a behavioural theory of the firm. Much less attention has been directed to an alternative conception based on complexity theory, yet in recent years complexity theory has increasingly been concerned with the general attributes of evolutionary natural and social systems. In this article we explore the idea of the economic landscape as a complex adaptive system. We identify several key notions of what is being called the new ‘complexity economics’, and examine whether and in what ways these can be used to help inform an evolutionary perspective for understanding the uneven development and adaptive transformation of the economic landscape.

title: The n-of-1 clinical trial: the ultimate strategy for individualizing medicine?
abstract: N-of-1 clinical trials, which treat the individual patient as the sole unit of observation, offer a rigorous, data-driven approach for determining optimal therapeutic interventions tailored to unique patient characteristics. While traditional randomized controlled trials (RCTs) remain the gold standard for evaluating treatment efficacy at the population level, they often fail to address the heterogeneity inherent in individual responses, especially in the context of chronic and complex conditions. This review examines the history, design, and implementation of n-of-1 trials, highlighting their potential to advance truly individualized medicine beyond current stratification strategies based on genetic or phenotypic subgroups. Despite their promise and established use in educational and behavioral research, n-of-1 trials are underutilized in clinical practice due to perceived challenges in cost, logistics, and generalizability. However, advances in wireless health monitoring technologies may facilitate broader adoption by enabling objective, real-time data collection and remote assessment. The authors argue that n-of-1 trials warrant greater attention as a practical strategy for personalizing care, improving comparative effectiveness research, and ultimately enhancing patient outcomes in an era increasingly focused on precision medicine.

title: Sanitation and Health
abstract: Adequate sanitation is fundamental to public health, yet over 2.6 billion people worldwide lack access to safe disposal of human excreta, contributing to approximately 10% of the global disease burden, primarily through diarrhoeal diseases. This paper reviews the latest evidence on the health impacts of poor sanitation, highlighting its strong association with diarrhoeal diseases, neglected tropical diseases, acute respiratory infections, and undernutrition, particularly among children in developing countries. Improved sanitation can reduce rates of diarrhoeal disease by up to 37% and plays a crucial role in controlling diseases such as trachoma, soil-transmitted helminthiases, and schistosomiasis. Despite these benefits, progress in sanitation coverage has been slow due to insufficient policy focus and reliance on infrastructure provision rather than behavior change. The paper argues for a multidisciplinary approach involving engineers, social scientists, health professionals, and communities themselves to achieve sustainable improvements. Beyond health, improved sanitation yields significant social and economic benefits, including enhanced privacy, dignity, and safety—especially for women. The health sector has a vital role in policy development and program implementation to accelerate progress toward universal sanitation coverage and maximize its broad benefits for society.

title: New advances in nanographene chemistry.
abstract: Nanographenes, or extended polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, have been attracting renewed and more widespread attention since the first experimental demonstration of graphene in 2004. However, the atomically precise fabrication of nanographenes has thus far been achieved only through synthetic organic chemistry. The precise synthesis of quasi-zero-dimensional nanographenes, i.e. graphene molecules, has witnessed rapid developments over the past few years, and these developments can be summarized in four categories: (1) non-conventional methods, (2) structures incorporating seven- or eight-membered rings, (3) selective heteroatom doping, and (4) direct edge functionalization. On the other hand, one-dimensional extension of the graphene molecules leads to the formation of graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) with high aspect ratios. The synthesis of structurally well-defined GNRs has been achieved by extending nanographene synthesis to longitudinally extended polymeric systems. Access to GNRs thus becomes possible through the solution-mediated or surface-assisted cyclodehydrogenation, or 'graphitization,' of tailor-made polyphenylene precursors. In this review, we describe recent progress in the 'bottom-up' chemical syntheses of structurally well-defined nanographenes, namely graphene molecules and GNRs.

title: Green supply chain management practices and performance
abstract: This study investigates the influence of pro-active and re-active green supply chain management (GSCM) practices on environmental, economic, and intangible performance outcomes in ISO 14001 certified manufacturing firms in Thailand, with business strategy as a contextual variable. Using survey data from 190 companies, factor analysis and multivariate linear regression were employed to validate constructs and test hypotheses. Findings reveal that re-active practices driven by legislative and regulatory pressures significantly enhance all dimensions of performance, while pro-active practices such as reverse logistics show low adoption rates and lack significant impact on GSCM performance. The study highlights the potential negative consequences of a low-cost strategy on GSCM investment and underscores the importance of considering both institutional drivers and business strategy in GSCM implementation. By focusing on an emerging economy context and including intangible performance measures, this research contributes novel insights to the literature on sustainable supply chain management.

title: Mathematics Is Biology's Next Microscope, Only Better; Biology Is Mathematics' Next Physics, Only Better
abstract: This paper explores the evolving and reciprocal relationship between mathematics and biology, arguing that mathematics serves as biology’s next microscope by enabling the discovery and interpretation of complex biological phenomena beyond the reach of traditional observation, while biology is poised to become mathematics’ next physics by inspiring fundamentally new mathematical concepts and methods. Drawing on historical milestones such as Harvey’s quantification of blood circulation and Mendel’s genetic laws, the paper illustrates how mathematical reasoning has been integral to major advances in biology. It highlights the unique challenges posed by biological heterogeneity and diversity, which surpass those found in non-living systems and demand novel mathematical frameworks. The discussion traces the mutual enrichment of both fields over centuries, emphasizing that future progress in understanding life’s complexity will require deeper integration of mathematical innovation driven by biological questions, ultimately transforming both disciplines.

title: Business Process Modeling, Simulation and Design
abstract: Business Process Modeling, Simulation and Design, Third Edition provides students with a comprehensive coverage of a range of analytical tools used to model, analyze, understand, and ultimately design business processes.  The new edition of this very successful textbook includes a wide range of approaches such as graphical flowcharting tools, cycle time and capacity analyses, queuing models, discrete-event simulation, simulation-optimization, and data mining for process analytics.  While most textbooks on business process management either focus on the intricacies of computer simulation or managerial aspects of business processes, this textbook does both. It presents the tools to design business processes and management techniques on operating them efficiently.  The book focuses on the use of discrete event simulation as the main tool for analyzing, modeling, and designing effective business processes. The integration of graphic user-friendly simulation software enables a systematic approach to create optimal designs.

title: Six Degrees: The Science of a Connected Age
abstract: 'Six degrees of separation' is a cliche, as is 'it's a small world', both cliches of the language and cliches of everyone's experience. We all live in tightly bonded social networks, yet linked to vast numbers of other people more closely than we sometimes think. Only in recent years, however, have scientists begun to apply insights from the theoretical study of networks to understand forms of network as superficially different as social networks and electrical networks, computer networks and economic networks, and to show how common principles underlie them all. Duncan Watts explores the science of networks and its implications, ranging from the Dutch tulipmania of the 17th century to the success of Harry Potter, from the impact of September 11 on Manhattan to the brain of the sea-slug, from the processes that lead to stockmarket crashes to the structure of the world wide web. As stimulating and life-changing as James Gleick's Chaos, Six Degrees is a ground-breaking and important book.

title: Using critical consciousness to inform health professions education
abstract: To explore how, in health professions education (HPE), the concept of critical consciousness has been defined and discussed, and to consider and suggest how critical pedagogy could be applied in practice. This exploration responds to increasing calls in the literature for HPE to foster compassionate care and social consciousness through the social sciences and humanities. The authors searched Medline/PubMed, ERIC and Web of Science for articles focusing on critical consciousness and/or critical pedagogy involving health professions. A thematic analysis aimed to identify key themes of critical consciousness in HPE literature. The authors included 30 papers in their review. Key themes related to defining and discussing core attributes of critical consciousness in HPE were: 1) appreciating context in education and practice; 2) illuminating power structures; 3) moving beyond ‘procedural’; 4) enacting reflection; and 5) promoting equity and social justice. Critical consciousness may inform an appropriate critical pedagogy for fostering compassionate, humanistic, socially conscious health professionals who act as agents of change. While the authors share critical teaching practices for educators, considerable care must be taken in efforts to use critical pedagogy within the current structures of HPE programmes. The authors suggest attending to the philosophical and theoretical origins of critical consciousness and those of the dominant models of contemporary HPE (e. g. competency-based approaches) in order to ensure the tenets of critical pedagogy can be enacted authentically.

title: Practice Guidelines for the Management of Community-Acquired Pneumonia in Adults
abstract: This paper presents updated practice guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America for the management of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in immunocompetent adults. The guidelines address diagnostic evaluation, site-of-care decisions, laboratory testing, antimicrobial therapy, and prevention strategies, incorporating recent advances in pathogen identification, diagnostic methods, and antimicrobial agents. Recommendations are graded by strength and quality of supporting evidence. Key elements include the use of chest radiography for diagnosis, risk stratification for hospitalization based on clinical prediction rules, and targeted laboratory studies to guide pathogen-specific therapy and reduce inappropriate antibiotic use. Empirical antimicrobial regimens are tailored to illness severity, likely pathogens, resistance patterns, and comorbidities, with specific guidance for outpatient, inpatient, and intensive care unit settings. The guidelines emphasize early initiation of appropriate antibiotics, switching to oral therapy when clinically indicated, and monitoring for treatment response. Prevention measures focus on influenza and pneumococcal vaccination. Performance indicators are proposed to assess adherence to recommended practices. These evidence-based recommendations aim to optimize clinical outcomes, minimize antibiotic resistance, and standardize care for adults with CAP.

title: Towards a pedagogy of love: exploring pre-service teachers’ and youth’s experiences of an activist sport pedagogical model
abstract: Introduction: Several studies demonstrate the benefits of socially critical work in physical education and sport which value the importance of taking action intended for democracy, empowerment and critical reflection [Devis-devis, Jose. 2006. “Socially Critical Research Perspectives in Physical Education.” In The Handbook of Physical Education, edited by David Kirk, Doune MacDavid, and Mary O’Sullivan, Vol. 9, 37–58. London: Sage]. An ‘ethic of care’ has been proposed as a moral basis for socio-critical work, describing caring or love as being the basis for pedagogic dialogue and commitment to young people [Rovegno, Inez, and David Kirk. 1995. “Articulations and Silences in Socially Critical Work on Physical Education: Toward a Broader Agenda.” Quest (Grand Rapids, Mich) 47 (4): 447–474]. Although we have a body of research on socially critical pedagogy in physical education and sport that highlights the importance of an ethic of care (e.g. Ennis, Catherine D. 1999. “Creating a Culturally Relevant Curriculum for Disengaged Girls.” Sport, Education and Society 4: 31–49; Hellison, Don. 1978. Beyond Balls and Bats. Washington: American Alliance for Health Physical], there is little research that aims to explore teachers’ and youth’s experiences in living this kind of pedagogy. Purpose: The aim of this study was to explore both pre-service teachers’ and youth’s experiences of an activist sport pedagogical model for working with youth from socially vulnerable backgrounds and to interrogate the way in which a pedagogy of love emerged. Participants and settings: Participatory action research framed this 3-semester study (18 months). Participants included 10 pre-service-teachers (PSTs), 90 youths and a researcher (the lead author). Data collection/analysis: Data collected included: (a) lead researcher observations collected as field notes; (b) collaborative PSTs group meetings; (c) PSTs’ reflective diaries after each teaching episode; (d) PSTs and youth generated artefacts; and (e) PSTs and youth focus groups and interviews. Data analysis involved induction and constant comparison. Findings: A pedagogy of love emerged when we implemented the activist sport pedagogical model across three semesters in a socially vulnerable context with pre-service teachers and youth. First, a pedagogy of love involved repeatedly challenging inequities. Second, it valued solidarity thereby cultivating a learning community. Finally, it fostered hope and imagination in all participants in order to persevere despite barriers. Implications: We suggest that the activist sport approach could be considered a holistic approach in which teacher/coach and youth interact affectively [Hellison, Don. 1978. Beyond Balls and Bats. Washington: American Alliance for Health Physical] and showed profound commitment to humanity, conscientization and pedagogic dialogue [Freire, Paulo. 2005. Teachers as Cultural Workers: Letters to Those Who Dare Teach. Boulder, CO: Westview Press].

title: Building optimism at the environmental science-policy-practice interface through the study of bright spots
abstract: Effectively bridging the gap between environmental science, policy, and practice is critical for addressing contemporary environmental challenges, yet efforts to integrate scientific knowledge into decision-making often focus on barriers and failures, perpetuating a narrative of pessimism. This paper argues for a paradigm shift towards studying 'bright spots'—instances where science has successfully influenced policy and practice—to foster optimism and inspire action among scientists and decision-makers. Drawing on examples from environmental management and fisheries, the authors demonstrate how documenting and analyzing these successes can reveal key principles, such as building trusted relationships, co-developing research questions, and maintaining ongoing stakeholder engagement. The cultivation of optimism, informed by lessons from psychology and organizational behavior, is shown to enhance individual resilience, team collaboration, creativity, and innovation—factors essential for overcoming entrenched institutional barriers and achieving sustainability goals. Ultimately, the systematic study of bright spots offers a constructive approach to strengthening the science-policy-practice interface and promoting evidence-informed environmental decision-making.

title: From big data analysis to personalized medicine for all: challenges and opportunities
abstract: Recent advances in high-throughput technologies have led to the emergence of systems biology as a holistic science to achieve more precise modeling of complex diseases. Many predict the emergence of personalized medicine in the near future. We are, however, moving from two-tiered health systems to a two-tiered personalized medicine. Omics facilities are restricted to affluent regions, and personalized medicine is likely to widen the growing gap in health systems between high and low-income countries. This is mirrored by an increasing lag between our ability to generate and analyze big data. Several bottlenecks slow-down the transition from conventional to personalized medicine: generation of cost-effective high-throughput data; hybrid education and multidisciplinary teams; data storage and processing; data integration and interpretation; and individual and global economic relevance. This review provides an update of important developments in the analysis of big data and forward strategies to accelerate the global transition to personalized medicine.

title: Examining Science Education in ChatGPT: An Exploratory Study of Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The advent of generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers transformative potential in the field of education. The study explores three main areas: (1) How did ChatGPT answer questions related to science education? (2) What are some ways educators could utilise ChatGPT in their science pedagogy? and (3) How has ChatGPT been utilised in this study, and what are my reflections about its use as a research tool? This exploratory research applies a self-study methodology to investigate the technology. Impressively, ChatGPT’s output often aligned with key themes in the research. However, as it currently stands, ChatGPT runs the risk of positioning itself as the ultimate epistemic authority, where a single truth is assumed without a proper grounding in evidence or presented with sufficient qualifications. Key ethical concerns associated with AI include its potential environmental impact, issues related to content moderation, and the risk of copyright infringement. It is important for educators to model responsible use of ChatGPT, prioritise critical thinking, and be clear about expectations. ChatGPT is likely to be a useful tool for educators designing science units, rubrics, and quizzes. Educators should critically evaluate any AI-generated resource and adapt it to their specific teaching contexts. ChatGPT was used as a research tool for assistance with editing and to experiment with making the research narrative clearer. The intention of the paper is to act as a catalyst for a broader conversation about the use of generative AI in science education.
venue: Journal of Science Education and Technology

title: Biology of breast cancer in young women
abstract: Breast cancer in young women, though relatively rare, is characterized by more aggressive pathological features and poorer outcomes compared to older patients. Young women are more likely to present with larger, higher-grade, node-positive, and endocrine receptor-negative tumors, as well as higher rates of HER2 positivity and basal-like subtypes. Distinct molecular and genomic profiles, including increased PI3K and Myc pathway deregulation, further differentiate these tumors from those in older women. Genetic predisposition is more common in this population, and reproductive factors such as pregnancy and breastfeeding may influence tumor biology and subtype distribution. Despite these differences, treatment strategies for young women largely mirror those for older patients, highlighting a need for research focused on the unique biology of breast cancer in this group to inform prognosis and guide tailored therapies. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the pathological and molecular characteristics of breast cancer in young women, explores the impact of reproductive behaviors, and discusses implications for clinical management.

title: The DAVID Gene Functional Classification Tool: a novel biological module-centric algorithm to functionally analyze large gene lists
abstract: The DAVID Gene Functional Classification Tool introduces a novel module-centric algorithm that organizes large gene lists into biologically meaningful groups by leveraging a fuzzy agglomeration approach based on global annotation profile similarity. Unlike traditional methods that rely on sequence homology or predefined categories, DAVID measures functional relationships between genes by analyzing the overlap of diverse annotation terms from multiple databases, enabling the identification of broader and more functionally relevant gene modules. The tool’s fuzzy clustering allows genes and terms to participate in multiple modules, reflecting the complex many-to-many relationships inherent in biological systems. This approach reduces redundancy, enhances interpretability, and facilitates visualization of gene-term networks, providing researchers with an efficient means to extract biological insights from high-throughput genomic or proteomic data. The paper details the underlying algorithms, demonstrates key functionalities, and highlights how DAVID enables rapid and comprehensive functional analysis of large-scale gene lists.

title: An Introduction to Optimization on Smooth Manifolds
abstract: Optimization on Riemannian manifolds-the result of smooth geometry and optimization merging into one elegant modern framework-spans many areas of science and engineering, including machine learning, computer vision, signal processing, dynamical systems and scientific computing. This text introduces the differential geometry and Riemannian geometry concepts that will help students and researchers in applied mathematics, computer science and engineering gain a firm mathematical grounding to use these tools confidently in their research. Its charts-last approach will prove more intuitive from an optimizer's viewpoint, and all definitions and theorems are motivated to build time-tested optimization algorithms. Starting from first principles, the text goes on to cover current research on topics including worst-case complexity and geodesic convexity. Readers will appreciate the tricks of the trade for conducting research and for numerical implementations sprinkled throughout the book.

title: The Negative Influences of Exam-Oriented Education on Chinese High School Students: Backwash from Classroom to Child
abstract: This study investigates the detrimental effects of exam-oriented education on Chinese high school students, focusing on the phenomenon of backwash—the influence of testing on teaching and learning. Drawing on survey data from 43 students in Yunnan Province, alongside interviews and focus groups, the research explores how a system centered on high-stakes examinations shapes classroom practices and student experiences. The findings reveal that the pervasive emphasis on testing fosters excessive academic pressure, narrows curricular focus, and undermines creativity, imagination, and personal development. Students report viewing education primarily as a means to pass exams, resulting in diminished motivation for genuine learning and limited opportunities for extracurricular engagement. The study further discusses policy assumptions underpinning this approach and highlights widespread dissatisfaction among students and educators. Ultimately, the research suggests that reducing the dominance of high-stakes testing and promoting a more balanced educational environment can enhance student well-being, foster holistic development, and better prepare students for productive adulthood.

title: The Deluge of Spurious Correlations in Big Data
abstract: The rapid expansion of big data has fueled claims that data-driven correlations can supplant traditional scientific methods, suggesting that with sufficient data, statistical associations alone are sufficient for prediction and decision-making, rendering causal understanding and theoretical models obsolete. This paper challenges such assertions by drawing on results from ergodic theory, Ramsey theory, and algorithmic information theory to demonstrate that very large datasets inevitably contain numerous arbitrary correlations that arise purely due to their size rather than any underlying causal structure. These spurious correlations, which can be found even in randomly generated large datasets, undermine the reliability of conclusions drawn solely from data mining without scientific interpretation. The analysis shows that an overabundance of information can paradoxically mimic the effects of having too little, leading to misleading patterns and false insights. The authors argue that while computational tools and large-scale data analysis can enrich scientific inquiry, they cannot replace the need for hypothesis-driven research, critical thinking, and the search for meaning through causal explanation.

title: The physics of brain network structure, function and control
abstract: The brain’s remarkable cognitive abilities arise from complex networks of structural connections that underpin diverse functions and behaviors. Advances in noninvasive imaging have enabled detailed mapping of these networks, yet understanding how their architecture supports cognition and behavior remains a central challenge. This review synthesizes recent progress at the intersection of physics and neuroscience, highlighting how concepts from statistical mechanics, information theory, dynamical systems, and control theory inform our understanding of brain network structure, function, and control. We discuss the organizing principles governing brain network architecture, including symmetry, spatial embedding, and energy constraints, and explore models describing how neural activity propagates through these networks to generate collective dynamics. The review also examines experimental and theoretical approaches to brain network control, with implications for targeted interventions in neurological and psychiatric disorders. Throughout, we emphasize open questions and the need for continued interdisciplinary collaboration to unravel the physical principles underlying the brain’s structure-function relationships.

title: Biochar Aging: Mechanisms, Physicochemical Changes, Assessment, And Implications for Field Applications.
abstract: Biochar, a carbon-rich material with promising applications in soil amendment, pollutant remediation, and climate change mitigation, undergoes significant physicochemical transformations after field application due to environmental factors such as temperature fluctuations, precipitation, and microbial activity. These aging processes alter biochar’s structure, surface chemistry, and functionality, impacting its long-term effectiveness and stability in soils. This critical review synthesizes current understanding of natural and artificial biochar aging mechanisms—including physical fragmentation, chemical oxidation, mineral interactions, and biological processes—and evaluates their effects on key biochar properties such as porosity, surface area, elemental composition, and contaminant sorption capacity. The review also assesses artificial aging methods designed to simulate natural weathering and highlights the need for more quantitative approaches to better predict field performance. Implications for the deployment of biochar as a sustainable soil amendment are discussed, emphasizing that engineered pre-aging strategies could enhance biochar’s environmental benefits. Future research directions are proposed to bridge knowledge gaps in long-term field behavior and optimize biochar design for agricultural and remediation applications.

title: Transformative learning as pedagogy for the health professions: a scoping review
abstract: This scoping review synthesizes the current representation and application of transformative learning (TL) as a pedagogical approach in health professions education. Employing Arksey and O’Malley’s six-step framework, the authors systematically reviewed literature from 2006 to 2018 across ten databases, identifying 99 relevant studies after screening 1532 initial records. The included literature comprised both conceptual and empirical works, predominantly from the USA, UK, and Australia, utilizing diverse qualitative methodologies. Findings revealed that opportunities for TL are intentionally created within curricula and are often grounded in the theories of key scholars such as Mezirow. TL was found to manifest through experiences that challenge learners’ assumptions, foster reflective practice, and promote shifts in perspectives and behaviors. The review highlights considerable congruence in how TL is conceptualized and experienced, emphasizing its value in preparing health professionals for complex, uncertain environments. The authors conclude that TL offers a robust theoretical lens for understanding and enhancing student learning in health professions education, advocating for its continued integration to support the development of adaptive, reflective practitioners.

title: The Cosmological Constant
abstract: This is a review of the physics and cosmology of the cosmological constant. Focusing on recent developments, I present a pedagogical overview of cosmology in the presence of a cosmological constant, observational constraints on its magnitude, and the physics of a small (and potentially nonzero) vacuum energy.

title: Building optimism at the environmental science-policy-practice interface through the study of bright spots
abstract: Effectively translating scientific knowledge into policy and practice is essential for helping humanity navigate contemporary environmental challenges. The likelihood of achieving this can be increased through the study of bright spots—instances where science has successfully influenced policy and practice—and the sense of optimism that this can inspire.

title: Key Scientific Issues in the Health Risk Assessment of Trichloroethylene
abstract: Trichloroethylene (TCE) is a widespread environmental contaminant with complex pharmacokinetics and toxicity, posing significant challenges for health risk assessment. This paper reviews key scientific issues critical to the hazard and dose–response characterization of TCE, including its metabolism, mode(s) of action, and cancer epidemiology. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has engaged diverse scientific perspectives to address these complexities, culminating in state-of-the-science reviews and ongoing consultations with the National Academy of Sciences. Recent advances in pharmacokinetic modeling, mechanistic understanding of TCE metabolites, and epidemiological evidence are highlighted, along with persistent uncertainties regarding metabolite-specific toxicity and interspecies variability. The mini-monograph synthesizes current research to inform future revisions of TCE risk assessment, emphasizing the need for continued research on unresolved scientific controversies affecting regulatory decisions.

title: Heart Valve Tissue Engineering: Concepts, Approaches, Progress, and Challenges
abstract: Heart valve tissue engineering represents a promising frontier in regenerative medicine, aiming to overcome the limitations of current prosthetic and bioprosthetic valve replacements, particularly for pediatric and young adult patients. This review synthesizes the fundamental concepts underlying heart valve structure, function, and biomechanics, and examines the principles of tissue engineering as applied to heart valves. Three primary approaches are discussed: cell seeding of biodegradable synthetic scaffolds, cell seeding of processed tissue scaffolds, and in-vivo repopulation by endogenous cells without prior in-vitro seeding. Progress in these areas is evaluated alongside persistent challenges such as achieving appropriate mechanical properties, durability, biocompatibility, and the capacity for growth and remodeling. The review highlights the need for advances in scaffold materials, cellular manipulation, extracellular matrix reconstruction, and non-invasive assessment techniques. It also addresses regulatory considerations crucial for clinical translation. Ultimately, the successful development of engineered heart valves will depend on multidisciplinary integration of biological, engineering, and technological innovations to meet clinical demands and improve patient outcomes.

title: The Physics of the B Factories
abstract: This comprehensive review details the conception, operation, and scientific achievements of the B Factories—two major experimental facilities at SLAC and KEK—built to investigate the origins of matter-antimatter asymmetry through precise studies of CP violation in the B meson system. The book outlines the historical context, detector technologies, data acquisition and analysis methodologies, and provides an in-depth pedagogical discussion of the theoretical framework underpinning CP violation and flavor mixing. It documents how high-luminosity asymmetric electron-positron collisions at the B Factories enabled precise measurements of mixing angles and confirmed that quark flavor mixing is the dominant source of CP violation observed in laboratory experiments, thus validating key aspects of the Standard Model. The review also addresses ongoing challenges, such as the inability of the Standard Model to fully account for the observed matter dominance in the universe, and highlights prospects for future discoveries at next-generation Super B Factories. This work serves as both a reference for experts and an educational resource for students, reflecting collaborative efforts across experimental and theoretical communities.

title: Variety of Methodological Approach in Economics
abstract: This paper examines the increasing methodological variety within economics, challenging the traditional binary distinction between orthodox and heterodox approaches. Drawing on recent literature and historical developments, it explores how economic theory has become more pluralistic, with fragmentation and specialization both within and across schools of thought. The analysis distinguishes between variety at different levels—reality, methodology, method, and theory—and considers the implications of pluralism for the discipline’s coherence and progress. While the expansion of methodological approaches offers opportunities for richer analysis and cross-disciplinary engagement, the paper cautions against unstructured eclecticism that undermines critical standards. It concludes that greater openness to methodological diversity, coupled with constructive critique, is essential for advancing economic knowledge and improving communication across specializations. The concepts of orthodoxy and heterodoxy remain relevant as meta-methodological categories for understanding this evolving landscape.

title: Rational Choice, Deterrence, and Social Learning Theory in Criminology: The Path Not Taken
abstract: This article critically examines the integration of rational choice and deterrence theories into criminology, arguing that their core concepts are not distinct theoretical advances but are instead special cases within the broader framework of social learning theory. While rational choice models, rooted in economic expected utility principles, have stimulated quantitative research and policy analysis in criminology, they have not contributed fundamentally new propositions to the understanding of criminal behavior. The article demonstrates that both deterrence (focused on fear of punishment) and rational choice (centered on cost-benefit calculations) can be subsumed under the differential reinforcement processes central to social learning theory, which accounts for a wider range of behavioral influences including rewards, punishments, and social context. The author contends that the relevance of learning principles to deterrence has been underappreciated and their applicability to rational choice largely ignored in criminological literature. By tracing the intellectual lineage and empirical applications of these theories, the article advocates for a more comprehensive behavioral approach that recognizes rational decision-making as one component within the general principles of social learning, thus charting a path for future theoretical development in criminology.

title: Harmonized guidelines for single-laboratory validation of methods of analysis (IUPAC Technical Report)
abstract: This technical report presents harmonized guidelines for the single-laboratory validation of analytical methods, developed under the auspices of IUPAC in collaboration with ISO and AOAC International. Recognizing the critical role of method validation in laboratory quality assurance and regulatory compliance, the guidelines provide minimum recommendations for procedures to ensure reliable analytical results when full interlaboratory validation is impractical or unnecessary. The document consolidates existing international protocols and standards, clarifies relevant terminology, and outlines essential performance characteristics to be evaluated—including applicability, selectivity, calibration, trueness, precision, recovery, range, detection limits, sensitivity, ruggedness, and measurement uncertainty. Detailed guidance is given on the design and conduct of validation studies, the extent of required validation, and considerations for uncertainty estimation. These harmonized guidelines aim to promote best practices in single-laboratory validation across diverse analytical fields, supporting laboratories in demonstrating method fitness-for-purpose and meeting legislative or client requirements.

title: Engineering orthopedic tissue interfaces.
abstract: Orthopedic tissue interfaces, which connect tissues with distinct biochemical and mechanical properties, play a critical role in load transfer and functional integration within the musculoskeletal system. Despite significant advances in engineering individual orthopedic tissues, the regeneration of these specialized interfaces has received comparatively less attention. This review highlights the unique biological and mechanical characteristics of key orthopedic interfaces—including cartilage–bone, ligament–bone, meniscus–bone, and muscle–tendon—and discusses their importance in restoring native function following injury or disease. Current strategies in interfacial tissue engineering are examined, distinguishing between approaches that aim to recreate the interface itself versus those that generate integrated tissue units such as osteochondral plugs. The paper summarizes state-of-the-art scaffold designs, cell sources, and bioactive factors used to engineer these complex regions, emphasizing the challenges of achieving proper biochemical gradients, mechanical transitions, and tissue integration. Advances and ongoing challenges specific to regenerating orthopedic interfaces are reviewed to inform future research directions in this emerging field.

title: Nitrate radicals and biogenic volatile organic compounds: oxidation, mechanisms, and organic aerosol
abstract: Oxidation of biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOC) by the nitrate radical (NO3) represents one of the important interactions between anthropogenic emissions related to combustion and natural emissions from the biosphere. This interaction has been recognized for more than 3 decades, during which time a large body of research has emerged from laboratory, field, and modeling studies. NO3-BVOC reactions influence air quality, climate and visibility through regional and global budgets for reactive nitrogen (particularly organic nitrates), ozone, and organic aerosol. Despite its long history of research and the significance of this topic in atmospheric chemistry, a number of important uncertainties remain. These include an incomplete understanding of the rates, mechanisms, and organic aerosol yields for NO3-BVOC reactions, lack of constraints on the role of heterogeneous oxidative processes associated with the NO3 radical, the difficulty of characterizing the spatial distributions of BVOC and NO3 within the poorly mixed nocturnal atmosphere, and the challenge of constructing appropriate boundary layer schemes and non-photochemical mechanisms for use in state-of-the-art chemical transport and chemistry–climate models. This review is the result of a workshop of the same title held at the Georgia Institute of Technology in June 2015. The first half of the review summarizes the current literature on NO3-BVOC chemistry, with a particular focus on recent advances in instrumentation and models, and in organic nitrate and secondary organic aerosol (SOA) formation chemistry. Building on this current understanding, the second half of the review outlines impacts of NO3-BVOC chemistry on air quality and climate, and suggests critical research needs to better constrain this interaction to improve the predictive capabilities of atmospheric models.

title: On the application of x-ray microtomography in the field of materials science
abstract: The principle of the tomography technique and the different possible set-ups, which can be used to obtain medium-(10 lm) and high(1 lm) resolution, three-dimensional, non-destructive images, are shown in this paper. Illustrations are made of the applications of the technique in the field of materials science. Examples are given for medium-resolution images of metallic foams and model metal matrix composites that are reinforced with spherical particles. High-resolution examples are shown for aluminium alloys. For low-absorbent materials we show that the phase contrast obtained using synchrotron radiation can provide a valuable solution. The quantitative use of these images, coupled with in-situ tensile tests or used for the simple analysis of the initial microstructure of several structural materials, is also described.

title: Vascularization strategies for tissue engineering.
abstract: Tissue engineering faces critical challenges due to insufficient vascularization, which limits nutrient and oxygen transport and restricts construct size and integration in vivo. This review examines current strategies to overcome these barriers, including scaffold functionalization with angiogenic factors, advanced scaffold design, bioreactor systems, microfabrication approaches, endothelial cell seeding, modular assembly, and in vivo vascularization techniques. Quantitative modeling and measurement of oxygen diffusion and consumption are highlighted as essential tools for optimizing these strategies and ensuring cell viability throughout engineered tissues. The strengths and limitations of each approach are discussed with emphasis on their capacity to promote functional vascular networks and facilitate anastomosis with host vasculature. By integrating advances in material science, cellular engineering, and quantitative analysis, this review outlines the fundamental requirements for achieving clinically relevant vascularized tissues both in vitro and in vivo.

title: Asymmetric Price Transmission: A Survey
abstract: Asymmetric price transmission has been the subject of considerable attention in agricultural economics. It is not only important because it may point to gaps in economic theory, but also because its presence is often considered for policy purposes to be evidence of market failure. In this paper we survey the literature on asymmetric price transmission. A wide variety of often conflicting theories of, and empirical tests for, asymmetry co‐exist in this literature. We classify the different types and causes of asymmetric price transmission and describe the econometric techniques used to quantify it. We also briefly review the results of empirical applications. Outstanding methodological problems and suggestions for future research are discussed. Our main conclusion is that the existing literature is far from being unified or conclusive, and that it has often been largely method‐driven, with little attention devoted to theoretical underpinnings and the plausible interpretation of results. Hence, much interesting theoretical and empirical work remains to be done.

title: Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics
abstract: European scale harmonized monitoring of atmospheric composition was initiated in the early 1970s, and the activity has generated a comprehensive dataset (available at http://www.emep.int) which allows the evaluation of regional and spatial trends of air pollution during a period of nearly 40 years. Results from the monitoring made within EMEP, the European Monitoring and Evaluation Programme, show large reductions in ambient concentrations and deposition of sulphur species during the last decades. Reductions are in the order of 70–90% since the year 1980, and correspond well with reported emission changes. Also reduction in emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) are reflected in the measurements, with an average decrease of nitrogen dioxide and nitrate in precipitation by about 23% and 25% respectively since 1990. Only minor reductions are however seen since the late 1990s. The concentrations of total nitrate in air have decreased on average only by 8% since 1990, and fewer sites show a significant trend. A majority of the EMEP sites show a decreasing trend in reduced nitrogen both in air and precipitation on the order of 25% since 1990. Deposition of base cations has decreased during the past 30 years, and the pH in precipitation has increased across Europe. Large inter annual variations in the particulate matter mass concentrations reflect meteorological variability, but still there is a relatively clear overall decrease at several sites during the last decade. With few observations going back to the 1990s, the observed chemical composition is applied to document a change in particulate matter (PM) mass even since 1980. These data indicate an overall reduction of about 5 μg/m3 from sulphate alone. Despite the significant reductions in sulphur emissions, sulphate still remains one of the single most important compounds contributing to regional scale aerosol mass concentration. Long-term ozone trends at EMEP sites show a mixed pattern. The year-to-year variability in ozone due to varying meteorological conditions is substantial, making it hard to separate the trends caused by emission change from other effects. For the Nordic countries the data indicate a reduced occurrence of very low concentrations. The most pronounced change in the frequency distribution is seen at sites in the UK and the Netherlands, showing a reduction in the higher values. Smaller changes are seen in Germany, while in Switzerland and Austria, no change is seen in the frequency distribution of ozone. The lack of long-term data series is a major obstacle for studying trends in volatile organic compounds (VOC). The scatter in the data is large, and significant changes are only found for certain components and stations. Concentrations of the heavy metals lead and cadmium have decreased in both air and precipitation during the last 20 years, with reductions in the order of 80–90% for Pb and 64–84% for Cd (precipitation and air respectively). The measurements of total gaseous mercury indicate a dramatic decrease in concentrations during 1980 to about 1993. Trends in hexachlorocyclohexanes (HCHs) show a significant decrease in annual average air concentrations. For other persistent organic pollutants (POPs) the patterns is mixed, and differs between sites and between measurements in air versus precipitation.

title: Blockchain for Supply Chain Traceability: Business Requirements and Critical Success Factors
abstract: This paper examines the implementation of blockchain technology for supply chain traceability by identifying key business requirements and critical success factors through thematic analysis of practitioner and academic literature. Using cobalt mining and pharmaceuticals as illustrative cases, the study highlights the need for traceability systems to address issues such as curbing illegal practices, enhancing sustainability, improving operational efficiency, strengthening supply chain coordination, and sensing market trends. The analysis identifies stakeholders’ needs—including those of suppliers, consumers, and regulators—and outlines critical success factors such as organizational capabilities, collaboration, technology maturity, supply chain practices, leadership, and governance. The findings provide an initial measurement model to support empirical research and offer a foundation for further descriptive and normative studies on blockchain applications in supply chain traceability.

title: Challenges of unculturable bacteria: environmental perspectives
abstract: Environmental biotechnology offers several promising techniques for the rehabilitation of polluted environments. The modern industrialized world presents novel challenges to the environmental sciences, requiring a constant development and deepening of knowledge to enable the characterization of novel pollutants and a better understanding of the bioremediation strategies as well as their limiting factors. The success of bioremediation depends heavily on the survival and activities of indigenous microbial communities and their interaction with introduced microorganisms. The majority of natural microbiomes remain uncultivated; therefore, further investigations focusing on their intrinsic functions in ecosystems are needed. In this review, we aimed to provide (a) a comprehensive overview of the presence of viable but nonculturable bacteria and yet-to-be-cultivated cells in nature and their diverse awakening strategies in response to, among other factors, signalling extracellular metabolites (autoinducers, resuscitation promoting factors, and siderophores); (b) an outline of the trends in isolating unculturable bacteria; and (c) the potential applications of these hidden players in rehabilitation processes.
venue: Reviews in Environmental Science and Bio\/technology

title: Is Cosmic Speed-Up Due to New Gravitational Physics?
abstract: We show that cosmic acceleration can arise due to very tiny corrections to the usual gravitational action of general relativity, of the form ${R}^{\ensuremath{-}n}$ with $ng0.$ This model eliminates the need for a nonzero cosmological constant or any other form of dark energy, attributing a purely gravitational origin to the acceleration of the universe.

title: Quantum Theory of Angular Momentum: Irreducible Tensors, Spherical Harmonics, Vector Coupling Coefficients, 3nj Symbols
abstract: This is the most complete handbook on the quantum theory of angular momentum. Containing basic definitions and theorems as well as relations, tables of formula and numerical tables which are essential for applications to many physical problems, the book is useful for specialists in nuclear and particle physics, atomic and molecular spectroscopy, plasma physics, collision and reaction theory, quantum chemistry, etc. The authors take pains to write many formulae in different coordinate systems thus providing users with added ease in consulting this book. Each chapter opens with a comprehensive list of its contents to ease the search for any information needed later. New results relating to different aspects of the angular momentum thoery are also included. Containing close to 500 pages this book also gathers together many useful formulae besides those related to angular momentum. The book also compares different notations used by previous authors.

title: Biology and biotechnology of Trichoderma
abstract: Fungi of the genus Trichoderma are soilborne, green-spored ascomycetes that can be found all over the world. They have been studied with respect to various characteristics and applications and are known as successful colonizers of their habitats, efficiently fighting their competitors. Once established, they launch their potent degradative machinery for decomposition of the often heterogeneous substrate at hand. Therefore, distribution and phylogeny, defense mechanisms, beneficial as well as deleterious interaction with hosts, enzyme production and secretion, sexual development, and response to environmental conditions such as nutrients and light have been studied in great detail with many species of this genus, thus rendering Trichoderma one of the best studied fungi with the genome of three species currently available. Efficient biocontrol strains of the genus are being developed as promising biological fungicides, and their weaponry for this function also includes secondary metabolites with potential applications as novel antibiotics. The cellulases produced by Trichoderma reesei, the biotechnological workhorse of the genus, are important industrial products, especially with respect to production of second generation biofuels from cellulosic waste. Genetic engineering not only led to significant improvements in industrial processes but also to intriguing insights into the biology of these fungi and is now complemented by the availability of a sexual cycle in T. reesei/Hypocrea jecorina, which significantly facilitates both industrial and basic research. This review aims to give a broad overview on the qualities and versatility of the best studied Trichoderma species and to highlight intriguing findings as well as promising applications.

title: Injectable hydrogels for cartilage and bone tissue engineering
abstract: Injectable hydrogels have emerged as promising scaffolds for cartilage and bone tissue engineering due to their high water content, structural similarity to the extracellular matrix, and ability to conform to irregular defects through minimally invasive delivery. This review summarizes the selection of biomaterials—both natural and synthetic—and fabrication methods, such as physical and chemical cross-linking, for developing novel injectable hydrogels tailored to cartilage and bone regeneration.
