The biological characteristics of cartilage and bone extracellular matrices are discussed to highlight the importance of mimicking native tissue architecture and composition. Despite advances in hydrogel design, challenges remain in achieving optimal biocompatibility, mechanical properties, and integration with host tissue for clinical applications. Future perspectives emphasize the need for innovative materials and fabrication strategies to realize the full therapeutic potential of injectable hydrogels in cartilage and bone tissue engineering.

title: Beyond the Lecture: Case Teaching and the Learning of Economic Theory
abstract: The use of the case method in a liberal arts college and a research university is discussed. The students' reactions a re reported as overwhelmingly positive. They felt that the cases were more useful than texts and lectures in learning about institutional arrangements, how to use economic data, and how to use economics to solve real problems.

title: Active learning in materials science with emphasis on adaptive sampling using uncertainties for targeted design
abstract: This review examines the role of active learning and adaptive sampling strategies in accelerating materials discovery, with a focus on leveraging uncertainties for targeted design. Traditional trial-and-error approaches are inefficient given the vast, high-dimensional search space of possible materials. We discuss how concepts from information science, such as surrogate modeling, utility functions, and Bayesian optimization, enable systematic exploration by prioritizing experiments or calculations that maximize expected information gain. The review outlines the integration of uncertainty quantification into decision-making processes, compares various utility functions, and demonstrates their application in both experimental and computational materials research. We highlight advances in adaptive sampling for optimizing material properties, address challenges related to multi-property and multi-fidelity data, and identify future opportunities for materials informatics to transform the discovery process through optimal experimental design.

title: Designing the next generation of medicines for malaria control and eradication
abstract: The ongoing challenge of malaria control and eradication necessitates the development of next-generation medicines that address both current and emerging needs. While artemisinin-based combination therapies have significantly reduced malaria morbidity and mortality, the emergence of drug resistance, limitations in treatment regimens, and the need for improved safety, affordability, and stability highlight the urgency for new therapeutic options. This review outlines the ideal and minimally acceptable characteristics for clinical candidate molecules (target candidate profiles) and combination medicines (target product profiles) required to achieve effective malaria control and eventual eradication. Key considerations include activity against resistant strains, single-dose regimens, transmission-blocking potential, relapse prevention, chemoprotection for vulnerable populations, compatibility with co-morbidities such as HIV and tuberculosis, and chemical stability in challenging environments. The Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) proposes a framework for integrating these attributes into new medicines through sustained investment in discovery and development. Defining clear target profiles is essential to guide research priorities, ensure adaptability to evolving public health landscapes, and optimize the long-term impact of antimalarial interventions.

title: Discrete convex analysis: A tool for economics and game theory
abstract: This paper presents discrete convex analysis as a tool for use in economics and game theory. Discrete convex analysis is a new framework of discrete mathematics and optimization, developed during the last two decades. Recently, it has been recognized as a powerful tool for analyzing economic or game models with indivisibilities. The main feature of discrete convex analysis is the distinction of two convexity concepts, M-convexity and L-convexity, for functions in integer or binary variables, together with their conjugacy relationship. The crucial fact is that M-concavity in its variant is equivalent to the gross substitutes property in economics. Fundamental theorems in discrete convex analysis such as the M-L conjugacy theorems, discrete separation theorems and discrete fixed point theorems yield structural results in economics such as the existence of equilibria and the lattice structure of equilibrium price vectors. Algorithms in discrete convex analysis provide iterative auction algorithms for finding equilibria.

title: A Critical Success Factors Model for ERP Implementation
abstract: An effective IT infrastructure can support a business vision and strategy; a poor, decentralized one can break a company. More and more companies are turning to off-the-shelf ERP (enterprise resource planning) solutions for IT planning and legacy systems management. The authors have developed a framework to help managers successfully plan and implement an ERP project.

title: Engineering orthopedic tissue interfaces.
abstract: While a wide variety of approaches to engineering orthopedic tissues have been proposed, less attention has been paid to the interfaces, the specialized areas that connect two tissues of different biochemical and mechanical properties. The interface tissue plays an important role in transitioning mechanical load between disparate tissues. Thus, the relatively new field of interfacial tissue engineering presents new challenges--to not only consider the regeneration of individual orthopedic tissues, but also to design the biochemical and cellular composition of the linking tissue. Approaches to interfacial tissue engineering may be distinguished based on if the goal is to recreate the interface itself, or generate an entire integrated tissue unit (such as an osteochondral plug). As background for future efforts in engineering orthopedic interfaces, a brief review of the biology and mechanics of each interface (cartilage-bone, ligament-bone, meniscus-bone, and muscle-tendon) is presented, followed by an overview of the state-of-the-art in engineering each tissue, including advances and challenges specific to regenerating the interfaces.

title: Cosmic rays and particle physics
abstract: The study of high-energy cosmic rays serves as a crucial intersection between astrophysics, particle physics, and cosmology, addressing fundamental questions about the acceleration mechanisms of charged particles, their propagation through galactic and extragalactic environments, and their implications for dark matter and physics beyond the Standard Model. This paper reviews the historical development of cosmic ray research, from early discoveries of new particles to current investigations into the cosmic ray energy spectrum, including notable features such as the knee and ankle. It highlights the role of direct measurements from balloon and satellite experiments in probing the origins, composition, and transport properties of cosmic rays, as well as their use in searches for dark matter and antimatter through antiproton and antinuclei fluxes. The interplay between accelerator-based nuclear and particle physics data and cosmic ray observations is emphasized, particularly in understanding secondary particle production and constraining models of cosmic ray propagation. Recent experimental efforts are discussed in the context of their contributions to neutrino physics and dark matter searches, illustrating the increasingly symbiotic relationship between cosmic ray studies and other fields in modern particle astrophysics.

title: Searching for materials with high refractive index and wide band gap: A first-principles high-throughput study
abstract: We present a first-principles high-throughput study of over 4000 semiconductors, with a focus on oxides, to identify materials that simultaneously exhibit a high refractive index and a wide band gap—properties critical for advanced optoelectronic and photonic applications. Our comprehensive dataset confirms the well-known inverse correlation between refractive index and band gap but also reveals notable outliers that defy this trend. By analyzing the results with a simple two-descriptor model based on the average optical gap and effective frequency, we elucidate key factors that enable certain materials to achieve both desirable properties. Specifically, we show that minimizing the energy difference between direct band gap and average optical gap, as well as maximizing the number or probability of optical transitions, can counterbalance the inverse relationship. Focusing on oxides, we further explore how chemical composition influences this interplay and highlight promising material classes for future exploration. Our findings provide valuable guidelines for the targeted discovery of new materials for both linear and nonlinear optical devices.

title: Density of states prediction for materials discovery via contrastive learning from probabilistic embeddings
abstract: We present Mat2Spec, a machine learning framework for predicting spectral properties of crystalline materials, specifically phonon and electronic densities of states (phDOS and eDOS), using contrastive learning from probabilistic embeddings. Building on graph attention networks for crystal structure encoding, Mat2Spec introduces a probabilistic embedding generator aligned with supervised contrastive learning to capture correlations between material features and spectral labels. Evaluated on datasets from the Materials Project, Mat2Spec demonstrates superior performance over state-of-the-art methods for ab initio phDOS and eDOS prediction. The model enables efficient identification of materials with targeted electronic features, such as eDOS gaps near the Fermi energy, facilitating the discovery of candidate thermoelectrics and transparent conductors. Our results highlight Mat2Spec as a generalizable and effective approach for accelerating materials discovery through accurate spectral property prediction.

title: Formação de professores no Brasil: características e problemas
abstract: This article analyzes teacher education in Brazil by examining four key dimensions: relevant legislation, the socio-educational profile of prospective teachers, the characteristics of teacher education programs, and the curricula of degrees in Pedagogy, Portuguese, Mathematics, and Biological Sciences. Drawing on research from 2008 and 2009, the study highlights persistent challenges such as ambiguities in regulatory frameworks, fragmentation within and between courses, and limited curricular emphasis on practical teaching preparation. The historical evolution of teacher training is discussed, revealing a longstanding division between polyvalent teachers for early education and subject specialists for higher grades, a distinction reinforced by institutional structures and social perceptions. The paper argues that these factors contribute to a fragmented and often inadequate preparation of teachers for basic education, underscoring the need for more integrated and coherent approaches to curriculum design, professionalization, and institutional organization in Brazilian teacher education.

title: Actionable Knowledge for Environmental Decision Making: Broadening the Usability of Climate Science
abstract: This paper reviews the evolution of science-policy models and their implications for the usability of climate science in environmental decision making. Despite advances in participatory approaches and boundary organizations designed to bridge the gap between scientific knowledge production and its application, the uptake of climate information by decision makers remains limited. The authors synthesize empirical research on factors influencing the use of scientific information, highlighting how perceptions, institutional contexts, and producer-user interactions shape usability. They argue that current efforts often focus too narrowly on individual users or small groups, overlooking the need to address a broader diversity of decision makers. To address this gap, the paper proposes a conceptual framework based on a typology of users at the aggregate level, offering a pathway to scale up the provision of actionable climate information while maintaining or enhancing its relevance and usability. The review concludes by identifying key challenges and opportunities for advancing the co-production and institutionalization of usable climate knowledge, with particular attention to supporting adaptation decisions in the face of accelerating climate change.

title: Transition pedagogy: A third generation approach to FYE - A case study of policy and practice for the higher education sector
abstract: Current research and practice related to the first year experience (FYE) of commencing higher education students are still mainly piecemeal rather than institution-wide with institutions struggling to achieve cross-institutional integration, coordination and coherence of FYE policy and practice. Drawing on a decade of FYE-related research including an ALTC Senior Fellowship and evidence at a large Australian metropolitan university, this paper explores how one institution has addressed that issue by tracing the evolution and maturation of strategies that ultimately conceptualize FYE as “everybody's business.” It is argued that, when first generation co-curricular and second generation curricular approaches are integrated and implemented through an intentionally designed curriculum by seamless partnerships of academic and professional staff in a whole-of-institution transformation, we have a third generation approach labelled here as transition pedagogy. It is suggested that transition pedagogy provides the optimal vehicle for dealing with the increasingly diverse commencing student cohorts by facilitating a sense of engagement, support and belonging. What is presented here is an example of transition pedagogy in action.

title: Sedimentation engineering : processes, measurements, modeling, and practice
abstract: Sedimentation Engineering: Processes, Measurements, Modeling, and Practice provides a comprehensive overview of current research and practical approaches to understanding sedimentation processes in diverse aquatic environments. Edited by Ata Amini, this volume compiles ten chapters contributed by international experts, addressing sediment dynamics in marshes, harbor estuaries, offshore regions, hydraulic turbines, and volcanic areas. The book emphasizes the integration of watershed management with sedimentation engineering and explores both the physical and chemical aspects of sediment transport and contamination, including case studies on persistent organic pollutants and heavy metals. By combining theoretical frameworks, measurement techniques, modeling strategies, and real-world applications, the book aims to enhance problem-solving capabilities for researchers, professionals, and students in water resources, environmental science, and related fields.

title: The physics of optical computing
abstract: Optical computing has the potential to be faster and more energy-efficient than conventional digital-electronic computing for certain applications. This Perspective article surveys the differences between optics and electronics that could be exploited, and explores the physics and engineering challenges in realizing useful optical computers. There has been a resurgence of interest in optical computing since the early 2010s, both in academia and in industry, with much of the excitement centred around special-purpose optical computers for neural-network processing. Optical computing has been a topic of periodic study since the 1960s, including for neural networks in the 1980s and early 1990s, and a wide variety of optical-computing schemes and architectures have been proposed. In this Perspective article, we provide a systematic explanation of why and how optics might be able to give speed or energy-efficiency benefits over electronics for computing, enumerating 11 features of optics that can be harnessed when designing an optical computer. One often-mentioned motivation for optical computing — that the speed of light is fast — is emphatically not a key differentiating physical property of optics for computing; understanding where an advantage could come from is more subtle. We discuss how gaining an advantage over state-of-the-art electronic processors will likely only be achievable by careful design that harnesses more than 1 of the 11 features, while avoiding a number of pitfalls that we describe.

title: Named Entity Recognition and Normalization Applied to Large-Scale Information Extraction from the Materials Science Literature
abstract: The exponential growth of materials science literature has created significant challenges in efficiently accessing and connecting new research with existing knowledge. This study presents a large-scale information extraction framework that applies supervised machine learning-based named entity recognition (NER) and entity normalization to over 3.27 million materials science abstracts. Using a recurrent neural network architecture, the NER model achieves an F1 score of 87%, extracting key summary-level entities such as inorganic material mentions, sample descriptors, phase labels, material properties, applications, and synthesis or characterization methods. Entity normalization, with an F1 score of 95%, enables the consolidation of synonymous terms, greatly enhancing recall in document retrieval compared to traditional keyword searches. The resulting structured database comprises more than 80 million materials-science-related entities and supports complex queries that previously required extensive manual effort. All data, models, and tools are made publicly available through bulk downloads, an API, and a web interface, providing unprecedented access to targeted information and accelerating materials discovery by enabling rapid, programmatic exploration of the literature.
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: The Oxford handbook of sociology, social theory, and organization studies : contemporary currents
abstract: Sociology and social theory has always been a major source of new perspectives for organization studies. Access to a series of authoritative accounts of theorists and research themes in sociology and social theory which have influenced developments in organization studies is essential for those wishing to deepen and extend their knowledge of the intersection of sociology and organization studies. This goal is achieved by drawing on a group of internationally renowned scholars committed in their own work to strengthening these links and asking them to provide critical accounts of particular theorists and research themes which have straddled this divide.  This volume aims to strengthen ties between organization studies and contemporary sociological work at a time when there are increasing institutional barriers to such cooperation, potentially generating a myopia that constricts new developments. Used in conjunction with its companion volume, The Oxford Handbook of Sociology and Organization Studies: Classical Foundations, the reader is provided with a comprehensive account of the productive and critical interaction between sociology and organization studies over many decades.

title: A Method of Automated Nonparametric Content Analysis for Social Science
abstract: The increasing availability of digitized text presents enormous opportunities for social scientists. Yet hand coding many blogs, speeches, government records, newspapers, or other sources of unstructured text is infeasible. Although computer scientists have methods for automated content analysis, most are optimized to classify individual documents, whereas social scientists instead want generalizations about the population of documents, such as the proportion in a given category. Unfortunately, even a method with a high percent of individual documents correctly classified can be hugely biased when estimating category proportions. By directly optimizing for this social science goal, we develop a method that gives approximately unbiased estimates of category proportions even when the optimal classifier performs poorly. We illustrate with diverse data sets, including the daily expressed opinions of thousands of people about the U.S. presidency. We also make available software that implements our methods and large corpora of text for further analysis.

title: The Business of Sport Management
abstract: This review critically examines The Business of Sport Management, edited by John Beech and Simon Chadwick, highlighting its comprehensive and engaging approach to the evolving field of sport management. The book distinguishes itself by moving beyond the typical reliance on American case studies, offering a global perspective and integrating humor to enhance accessibility. Contributions from twenty diverse authors cover the historical progression from amateurism to commercialism, address contemporary issues such as player contracts, e-business strategies, and legal considerations, and consistently link theory to real-world examples. While the text occasionally presents contradictory viewpoints and could benefit from additional operational insights, it effectively challenges readers to apply concepts and anticipate industry trends. The final chapters provide forward-looking analysis on the future of sport business, emphasizing innovation, customer engagement, and brand diversification. Overall, the book is recommended as an essential resource for students and practitioners seeking both theoretical grounding and practical guidance in sport management.

title: Nitrile-containing pharmaceuticals: efficacious roles of the nitrile pharmacophore.
abstract: Nitrile-containing pharmaceuticals represent a rapidly expanding class of medicinal agents with over 30 approved drugs and numerous clinical candidates, reflecting the unique biocompatibility and versatile roles of the nitrile pharmacophore. This review examines the structural and functional contributions of the nitrile group in drug design, highlighting its metabolic stability, minimal steric demand, and capacity for polar interactions and hydrogen bonding within protein binding sites. Detailed analysis of crystal structures reveals that nitriles frequently act as bioisosteres for carbonyl groups, facilitating key interactions with amino acid residues and enhancing pharmacokinetic properties. The survey is organized by the nature of the nitrile-bearing substituent, with a focus on aromatic nitriles that dominate current therapeutics, as well as aliphatic, alkene, and nitrogen-bearing nitriles. Case studies of clinically relevant compounds illustrate how strategic placement of the nitrile group can optimize efficacy, selectivity, and metabolic profiles across diverse therapeutic areas including oncology, endocrinology, and metabolic diseases. The findings underscore the value of the nitrile pharmacophore in modern drug discovery and support its continued deployment in the development of novel pharmaceuticals.

title: Molecular Weight Dependence of Polymersome Membrane Structure, Elasticity, and Stability
abstract: Vesicles prepared in water from a series of diblock copolymers“polymersomes”are physically characterized. With increasing molecular weight Mn, the hydrophobic core thickness for self-assembled bilayers of poly(ethylene oxide)−polybutadiene increases up to ∼20 nm, which is considerably greater than any previously studied lipid or polymersome system. Micromanipulation of vesicles demonstrates an interface-dominated elasticity that is independent of Mn. Furthermore, membrane stability as defined by the maximal areal strain increases with Mn, approaching a universal limit predicted by mean-field ideas and set by the interfacial tension. Nonlinear responses and memory effects also emerge with increasing Mn, indicating the onset of chain entanglements at higher Mn. The results highlight the interfacial limits and transitions to bulk responses of self-assemblies.

title: How to measure the impact of citizen science on environmental attitudes, behaviour and knowledge? A review of state-of-the-art approaches
abstract: Citizen science projects are increasingly recognized for their potential to influence participants’ environmental attitudes, behaviour, and knowledge, yet impact assessments in this domain often lack methodological rigor and consistency. This systematic literature review examines state-of-the-art approaches from environmental psychology for measuring these key outcomes in the context of citizen science. By analyzing relevant frameworks, scales, and assessment methods, the review identifies five validated approaches suitable for evaluating changes in environmental attitudes, behaviour, and knowledge among citizen scientists. The findings highlight a significant gap between established measurement practices in related scientific fields and their application within citizen science impact evaluations. Integrating these robust assessment tools can enhance the validity of project evaluations and support a more comprehensive understanding of citizen science impacts, ultimately informing better project design and implementation.

title: Universally Sloppy Parameter Sensitivities in Systems Biology Models
abstract: Quantitative models in systems biology often involve numerous parameters whose precise values are difficult to determine, posing a challenge for model development and predictive accuracy. Previous studies have shown that even when individual parameter values are poorly constrained, collective fitting to experimental data can still yield reliable model predictions, a phenomenon attributed to “sloppy” parameter sensitivities—where model behavior is highly sensitive to only a few specific parameter combinations. In this study, we systematically analyze 17 published systems biology models and find that all exhibit sloppy spectra of parameter sensitivities, suggesting that sloppiness is a universal feature of such models. We demonstrate that, due to this sloppiness, collective fitting to extensive time-series data typically leaves many parameters poorly constrained, while direct parameter measurements would need to be exceptionally precise and comprehensive to significantly improve predictive power. These findings highlight the limitations of focusing on individual parameter estimation and suggest that modelers should prioritize predictive accuracy over parameter precision when developing and validating systems biology models.

title: The Values and Value of Patient-Centered Care
abstract: Patient-centered care has emerged as a central tenet of high-quality healthcare, emphasizing respect for patients as unique individuals and involving them meaningfully in their care. This editorial explores the foundational values and practical value of patient-centered care, clarifying its moral underpinnings, its integration with evidence-based medicine, and the importance of fostering patient-clinician partnerships at personal, professional, and organizational levels. The authors critique superficial implementations that conflate amenities or infrastructural changes with genuine patient-centeredness and highlight the need for robust measures to assess whether interventions truly enhance patient engagement, understanding, and shared decision-making. They identify challenges in current assessment approaches, including the conflation of behaviors with outcomes, reliance on patient self-reporting, and discrepancies between patient, clinician, and expert evaluations of encounters. The editorial calls for the development of more nuanced, context-sensitive tools that capture the complex realities of patient-centered care and provide actionable feedback to improve practice. Ultimately, the authors argue that patient-centered care is both a moral imperative and a pathway to better health outcomes, requiring ongoing commitment to measurement and meaningful engagement at all levels of the healthcare system.

title: The Art, Science, and Engineering of Fuzzing: A Survey
abstract: Fuzzing has emerged as a cornerstone technique for software vulnerability discovery due to its simplicity, effectiveness, and widespread adoption in both industry and academia. Despite significant advances and a rapidly expanding body of research, the field suffers from fragmented terminology, inconsistent documentation, and a lack of unified frameworks, which impede systematic progress. This survey addresses these challenges by presenting a comprehensive model and taxonomy of fuzzing, consolidating terminology, and analyzing the design decisions that underpin modern fuzzers. Drawing from an extensive review of recent literature and major security conferences, the paper systematically explores the art, science, and engineering aspects of fuzzing, highlighting key innovations, trade-offs, and engineering practices that contribute to its success. The result is a coherent synthesis that aims to guide future research and practice in automated software testing for security.

title: Semiconductor nanocrystals: structure, properties, and band gap engineering.
abstract: Semiconductor nanocrystals are tiny light-emitting particles on the nanometer scale. Researchers have studied these particles intensely and have developed them for broad applications in solar energy conversion, optoelectronic devices, molecular and cellular imaging, and ultrasensitive detection. A major feature of semiconductor nanocrystals is the quantum confinement effect, which leads to spatial enclosure of the electronic charge carriers within the nanocrystal. Because of this effect, researchers can use the size and shape of these 'artificial atoms' to widely and precisely tune the energy of discrete electronic energy states and optical transitions. As a result, researchers can tune the light emission from these particles throughout the ultraviolet, visible, near-infrared, and mid-infrared spectral ranges. These particles also span the transition between small molecules and bulk crystals, instilling novel optical properties such as carrier multiplication, single-particle blinking, and spectral diffusion. In addition, semiconductor nanocrystals provide a versatile building block for developing complex nanostructures such as superlattices and multimodal agents for molecular imaging and targeted therapy. In this Account, we discuss recent advances in the understanding of the atomic structure and optical properties of semiconductor nanocrystals. We also discuss new strategies for band gap and electronic wave function engineering to control the location of charge carriers. New methodologies such as alloying, doping, strain-tuning, and band-edge warping will likely play key roles in the further development of these particles for optoelectronic and biomedical applications.

title: Personalized medicine in psychiatry: problems and promises
abstract: Personalized medicine in psychiatry aims to tailor prevention, diagnosis, and treatment strategies to individual biological and environmental profiles, with the promise of improving outcomes in major psychiatric disorders such as major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. This review examines the current state of personalized approaches in psychiatry, highlighting advances in genetic, epigenetic, and biomarker research that contribute to understanding disease susceptibility and therapeutic response. Despite notable progress, particularly in identifying genetic variants and neurobiological markers associated with psychiatric conditions, significant challenges remain due to the complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and clinical factors underlying these disorders. The review also discusses emerging technologies such as neuroimaging and pharmacogenomics that may enhance individualized care. Ultimately, while personalized medicine holds considerable promise for reducing morbidity and mortality in psychiatric populations, further research is needed to overcome barriers related to heritability, biomarker validation, and clinical implementation.

title: The rise of graphene.
abstract: Graphene, a single atomic layer of carbon atoms arranged in a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice, has emerged as a groundbreaking material in condensed-matter physics and materials science. Long considered theoretically intriguing but experimentally unattainable due to presumed thermodynamic instability, graphene was isolated in 2004, overturning established beliefs about the existence of free-standing two-dimensional crystals. This discovery revealed that graphene possesses exceptional crystal quality and unique electronic properties, including charge carriers behaving as massless Dirac fermions, which enable the exploration of relativistic quantum phenomena in accessible laboratory settings. The rapid evolution of methods for producing graphene, from micromechanical cleavage to epitaxial growth, has facilitated extensive research into its fundamental physics and potential technological applications. Graphene’s status as the basic building block for all graphitic forms and its conceptualization as a new class of atomically thin materials have opened new avenues in low-dimensional physics and device engineering, marking it as a transformative material with enduring scientific and practical significance.

title: Translational Systems Biology of Inflammation
abstract: Inflammation is a complex, multi-scale biological process essential for immune defense and tissue repair, yet its dysregulation underlies numerous diseases such as sepsis, trauma, and autoimmune disorders. Despite extensive molecular and cellular data, effective clinical therapies for severe inflammatory syndromes remain elusive due to the limitations of reductionist approaches. This review outlines the emergence of translational systems biology as an integrative discipline combining experimental data with dynamic mathematical modeling—such as agent-based and equation-based models—to bridge the gap between basic research and clinical application. Focusing on acute inflammation and sepsis, the paper highlights how these computational frameworks facilitate mechanistic insights across biological scales, support in silico clinical trials, and inform rational drug and device design. The authors emphasize the necessity of interdisciplinary collaboration among biologists, clinicians, and computational scientists to develop predictive models that can guide both fundamental discovery and translational strategies. Progress in this field demonstrates the promise of systems-level approaches for addressing complex medical challenges, with future advances hinging on methodological innovation and deeper integration of computational tools into biomedical research and practice.

title: Improving Health Care Globally: A Critical Review of the Necessity of Family Medicine Research and Recommendations to Build Research Capacity
abstract: This paper critically reviews the necessity of family medicine research in improving global health care and presents recommendations to build research capacity worldwide. Drawing on the proceedings of an international conference organized by the World Organization of Family Doctors (Wonca) with delegates from 34 countries, the paper underscores the essential role of evidence-based primary care and family medicine in delivering accessible, equitable, and effective health services. The conference identified key challenges, including limited recognition of family medicine research, insufficient infrastructure, and barriers to knowledge dissemination. Through collaborative discussions and review of eight foundational papers, participants formulated nine strategic recommendations: systematically showcasing research achievements to policymakers, developing sentinel practice systems for community health surveillance, establishing a central clearinghouse for research expertise and training, creating national research institutes and university departments with a research focus, expanding practice-based research networks globally, strengthening dissemination channels such as journals and conferences, facilitating funding for international collaborative studies, developing international ethical guidelines for participatory research, and addressing the specific needs of developing countries. The paper concludes that implementing these recommendations requires coordinated efforts among individuals, organizations, and governments to strengthen the global impact of family medicine research and ultimately improve health outcomes.

title: The physics of dipolar bosonic quantum gases
abstract: This paper reviews the recent theoretical and experimental advances in the study of ultra-cold gases made of bosonic particles interacting via the long-range, anisotropic dipole–dipole interaction, in addition to the short-range and isotropic contact interaction usually at work in ultra-cold gases. The specific properties emerging from the dipolar interaction are emphasized, from the mean-field regime valid for dilute Bose–Einstein condensates, to the strongly correlated regimes reached for dipolar bosons in optical lattices.

title: Telocytes in regenerative medicine
abstract: Telocytes (TCs) are a distinct type of interstitial cells characterized by a small cell body and extremely long and thin telopodes (Tps). The presence of TCs has been documented in many tissues and organs (go to http://www.telocytes.com). Functionally, TCs form a three‐dimensional (3D) interstitial network by homocellular and heterocellular communication and are involved in the maintenance of tissue homeostasis. As important interstitial cells to guide or nurse putative stem and progenitor cells in stem cell niches in a spectrum of tissues and organs, TCs contribute to tissue repair and regeneration. This review focuses on the latest progresses regarding TCs in the repair and regeneration of different tissues and organs, including heart, lung, skeletal muscle, skin, meninges and choroid plexus, eye, liver, uterus and urinary system. By targeting TCs alone or in tandem with stem cells, we might promote regeneration and prevent the evolution to irreversible tissue damage. Exploring pharmacological or non‐pharmacological methods to enhance the growth of TCs would be a novel therapeutic strategy besides exogenous transplantation for many diseased disorders.
venue: Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine

title: What Is (Business) Management? Laying the Ground for a Philosophy of Management
abstract: This article critically examines the foundational question of what constitutes business management, moving beyond prevailing political and control-oriented paradigms to lay the groundwork for a philosophy of management. By juxtaposing ancient and contemporary definitions, the study challenges the self-evident conceptualization of management as mere managerial power or mechanism of control. Employing an explorative and confrontational philosophical method, the paper identifies limitations in traditional theories and introduces a framework comprising six dimensions—management control, people management, asset management and entrepreneurial action, participation, responsive action, and constituting meaning—that collectively capture the multifaceted nature of business management. This framework aims to open new avenues for philosophical and empirical inquiry, encouraging a more nuanced understanding of management that transcends reductionist models and addresses its broader organizational, social, and ethical implications.

title: TWO-PERIOD GREEN'S FUNCTION IN STATISTICAL PHYSICS
abstract: Various aspects of the application of Green's functions in statistical physics are reviewed, and the future applications of two-period functions (retarding and advancing) are analyzed. The principle properties of the two- period Green's function and their simplest application in irreversible process theory, in the theory of superconductors, in ferromagnetics, and in electron- lattice reactions in common metals and semiconductors are discussed. It is also shown that the causal Green's functions can be successfully replaced with retarding and advancing Green's functions in the analytical expansion of the complex plane. Statistical mechanics sometimes employs the Motsubara temperature Green's functions which are not related to time; however, they are less adaptable than the temperature-time Green's functions. (R.V.J.)

title: Social Control Theory and Delinquency.
abstract: This dissertation examines the relationship between social control theory and delinquency, with a focus on extending Travis Hirschi’s influential model by incorporating the effects of educational experiences and social class background. Drawing on longitudinal data from the Marion County Youth Study, which followed a panel of male high school juniors from 1964 to 1967, the research replicates and expands upon Hirschi’s findings regarding the formation and stability of the social bond in adolescence. The study finds that while the social bond is initially formed within the family, its elements can change over time in response to school experiences and class position. Contrary to Hirschi’s assertion that social class is unrelated to delinquency or bond strength, this research demonstrates significant associations between social class, changes in the social bond, and rates of delinquent behavior. The results suggest that both primary group socialization and secondary institutional factors such as educational policies play important roles in shaping adolescent delinquency, highlighting the need for a more comprehensive model of social control that accounts for broader structural influences.

title: On the Economics and Biology of Trust
abstract: This paper examines the multifaceted nature of trust by integrating insights from economics and biology, focusing on its definition, measurement, and causal role in economic outcomes. Employing a behavioral definition rooted in preferences and beliefs, the study reviews experimental, neurobiological, and genetic evidence to demonstrate that trust is not merely a function of risk-taking or beliefs about others’ trustworthiness, but is also shaped by social preferences such as betrayal aversion. The analysis highlights that both survey and behavioral measures of trust are influenced by individual risk attitudes and social preferences, and that differences in national and ethnic trust can be traced to variations in these underlying factors. The paper also addresses the endogeneity of trust beliefs and critically evaluates existing empirical approaches to establishing the causal impact of trust on aggregate economic variables. Despite substantial progress in understanding the determinants and correlates of trust, the paper concludes that robust evidence for its independent causal effect on economic performance remains elusive, underscoring the need for further research using more rigorous identification strategies.

title: Handbook of constructionist research
abstract: The Handbook of Constructionist Research, edited by James A. Holstein and Jaber F. Gubrium, offers a comprehensive exploration of the diverse and evolving field of constructionist inquiry within sociology and related disciplines. Rather than seeking to rigidly define constructionism, the volume presents a mosaic of theoretical, methodological, and empirical contributions that collectively illustrate the versatility and richness of constructionist approaches. Spanning historical context, multidisciplinary perspectives, epistemological debates, and practical strategies, the handbook addresses key areas such as identity, health, gender, race, ethnicity, and national belonging through a constructionist lens. Notable sections highlight innovative methodologies like autoethnography and examine the social processes underlying medical knowledge and expertise. The final part engages with ongoing challenges and intersections with other research paradigms, stimulating critical reflection on the future directions of constructionist research. While some emerging topics are underrepresented, the handbook remains an essential resource for scholars and doctoral students seeking to deepen their understanding of social construction and to innovate within sociological research methodologies.

title: Host Biology in Light of the Microbiome: Ten Principles of Holobionts and Hologenomes
abstract: The holobiont and hologenome concepts redefine animals and plants as integrated units comprising hosts and their symbiotic microbes, challenging traditional, nucleocentric views of biology. This essay synthesizes historical and contemporary perspectives to articulate ten foundational principles that clarify the nature, scope, and implications of holobionts and hologenomes. These principles distinguish holobionts from other biological assemblages, position the hologenome as a comprehensive gene system, and highlight the roles of both selection and neutrality in shaping host-microbe associations. The framework extends classical evolutionary theory by incorporating intergenomic interactions, mechanisms of inheritance beyond Mendelian genetics, and multilevel selection. By providing a predictive and testable foundation, this work aims to unify subdisciplines across the life sciences and catalyze hypothesis-driven research that fully integrates microbiology into our understanding of host biology.

title: 'Translanguaging' as a socially just pedagogy
abstract: This article examines translanguaging as a socially just pedagogy within the context of South African higher education, where English dominance perpetuates colonial legacies and disadvantages multilingual students. Drawing on theoretical frameworks of decoloniality and language as a social practice, the authors analyze the implementation of translanguaging pedagogies in an introductory course at the University of Cape Town. Through lecturer reflections, classroom practices, and student assessments, the study demonstrates how translanguaging empowers students marginalized by English monolingualism, fosters greater participation, and affirms linguistic identities. The findings highlight positive student responses and suggest that multilingual pedagogies are essential for addressing structural inequalities and advancing social justice in postcolonial educational settings.

title: Systems biology and genomics of breast cancer.
abstract: Breast cancer is now recognized as a heterogeneous disease comprising multiple subtypes with distinct molecular and clinical characteristics. Systems biology approaches, particularly gene expression profiling using DNA microarrays, have enabled the identification of intrinsic breast cancer subtypes—luminal A, luminal B, HER2-enriched, basal-like, and normal breast-like—which are conserved across populations and stages of disease. These subtypes, defined by unique gene expression signatures and validated across numerous independent datasets, correlate strongly with hormone receptor status, genetic alterations, prognosis, and response to therapy. The development of robust classification tools such as the Single Sample Predictor and the PAM50 gene set has facilitated reproducible subtype assignment in clinical samples, including formalin-fixed tissues. Understanding the biology underlying each subtype has revealed key differences in tumor behavior, genetic mutations, and therapeutic vulnerabilities, underscoring the importance of molecular taxonomy in guiding personalized breast cancer management and advancing research into tumor progression and metastasis.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology

title: Avogadro: an advanced semantic chemical editor, visualization, and analysis platform
abstract: The Avogadro project has developed an advanced molecule editor and visualizer designed for cross-platform use in computational chemistry, molecular modeling, bioinformatics, materials science, and related areas. It offers flexible, high quality rendering, and a powerful plugin architecture. Typical uses include building molecular structures, formatting input files, and analyzing output of a wide variety of computational chemistry packages. By using the CML file format as its native document type, Avogadro seeks to enhance the semantic accessibility of chemical data types.ResultsThe work presented here details the Avogadro library, which is a framework providing a code library and application programming interface (API) with three-dimensional visualization capabilities; and has direct applications to research and education in the fields of chemistry, physics, materials science, and biology. The Avogadro application provides a rich graphical interface using dynamically loaded plugins through the library itself. The application and library can each be extended by implementing a plugin module in C++ or Python to explore different visualization techniques, build/manipulate molecular structures, and interact with other programs. We describe some example extensions, one which uses a genetic algorithm to find stable crystal structures, and one which interfaces with the PackMol program to create packed, solvated structures for molecular dynamics simulations. The 1.0 release series of Avogadro is the main focus of the results discussed here.ConclusionsAvogadro offers a semantic chemical builder and platform for visualization and analysis. For users, it offers an easy-to-use builder, integrated support for downloading from common databases such as PubChem and the Protein Data Bank, extracting chemical data from a wide variety of formats, including computational chemistry output, and native, semantic support for the CML file format. For developers, it can be easily extended via a powerful plugin mechanism to support new features in organic chemistry, inorganic complexes, drug design, materials, biomolecules, and simulations. Avogadro is freely available under an open-source license from http://avogadro.openmolecules.net.

title: TWO-PERIOD GREEN'S FUNCTION IN STATISTICAL PHYSICS
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of two-period (two-time) Green's functions within the framework of statistical physics, emphasizing their foundational role in the study of systems with a large number of interacting particles. Building on the formalism of quantum field theory, the work introduces temperature-dependent two-time Green's functions—causal, retarded, and advanced—as generalizations of correlation functions, highlighting their advantages for calculating observable quantities and constructing equations of motion. The spectral representations of these functions are discussed, demonstrating their utility in addressing the challenges posed by continuous energy spectra and large system sizes, where traditional perturbation theory encounters difficulties. The paper explores applications to the theory of irreversible processes, ideal quantum gases, superconductivity, ferromagnetism, and electron-lattice interactions in metals and semiconductors. By employing two-time retarded and advanced Green's functions instead of conventional causal functions, the approach facilitates analytic continuation in the complex plane and provides a unified framework for tackling a wide range of problems in quantum statistical mechanics. The results underscore the effectiveness and versatility of two-period Green's function methods for analyzing equilibrium and nonequilibrium phenomena in many-body systems.

title: A conceptual framework for integrated STEM education
abstract: The global urgency to improve STEM education may be driven by environmental and social impacts of the twenty-first century which in turn jeopardizes global security and economic stability. The complexity of these global factors reach beyond just helping students achieve high scores in math and science assessments. Friedman (The world is flat: A brief history of the twenty-first century, 2005) helped illustrate the complexity of a global society, and educators must help students prepare for this global shift. In response to these challenges, the USA experienced massive STEM educational reforms in the last two decades. In practice, STEM educators lack cohesive understanding of STEM education. Therefore, they could benefit from a STEM education conceptual framework. The process of integrating science, technology, engineering, and mathematics in authentic contexts can be as complex as the global challenges that demand a new generation of STEM experts. Educational researchers indicate that teachers struggle to make connections across the STEM disciplines. Consequently, students are often disinterested in science and math when they learn in an isolated and disjoined manner missing connections to crosscutting concepts and real-world applications. The following paper will operationalize STEM education key concepts and blend learning theories to build an integrated STEM education framework to assist in further researching integrated STEM education.

title: Introduction to chemical engineering thermodynamics
abstract: This comprehensive text provides a foundational and advanced exploration of chemical engineering thermodynamics, systematically covering the principles, laws, and applications essential to the discipline. Beginning with fundamental concepts such as energy, work, heat, and state functions, the book progresses through the first and second laws of thermodynamics, volumetric properties of pure fluids, heat effects, and entropy. It addresses the thermodynamic properties of fluids, flow processes, power generation from heat, refrigeration, and liquefaction. The treatment extends to solution thermodynamics, phase equilibria, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE), and chemical-reaction equilibria, integrating theoretical frameworks with practical applications. Emphasis is placed on the use of equations of state, property correlations, and computational methods for analyzing real-world chemical processes. The text is supported by extensive tables, diagrams, and example problems to facilitate understanding and application in engineering practice. This work serves as both an instructional resource for students and a reference for practicing engineers seeking a thorough grounding in chemical engineering thermodynamics.

title: Pedagogical content knowledge in science education: perspectives and potential for progress
abstract: Pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), since its inception as teacher‐specific professional knowledge, has been researched extensively. Drawing on a wide range of literature, this paper seeks to clarify how the potential offered by PCK could be utilised to further develop science teacher education. An analysis of PCK models proposed by various researchers, together with methods of elucidating PCK in experienced and novice teachers, is provided. The paper argues that making PCK more explicit in the teacher education process may help novices adjust to teaching, as well as aiding experienced teachers in developing more reflective practices.

title: Energy band-gap engineering of graphene nanoribbons.
abstract: We investigate electronic transport in lithographically patterned graphene ribbon structures where the lateral confinement of charge carriers creates an energy gap near the charge neutrality point. Individual graphene layers are contacted with metal electrodes and patterned into ribbons of varying widths and different crystallographic orientations. The temperature dependent conductance measurements show larger energy gaps opening for narrower ribbons. The sizes of these energy gaps are investigated by measuring the conductance in the nonlinear response regime at low temperatures. We find that the energy gap scales inversely with the ribbon width, thus demonstrating the ability to engineer the band gap of graphene nanostructures by lithographic processes.

title: Biostimulants in Plant Science: A Global Perspective
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive global analysis of plant biostimulants, examining their diverse origins, mechanisms of action, and roles in enhancing plant productivity and stress resilience. The paper traces the historical development of biostimulant science, clarifies conceptual definitions to distinguish biostimulants from fertilizers, plant growth regulators, and protective compounds, and highlights the challenges posed by their complex compositions and undefined modes of action. Emphasizing the importance of efficacy and safety validation over precise mechanistic elucidation, the authors advocate for a science-based framework for biostimulant classification, regulation, and application. The review synthesizes methodological advances, including chemical characterization, agronomic trials, and -omics technologies, and underscores the potential of biostimulants to uncover novel biological pathways and contribute to sustainable agricultural innovation.

title: The Physics of Cosmic Acceleration
abstract: The discovery of cosmic acceleration has fundamentally challenged our understanding of gravity and the large-scale dynamics of the universe, prompting a surge of theoretical and observational research in cosmology and fundamental physics. This review summarizes the evidence for accelerated expansion, primarily from supernovae, cosmic microwave background measurements, and large-scale structure surveys, and explores leading theoretical frameworks proposed to explain it. The simplest explanation invokes a cosmological constant, but its unnaturally small value relative to quantum field theory expectations motivates alternatives such as dynamical dark energy (e.g., quintessence, mass-varying neutrinos, phantom energy) and modifications to general relativity (including scalar-tensor theories, f(R) gravity, and braneworld models). Each scenario introduces new parameters or fine-tuning issues and raises the coincidence problem regarding the timing of acceleration. The review discusses how current and future experiments—probing the expansion history, growth of structure, and potential deviations from Lorentz invariance—can help discriminate among these models. Ultimately, resolving the physics of cosmic acceleration will require both deeper theoretical insight and more precise observational data to determine whether the phenomenon arises from new energy components or a breakdown of general relativity on cosmological scales.

title: Plasma physics of liquids—A focused review
abstract: The interaction of plasma with liquids has led to various established industrial implementations as well as promising applications, including high-voltage switching, chemical analysis, nanomaterial synthesis, and plasma medicine. Along with these numerous accomplishments, the physics of plasma in liquid or in contact with a liquid surface has emerged as a bipartite research field, for which we introduce here the term “plasma physics of liquids.” Despite the intensive research investments during the recent decennia, this field is plagued by some controversies and gaps in knowledge, which might restrict further progress. The main difficulties in understanding revolve around the basic mechanisms of plasma initiation in the liquid phase and the electrical interactions at a plasma-liquid interface, which require an interdisciplinary approach. This review aims to provide the wide applied physics community with a general overview of the field, as well as the opportunities for interdisciplinary research on topics, such as nanobubbles and the floating water bridge, and involving the research domains of amorphous semiconductors, solid state physics, thermodynamics, material science, analytical chemistry, electrochemistry, and molecular dynamics simulations. In addition, we provoke awareness of experts in the field on yet underappreciated question marks. Accordingly, a strategy for future experimental and simulation work is proposed.

title: Engineering and the Problem of Moral Overload
abstract: When thinking about ethics, technology is often only mentioned as the source of our problems, not as a potential solution to our moral dilemmas. When thinking about technology, ethics is often only mentioned as a constraint on developments, not as a source and spring of innovation. In this paper, we argue that ethics can be the source of technological development rather than just a constraint and technological progress can create moral progress rather than just moral problems. We show this by an analysis of how technology can contribute to the solution of so-called moral overload or moral dilemmas. Such dilemmas typically create a moral residue that is the basis of a second-order principle that tells us to reshape the world so that we can meet all our moral obligations. We can do so, among other things, through guided technological innovation.

title: The Virtues and Vices of Equilibrium and the Future of Financial Economics
abstract: The use of equilibrium models in economics springs from the desire for parsimonious models of economic phenomena that take human reasoning into account. This approach has been the cornerstone of modern economic theory. We explain why this is so, extolling the virtues of equilibrium theory; then we present a critique and describe why this approach is inherently limited, and why economics needs to move in new directions if it is to continue to make progress. We stress that this shouldn't be a question of dogma, but should be resolved empirically. There are situations where equilibrium models provide useful predictions and there are situations where they can never provide useful predictions. There are also many situations where the jury is still out, i.e., where so far they fail to provide a good description of the world, but where proper extensions might change this. Our goal is to convince the skeptics that equilibrium models can be useful, but also to make traditional economists more aware of the limitations of equilibrium models. We sketch some alternative approaches and discuss why they should play an important role in future research in economics.

title: Physics and financial economics (1776–2014): puzzles, Ising and agent-based models
abstract: This review traces the historical and conceptual interplay between physics and financial economics from the late 18th century to the present, highlighting how physical models and concepts have informed economic thought and vice versa. It examines key puzzles in financial economics, such as the volatility smile and excess volatility, through the contrasting lenses of economics and physics. The paper explores the application of the Ising model and its generalizations to social and financial systems, drawing analogies between statistical mechanics (e.g., Boltzmann factor, logit models) and decision-making in markets. Recent developments including quantum decision theory and agent-based models (ABMs) are discussed as powerful tools for capturing heterogeneity, out-of-equilibrium dynamics, and collective phenomena such as bubbles and crashes. The review introduces the “Emerging Market Intelligence Hypothesis” to reconcile persistent market inefficiencies with near-efficient outcomes, and argues that evolutionary biology is increasingly influential in modeling financial markets. Overall, the paper underscores the value of interdisciplinary approaches—particularly those rooted in complex systems science—for understanding the adaptive, dynamic, and often unpredictable nature of financial markets.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Discrete convex analysis: A tool for economics and game theory
abstract: This paper introduces discrete convex analysis as a foundational framework for addressing economic and game-theoretic models characterized by indivisibilities. Discrete convex analysis extends classical convex analysis to discrete settings, distinguishing between M-convexity and L-convexity for functions on integer or binary domains and elucidating their conjugacy relationship. A central insight is the equivalence between M-concavity and the gross substitutes property, which underpins key results in market equilibrium theory. The paper surveys fundamental theorems such as discrete separation and fixed point theorems, demonstrating their implications for equilibrium existence and the lattice structure of price vectors. Additionally, it highlights algorithmic developments, including iterative auction mechanisms derived from discrete convex analysis, and explores applications to matching markets, assignment problems, and submodular flows. By providing rigorous definitions, structural results, and computational tools, this work establishes discrete convex analysis as a versatile and powerful tool for economic theory and combinatorial optimization in environments with discrete choices.

title: Ultracold atomic gases in optical lattices: mimicking condensed matter physics and beyond
abstract: We review recent developments in the physics of ultracold atomic and molecular gases in optical lattices. Such systems are nearly perfect realisations of various kinds of Hubbard models, and as such may very well serve to mimic condensed matter phenomena. We show how these systems may be employed as quantum simulators to answer some challenging open questions of condensed matter, and even high energy physics. After a short presentation of the models and the methods of treatment of such systems, we discuss in detail, which challenges of condensed matter physics can be addressed with (i) disordered ultracold lattice gases, (ii) frustrated ultracold gases, (iii) spinor lattice gases, (iv) lattice gases in “artificial” magnetic fields, and, last but not least, (v) quantum information processing in lattice gases. For completeness, also some recent progress related to the above topics with trapped cold gases will be discussed. Motto: There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, Than are dreamt of in your philosophy 1

title: Engineering precision nanoparticles for drug delivery
abstract: Engineered nanoparticles offer significant potential to enhance drug delivery by overcoming biological barriers and improving therapeutic specificity. Despite extensive research and advances in nanoparticle design, clinical translation has been limited by challenges such as interspecies physiological differences, patient heterogeneity, and incomplete understanding of nanoparticle interactions in complex biological environments. Recent innovations in nanoparticle engineering—including the development of lipid-based, polymeric, and inorganic nanoparticles with tailored architectures and bioresponsive features—have enabled more precise targeting, improved stability, and controlled release of therapeutics. These advances align with the goals of precision medicine by facilitating individualized treatment strategies that account for genetic, environmental, and pathological variability among patients. This review discusses the progress in nanoparticle technologies for drug delivery, highlights strategies to address translational barriers, and emphasizes the importance of rational nanoparticle design to optimize both general and patient-specific therapeutic outcomes. The integration of biomaterials science and precision medicine principles is poised to drive the next generation of clinically effective nanomedicines for applications including cancer therapy, immunomodulation, and gene editing.

title: Adiabatic quantum computation is equivalent to standard quantum computation
abstract: We prove that adiabatic quantum computation, in which a quantum system evolves under a slowly varying local Hamiltonian, is polynomially equivalent to the standard quantum circuit model. Specifically, we construct an efficient adiabatic simulation of any quantum algorithm, demonstrating that both models have the same computational power. This equivalence extends to physically realistic settings involving particles on a two-dimensional grid with nearest-neighbor interactions and to sparse Hamiltonians, making the results broadly applicable. Our findings provide a new perspective for designing quantum algorithms and studying fault tolerance by relating algorithmic questions to spectral properties of Hermitian matrices, thereby connecting quantum computation with areas such as mathematical physics, expander theory, and Markov chains. This work establishes adiabatic computation as a universal model for quantum computing and motivates further exploration of its practical and theoretical advantages.
venue: 45th Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science

title: Oligodendrocytes: biology and pathology
abstract: Oligodendrocytes are the myelinating cells of the central nervous system (CNS). They are the end product of a cell lineage which has to undergo a complex and precisely timed program of proliferation, migration, differentiation, and myelination to finally produce the insulating sheath of axons. Due to this complex differentiation program, and due to their unique metabolism/physiology, oligodendrocytes count among the most vulnerable cells of the CNS. In this review, we first describe the different steps eventually culminating in the formation of mature oligodendrocytes and myelin sheaths, as they were revealed by studies in rodents. We will then show differences and similarities of human oligodendrocyte development. Finally, we will lay out the different pathways leading to oligodendrocyte and myelin loss in human CNS diseases, and we will reveal the different principles leading to the restoration of myelin sheaths or to a failure to do so.

title: A review of metasurfaces: physics and applications
abstract: Metamaterials are composed of periodic subwavelength metal/dielectric structures that resonantly couple to the electric and/or magnetic components of the incident electromagnetic fields, exhibiting properties that are not found in nature. This class of micro- and nano-structured artificial media have attracted great interest during the past 15 years and yielded ground-breaking electromagnetic and photonic phenomena. However, the high losses and strong dispersion associated with the resonant responses and the use of metallic structures, as well as the difficulty in fabricating the micro- and nanoscale 3D structures, have hindered practical applications of metamaterials. Planar metamaterials with subwavelength thickness, or metasurfaces, consisting of single-layer or few-layer stacks of planar structures, can be readily fabricated using lithography and nanoprinting methods, and the ultrathin thickness in the wave propagation direction can greatly suppress the undesirable losses. Metasurfaces enable a spatially varying optical response (e.g. scattering amplitude, phase, and polarization), mold optical wavefronts into shapes that can be designed at will, and facilitate the integration of functional materials to accomplish active control and greatly enhanced nonlinear response. This paper reviews recent progress in the physics of metasurfaces operating at wavelengths ranging from microwave to visible. We provide an overview of key metasurface concepts such as anomalous reflection and refraction, and introduce metasurfaces based on the Pancharatnam–Berry phase and Huygens’ metasurfaces, as well as their use in wavefront shaping and beam forming applications, followed by a discussion of polarization conversion in few-layer metasurfaces and their related properties. An overview of dielectric metasurfaces reveals their ability to realize unique functionalities coupled with Mie resonances and their low ohmic losses. We also describe metasurfaces for wave guidance and radiation control, as well as active and nonlinear metasurfaces. Finally, we conclude by providing our opinions of opportunities and challenges in this rapidly developing research field.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Between activism and science: Grassroots concepts for sustainability coined by Environmental Justice Organizations
abstract: This paper examines the emergence and evolution of key sustainability concepts developed by Environmental Justice Organizations (EJOs) since the early 1980s, highlighting their dual role as both activists and contributors to political ecology. Drawing on collaborative research projects and case studies, the authors trace how EJOs have coined and popularized terms such as environmental justice, ecological debt, popular epidemiology, environmental racism, climate justice, food sovereignty, and others, which have subsequently influenced academic research and policy discourse. The analysis explores the contexts in which these grassroots concepts arose, their definitions, and the interconnections among them, demonstrating a dynamic process of mutual reinforcement between activism and scholarship. The paper argues that this iterative exchange has led to the co-production of a social science of sustainability rooted in activist knowledge, advancing both theoretical understanding and practical action for environmental justice.

title: Polymer Science and Technology
abstract: At least dozens of good introductory textbooks on polymer science and engineering are now available. Why then has yet another book been written? The decision was based on my belief that none of the available texts fully addresses the needs of students in chemical engineering. It is not that chemical engineers are a rare breed, but rather that they have special training in areas of thermodynamics and transport phenomena that is seldom challenged by texts designed primarily for students of chemistry or materials science. This has been a frustration of mine and of many of my students for the past 15 years during which I have taught an introductory course, Polymer Technology, to some 350 chemical engineering seniors. In response to this perceived need, I had written nine review articles that appeared in the SPE publication Plastics Engineering from 1982 to 1984. These served as hard copy for my students to supplement their classroom notes but fell short of a complete solution. In writing this text, it was my objective to first provide the basic building blocks of polymer science and engineering by coverage of fundamental polymer chemistry and materials topics given in Chapters 1 through 7. As a supplement to the traditional coverage of polymer thermodynamics, extensive discussion of phase equilibria, equation-of- state theories, and UNIFAC has been included in Chapter 3. Coverage of rheology, including the use of constitutive equations and the modeling of simple flow geometries, and the fundamentals of polymer processing operations are given in Chapter 11. Finally, I wanted to provide information on the exciting new materialsnowavailable and the emerging areas of technological growth that could motivate a new generation of scientists and engineers. For this reason, engineering and specialty polymers are surveyed in Chapter 10 and important new applications for polymers in separations (membrane separations), electronics (conducting polymers), biotechnology (controlled drug release), and other specialized areas of engineering are given in Chapter 12. In all, this has been an ambitious undertaking and I hope that I have succeeded in at least some of these goals. Although the intended audience for this text is advanced undergraduates and graduate students in chemical engineering, the coverage of polymer science fundamentals (Chapters 1 through 7) should be suitable for a semester course in a materials science or chemistry curriculum. Chapters 8 through 10 intended as survey chapters of the principal categories of polymers commodity thermoplastics and fibers, network polymers (elastomers and thermosets), and engineering and specialty polymers may be included to supplement and reinforce the material presented in the chapters on fundamentals and should serve as a useful reference source for the practicing scientist or engineer in the plastics industry.

title: Deep Learning and Its Application to LHC Physics
abstract: Machine learning has played an important role in the analysis of high-energy physics data for decades. The emergence of deep learning in 2012 allowed for machine learning tools which could adeptly handle higher-dimensional and more complex problems than previously feasible. This review is aimed at the reader who is familiar with high-energy physics but not machine learning. The connections between machine learning and high-energy physics data analysis are explored, followed by an introduction to the core concepts of neural networks, examples of the key results demonstrating the power of deep learning for analysis of LHC data, and discussion of future prospects and concerns.
venue: Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science

title: Attosecond physics at the nanoscale
abstract: Attosecond physics at the nanoscale represents a rapidly emerging field at the intersection of ultrafast laser science and nanotechnology, enabling the exploration of electron dynamics on attosecond temporal and nanometer spatial scales. This report provides a comprehensive overview of recent experimental and theoretical advances in understanding how intense, ultrashort laser pulses interact with nanosystems such as metallic and dielectric nanostructures. Key topics include the generation and characterization of spatially inhomogeneous near-fields, their impact on fundamental processes like above-threshold ionization and high-order harmonic generation, and the development of advanced techniques such as attosecond streaking and waveform-controlled electron emission imaging. The interplay between localized plasmonic fields and strong-field phenomena is examined, alongside discussions of fabrication methods for nanoscale targets and the theoretical frameworks required to describe electron dynamics in these complex environments. The review highlights open questions, challenges, and future prospects for atto-nanophysics, emphasizing its potential to unlock new regimes of light-matter interaction and drive technological innovations in ultrafast science.
venue: Reports on progress in physics. Physical Society

title: Effects and treatment methods of acupuncture and herbal medicine for premenstrual syndrome/premenstrual dysphoric disorder: systematic review
abstract: This systematic review evaluated the efficacy and safety of acupuncture and herbal medicine in the treatment of premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) by analyzing randomized controlled trials published between 2002 and 2012. Nineteen studies met inclusion criteria, comprising eight on acupuncture and eleven on various herbal medicines, including Vitex Agnus castus, Hypericum perforatum, Xiao yao san, Elsholtzia splendens, Cirsium japonicum, and Ginkgo biloba L. The interventions demonstrated significant improvement in PMS/PMDD symptoms, with most studies reporting a 50% or greater reduction in symptom severity compared to baseline. No serious adverse events were associated with either acupuncture or herbal medicine treatments.
