abstract: This review provides a comprehensive overview of natural hydrogels and their applications in regenerative medicine, emphasizing their synthesis, characterization, and functional properties. Natural hydrogels, derived from protein-based materials such as collagen, elastin, fibrin, and silk fibroin, as well as polysaccharide-based materials like glycosaminoglycans, alginate, and chitosan, offer significant advantages including biocompatibility, biodegradability, and similarity to native extracellular matrix. The review discusses various methods for hydrogel preparation—both chemical and physical crosslinking—and highlights the importance of characterizing mechanical properties, swelling behavior, and degradation kinetics to tailor hydrogels for specific biomedical uses. Additionally, the incorporation of decellularized tissues into hydrogels is explored for its potential to preserve bioactive molecules that promote cell growth and tissue regeneration. Despite challenges such as limited mechanical strength and batch-to-batch variability, natural hydrogels remain highly versatile platforms for applications in drug delivery, tissue engineering, and cell culture systems. The article concludes by summarizing recent advances and future perspectives in the development of natural hydrogels for regenerative medicine.
venue: Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Medicine

title: Diffusion of synthetic biology: a challenge to biosafety
abstract: Synthetic biology aims to simplify the engineering of biological systems, enabling broader participation and accelerating innovation. However, this democratization and “de-skilling” of biotechnology pose significant biosafety challenges, as individuals outside traditional scientific disciplines gain access to powerful tools for creating self-replicating organisms. The rise of interdisciplinary practitioners and “biohackers,” often lacking formal biosafety training or regulatory oversight, increases the risk of accidental or deliberate misuse, including home-based genetic engineering and the potential for illicit production of drugs and other substances. Existing strategies such as biosafety education, specialized manuals, and expanded institutional oversight may mitigate risks within professional settings but are insufficient for unregulated environments. As synthetic biology continues to diffuse, urgent development and implementation of robust safety standards are essential to address the unprecedented risks to public health, the environment, and security.
venue: Journal of Systems and Synthetic Biology

title: Employability attributes and personality preferences of postgraduate business management students
abstract: This study investigates the relationship between employability attributes and personality preferences among postgraduate business management students in South Africa. Employability attributes, encompassing career self-management, cultural competence, and self-efficacy, are increasingly recognized as essential for graduates navigating a dynamic and uncertain labor market. Using a quantitative survey design, data were collected from 304 early career adults enrolled in an Honours business management program at an open distance learning institution. The Employability Attributes Scale and the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (Form M) were administered to assess participants’ employability-related competencies and personality preferences, respectively. Correlational and multiple regression analyses revealed significant associations between specific personality preferences and employability attributes, highlighting the influence of dispositional factors on proactive career behaviors. The findings underscore the importance for career counselors and human resource practitioners to consider personality preferences in supporting students’ and employees’ career development and employability. This research contributes to the literature on career meta-competencies by providing insights into how personality shapes employability, offering practical implications for organizational career development interventions in multicultural contexts.

title: Engineering BioBrick vectors from BioBrick parts
abstract: The underlying goal of synthetic biology is to make the process of engineering biological systems easier. Recent work has focused on defining and developing standard biological parts. The technical standard that has gained the most traction in the synthetic biology community is the BioBrick standard for physical composition of genetic parts. Parts that conform to the BioBrick assembly standard are BioBrick standard biological parts. To date, over 2,000 BioBrick parts have been contributed to, and are available from, the Registry of Standard Biological Parts.ResultsHere we extended the same advantages of BioBrick standard biological parts to the plasmid-based vectors that are used to provide and propagate BioBrick parts. We developed a process for engineering BioBrick vectors from BioBrick parts. We designed a new set of BioBrick parts that encode many useful vector functions. We combined the new parts to make a BioBrick base vector that facilitates BioBrick vector construction. We demonstrated the utility of the process by constructing seven new BioBrick vectors. We also successfully used the resulting vectors to assemble and propagate other BioBrick standard biological parts.ConclusionWe extended the principles of part reuse and standardization to BioBrick vectors. As a result, myriad new BioBrick vectors can be readily produced from all existing and newly designed BioBrick parts. We invite the synthetic biology community to (1) use the process to make and share new BioBrick vectors; (2) expand the current collection of BioBrick vector parts; and (3) characterize and improve the available collection of BioBrick vector parts.

title: Researching and Practicing Positive Psychology in Second/Foreign Language Learning and Teaching: The Past, Current Status and Future Directions
abstract: This conceptual review examines the evolution, current landscape, and future directions of positive psychology in second and foreign language (L2) learning and teaching. Drawing on the broaden-and-build theory of positive emotions, the paper highlights how positive psychological constructs—such as academic engagement, emotion regulation, enjoyment, grit, loving pedagogy, resilience, and well-being—contribute to more effective and fulfilling L2 educational experiences. The review traces the shift from a traditional focus on negative emotions like anxiety and burnout to a more balanced perspective that recognizes the interplay between positive and negative affect in language education. It synthesizes key theoretical frameworks and recent empirical advances, identifies underexplored areas such as positive institutions, and discusses practical implications for educators and stakeholders aiming to foster flourishing language learning environments. The paper concludes with recommendations for future research to address existing gaps and further integrate positive psychology principles into L2 education.

title: Radiation Oncology Physics: A Handbook for Teachers and Students
abstract: This book, published in 2005 by the International Atomic Energy Agency, is a comprehensive compendium of all of the topics that should be covered by a radiation oncology physics course, from basic physics to dosimetry, commissioning and quality assurance of equipment, treatment planning and radiation protection and safety. It has an extensive section on brachytherapy, some basic radiation biology and a chapter on special procedures and techniques. As a handbook, as opposed to a textbook, it contains a large number of useful data tables and basic formulae, but in places it does not go deep enough into the issues that are of current concern in the radiotherapy physics community. It has a comprehensive review of various calibration methods for both photon and electron beams, but it does not reproduce the basic tables of the most recent protocols. It also has a reasonably up to date review of the various radiation distribution algorithms employed by modern treatment planning systems, but it does not discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the various approaches. In general, it is a little disappointing that such a recent publication is not more focused on new developments in radiotherapy and their implications for the physicists' workload. The section on radiation producing equipment is historically inclusive of somewhat outdated models, but it hardly touches on the newer developments, such as cyclotrons or synchrotrons for proton therapy. Multi-leaf Collimators are not even included in this chapter, despite their wide availability, confining them to the special techniques chapter. Virtual simulators are presented alongside conventional ones, but their impact on the treatment planning process is not discussed. The Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy Section in the otherwise comprehensive section on special procedures is inadequate. Given its great and wide impact on recent practice, one would have expected the Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy Section to warrant a chapter of its own, with a detailed discussion on the associated quality assurance and its analysis. References to the up and coming heavy particle therapy, such as neutrons, protons and carbon ions, and their physical characteristics, are very sparse. In summary, this book is a worthwhile addition to the library of any university or hospital department of medical physics, but has a slightly dated feel despite its age.

title: Gold nanoparticles for biology and medicine.
abstract: Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) have emerged as versatile platforms in biology and medicine due to their unique size- and shape-dependent properties, ease of synthesis, and capacity for diverse surface functionalization. This review summarizes recent advances in the synthesis of AuNPs, methods for their bioconjugation with ligands such as citrate, amines, nucleic acids, peptides, antibodies, and lipids, and their applications in cellular systems. AuNPs have enabled the development of highly sensitive assays for biodetection and diagnostics, and their ability to enter living cells has opened new avenues for therapeutic applications including gene regulation, drug delivery, imaging, and photoresponsive therapies. The distinct physical and chemical characteristics of gold nanoconjugates confer advantages over traditional molecular systems, offering improved cellular uptake, stability, and multifunctionality. Key challenges remain in understanding cellular interactions, optimizing surface chemistry for specific applications, and addressing cytotoxicity concerns. Continued research into the design and biological interface of AuNPs is expected to drive further innovations in nanomedicine.

title: Emerging learning environments in engineering education
abstract: Three major challenges, sustainability, the fourth industrial revolution, and employability, will require new types of engineering programs, to help students develop skills in cross-disciplinarity, complexity, and contextual understanding. Future engineering students should be able to understand the needs for technological, sustainable solutions in context. The engineering graduates should be able to act in complex and chaotic situations. The question is how engineering institutions are responding now and how they should respond in the future. This article analyses the general responses from engineering education over the last 20 years. These responses are student-centred learning, integration of theory and practice, digital and online learning, and the definition of professional competencies. Examples are given of institutions that are already applying several of these components in the curriculum. On the long-term horizon, more personalised curriculum models are emerging based on students developing and documenting their own learning and career trajectories, as part of their lifelong learning strategy.

title: Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics
abstract: This article introduces the second special issue of the Geoengineering Model Intercomparison Project (GeoMIP), highlighting its evolution, achievements, and ongoing challenges in understanding climate model responses to solar geoengineering. Building on the first special issue, which primarily addressed idealized scenarios such as abrupt CO2 increases offset by solar irradiance reduction, the second issue expands the scope to include marine cloud brightening and other geoengineering techniques. The paper reviews advances in multi-model experiments, particularly those examining sea spray injections and their effects on albedo and climate controllability. It also discusses persistent uncertainties, the need for deeper exploration of hydrologic, cryospheric, and extreme event impacts, and the importance of standardized protocols for robust inter-model comparisons. The article concludes by outlining future directions for GeoMIP and the broader field of geoengineering research, emphasizing the project's unique role in revealing model commonalities and differences under coordinated scenarios.

title: Bioorthogonal chemistry: fishing for selectivity in a sea of functionality.
abstract: The study of biomolecules in their native environments is a challenging task because of the vast complexity of cellular systems. Technologies developed in the last few years for the selective modification of biological species in living systems have yielded new insights into cellular processes. Key to these new techniques are bioorthogonal chemical reactions, whose components must react rapidly and selectively with each other under physiological conditions in the presence of the plethora of functionality necessary to sustain life. Herein we describe the bioorthogonal chemical reactions developed to date and how they can be used to study biomolecules.

title: Reconciling evidence-based medicine and precision medicine in the era of big data: challenges and opportunities
abstract: The convergence of high-throughput technologies, advanced bioinformatics, and empowered patients is transforming medicine by enabling the collection and analysis of vast, multidimensional health datasets. This evolution underpins precision medicine, which aims to tailor healthcare to individual variability, yet presents significant challenges when contrasted with the established paradigm of evidence-based medicine that relies on population-level data and generalized recommendations. This paper explores the conceptual and practical tensions between these approaches, highlighting the inadequacy of one-size-fits-all solutions for individual outliers and advocating for a synergistic model that integrates both frameworks. Achieving evidence-based precision medicine will require global data sharing, standardized clinical bioinformatics, and updated training for healthcare professionals. The authors argue that overcoming these challenges will shift healthcare from reactive treatment to proactive prevention, fostering improved patient outcomes, citizen-centered care, and sustained well-being in the era of big data.

title: PEG Hydrogels for the Controlled Release of Biomolecules in Regenerative Medicine
abstract: Polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels have emerged as versatile platforms for the controlled release of biomolecules in regenerative medicine due to their tunable physicochemical properties and excellent biocompatibility. This review examines the fundamental gelation mechanisms of PEG hydrogels, including chain-growth, step-growth, and mixed-mode polymerizations, and discusses how these influence network structure, degradation, and release kinetics. Critical design considerations such as gel crosslinking density, incorporation of functional moieties, and strategies for loading and preserving bioactive molecules are addressed in the context of optimizing therapeutic efficacy and minimizing adverse reactions. The article highlights advances in spatiotemporal control of biomolecule delivery, hybrid hydrogel systems, and PEG-based matrices engineered to direct stem cell fate. By integrating recent developments with established principles, this review provides a comprehensive perspective on the current challenges and future directions for PEG hydrogels in facilitating targeted, sustained delivery of therapeutics for tissue regeneration.

title: The Matthew effect in environmental science publication: A bibliometric analysis of chemical substances in journal articles
abstract: This study investigates the distribution of research attention among environmental chemicals in scientific literature, examining whether a Matthew effect—where well-studied substances continue to dominate research—exists in environmental science publications. Using bibliometric analysis of 119,636 articles from 78 major journals published between 2000 and 2009, we identified 760,056 Chemical Abstract Service (CAS) number links and ranked chemicals by publication frequency. Results reveal that the top-20 substances, primarily metals and persistent organic pollutants, accounted for 12% of all CAS links, with each covered by thousands of articles over the decade. In contrast, chemicals prioritized by regulatory agencies due to insufficient documentation received minimal research attention. The prominence of top chemicals was only weakly associated with publication in high-impact journals, though some achieved high citation rates. These findings suggest a self-reinforcing bias in environmental science literature that favors already well-studied chemicals, potentially at the expense of emerging or less-documented hazards, thereby limiting innovation and impeding societal needs for comprehensive risk assessment.

title: Deep Mining: A Rock Engineering Challenge
abstract: Increasing demand for metals caused by global economic growth and exploitation of shallow mineral deposits forces mineral extraction to go deeper. A direct consequence of this development is an increase in rock pressure-related mining problems. The role of rock engineering in the design and operation of deep mines is discussed in detail. Critical issues are the rock fracturing around mining excavations, the support and control of the fractured rock, and the rock mechanics design of mine infrastructure and extraction (stoping) systems. Progress of the science of rock mechanics in the areas related to these issues is highlighted and critically examined. Specific areas are the prediction and assessment of the mechanical properties of rock mass, the mechanics of controlling fractured rock around deep mining excavations and the resulting demands on support systems. Rock engineering aspects of stoping systems and the regional stress changes resulting from the extraction of large mineral bodies are discussed in detail. The progress in design concepts for open stopes and stopes with caving of the roof strata is illustrated. It is shown that the stress environment in deep mines does not favour the highly productive caving systems of stoping. The value of energy-based design concepts for very deep mines exploiting tabular mineral deposits is shown. Despite the considerable progress that has been made in the science of rock mechanics since the 1950s, progress in applying this knowledge to solve rock pressure problems in deep mines has been rather slow. The tools are available. What is needed is the development of robust design criteria for mine infrastructure, excavations and support systems for dynamic and changing stress environments. The second critical issue is the lack of highly qualified rock engineering personnel on the mines. This has been recognized by the European mining industry through supporting a continued education programme in rock engineering for deep mines.

title: Personalized medicine and human genetic diversity.
abstract: Human genetic diversity plays a critical role in understanding disease susceptibility, evolutionary history, and the development of personalized medicine. This paper reviews the evolution of scientific thought regarding human genetic variation, from early 20th-century theories and biased physical measurements to modern genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and next-generation sequencing. Landmark discoveries, such as the ABO blood group system and Lewontin’s demonstration that most genetic diversity exists within rather than between populations, have shifted perspectives on race and genetics. The paper highlights how both rare and common genetic variants contribute to disease risk and treatment response, using examples like sickle cell anemia, Tay–Sachs disease, and hepatitis C. It also addresses the limitations of current genomics research, which is disproportionately focused on populations of European ancestry, potentially exacerbating health disparities. The authors argue that a comprehensive understanding of human genetic diversity is essential for advancing medical genetics, reducing health inequities, and realizing the full potential of personalized medicine.
venue: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Medicine

title: The Materials Science beamline upgrade at the Swiss Light Source
abstract: The Materials Science beamline at the Swiss Light Source underwent a major upgrade with the replacement of its original wiggler source by a state-of-the-art in-vacuum cryogenically cooled permanent-magnet undulator (CPMU), enabling access to higher photon energies and significantly increased brilliance in a medium-energy storage ring. This paper details the design, implementation, and performance of the new U14 undulator and associated beamline components, including redesigned front-end and X-ray optics optimized for the reduced beam divergence and enhanced coherent fraction. The upgrade supports advanced experimental techniques such as coherent X-ray diffraction imaging and micro Laue diffraction, while also improving flux, energy resolution, and beam stability for powder and surface diffraction applications. Performance metrics post-upgrade demonstrate substantial gains in photon flux and energy range, establishing the upgraded beamline as a versatile platform for cutting-edge materials science research.

title: Green supply chain management practices and performance
abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this study is to examine the deployment of pro‐active and re‐active practices in the implementation of green supply chain management (GSCM) and analyze their impact on environmental, economic, and intangible performance by considering business strategy as organizational focus.Design/methodology/approach – Data were collected from a sample of 190 ISO 14001 certified manufacturing companies in Thailand and used to test the research hypotheses. Factor analysis was used to examine the construct validity while multivariate linear regression was used to test criteria validity.Findings – The threat of legislation and regulation (re‐active practices) was a consideration that resulted in companies enhancing their environmental, economic, and intangible performance. Reverse logistics practices (pro‐active practices) had low levels of adoption and do not have a significant impact on GSCM performance.Research limitations/implications – This study did not consider some aspects of organizationa...

title: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine
abstract: New knowledge drives medical progress and improves patient care. The rapid growth of this knowledge in skin diseases and skin biology makes publication of the eighth edition of Fitzpatrick's Dermatology in General Medicine (DIGM) particularly timely. Forty years ago, the first edition of “Fitz” was a critical textbook devoted to providing a comprehensive knowledge of dermatology. The relevance of dermatology to general medicine and the basic science foundations of the specialty were defining elements of the new text. This edition, more than ever, reinforces those earlier goals and is designed to be easily accessible to those interested in the clinical and basic science of dermatology. This reference text also highlights the relevance of dermatology to general internal medicine and other disciplines of medicine and surgery. It is written for experienced clinicians and skin biologists worldwide as well as for those in training.

title: Cosmology and Fundamental Physics with the Euclid Satellite
abstract: Euclid is a European Space Agency medium-class mission selected for launch in 2019 within the Cosmic Vision 2015–2025 program. The main goal of Euclid is to understand the origin of the accelerated expansion of the universe. Euclid will explore the expansion history of the universe and the evolution of cosmic structures by measuring shapes and red-shifts of galaxies as well as the distribution of clusters of galaxies over a large fraction of the sky.Although the main driver for Euclid is the nature of dark energy, Euclid science covers a vast range of topics, from cosmology to galaxy evolution to planetary research. In this review we focus on cosmology and fundamental physics, with a strong emphasis on science beyond the current standard models. We discuss five broad topics: dark energy and modified gravity, dark matter, initial conditions, basic assumptions and questions of methodology in the data analysis.This review has been planned and carried out within Euclid’s Theory Working Group and is meant to provide a guide to the scientific themes that will underlie the activity of the group during the preparation of the Euclid mission.

title: Constructivism: reflections on twenty five years teaching the constructivist approach in medical education
abstract: This paper reflects on twenty-five years of teaching the constructivist approach in medical education, exploring its theoretical foundations, practical implications, and connections to related domains such as communication, psychotherapy, and neuroscience. The author argues that constructivism, rooted in the work of Kant, Piaget, and Vygotsky, provides a unifying framework for understanding learning as an active process in which new knowledge is assimilated through interaction with prior knowledge. The paper highlights the parallels between constructivist learning and scientific reasoning, particularly the hypothetico-deductive method, and demonstrates how this model underpins clinical diagnostic reasoning in medicine. Emphasis is placed on the importance of recognizing students’ pre-existing mental models and the role of imagination in resolving cognitive dissonance. The discussion suggests that constructivism offers valuable insights for medical educators by promoting active engagement, critical thinking, and adaptive expertise in learners. The author concludes that constructivism remains a robust and integrative approach for guiding educational practice in medicine and beyond.

title: Nickel-catalyzed cross-couplings involving carbon-oxygen bonds.
abstract: Nickel-Catalyzed Cross-Couplings Involving Carbon-Oxygen Bonds Brad M. Rosen, Kyle W. Quasdorf, Daniella A. Wilson, Na Zhang, Ana-Maria Resmerita, Neil K. Garg,* and Virgil Percec* Roy & Diana Vagelos Laboratories, Department of Chemistry, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19104-6323, United States Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California, Los Angeles, California 90095, United States

title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
abstract: This systematic review examines the landscape of research on artificial intelligence (AI) applications in higher education, with a particular focus on the involvement of educators. Analyzing 146 articles published between 2007 and 2018, the study finds that most research originates from computer science and STEM disciplines, employing predominantly quantitative methods. Four primary areas of AI application are identified: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalization, and intelligent tutoring systems. The review highlights a notable lack of critical engagement with ethical challenges, risks, and pedagogical theories within the literature. The findings underscore the need for greater educator involvement and deeper exploration of ethical, theoretical, and educational dimensions to ensure meaningful integration of AI in higher education contexts.
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education

title: Personal Knowledge: Towards a post-critical philosophy
abstract: This paper advances a post-critical philosophy of knowledge by challenging the traditional dichotomy between objectivity and subjectivity, arguing that all knowing is inherently personal and rooted in tacit, embodied skills. Through a systematic exploration of concepts such as probability, order, intellectual passions, and conviviality, the work contends that scientific inquiry and human understanding are shaped by personal commitment and active participation rather than detached observation. The analysis critiques the logic of doubt and affirms the necessity of personal involvement in the justification of knowledge claims. By articulating the tacit dimension of knowing and emphasizing the creative, communal, and existential aspects of knowledge, the paper proposes a new framework for epistemology that integrates personal experience with rational affirmation, ultimately redefining what it means to know and to be.

title: The chemistry of isoindole natural products
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive overview of the chemistry of isoindole natural products, focusing on their structural diversity, biological activities, and synthetic approaches. Isoindole scaffolds, present in both oxidized and reduced forms, are found in a range of natural products including indolocarbazoles, macrocyclic polyketides, aporhoeadane alkaloids, meroterpenoids, and anthraquinone-type alkaloids. The article discusses key examples such as staurosporine and rebeccamycin, highlighting their biosynthetic origins from tryptophan derivatives and their significant roles as protein kinase inhibitors and antitumor agents. Synthetic strategies for constructing the isoindole core, including Diels–Alder reactions and recent enantioselective methods, are examined alongside notable total syntheses. The review also addresses the application of isoindole derivatives as dyes and analytical markers. By elucidating the molecular structures, biosynthetic pathways, and synthetic methodologies of these compounds, this work underscores the importance of isoindole natural products in medicinal chemistry and inspires further research into their chemical biology and therapeutic potential.

title: Handbook of freshwater fishery biology
abstract: This handbook provides a comprehensive compilation of tabular data on the growth, length-weight relationships, condition indices, fecundity, and life histories of freshwater fish species found in the United States and Canada. Designed as a reference source for conservationists, biologists, and researchers, it consolidates widely scattered fishery information from both published and unpublished sources to facilitate comparative studies and bibliographical research. The handbook includes detailed instructions for interpreting tables, addresses methodological variations in fish measurement, and highlights the importance of sample size and statistical analysis in evaluating population data. By systematically organizing species-specific data and offering conversion tables and bibliographic codes, this work aims to support efficient access to essential fishery biology information while encouraging further publication of unpublished data and careful application of summarized findings across diverse aquatic environments.

title: Adipose tissue engineering for soft tissue regeneration.
abstract: Current treatment modalities for soft tissue defects caused by various pathologies and trauma include autologous grafting and commercially available fillers. However, these treatment methods present a number of challenges and limitations, such as donor-site morbidity and volume loss over time. As such, improved therapeutic modalities need to be developed. Tissue engineering techniques offer novel solutions to these problems through development of bioactive tissue constructs that can regenerate adipose tissue in both structure and function. Recently, a number of studies have been designed to explore various methods to engineer human adipose tissue. This review will focus on these developments in the area of adipose tissue engineering for soft tissue replacement. The physiology of adipose tissue and current surgical therapies used to replace lost tissue volume, specifically in breast tissue, are introduced, and current biomaterials, cell sources, and tissue culture strategies are discussed. We discuss future areas of study in adipose tissue engineering.

title: A typology of Indigenous engagement in Australian environmental management: Implications for knowledge integration and social-ecological system sustainability
abstract: Indigenous peoples now engage with many decentralized approaches to environmental management that offer opportunities for integration of Indigenous Ecological Knowledge (IEK) and western science to promote cultural diversity in the management of social-ecological system sustainability. Nevertheless, processes of combining IEK with western science are diverse and affected by numerous factors, including the adaptive co-management context, the intrinsic characteristics of the natural resources, and the governance systems. We present a typology of Indigenous engagement in environmental management, derived through comparative analysis of 21 Australian case studies, and consider its implications for the integration of IEK with western science. Sociological and rational choice institutionalism underpin our analytical framework, which differentiates on three axes: (1) power sharing, incorporating decision making, rules definition, resource values and property rights; (2) participation, incorporating participatory processes, organizations engaged, and coordination approaches; (3) intercultural purpose, incorporating purposes of environmental management, Indigenous engagement, Indigenous development and capacity building. Our typology groups engagement into four types: Indigenous governed collaborations; Indigenous-driven co-governance; agency-driven co-governance; and agency governance. From our analysis of manifestations of knowledge integration across the types, we argue that Indigenous governance and Indigenous-driven co-governance provides better prospects for integration of IEK and western science for sustainability of social-ecological systems. Supporting Indigenous governance without, or with only a limited requirement for power sharing with other agencies sustains the distinct Indigenous cultural purposes underpinning IEK, and benefits knowledge integration. We conclude by advocating that the typology be applied to test its general effectiveness in guiding practitioners and researchers to develop robust governance for Indigenous knowledge integration in environmental management.

title: In situ click chemistry generation of cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors
abstract: Cyclooxygenase-2 isozyme is a promising anti-inflammatory drug target, and overexpression of this enzyme is also associated with several cancers and neurodegenerative diseases. The amino-acid sequence and structural similarity between inducible cyclooxygenase-2 and housekeeping cyclooxygenase-1 isoforms present a significant challenge to design selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors. Herein, we describe the use of the cyclooxygenase-2 active site as a reaction vessel for the in situ generation of its own highly specific inhibitors. Multi-component competitive-binding studies confirmed that the cyclooxygenase-2 isozyme can judiciously select most appropriate chemical building blocks from a pool of chemicals to build its own highly potent inhibitor. Herein, with the use of kinetic target-guided synthesis, also termed as in situ click chemistry, we describe the discovery of two highly potent and selective cyclooxygenase-2 isozyme inhibitors. The in vivo anti-inflammatory activity of these two novel small molecules is significantly higher than that of widely used selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors.Traditional inflammation and pain relief drugs target both cyclooxygenase 1 and 2 (COX-1 and COX-2), causing severe side effects. Here, the authors use in situ click chemistry to develop COX-2 specific inhibitors with high in vivo anti-inflammatory activity.

title: The physics of financial networks
abstract: This paper addresses the longstanding challenge of achieving energy stability in global radial basis function (RBF) methods for linear advection problems, particularly in the presence of boundary conditions. Traditional RBF approaches that strongly enforce boundary conditions often suffer from stability issues, leading to unreliable numerical solutions. To overcome this, we propose two novel RBF schemes that weakly enforce boundary conditions: one inspired by flux reconstruction (FR) techniques and another based on simultaneous approximation terms (SATs). We rigorously prove that both methods are energy stable for linear advection equations and demonstrate their conservation properties. Numerical experiments in one and two spatial dimensions, for both scalar equations and systems, validate the theoretical findings and highlight the advantages and limitations of each approach. Our results establish a foundation for more robust RBF methods and reveal connections to classical finite difference and finite element schemes, paving the way for further advancements in stable numerical methods for partial differential equations.

title: On the application of x-ray microtomography in the field of materials science
abstract: This paper presents the principles and applications of x-ray microtomography in materials science, highlighting its ability to provide non-destructive, three-dimensional imaging at both medium (10 μm) and high (1 μm) resolutions. The technique is demonstrated through examples involving metallic foams, model metal matrix composites reinforced with spherical particles, and high-resolution studies of aluminum alloys. For low-absorbent materials, the use of phase contrast with synchrotron radiation is shown to enhance image quality. The study also discusses the quantitative analysis enabled by microtomography, including its integration with in-situ tensile testing and its use in characterizing the initial microstructure of various structural materials. Overall, x-ray microtomography is established as a powerful tool for investigating the internal structure and properties of materials in a non-destructive manner.

title: Science friction: Data, metadata, and collaboration
abstract: When scientists from two or more disciplines work together on related problems, they often face what we call ‘science friction’. As science becomes more data-driven, collaborative, and interdisciplinary, demand increases for interoperability among data, tools, and services. Metadata – usually viewed simply as ‘data about data’, describing objects such as books, journal articles, or datasets – serve key roles in interoperability. Yet we find that metadata may be a source of friction between scientific collaborators, impeding data sharing. We propose an alternative view of metadata, focusing on its role in an ephemeral process of scientific communication, rather than as an enduring outcome or product. We report examples of highly useful, yet ad hoc, incomplete, loosely structured, and mutable, descriptions of data found in our ethnographic studies of several large projects in the environmental sciences. Based on this evidence, we argue that while metadata products can be powerful resources, usually they must be supplemented with metadata processes. Metadata-as-process suggests the very large role of the ad hoc, the incomplete, and the unfinished in everyday scientific work.

title: Evoked potentials in clinical medicine.
abstract: Recent technological advances have facilitated the conduct of evoked potential studies, and permitted their wider use in a clinical context. Evoked potential studies are performed to determine the presence, extent and site of disease of the peripheral and central sensory pathways. This may be helpful for diagnostic purposes, and for characterizing more completely the changes occurring in various diseases. Certain evoked potential components have also been used in the evaluation of cognitive function. The major uses and limitations of evoked potential studies in clinical medicine are reviewed, but technical details are not provided in the interest of simplicity.

title: A materials-science perspective on tackling COVID-19
abstract: This review examines the pivotal role of materials science in addressing the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting how advances in materials have enabled breakthroughs in viral detection, protection, and treatment. The authors discuss the development of imaging and microfluidic technologies for real-time investigation of viral structure and transmission, as well as material-based platforms for rapid and accurate virus detection and targeted drug and vaccine delivery. The review details contributions to personal protective equipment design and the creation of low-cost diagnostic devices, emphasizing the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration. Looking forward, the paper explores future opportunities for materials science in antiviral research, including synthetic platforms for organoids and organs-on-a-chip, improved drug delivery systems, and scalable production of medical equipment. The authors argue that materials-science-based technologies are essential not only for combating SARS-CoV-2 but also for preparing for future viral outbreaks by enabling universal platforms for understanding, protecting against, detecting, and treating infectious diseases.

title: Quantifying the Impoverishing Effects of Purchasing Medicines: A Cross-Country Comparison of the Affordability of Medicines in the Developing World
abstract: This study assesses the impoverishing effects of purchasing essential medicines in 16 low- and middle-income countries by quantifying the proportion of the population pushed below international poverty lines (US$1.25 and US$2 per day) after buying four commonly used medicines. Using standardized facility-based price surveys and World Bank household expenditure data, the analysis reveals that medicine purchases can impoverish significant portions of national populations, with up to 86% affected in some settings. Originator brand medicines are consistently less affordable than lowest-priced generics, with marked differences observed in countries such as the Philippines. The findings highlight the widespread unaffordability of essential medicines and underscore the urgent need for policy interventions to promote access, including increased use of quality-assured generics and expansion of health insurance coverage.

title: Polymeric nanofibers in tissue engineering.
abstract: Polymeric nanofibers have emerged as versatile scaffolds in tissue engineering due to their structural similarity to extracellular matrix components, high surface area for cell attachment, and capacity for bioactive factor delivery. This review examines the primary fabrication methods—electrospinning, phase separation, and self-assembly—highlighting how each technique influences fiber diameter, alignment, porosity, mechanical properties, and degradation profiles. The ability to tailor these characteristics enables the design of scaffolds optimized for specific tissue engineering applications. The review also discusses strategies for incorporating bioactive molecules into nanofibers to enhance cellular responses and tissue regeneration. Applications in bone, cartilage, ligament and tendon, cardiovascular, and neural tissue engineering are explored, demonstrating the broad utility of polymeric nanofibers. Overall, advances in nanofiber fabrication and functionalization continue to expand their potential as biomimetic scaffolds for regenerative medicine.

title: Avogadro: an advanced semantic chemical editor, visualization, and analysis platform
abstract: Avogadro is an advanced, open-source molecular editor and visualization platform designed to address the limitations of existing chemical software by providing a flexible, extensible, and cross-platform solution for computational chemistry, molecular modeling, bioinformatics, and materials science. Utilizing a robust plugin architecture and supporting both C++ and Python, Avogadro enables users and developers to build, manipulate, and analyze molecular structures with high-quality three-dimensional rendering and semantic data support via the Chemical Markup Language (CML) file format. The platform integrates with widely used libraries such as Qt and Open Babel, offers native support for multiple operating systems, and facilitates interoperability with other scientific software. Avogadro’s modular design allows for rapid extension to new domains, including drug design, materials science, and biomolecular simulations, while its user-friendly interface supports tasks such as structure building, input/output formatting for computational packages, and data extraction from public databases. Freely available under an open-source license, Avogadro represents a significant advancement in accessible chemical informatics tools for both research and education.

title: Fat-Tailed Uncertainty in the Economics of Catastrophic Climate Change
abstract: In this article, I revisit some basic issues concerning structural uncertainty and catastrophic climate change. My target audience here are general economists, so this article could also be viewed as a somewhat less technical exposition that supplements my previous work. Using empirical examples, I argue that it is implausible that low-probability, high-negative impact events would not much influence an economic analysis of climate change. I then try to integrate the empirical examples and the theory together into a unified package with a unified message that the possibility of catastrophic climate change needs to be taken seriously.
venue: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy

title: Multicomponent reactions
abstract: Chemistry as a central science is facing a steadily increasing demand for new chemical entities (NCE). Innovative solutions, in all kinds of disciplines that depend on chemistry, require new molecules with specific properties, and their societal consequences are fundamental and pioneering. However, NCE not only demand a realistic structural space but also their feasibility poses challenges to synthetic chemists. Nowadays the question of how to perform a synthesis has become most crucial.

title: Physics, Astrophysics and Cosmology with Gravitational Waves
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of gravitational wave astronomy, examining the fundamental physics of gravitational waves, their interaction with detectors, and the operational principles of current and planned detection technologies. It surveys the primary astrophysical and cosmological sources of gravitational waves, including binary systems, black holes, neutron stars, and stochastic backgrounds, and details the data analysis techniques used to extract weak signals from noisy measurements. The review explores the profound implications of gravitational wave observations for testing general relativity, probing the properties of compact objects, investigating stellar evolution, and measuring cosmological parameters. By synthesizing recent advances in detector sensitivity and outlining future prospects, this work highlights the transformative potential of gravitational waves for advancing our understanding of physics, astrophysics, and cosmology.

title: Dental pulp stem cells: function, isolation and applications in regenerative medicine
abstract: Dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) are a unique population of mesenchymal stem cells derived from the neural crest, residing within the dental pulp and exhibiting the capacity for self-renewal and multilineage differentiation. Their primary physiological role involves the generation of odontoblasts for reparative dentin formation, contributing to tooth homeostasis and repair. DPSCs can be efficiently isolated from both permanent and deciduous teeth using enzymatic digestion or tissue outgrowth methods, with advances in culture techniques enabling expansion and cryopreservation for future clinical use. Compared to bone marrow stromal cells, DPSCs display distinct phenotypic markers and enhanced neuroglial differentiation potential, broadening their applicability beyond dental tissue regeneration. In regenerative medicine, DPSCs have demonstrated promise in dental pulp and dentin regeneration, bone repair, neural regeneration, and angiogenesis, supported by in vivo studies showing their ability to generate dentin-pulp-like complexes and vascularized tissues. The accessibility of DPSCs from discarded teeth, their robust proliferative capacity, and their versatility in tissue engineering underscore their significant potential as an autologous cell source for a wide range of regenerative therapies.
venue: Journal of Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Medicine

title: Economics of Crime
abstract: This paper starts with a review the economics of criminal behavior. Then, the authors discuss the theory of public enforcement. The economic analysis of criminal behavior and criminal law has been a hugely successful enterprise. As an academic enterprise, it has achieved the goal of research—it has generated a large and growing literature. More important than academic success, however, has been the influence of this branch of learning on actual practice. The understanding of deterrence effects and rational responses by criminals has substantially changed the purpose and functioning of the criminal justice system.

title: Intrinsically Disordered Proteins and Their “Mysterious” (Meta)Physics
abstract: Recognition of the natural abundance and functional importance of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and hybrid proteins containing ordered and intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDPRs) is changing protein science. IDPs and IDPRs; i.e., functional proteins and protein regions without unique structures, are commonly found in all organisms, where they have crucial roles in various biological processes. Disorder-based functionality complements functions of ordered proteins and domains. However, by virtue of their existence, IDPs/IDPRs, which are characterized by the remarkable conformational flexibility and structural plasticity, break multiple rules elaborated over the years to explain structure, folding, and functionality of well-folded proteins with unique structures. Despite the general believe, which dominated in protein science for more than a century, that unique biological functions of proteins require unique 3D-structures, structure-less IDPs/IDPRs are functional, being able to perform impossible tricks and to be engaged in biological activities, which are improbable for ordered proteins. With their exceptional spatio-temporal heterogeneity and high conformational flexibility, IDPs/IDPRs represent complex systems that act at the edge of chaos and are specifically tunable by various means. In this article, some of the wanders of intrinsic disorder are discussed as illustrations of their ‘mysterious’ (meta)physics.

title: Teachers’ perception of STEM integration and education: a systematic literature review
abstract: For schools to include quality STEM education, it is important to understand teachers’ beliefs and perceptions related to STEM talent development. Teachers, as important persons within a student’s talent development, hold prior views and experiences that will influence their STEM instruction. This study attempts to understand what is known about teachers’ perceptions of STEM education by examining existing literature.ResultsStudy inclusion criteria consisted of empirical articles, which aligned with research questions, published in a scholarly journal between 2000 and 2016 in English. Participants included in primary studies were preK-12 teachers. After quality assessment, 25 articles were included in the analysis. Thematic analysis was used to find themes within the data. Findings indicate that while teachers value STEM education, they reported barriers such as pedagogical challenges, curriculum challenges, structural challenges, concerns about students, concerns about assessments, and lack of teacher support. Teachers felt supports that would improve their effort to implement STEM education included collaboration with peers, quality curriculum, district support, prior experiences, and effective professional development.ConclusionsRecommendations for practice include quality in-service instruction over STEM pedagogy best practices and district support of collaboration time with peer teachers. Recommendations for future research are given.

title: Evidence based medicine: a movement in crisis?
abstract: Trisha Greenhalgh and colleagues argue that, although evidence based medicine has had many benefits, it has also had some negative unintended consequences. They offer a preliminary agenda for the movement’s renaissance, refocusing on providing useable evidence that can be combined with context and professional expertise so that individual patients get optimal treatment

title: Physics of thin-film ferroelectric oxides
abstract: This review provides a comprehensive account of recent advances in the physics of thin-film ferroelectric oxides, with a focus on phenomena unique to the thin-film form. The authors discuss the development and application of ferroelectric thin films in electronic devices, addressing key physical mechanisms that influence device performance and failure, such as polarization switching, domain-wall motion, and conduction processes. The review highlights significant progress in first-principles computational approaches for understanding ferroelectric behavior at the atomic scale, particularly as film thickness approaches the nanoscale. The critical impact of strain imposed by substrates on epitaxial thin films is examined, revealing how strain engineering can modify ferroelectric properties. Finally, emerging directions in nanoscale ferroelectrics are explored, including quantum confinement effects and novel geometries such as ferroelectric nanotubes. By integrating experimental findings with theoretical insights, this work elucidates the interplay between structure, properties, and device functionality in thin-film ferroelectric oxides, offering guidance for future research and technological applications.

title: Naturally occurring anti-cancer compounds: shining from Chinese herbal medicine
abstract: Chinese herbal medicine is a rich source of naturally occurring compounds with significant anti-cancer activities, including anti-proliferative, pro-apoptotic, anti-metastatic, and anti-angiogenic effects, as well as the ability to regulate autophagy, reverse multidrug resistance, modulate immunity, and enhance chemotherapy. This review systematically summarizes recent advances since 2011 in the pharmacological effects, mechanisms of action, clinical studies, and innovative therapeutic applications of key bioactive compounds such as curcumin, epigallocatechin gallate, berberine, artemisinin, ginsenoside Rg3, ursolic acid, silibinin, emodin, triptolide, cucurbitacin B, tanshinone I, oridonin, shikonin, gambogic acid, artesunate, wogonin, β-elemene, and cepharanthine. Additional promising agents including dihydroartemisinin, ginsenoside Rh2, compound K, cucurbitacins D/E/I, tanshinone IIA and cryptotanshinone are also discussed for their emerging roles in cancer therapy. The review highlights both the advantages and limitations of these compounds across various cancer types and emphasizes the need for further research into their immunomodulatory effects and mechanisms as immune checkpoint modulators. Despite growing evidence supporting their potential clinical utility, more comprehensive studies are required to fully elucidate their therapeutic value and optimize their integration into modern oncology.

title: Hermione and the Secretary: how gendered task division in introductory physics labs can disrupt equitable learning
abstract: Physics labs provide a unique opportunity for students to grow their physics identity and science identity in general since they provide students with an opportunity to tinker with experiments and analyze data in a low-stakes environment. However, it is important to ensure that all students are benefiting from the labs equally and have a positive growth trajectory. Through interviews and reflexive ethnographic observations, we identify and analyze two common modes of work that may disadvantage female students in introductory physics labs. Students who adopt the Secretary archetype are relegated to recording and analyzing data, and thus may miss out on much of the opportunity to grow their physics and science identities by engaging fully in the experimental work. Meanwhile, students in the Hermione archetype shoulder a disproportionate amount of managerial work, and also may not get an adequate opportunity to engage with different aspects of the experimental work that is essential for helping them develop their physics and science identities. We use a physics identity framework to investigate how students under these modes of work may experience stunted growth in their physics and science identity trajectories in their physics lab course. This stunted growth can then perpetuate and reinforce societal stereotypes and biases about who does physics. Our categorization not only gives a vocabulary to discussions about equity in the physics lab, but may also serve as a useful touchstone for those who seek to center equity in efforts to transform physics instruction.

title: Initial teacher education in England and the Covid-19 pandemic: challenges and opportunities
abstract: This paper explores the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic on initial teacher education (ITE) in England, drawing on interviews with programme leaders from four university providers. The abrupt closure of schools and universities in spring 2020 disrupted traditional school placements and necessitated a rapid shift to online provision, raising significant challenges related to equity, pedagogy, and the balance between practical and theoretical learning. The study finds that while the loss of in-person practicum limited opportunities for classroom experience, it also created space for increased reflection and engagement with educational theory. The authors present a model for digital pedagogy in ITE and argue that the crisis offers a unique opportunity to reconsider the role of practicum within teacher education, suggesting that while practical experience is essential, it may not be sufficient on its own for effective teacher learning. The paper concludes by highlighting both the challenges and new possibilities for ITE as the sector adapts to a post-Covid landscape.

title: Symbolic regression in materials science
abstract: Symbolic regression offers a promising alternative to traditional machine learning approaches for discovering governing relationships in materials science, particularly in the era of big data enabled by advanced experimental and computational techniques. This perspective introduces genetic programming-based symbolic regression (GPSR) and recent methodological advances, highlighting its ability to autonomously identify both the functional form and parameters of models directly from data without prior assumptions. We discuss the limited but growing adoption of symbolic regression in materials science compared to other domains, and illustrate its utility through two case studies: learning the Johnson-Mehl-Avrami-Kolmogorov kinetics law for phase transformations and deriving the Landau free energy functional for structural transitions in perovskite LaNiO₃. The results demonstrate that GPSR can recover established physical laws and provide interpretable models, underscoring its potential as a tool for elucidating complex structure-property relationships. We advocate for broader adoption of symbolic regression techniques in materials research as a means to accelerate scientific discovery and advance the automation of knowledge extraction from large-scale materials datasets.

title: Higher Charmonia
abstract: We present a comprehensive theoretical study of the spectrum, electromagnetic transition rates, and open-charm strong decay amplitudes for all 40 expected charmonium (c̄c) states up to the 4S multiplet, just above 4.4 GeV. The mass spectrum and E1 radiative partial widths (with selected M1 transitions) are calculated using both the relativized Godfrey-Isgur model and a nonrelativistic potential model, incorporating Coulomb plus linear confining potentials with smeared hyperfine interactions. Electromagnetic transitions are evaluated using wavefunctions from these models, while open-flavor strong decay amplitudes are determined via the 3P0 decay model with harmonic oscillator wavefunctions. Our results provide detailed predictions for higher-mass charmonia, addressing current experimental interests such as missing states, the Lorentz structure of confinement, exotic hybrid candidates, and mixing effects with meson continua. These predictions aim to guide and interpret forthcoming high-statistics data from facilities including BES, CLEO, and GSI, thereby advancing the understanding of charmonium spectroscopy above open-charm threshold.

title: The information paradox: a pedagogical introduction
abstract: The black hole information paradox challenges the compatibility of quantum mechanics and general relativity by questioning whether information is lost during black hole evaporation. This pedagogical introduction clarifies the precise formulation of Hawking’s argument, demonstrating that small quantum corrections to Hawking radiation cannot restore unitarity or eliminate entanglement between radiation and the black hole. The analysis formalizes the paradox as a theorem: under standard assumptions of locality and regular physics at the horizon, one is forced to accept either mixed final states or remnants, both of which are problematic. The paper further argues that appeals to AdS/CFT duality do not resolve the paradox within semiclassical gravity. Recent developments in string theory, particularly the fuzzball proposal, suggest that black holes possess a rich microstate structure without traditional horizons, offering a resolution to the paradox and illustrating how classical intuition breaks down in quantum gravitational regimes.

title: Designing the next generation of medicines for malaria control and eradication
abstract: In the fight against malaria new medicines are an essential weapon. For the parts of the world where the current gold standard artemisinin combination therapies are active, significant improvements can still be made: for example combination medicines which allow for single dose regimens, cheaper, safer and more effective medicines, or improved stability under field conditions. For those parts of the world where the existing combinations show less than optimal activity, the priority is to have activity against emerging resistant strains, and other criteria take a secondary role. For new medicines to be optimal in malaria control they must also be able to reduce transmission and prevent relapse of dormant forms: additional constraints on a combination medicine. In the absence of a highly effective vaccine, new medicines are also needed to protect patient populations. In this paper, an outline definition of the ideal and minimally acceptable characteristics of the types of clinical candidate molecule which are needed (target candidate profiles) is suggested. In addition, the optimal and minimally acceptable characteristics of combination medicines are outlined (target product profiles). MMV presents now a suggested framework for combining the new candidates to produce the new medicines. Sustained investment over the next decade in discovery and development of new molecules is essential to enable the long-term delivery of the medicines needed to combat malaria.

title: Quantum computing
abstract: The subject of quantum computing brings together ideas from classical information theory, computer science, and quantum physics. This review aims to summarize not just quantum computing, but the whole subject of quantum information theory. Information can be identified as the most general thing which must propagate from a cause to an effect. It therefore has a fundamentally important role in the science of physics. However, the mathematical treatment of information, especially information processing, is quite recent, dating from the mid-20th century. This has meant that the full significance of information as a basic concept in physics is only now being discovered. This is especially true in quantum mechanics. The theory of quantum information and computing puts this significance on a firm footing, and has led to some profound and exciting new insights into the natural world. Among these are the use of quantum states to permit the secure transmission of classical information (quantum cryptography), the use of quantum entanglement to permit reliable transmission of quantum states (teleportation), the possibility of preserving quantum coherence in the presence of irreversible noise processes (quantum error correction), and the use of controlled quantum evolution for efficient computation (quantum computation). The common theme of all these insights is the use of quantum entanglement as a computational resource. It turns out that information theory and quantum mechanics fit together very well. In order to explain their relationship, this review begins with an introduction to classical information theory and computer science, including Shannon's theorem, error correcting codes, Turing machines and computational complexity. The principles of quantum mechanics are then outlined, and the Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen (EPR) experiment described. The EPR-Bell correlations, and quantum entanglement in general, form the essential new ingredient which distinguishes quantum from classical information theory and, arguably, quantum from classical physics. Basic quantum information ideas are next outlined, including qubits and data compression, quantum gates, the `no cloning' property and teleportation. Quantum cryptography is briefly sketched. The universal quantum computer (QC) is described, based on the Church-Turing principle and a network model of computation. Algorithms for such a computer are discussed, especially those for finding the period of a function, and searching a random list. Such algorithms prove that a QC of sufficiently precise construction is not only fundamentally different from any computer which can only manipulate classical information, but can compute a small class of functions with greater efficiency. This implies that some important computational tasks are impossible for any device apart from a QC. To build a universal QC is well beyond the abilities of current technology. However, the principles of quantum information physics can be tested on smaller devices. The current experimental situation is reviewed, with emphasis on the linear ion trap, high-Q optical cavities, and nuclear magnetic resonance methods. These allow coherent control in a Hilbert space of eight dimensions (three qubits) and should be extendable up to a thousand or more dimensions (10 qubits). Among other things, these systems will allow the feasibility of quantum computing to be assessed. In fact such experiments are so difficult that it seemed likely until recently that a practically useful QC (requiring, say, 1000 qubits) was actually ruled out by considerations of experimental imprecision and the unavoidable coupling between any system and its environment. However, a further fundamental part of quantum information physics provides a solution to this impasse. This is quantum error correction (QEC). An introduction to QEC is provided. The evolution of the QC is restricted to a carefully chosen subspace of its Hilbert space. Errors are almost certain to cause a departure from this subspace. QEC provides a means to detect and undo such departures without upsetting the quantum computation. This achieves the apparently impossible, since the computation preserves quantum coherence even though during its course all the qubits in the computer will have relaxed spontaneously many times. The review concludes with an outline of the main features of quantum information physics and avenues for future research.

title: Engineering Systems Multiple‐Domain Matrix: An organizing framework for modeling large‐scale complex systems
abstract: The increasing complexity and scale of modern engineering systems, driven by evolving technological, social, and market demands, challenge traditional modeling approaches and require new frameworks for effective analysis and management. This paper introduces the Engineering Systems Multiple-Domain Matrix (ESM), a conceptual and organizing framework designed to address theoretical gaps in representing and understanding large-scale complex systems. Building on a review of systems theory, socio-technical systems, and large technological systems literature, the ESM provides a structured methodology for identifying, tagging, and organizing diverse system information across technical, organizational, and social domains. The framework facilitates holistic knowledge capture, improved visualization, and enhanced discourse among engineers and managers. By enabling better collection, storage, processing, and analysis of systems engineering data, the ESM supports the development of a comprehensive knowledge basis that advances both scholarship and practice in engineering systems modeling.

title: SwissADME: a free web tool to evaluate pharmacokinetics, drug-likeness and medicinal chemistry friendliness of small molecules
abstract: To be effective as a drug, a potent molecule must reach its target in the body in sufficient concentration, and stay there in a bioactive form long enough for the expected biologic events to occur. Drug development involves assessment of absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion (ADME) increasingly earlier in the discovery process, at a stage when considered compounds are numerous but access to the physical samples is limited. In that context, computer models constitute valid alternatives to experiments. Here, we present the new SwissADME web tool that gives free access to a pool of fast yet robust predictive models for physicochemical properties, pharmacokinetics, drug-likeness and medicinal chemistry friendliness, among which in-house proficient methods such as the BOILED-Egg, iLOGP and Bioavailability Radar. Easy efficient input and interpretation are ensured thanks to a user-friendly interface through the login-free website http://www.swissadme.ch. Specialists, but also nonexpert in cheminformatics or computational chemistry can predict rapidly key parameters for a collection of molecules to support their drug discovery endeavours.

title: Balancing Technology, Pedagogy and the New Normal: Post-pandemic Challenges for Higher Education
abstract: This paper examines the post-pandemic challenges facing higher education as institutions seek to balance technology integration and pedagogical innovation within the emerging “new normal.” Drawing on recent literature and expert interviews, the study explores how the forced adoption of emergency remote teaching (ERT) during Covid-19 has prompted educators to reconsider their roles, support for student learning, and perceptions of students as autonomous agents. The analysis distinguishes between ERT and well-designed online learning and teaching (OLT), highlighting the limitations of crisis-driven digitalization and the underdevelopment of pedagogical strategies prior to the pandemic. Findings suggest that while the shift to ERT was often disruptive, it has also fostered openness to blended and flexible learning models. The authors argue that future higher education practices should prioritize pedagogical decision-making over mere digitalization, leveraging lessons from the pandemic to achieve a more harmonious integration of physical and digital tools. Ultimately, the paper advocates for a strategic approach that foregrounds active, meaningful learning and supports both teachers’ and students’ evolving needs in a post-Covid landscape.

title: Systems biology and the virtual physiological human
abstract: This editorial explores the relationship between systems biology and the virtual physiological human (VPH) initiative, highlighting how systems biology serves as a conceptual and methodological approach that integrates reductionist and integrative research across multiple biological scales. The VPH, a major European effort aligned with the international Physiome Project, aims to develop patient-specific computational models for personalized healthcare by treating the human body as a complex, multi-level system. The article discusses the challenges of defining systems biology, emphasizing its role as an approach rather than a discipline, and traces its roots to both historical physiology and recent advances in computational modeling. It argues that systems biology’s strength lies in its ability to unify experimental and computational techniques for quantitative analysis of biological entities and their interactions. The VPH exemplifies this approach by pursuing a 'middle-out' strategy—integrating data and models from genes to the whole organism—to achieve dynamic, multi-scale understanding of human physiology. The editorial concludes that systems biology provides the essential framework for realizing the VPH vision, enabling collaborative, quantitative investigation of biological systems for predictive and personalized medicine.

title: COVID-19 and digital disruption in UK universities: afflictions and affordances of emergency online migration
abstract: COVID-19 has caused the closure of university campuses around the world and migration of all learning, teaching, and assessment into online domains. The impacts of this on the academic community as frontline providers of higher education are profound. In this article, we report the findings from a survey of n = 1148 academics working in universities in the United Kingdom (UK) and representing all the major disciplines and career hierarchy. Respondents report an abundance of what we call ‘afflictions’ exacted upon their role as educators and in far fewer yet no less visible ways ‘affordances’ derived from their rapid transition to online provision and early ‘entry-level’ use of digital pedagogies. Overall, they suggest that online migration is engendering significant dysfunctionality and disturbance to their pedagogical roles and their personal lives. They also signpost online migration as a major challenge for student recruitment, market sustainability, an academic labour-market, and local economies.

title: Emerging learning environments in engineering education
abstract: This paper examines the evolving landscape of engineering education in response to three major challenges: sustainability, the fourth industrial revolution, and employability. It analyzes how these drivers necessitate new educational models that foster cross-disciplinary skills, systems thinking, and contextual understanding. The study reviews trends over the past two decades, highlighting shifts toward student-centered learning, integration of theory and practice, digital and online modalities, and a redefinition of professional competencies. Institutional examples illustrate early adoption of these approaches. The paper also explores the increasing complexity of engineering problems and the need for graduates to operate effectively in complex, interdisciplinary environments. Looking ahead, it identifies emerging personalized curriculum models that support lifelong learning and adaptability. The findings underscore the importance of integrating societal context, digital skills, and human values into engineering curricula to prepare graduates for rapidly changing technological and social landscapes.

title: Aquaporins in clinical medicine.
abstract: The aquaporins are a family of membrane water channels, some of which also transport glycerol. They are involved in a wide range of physiological functions (including water/salt homeostasis, exocrine fluid secretion, and epidermal hydration) and human diseases (including glaucoma, cancer, epilepsy, and obesity). At the cellular level, aquaporin-mediated osmotic water transport across cell plasma membranes facilitates transepithelial fluid transport, cell migration, and neuroexcitation; aquaporin-mediated glycerol transport regulates cell proliferation, adipocyte metabolism, and epidermal water retention. Genetic diseases caused by loss-of-function mutations in aquaporins include nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and congenital cataracts. The neuroinflammatory demyelinating disease neuromyelitis optica is marked by pathogenic autoantibodies against astrocyte water channel aquaporin-4. There remain broad opportunities for the development of aquaporin-based diagnostics and therapeutics. Disease-relevant aquaporin polymorphisms are beginning to be explored. There is great promise in the development of small-molecule aquaporin modulators for therapy of some types of refractory edema, brain swelling, neuroinflammation, glaucoma, epilepsy, cancer, pain, and obesity.

title: Lecture Notes in Economics and Mathematical Systems
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive overview of the book proposal process for the Lecture Notes in Economics and Mathematical Systems series, detailing the required information and guidelines for prospective authors and editors. It outlines the essential components of a successful submission, including author biographies, book descriptions, originality statements, estimated length and figures, table of contents, keywords, unique selling points, and audience analysis. The proposal form emphasizes the importance of search engine optimization (SEO) to maximize discoverability and provides instructions for open access options and competing title analysis. By systematically guiding applicants through each step, this resource aims to streamline the evaluation process for both authors and publishers while ensuring high-quality, targeted academic content for the economics and mathematical systems community.

title: Model-independent constraints on ΔF = 2 operators and the scale of new physics
abstract: We present updated, model-independent constraints on new physics contributions to ΔF = 2 processes using the latest experimental data and a generalized unitarity triangle analysis. By deriving upper bounds on the Wilson coefficients of the most general effective Hamiltonian for ΔF = 2 transitions, we translate these into lower bounds on the scale of new physics.
