Our results show that non-standard operators are significantly more constrained than the Standard Model operator due to enhancements in renormalization group evolution and matrix elements. Consequently, models generating new ΔF = 2 operators, such as those with next-to-minimal flavor violation, require a much higher new physics scale—often beyond the direct reach of the LHC—compared to minimal flavor violation scenarios. This highlights the continued importance of flavor physics as a probe for extensions of the Standard Model.

title: Probing Planck-scale physics with quantum optics
abstract: The search for experimental evidence of quantum gravitational effects remains a central challenge in unifying quantum mechanics and general relativity, as direct access to Planck-scale phenomena is beyond current technological capabilities. This paper proposes a novel quantum optical scheme to probe potential Planck-scale modifications of the canonical commutation relation, which are predicted by various approaches to quantum gravity and manifest as generalized uncertainty principles with a minimal measurable length. By employing optomechanical systems with masses approaching the Planck mass, the protocol enables direct measurement of the commutator of the center-of-mass mode through a sequence of interactions with strong optical fields. The resulting nonlinear enhancement allows deviations from standard quantum mechanics to be mapped onto measurable changes in the optical field, circumventing the need for Planck-scale position sensitivity. The analysis demonstrates that state-of-the-art technology can achieve unprecedented sensitivity to possible deformations of the commutator, opening a feasible pathway for table-top experiments to test quantum gravitational theories and explore the fundamental structure of space-time.

title: Hygiene, Sanitation, and Water: Forgotten Foundations of Health
abstract: Deficiencies in hygiene, sanitation, and water (HSW) remain major but often overlooked contributors to global disease burden, particularly among children in developing countries. This introductory article to a PLoS Medicine series highlights that inadequate HSW is responsible for millions of preventable deaths and a significant proportion of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), primarily through diarrhoeal diseases and malnutrition-related conditions. Despite proven, cost-effective interventions capable of reducing diarrhoeal disease by up to two-thirds, HSW receives insufficient attention from the public health community compared to higher-profile diseases. The paper reviews the extensive health impacts of poor HSW, including its role in infectious diseases, malnutrition, and broader child mortality, and emphasizes the need for effective behaviour change strategies and policy prioritization. The authors argue that the benefits of improving HSW extend beyond health outcomes to economic and social gains, underscoring the critical importance of renewed commitment from health professionals and policymakers to address these foundational determinants of health.

title: Information, physics, quantum: the search for links
abstract: This report reviews what quantum physics and information theory have to tell us about the age-old question, How come existence? No escape is evident from four conclusions: (1) The world cannot be a giant machine, ruled by any preestablished continuum physical law. (2) There is no such thing at the microscopic level as space or time or spacetime continuum. (3) The familiar probability function or functional, and wave equation or functional wave equation, of standard quantum theory provide mere continuum idealizations and by reason of this circumstance conceal the information-theoretic source from which they derive. (4) No element in the description of physics shows itself as closer to primordial than the elementary quantum phenomenon, that is, the elementary device-intermediated act of posing a yes-no physical question and eliciting an answer or, in brief, the elementary act of observer-participancy. Otherwise stated, every physical quantity, every it, derives its ultimate significance from bits, binary yes-or-no indications, a conclusion which we epitomize in the phrase, it from bit. Revolution in outlook though Kepler, Newton, and Einstein brought us [1-4], and still more startling the story of life [5-7] that evolution forced upon an unwilling world, the ultimate shock to preconceived ideas lies ahead, be it a decade hence, a century or a millenium. The overarching principle of 20th-century physics, the quantum [8] — and the principle of complementarity [9] that is central idea of the quantum — leaves us no escape, Niels Bohr tells us, [10] from 'a radical revision of our attitude as regards physical reality' and a 'fundamental modification of all ideas regarding the absolute character of physical phenomena.' Transcending Einstein's summons [11] of 1908, 'This quantum business is so incredibly important and difficult that everyone should busy himself with it,' Bohr's modest words direct us to the supreme goal: Deduce the quantum from an understanding of existence. How make headway toward a goal so great against difficulties so large? The search for understanding presents to us three questions, four no's and five clues:

title: Lange's Handbook of Chemistry
abstract: Lange's Handbook has served as a leading source of reliable chemical information and data for chemists, engineers, and other technical specialists since l934. This encyclopedic work includes authoritative coverage of atomic and molecular structure, organic chemistry (revised), inorganic, analytical, and electro- chemistry, mathematics as applied to chemistry, and more. It also includes nomenclature consistent with recommendations of the IUPAC Commission rules.

title: Direct human cartilage repair using three-dimensional bioprinting technology.
abstract: Current cartilage tissue engineering strategies cannot as yet fabricate new tissue that is indistinguishable from native cartilage with respect to zonal organization, extracellular matrix composition, and mechanical properties. Integration of implants with surrounding native tissues is crucial for long-term stability and enhanced functionality. In this study, we developed a bioprinting system with simultaneous photopolymerization capable for three-dimensional (3D) cartilage tissue engineering. Poly(ethylene glycol) dimethacrylate (PEGDMA) with human chondrocytes were printed to repair defects in osteochondral plugs (3D biopaper) in layer-by-layer assembly. Compressive modulus of printed PEGDMA was 395.73±80.40 kPa, which was close to the range of the properties of native human articular cartilage. Printed human chondrocytes maintained the initially deposited positions due to simultaneous photopolymerization of surrounded biomaterial scaffold, which is ideal in precise cell distribution for anatomic cartilage engineering. Viability of printed human chondrocytes increased 26% in simultaneous polymerization than polymerized after printing. Printed cartilage implant attached firmly with surrounding tissue and greater proteoglycan deposition was observed at the interface of implant and native cartilage in Safranin-O staining. This is consistent with the enhanced interface failure strength during the culture assessed by push-out testing. Printed cartilage in 3D biopaper had elevated glycosaminoglycan (GAG) content comparing to that without biopaper when normalized to DNA. These observations were consistent with gene expression results. This study indicates the importance of direct cartilage repair and promising anatomic cartilage engineering using 3D bioprinting technology.

title: Cultural stereotypes as gatekeepers: increasing girls’ interest in computer science and engineering by diversifying stereotypes
abstract: Despite having made significant inroads into many traditionally male-dominated fields (e.g., biology, chemistry), women continue to be underrepresented in computer science and engineering. We propose that students’ stereotypes about the culture of these fields—including the kind of people, the work involved, and the values of the field—steer girls away from choosing to enter them. Computer science and engineering are stereotyped in modern American culture as male-oriented fields that involve social isolation, an intense focus on machinery, and inborn brilliance. These stereotypes are compatible with qualities that are typically more valued in men than women in American culture. As a result, when computer science and engineering stereotypes are salient, girls report less interest in these fields than their male peers. However, altering these stereotypes—by broadening the representation of the people who do this work, the work itself, and the environments in which it occurs—significantly increases girls’ sense of belonging and interest in the field. Academic stereotypes thus serve as gatekeepers, driving girls away from certain fields and constraining their learning opportunities and career aspirations.

title: Role of platelet-derived growth factors in physiology and medicine.
abstract: Platelet-derived growth factors (PDGFs) and their receptors (PDGFRs) are key regulators of cell proliferation, migration, and survival, serving as paradigms for growth factor and receptor tyrosine kinase biology. This review synthesizes current understanding of PDGF biochemistry, receptor interactions, and signaling mechanisms, highlighting their essential roles in embryonic development, particularly in neural crest formation, organogenesis, and vascular development. Dysregulated PDGF signaling is implicated in a spectrum of human diseases, including cancers, fibrotic disorders, and vascular pathologies, through both autocrine and paracrine mechanisms. The discovery of additional PDGF family members and their evolutionary relationship to vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGFs) has expanded the functional landscape of these ligands across species. Recent advances in pharmacological modulation of PDGF pathways have led to clinical applications in oncology and regenerative medicine, with PDGF antagonists and recombinant ligands showing therapeutic promise. This review provides an integrated overview of PDGF structure-function relationships, developmental and pathological roles, regulatory mechanisms controlling ligand bioavailability, and the translational potential of targeting PDGF signaling in disease.

title: Statistical physics of social dynamics
abstract: Statistical physics has proven to be a fruitful framework to describe phenomena outside the realm of traditional physics. Recent years have witnessed an attempt by physicists to study collective phenomena emerging from the interactions of individuals as elementary units in social structures. A wide list of topics are reviewed ranging from opinion and cultural and language dynamics to crowd behavior, hierarchy formation, human dynamics, and social spreading. The connections between these problems and other, more traditional, topics of statistical physics are highlighted. Comparison of model results with empirical data from social systems are also emphasized.

title: Exposure Science: A View of the Past and Milestones for the Future
abstract: Exposure science has emerged as a critical discipline bridging environmental science and environmental health by quantifying and characterizing human contact with environmental toxicants. This review traces the historical development of exposure science, highlighting its roots in occupational hygiene and its evolution through key milestones such as the establishment of core principles, the creation of professional societies, and the development of exposure assessment models. Advances in understanding activity patterns and behavioral factors have enhanced the field’s ability to define and reduce exposures, informing risk management and public health interventions. Despite its growing relevance, exposure science remains underfunded and underrecognized compared to related fields, limiting its potential impact. The review underscores the need for greater integration of observational studies into epidemiologic research, adoption of innovative tools for hypothesis testing, and expanded training resources to ensure exposure science can fulfill its role in preventing excess risk and protecting public health in increasingly complex environmental contexts.

title: Handbook of Public Communication of Science and Technology
abstract: The third edition of the Handbook of Public Communication of Science and Technology offers a comprehensive and updated overview of the field, integrating interdisciplinary perspectives and global contexts. Edited by Massimiano Bucchi and Brian Trench, this volume features extensively revised chapters and introduces new contributions on enduring topics such as science publics and science-media theories, as well as emerging themes like art-science interactions and the conceptualization of science communication as a cultural and social process. Through its in-depth analyses and diverse viewpoints, the handbook serves as an essential resource for understanding the evolving landscape of how science and technology are communicated to and engaged with by the public.

title: Biological evolution and statistical physics
abstract: This review introduces physicists to the theoretical models and mathematical approaches used to study biological evolution, highlighting the strong parallels with methods from statistical physics. The paper is organized into three independent sections: the first explores evolution on fitness landscapes, covering Fisher’s theorem, adaptive walks, quasispecies models, finite population effects, and neutral evolution; the second examines coevolutionary models, including evolutionary game theory, kin and group selection, sexual selection, speciation, and host-parasite dynamics; the third discusses models of interacting species networks and extinction avalanches. Throughout, the review provides essential biological context, clarifies model assumptions and limitations, and emphasizes the interplay between biological complexity and statistical physics concepts in understanding evolutionary processes.

title: Nitrate radicals and biogenic volatile organic compounds: oxidation, mechanisms, and organic aerosol
abstract: Oxidation of biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOC) by nitrate radicals (NO3) constitutes a significant interface between anthropogenic and natural emissions, influencing regional and global budgets of reactive nitrogen, ozone, and organic aerosol. This review synthesizes three decades of laboratory, field, and modeling research on NO3-BVOC chemistry, emphasizing recent advances in instrumentation, mechanistic understanding, and the formation of organic nitrates and secondary organic aerosol (SOA). Despite progress, key uncertainties persist regarding reaction rates, mechanisms, SOA yields, the role of heterogeneous processes, spatial distributions in the nocturnal boundary layer, and representation in atmospheric models. The review highlights the importance of NO3-BVOC interactions for air quality and climate, identifies critical gaps in current knowledge—particularly concerning SOA production and organic nitrate formation—and outlines research priorities to improve predictive capabilities for atmospheric composition and impacts.

title: Graphene plasmonics
abstract: Two rich and vibrant fields of investigation—graphene physics and plasmonics—strongly overlap. Not only does graphene possess intrinsic plasmons that are tunable and adjustable, but a combination of graphene with noble-metal nanostructures promises a variety of exciting applications for conventional plasmonics. The versatility of graphene means that graphene-based plasmonics may enable the manufacture of novel optical devices working in different frequency ranges—from terahertz to the visible—with extremely high speed, low driving voltage, low power consumption and compact sizes. Here we review the field emerging at the intersection of graphene physics and plasmonics. Many researchers hope to merge plasmonics and graphene photonics to combine their useful features. The properties and characteristics of plasmons on graphene are reviewed. Prospects for possible future applications are discussed.

title: Conducting Polymers for Tissue Engineering.
abstract: Electrically conducting polymers such as polyaniline, polypyrrole, polythiophene, and their derivatives (mainly aniline oligomer and poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)) with good biocompatibility find wide applications in biomedical fields including bioactuators, biosensors, neural implants, drug delivery systems, and tissue engineering scaffolds. This review focuses on these conductive polymers for tissue engineering applications. Conductive polymers exhibit promising conductivity as bioactive scaffolds for tissue regeneration, and their conductive nature allows cells or tissue cultured on them to be stimulated by electrical signals. However, their mechanical brittleness and poor processability restrict their application. Therefore, conductive polymeric composites based on conductive polymers and biocompatible biodegradable polymers (natural or synthetic) were developed. The major objective of this review is to summarize the conductive biomaterials used in tissue engineering including conductive composite films, conductive nanofibers, conductive hydrogels, and conductive composite scaffolds fabricated by various methods such as electrospinning, coating, or deposition by in situ polymerization. Furthermore, recent progress in tissue engineering applications using these conductive biomaterials including bone tissue engineering, muscle tissue engineering, nerve tissue engineering, cardiac tissue engineering, and wound healing application are discussed in detail.

title: P4 medicine: how systems medicine will transform the healthcare sector and society.
abstract: Ten years ago, the proposition that healthcare is evolving from reactive disease care to care that is predictive, preventive, personalized and participatory was regarded as highly speculative. Today, the core elements of that vision are widely accepted and have been articulated in a series of recent reports by the US Institute of Medicine. Systems approaches to biology and medicine are now beginning to provide patients, consumers and physicians with personalized information about each individual's unique health experience of both health and disease at the molecular, cellular and organ levels. This information will make disease care radically more cost effective by personalizing care to each person's unique biology and by treating the causes rather than the symptoms of disease. It will also provide the basis for concrete action by consumers to improve their health as they observe the impact of lifestyle decisions. Working together in digitally powered familial and affinity networks, consumers will be able to reduce the incidence of the complex chronic diseases that currently account for 75% of disease-care costs in the USA.

title: ETHICS AND ECONOMIC INTERPRETATION
abstract: This paper examines the complex relationship between ethics and economic interpretation, focusing on the methodological and conceptual challenges that arise from their shared engagement with values. It critiques the traditional economic assumption of treating human desires as static data, arguing that such desires are inherently dynamic and shaped by cultural, social, and economic processes. The analysis highlights the limitations of viewing economics as a purely value-neutral science and questions whether ethical considerations can be meaningfully separated from economic reasoning. By exploring the evolving nature of human motivations and the interplay between individual conduct and societal norms, the paper contends that a rigid distinction between economics and ethics is untenable. Instead, it suggests that both disciplines are interdependent, with ethical reflection necessary for a fuller understanding of economic behavior and policy. The discussion ultimately calls for a more nuanced approach to economic theory—one that recognizes the fluidity of human values and the essential role of ethical critique in interpreting economic phenomena.

title: Molecular Biology, Nucleic Acids, and the Future of Medicine
abstract: This paper explores the transformative impact of molecular biology and nucleic acid research on the future of medicine, focusing on key problem areas such as viral diseases, hereditary metabolic disorders, developmental defects, and cancer. It discusses the anticipated advancements in understanding and controlling viral infections through immunological and chemical means, the identification and management of genetic metabolic disorders via improved diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, and the prevention or correction of developmental abnormalities through insights into gene regulation. The paper also highlights the promise of molecular biology in elucidating the causes of cancer and developing effective preventive and curative strategies. Central to these advances is the elucidation of DNA structure and function, particularly its role in heredity, replication, mutation, and protein synthesis. The discussion includes recent findings on DNA circularity, strandedness, and their implications for replication, repair, and transcription, as well as the molecular interactions of antibiotics with nucleic acids. The author concludes that the exponential growth of knowledge in molecular biology will continue to drive significant medical progress, provided broader societal challenges such as population growth are addressed.

title: Reactions at surfaces in the atmosphere: integration of experiments and theory as necessary (but not necessarily sufficient) for predicting the physical chemistry of aerosols.
abstract: While particles have significant deleterious impacts on human health, visibility and climate, quantitative understanding of their formation, composition and fates remains problematic. Indeed, in many cases, even qualitative understanding is lacking. One area of particular uncertainty is the nature of particle surfaces and how this determines interactions with gases in the atmosphere, including water, which is important for cloud formation and properties. The focus in this Perspective article is on some chemistry relevant to airborne particles and especially to reactions occurring on their surfaces. The intent is not to provide a comprehensive review, but rather to highlight a few selected examples of interface chemistry involving inorganic and organic species that may be important in the lower atmosphere. This includes sea salt chemistry, nitrate and nitrite ion photochemistry, organics on surfaces and heterogeneous reactions of oxides of nitrogen on proxies for airborne mineral dust and boundary layer surfaces. Emphasis is on the molecular level understanding that can only be gained by fully integrating experiment and theory to elucidate these complex systems.

title: Toxicity and Safety Implications of Herbal Medicines Used in Africa
abstract: The widespread use of herbal medicines in Africa is driven by cultural acceptance, accessibility, affordability, and the limitations of allopathic medicine. Despite their long-standing role in traditional healthcare systems and perceived safety, concerns about the toxicity and safety of these remedies have intensified due to reports of adverse effects, intrinsic toxicity of certain plant constituents, herb-drug interactions, poor manufacturing practices, regulatory gaps, and adulteration. This chapter critically examines the determinants of herbal medicine safety in Africa, reviewing evidence from animal and cellular toxicity studies and highlighting discrepancies between in vivo and in vitro findings. It underscores the importance of aligning toxicity assessments with traditional usage patterns to ensure rational evaluation and safe integration of herbal medicines into healthcare. While scientific validation has confirmed the efficacy and relative safety of many African medicinal plants, ongoing vigilance, responsible use, and strengthened regulatory oversight are essential to mitigate risks and maximize their therapeutic benefits.

title: Theoretical Nuclear Physics
abstract: This progress report presents advances in theoretical nuclear physics, focusing on the development and application of consistent relativistic Hartree and random phase approximations (RHA-RPA) for finite nuclei, and the exact treatment of vacuum polarization effects within finite nuclear systems. The RHA-RPA framework incorporates vacuum contributions via a derivative expansion of the one-loop effective action, with momentum cutoffs introduced to suppress unphysical short-range effects. Results demonstrate that the strength of spin-orbit potentials and collective excitation properties in finite nuclei are sensitive to the choice of cutoff, with physically motivated values providing improved agreement with experimental data. In parallel, the report details computational strategies for evaluating vacuum polarization in finite nuclei, highlighting limitations of traditional integration schemes and introducing a stable diagonalization method in a finite basis of free eigenstates. This approach enables accurate calculation of renormalized vacuum densities and self-consistent solutions, supplemented by local density approximation results for high-energy states. Additional topics include isovector correlations in quantum hadrodynamics, nuclear response functions in quasielastic electron scattering, charge density differences near lead isotopes, excitation mechanisms in oxygen-16, deformed chiral nucleons, new bases for vacuum calculations in three dimensions, second-order processes in electron-induced deuteron emission, scalar and vector contributions to nucleon-nucleon interactions, and radiative proton capture by light nuclei at low energies. Collectively, these studies advance the understanding of nuclear structure and dynamics through improved theoretical models and computational techniques.

title: Practical Physiological Chemistry
abstract: Practical Physiological Chemistry by Dr. R. H. Aders Plimmer represents a significant advancement in the teaching of physiological chemistry, offering a comprehensive and methodically structured manual primarily aimed at medical students. Distinct from previous works authored by physiologists, this book is written from a chemist’s perspective, emphasizing the integration of organic chemistry with physiological processes. The manual provides detailed, clearly presented laboratory exercises designed to be accessible and practical for students, addressing the increasing demands on medical curricula while underscoring the essential role of physiological chemistry in medical education and its close relationship to pathology. The book’s approach facilitates a deeper understanding of the chemical basis of biological function and serves as an indispensable resource for both students and instructors seeking a reliable guide to practical work in physiological chemistry.

title: Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics: From Air Pollution to Climate Change
abstract: Expanded and updated with new findings and new features • New chapter on Global Climate providing a self-contained treatment of climate forcing, feedbacks, and climate sensitivity • New chapter on Atmospheric Organic Aerosols and new treatment of the statistical method of Positive Matrix Factorization • Updated treatments of physical meteorology, atmospheric nucleation, aerosol-cloud relationships, chemistry of biogenic hydrocarbons • Each topic developed from the fundamental science to the point of application to real-world problems • New problems at an introductory level to aid in classroom teaching

title: A research framework of smart education
abstract: The development of new technologies enables learners to learn more effectively, efficiently, flexibly and comfortably. Learners utilize smart devices to access digital resources through wireless network and to immerse in both personalized and seamless learning. Smart education, a concept that describes learning in digital age, has gained increased attention. This paper discusses the definition of smart education and presents a conceptual framework. A four-tier framework of smart pedagogies and ten key features of smart learning environments are proposed for foster smart learners who need master knowledge and skills of the 21st century learning. The smart pedagogy framework includes class-based differentiated instruction, group-based collaborative learning, individual-based personalized learning and mass-based generative learning. Furthermore, a technological architecture of smart education, which emphasizes the role of smart computing, is proposed. The tri-tier architecture and key functions are all presented. Finally, challenges of smart education are discussed.

title: The Physics of the B Factories
abstract: We review recent progress at the two e+ e− B factories. The first measurement of CP violation and the prospects for measuring all the angles of the unitarity triangle are discussed.

title: Positive Education Pedagogy: Shifting Teacher Mindsets, Practice, and Language to Make Wellbeing Visible in Classrooms
abstract: This paper explores the evolution of positive education by advocating for a shift from solely explicit wellbeing programs to a broader positive education pedagogy that integrates both explicit and implicit approaches. It argues that while explicit curricula provide structured, expert-designed content to promote student wellbeing, they often neglect the contextual factors and teacher agency crucial for sustainable impact. The chapter highlights the limitations of content-focused interventions, such as their potential to disempower teachers and overlook the role of classroom environment and relationships in shaping wellbeing. By examining implicit approaches, the paper demonstrates how wellbeing can be embedded across academic subjects and daily school life, making it more accessible and contextually relevant. Drawing on research and case studies, it emphasizes the importance of empowering teachers to actively incorporate positive psychology principles into their pedagogical practice, thereby making wellbeing visible in classrooms. The paper concludes by calling for a balanced model that values both programmatic content and the cultivation of supportive contexts through teacher mindsets, practices, and language, ultimately fostering holistic student wellbeing.
venue: The Palgrave Handbook of Positive Education

title: Firmar a posição como professor, afirmar a profissão docente
abstract: The first section of the article discusses the need to think about teacher training as professional education. For this, it is fundamental to build a new institutional place, so that the profession occupy its place within the training institutions. Between the two sections, it is argued that training should consolidate the position of each person as a professional as well as the position of the profession itself. In the second section, the need to reorganize the place of teacher education is discussed, unfolding the concept of position in five movements: personal disposition, professional interposition, pedagogical composition, research recomposition and public exposition. The text concludes with a coda, which stresses the importance of the profession to the education of teachers and of teacher education to the profession.

title: Automated identification of media bias in news articles: an interdisciplinary literature review
abstract: This interdisciplinary literature review examines the automated identification of media bias in news articles by integrating perspectives from social sciences and computer science. The paper first establishes a conceptual framework for understanding media bias, drawing on established social science models that characterize various forms such as coverage, gatekeeping, and statement bias. It then reviews how these forms have traditionally been analyzed through manual, often labor-intensive methods in the social sciences, and contrasts them with automated, scalable techniques from computer science, particularly natural language processing. The review highlights that while computer science offers technically advanced tools for detecting bias, these approaches often lack the theoretical depth found in social science research. By systematically mapping social science concepts to computational methods, the authors demonstrate that existing automated techniques can be adapted to address different types of media bias. The review concludes that closer interdisciplinary collaboration can enhance the effectiveness and relevance of automated media bias detection, opening new avenues for research and practical applications in promoting balanced news coverage.

title: Initial teacher education in England and the Covid-19 pandemic: challenges and opportunities
abstract: This paper examines the impact and implications on initial teacher education (ITE) of the crisis brought about by the Covid-19 lockdown of schools and universities from the perspectives of four university providers in England. The start of the pandemic meant that, in England, schools were closed to all but vulnerable pupils and the children of ‘key workers’, and so the normal placements of students in teacher education (ITE students) could not continue. The ‘virtualisation’ of the ITE programmes by, in some cases, both schools and universities, raised significant issues of both equity and pedagogy. The loss of time on school placement had the effect of lost opportunities for practising teaching but increasing the time for reading and reflection. We consider the effects on a teacher education programme when the practicum experience is abruptly curtailed, yet the programme is able to continue in a different way. We present a model framework for a new digital pedagogy for ITE and discuss the opportunities and affordances available as the post-Covid educational landscape emerges, and suggest that the Covid-19 crisis provides an opportunity to reflect on the idea that practicum experience may be a necessary but not, in itself, a sufficient condition for teacher learning.

title: Benchmarking the performance of Bayesian optimization across multiple experimental materials science domains
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has been leveraged for guiding autonomous and high-throughput experiments in materials science. However, few have evaluated the efficiency of BO across a broad range of experimental materials domains. In this work, we quantify the performance of BO with a collection of surrogate model and acquisition function pairs across five diverse experimental materials systems. By defining acceleration and enhancement metrics for materials optimization objectives, we find that surrogate models such as Gaussian Process (GP) with anisotropic kernels and Random Forest (RF) have comparable performance in BO, and both outperform the commonly used GP with isotropic kernels. GP with anisotropic kernels has demonstrated the most robustness, yet RF is a close alternative and warrants more consideration because it is free from distribution assumptions, has smaller time complexity, and requires less effort in initial hyperparameter selection. We also raise awareness about the benefits of using GP with anisotropic kernels in future materials optimization campaigns.

title: The Negative Influences of Exam-Oriented Education on Chinese High School Students: Backwash from Classroom to Child
abstract: This essay describes the various problems China faces on account of its exam-centric education system and pedagogy. Along with interviews and focus groups, this study draws on survey responses from 43 Chinese high school students enrolled in the Yunnan Province's No. 10 school. Moreover, this essay explores the policy arguments and key assumptions underlying this pedagogical approach as well as the negative influences exam-oriented education systems have on Chinese students, who view education as nothing more than merely passing examinations. This particular approach, at its worst, can stifle a student's imagination, creativity, and sense of self, qualities crucial for a child's ultimate success in and out of the classroom. The study suggests moderate pressure to excel in school, when paired with deemphasizing high-stakes testing, better motivates students and improves student success and psychological health, both in terms of academic success and also a productive adulthood.

title: P4 medicine: how systems medicine will transform the healthcare sector and society.
abstract: P4 medicine, defined by its predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory approach, is poised to transform healthcare and society through the integration of systems biology, digital technologies, and active consumer engagement. This paper examines the convergence of these megatrends—advances in systems medicine, the digital revolution’s capacity for big data management, and empowered patients—to outline a new paradigm for disease care and wellness. Systems medicine leverages high-throughput omics technologies and computational modeling to stratify individuals and diseases, enabling earlier interventions, targeted therapies, and more cost-effective care by addressing disease causes rather than symptoms. The proliferation of personal health data tools and networked consumer communities further accelerates this shift by generating essential data for continuous innovation and supporting lifestyle changes that can reduce the incidence of complex chronic diseases. As patients become active participants in their health management, P4 medicine facilitates the emergence of a learning healthcare system that integrates discovery science with clinical practice. The resulting transformation promises not only improved health outcomes and reduced costs but also a redefinition of the roles of patients, providers, and society in healthcare.

title: Benchmarking the performance of Bayesian optimization across multiple experimental materials science domains
abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is increasingly used to accelerate experimental materials discovery, yet its comparative performance across diverse real-world materials domains remains underexplored. Here, we systematically benchmark BO using various surrogate model and acquisition function combinations on five experimental datasets spanning carbon nanotube-polymer blends, silver nanoparticles, lead-halide perovskites, and additively manufactured polymer structures. Employing pool-based active learning and quantitative metrics such as enhancement and acceleration factors, we find that BO with Gaussian Process (GP) models featuring anisotropic kernels and Random Forest (RF) surrogates consistently outperform the commonly used isotropic GP models. While GP with anisotropic kernels demonstrates the greatest robustness, RF offers comparable performance with advantages in computational efficiency and reduced hyperparameter tuning effort. Our results provide practical guidelines for surrogate model selection in autonomous materials optimization campaigns and are supported by open-source benchmarking code and datasets to facilitate future algorithm development in the field.

title: Coronavirus biology and replication: implications for SARS-CoV-2
abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic and its unprecedented global societal and economic disruptive impact has marked the third zoonotic introduction of a highly pathogenic coronavirus into the human population. Although the previous coronavirus SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV epidemics raised awareness of the need for clinically available therapeutic or preventive interventions, to date, no treatments with proven efficacy are available. The development of effective intervention strategies relies on the knowledge of molecular and cellular mechanisms of coronavirus infections, which highlights the significance of studying virus–host interactions at the molecular level to identify targets for antiviral intervention and to elucidate critical viral and host determinants that are decisive for the development of severe disease. In this Review, we summarize the first discoveries that shape our current understanding of SARS-CoV-2 infection throughout the intracellular viral life cycle and relate that to our knowledge of coronavirus biology. The elucidation of similarities and differences between SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses will support future preparedness and strategies to combat coronavirus infections. In this Review, Thiel and colleagues discuss the key aspects of coronavirus biology and their implications for SARS-CoV-2 infections as well as for treatment and prevention strategies.

title: Systems-biology dissection of eukaryotic cell growth
abstract: A recent article in BMC Biology illustrates the use of a systems-biology approach to integrate data across the transcriptome, proteome and metabolome of budding yeast in order to dissect the relationship between nutrient conditions and cell growth.See research article http://jbiol.com/content/6/2/4 and http://www.biomedcentral.com/1741-7007/8/68

title: Bioorthogonal chemistry: fishing for selectivity in a sea of functionality.
abstract: Bioorthogonal chemistry has emerged as a powerful approach for the selective modification and study of biomolecules within the complex environment of living systems, where traditional chemical methods often lack the necessary specificity. This review traces the historical development of bioorthogonal reactions, from early protein bioconjugation techniques targeting natural amino acid residues to modern strategies employing unnatural functional groups and metal-mediated transformations. The unique requirements for bioorthogonality—rapid and selective reactivity under physiological conditions without interfering with native biological processes—have driven innovation in reaction design, enabling precise labeling and manipulation of diverse biomolecules such as proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and glycans. We discuss the evolution of residue-specific and site-selective modification methods, advances in incorporating orthogonal functionalities into biomolecules, and the application of these chemistries to probe cellular processes in real time. The review concludes by highlighting ongoing challenges and future directions for expanding the repertoire of bioorthogonal reactions to access new biological insights.

title: Structural Design Elements in Biological Materials: Application to Bioinspiration
abstract: Biological materials exhibit a limited set of recurring structural motifs that have evolved to address diverse functional demands using a constrained palette of biopolymers and biominerals. This review identifies and systematizes eight common structural design elements—fibrous, helical, gradient, layered, tubular, cellular, suture, and overlapping structures—found across a wide range of animal taxa. Each element is analyzed in terms of its hierarchical organization, critical design parameters, and constitutive mechanical equations, with examples drawn from various organisms to illustrate their widespread occurrence and multifunctionality. These elements collectively enhance properties such as strength, stiffness, flexibility, fracture toughness, wear resistance, and energy absorption to fulfill roles including support, protection, mobility, and weight reduction. The unified framework presented here provides a foundational toolbox for understanding the structure–function relationships in biological materials and guides the rational design of bioinspired materials by leveraging these natural strategies for advanced structural applications.

title: METHODICAL APPROACH TO THE CHOICE OF A BUSINESS MANAGEMENT STRATEGY WITHIN THE FRAMEWORK OF A CHANGE IN COMMERCIAL ACTIVITIES
abstract: This study presents a methodical approach to selecting business management strategies in the context of changing commercial activities. Recognizing the dynamic and unpredictable nature of modern business environments, the research focuses on developing a systematic framework that enables enterprises to effectively manage strategic changes and maintain competitiveness. The proposed methodology utilizes block-object-oriented modeling to structure the stages of strategy formation, ensuring that each phase incorporates processes and actions responsive to both internal and external change drivers. By integrating literature review, trend analysis, and practical modeling techniques, the study offers a comprehensive tool for managers to assess readiness for change, align strategic decisions with organizational goals, and adapt to evolving market conditions. The novelty of this research lies in its structured, process-oriented approach to strategy selection, which enhances the capacity of enterprises to implement effective change management within commercial activities.

title: The role of chlorine in global tropospheric chemistry
abstract: Abstract. We present a comprehensive simulation of tropospheric chlorine within the GEOS-Chem global 3-D model of oxidant–aerosol–halogen atmospheric chemistry. The simulation includes explicit accounting of chloride mobilization from sea salt aerosol by acid displacement of HCl and by other heterogeneous processes. Additional small sources of tropospheric chlorine (combustion, organochlorines, transport from stratosphere) are also included. Reactive gas-phase chlorine Cl*, including Cl, ClO, Cl2, BrCl, ICl, HOCl, ClNO3, ClNO2, and minor species, is produced by the HCl+OH reaction and by heterogeneous conversion of sea salt aerosol chloride to BrCl, ClNO2, Cl2, and ICl. The model successfully simulates the observed mixing ratios of HCl in marine air (highest at northern midlatitudes) and the associated HNO3 decrease from acid displacement. It captures the high ClNO2 mixing ratios observed in continental surface air at night and attributes the chlorine to HCl volatilized from sea salt aerosol and transported inland following uptake by fine aerosol. The model successfully simulates the vertical profiles of HCl measured from aircraft, where enhancements in the continental boundary layer can again be largely explained by transport inland of the marine source. It does not reproduce the boundary layer Cl2 mixing ratios measured in the WINTER aircraft campaign (1–5 ppt in the daytime, low at night); the model is too high at night, which could be due to uncertainty in the rate of the ClNO2+Cl- reaction, but we have no explanation for the high observed Cl2 in daytime. The global mean tropospheric concentration of Cl atoms in the model is 620 cm−3 and contributes 1.0 % of the global oxidation of methane, 20 % of ethane, 14 % of propane, and 4 % of methanol. Chlorine chemistry increases global mean tropospheric BrO by 85 %, mainly through the HOBr+Cl- reaction, and decreases global burdens of tropospheric ozone by 7 % and OH by 3 % through the associated bromine radical chemistry. ClNO2 chemistry drives increases in ozone of up to 8 ppb over polluted continents in winter.

title: The physics of exceptional points
abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) are singularities in parameter-dependent eigenvalue problems where both eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce, leading to unique algebraic and physical properties distinct from conventional degeneracies. This paper provides an overview of the mathematical structure and physical manifestations of EPs, highlighting their occurrence across a wide range of systems including quantum mechanics, optics, atomic and molecular physics, nuclear physics, and classical mechanics. EPs are central to phenomena such as symmetry breaking in PT-symmetric Hamiltonians, quantum phase transitions, quantum chaos, and multichannel scattering, often resulting in dramatic effects due to their influence on spectral properties and system dynamics. The paper discusses experimental realizations, particularly in optical systems and microwave cavities, and explores the implications of EPs for approximation schemes and spectral analysis. The ubiquity and significance of EPs underscore their fundamental role in understanding non-Hermitian physics and the behavior of open or complex systems.

title: The economics of animal health and production.
abstract: During the last 200 years, there has been massive socio-economic change through industrial and agricultural revolutions. This change has been associated with rapid increases in human and domestic livestock populations, and a movement of people from rural to urban areas. More than half the people in the world now live in urban environments where they have bet- ter access to work, but limited or no access to land and livestock to produce food. This implies that a majority of people are dependent on others for raw, semi-processed and processed food products. The efficient functioning of the livestock sector, encompassing all facets of input sup- ply, production, processing and marketing, has become a critical issue for guaranteeing: ● that sufficient livestock products are available at affordable prices – food security; and ● that the livestock products are safe to eat – food safety. Within the livestock sector, the livestock producers and business people involved in input supply and output processing and marketing need to be able to plan, make a profit and have a sustainable livelihood. The State also plays a critical role in facilitating how the livestock sec- tor functions and develops in order to satisfy society’s needs. Therefore, both the private and public sectors require economic theory and tools to understand the drivers of change for the livestock sector, and how to assess the impact of future actions and investments.

title: Machine Learning in Medicine
abstract: Spurred by advances in processing power, memory, storage, and an unprecedented wealth of data, computers are being asked to tackle increasingly complex learning tasks, often with astonishing success. Computers have now mastered a popular variant of poker, learned the laws of physics from experimental data, and become experts in video games - tasks that would have been deemed impossible not too long ago. In parallel, the number of companies centered on applying complex data analysis to varying industries has exploded, and it is thus unsurprising that some analytic companies are turning attention to problems in health care. The purpose of this review is to explore what problems in medicine might benefit from such learning approaches and use examples from the literature to introduce basic concepts in machine learning. It is important to note that seemingly large enough medical data sets and adequate learning algorithms have been available for many decades, and yet, although there are thousands of papers applying machine learning algorithms to medical data, very few have contributed meaningfully to clinical care. This lack of impact stands in stark contrast to the enormous relevance of machine learning to many other industries. Thus, part of my effort will be to identify what obstacles there may be to changing the practice of medicine through statistical learning approaches, and discuss how these might be overcome.
venue: Mach. Learn. under Resour. Constraints Vol. 3

title: Self-organization and the physics of glassy networks
abstract: Network glasses exemplify self-organized systems whose unique glass-forming tendencies and phase behaviors elude explanation by conventional theories of gases, liquids, and crystals. This paper reviews the emergence of a topological theory that accounts for the formation and properties of glassy networks through simple, universal mechanisms based on network connectivity and constraints. The theory posits that the balance between interatomic constraints and degrees of freedom determines whether a network is floppy, rigid, or ideally isostatic, with the latter corresponding to an arrested, stress-free glassy state. Experimental evidence from chalcogenide alloys and other network glasses confirms key predictions, including the existence of a critical mean coordination number and the identification of two distinct topological transitions that bound an intermediate phase characterized by self-organization. This intermediate phase, observed in both insulating and electronic glasses, exhibits sharp compositional boundaries and is associated with a reversibility window in calorimetric measurements. The topological approach not only unifies understanding across diverse glassy materials but also establishes conceptual bridges to biophysical networks such as proteins, highlighting the broad applicability of self-organization principles in complex systems.

title: Unpacking “Participation” in the Adaptive Management of Social–ecological Systems: a Critical Review
abstract: Adaptive management has the potential to make environmental management more democratic through the involvement of different stakeholders. In this article, we examine three case studies at different scales that followed adaptive management processes, critically reflecting upon the role of stakeholder participation in each case. Specifically, we examine at which stages different types of stakeholders can play key roles and the ways that each might be involved. We show that a range of participatory mechanisms can be employed at different stages of the adaptive cycle, and can work together to create conditions for social learning and favorable outcomes for diverse stakeholders. This analysis highlights the need for greater reflection on case study research in order to further refine participatory processes within adaptive management. This should not only address the shortcomings and successes of adaptive management as a form of democratic environmental governance, but should also unpack the links between science, institutions, knowledge, and power.

title: Vascularization strategies for tissue engineering.
abstract: Tissue engineering is currently limited by the inability to adequately vascularize tissues in vitro or in vivo. Issues of nutrient perfusion and mass transport limitations, especially oxygen diffusion, restrict construct development to smaller than clinically relevant dimensions and limit the ability for in vivo integration. There is much interest in the field as researchers have undertaken a variety of approaches to vascularization, including material functionalization, scaffold design, microfabrication, bioreactor development, endothelial cell seeding, modular assembly, and in vivo systems. Efforts to model and measure oxygen diffusion and consumption within these engineered tissues have sought to quantitatively assess and improve these design strategies. This review assesses the current state of the field by outlining the prevailing approaches taken toward producing vascularized tissues and highlighting their strengths and weaknesses.

title: Decision-Making Processes in Social Contexts.
abstract: This article examines the limited integration of judgment and decision-making (JDM) research into sociology, despite decades of advances in understanding how individuals make choices. While JDM has focused on cognitive processes and deviations from rationality, often in de-socialized settings, sociological research emphasizes the influence of social environments on behavior but pays less attention to underlying decision mechanisms. We argue that bridging these traditions can enrich both fields, particularly for understanding choices characterized by ambiguity and obscurity rather than clear optimal solutions. The article reviews key theories, models, and data sources from decision research relevant to sociological inquiry, discusses methodological challenges and opportunities for observing decision processes in real-world social contexts, and highlights the potential for cross-fertilization between sociology and decision science. By integrating insights from cognitive science with sociological perspectives on context, researchers can better understand how individuals navigate complex social choices and how context shapes decision strategies and outcomes.

title: Ethics of AI in Education: Towards a Community-Wide Framework
abstract: This paper examines the pressing need for a comprehensive ethical framework to guide the development and deployment of artificial intelligence in education (AIED). While AIED research is motivated by the goal of enhancing student learning, ethical intentions alone are insufficient to address complex issues such as fairness, accountability, transparency, bias, autonomy, agency, and inclusion. Through a survey of leading AIED researchers, the study reveals a lack of consensus and preparedness within the community to tackle emerging ethical challenges. The findings highlight the absence of established guidelines or frameworks specific to AIED ethics and underscore the importance of multidisciplinary collaboration in developing robust, context-sensitive approaches. The paper concludes by advocating for a community-wide effort to create an actionable ethical framework that addresses both general AI concerns and the unique pedagogical dimensions of educational technology.
venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education

title: Agent-Based Business Process Management
abstract: This paper presents an agent-based approach to business process management developed within the ADEPT project, addressing the challenges of distributed, dynamic, and decentralized organizational environments. The proposed framework conceptualizes business processes as communities of autonomous, negotiating agents that encapsulate problem-solving capabilities and interact through service provision, negotiation, and information sharing. Each agent manages specific services or tasks and coordinates with others via service level agreements established through negotiation protocols, accommodating heterogeneous information models and organizational autonomy. The ADEPT agent architecture supports hierarchical and hybrid organizational structures by nesting agents and tasks, enabling flexible modeling of real-world business processes. The approach is demonstrated through its application to British Telecom’s customer quote process, highlighting the benefits of agent-based systems in managing complexity, supporting proactive and responsive decision-making, and maintaining organizational integrity. The paper contrasts this methodology with traditional business process management techniques and discusses ongoing research directions and open challenges in agent-based process management.
venue: International Journal of Cooperative Information Systems

title: Transformative learning as pedagogy for the health professions: a scoping review
abstract: Transformative learning (TL) has been described as learning that challenges established perspectives, leading to new ways of being in the world. As a learning theory it has resonated with educators globally, including those in the health professions. Described as a complex metatheory, TL has evolved over time, eliciting divergent interpretations of the construct. This scoping review provides a comprehensive synthesis of how TL is currently represented in the health professions education literature, including how it influences curricular activities, to inform its future application in the field.

title: Untangling the origins of competitive advantage
abstract: This paper begins to reconcile competing perspectives on the origins of competitive advantage by examining the adoption of ‘science-driven’ drug discovery, a performance-enhancing organizational practice. Science-driven drug discovery diffused slowly, allowing us to disentangle alternative theories of organizational heterogeneity. Adoption is driven by initial conditions, time-varying internal and external environmental conditions, and convergence (firms positioned least favorably adopt most aggressively). While accounting for initial conditions is critical, managers are sensitive to idiosyncratic environmental cues. The origins of competitive advantage may therefore lie in the ability to identify and respond to environmental cues well in advance of observing performance-oriented pay-offs. title: The genetic transformation of bone biology.
abstract: The skeleton, like every organ, has specific developmental and functional characteristics that define its identity in biologic and pathologic terms. Skeleton is composed of multiple elements of various shapes and origins spread throughout the body. Most of these skeletal elements are formed by two different tissues, cartilage and bone, and each of these two tissues has its own specific cell types: the chondrocyte in cartilage, and the osteoblast and osteoclast in bone. Finally, each of these cell types has its own differentiation pathway, physiological functions, and therefore pathological conditions. The complexity of this organ in terms of developmental biology, physiology, and pathology, along with the multitude of important conceptual advances in our understanding of skeletal biology, are such that it has become impossible to present in a short review an up-to-date summary of both cartilage and bone biology. Thus, this review will concentrate only on bone biology beyond embryonic patterning. The entire bone field is dominated by the impact of degenerative diseases, such as osteoporosis.
