title: THE APPLICATIONS OF INTERNATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF FUNCTIONING, DISABILITY AND HEALTH (ICF) BY WORLD HEALTH ORGANIZATION(WHO) IN REHABILITATION MEDICINE PRACTICE
abstract: Rehabilitation Medicine is dedicated to optimise patients function and health in the most comprehensive manner. ICF, the latest International Classification by World Health Organization (WHO) is a conceptual framework for the assessment of functioning, disability and health. The purpose of this paper is to describe the applications of ICF in Rehabilitation Medicine practice in the Medical Rehabilitation Unit, University of Malaya Medical Centre (UMMC), Kuala Lumpur. Issues: ICF consists of body function, structure, activity, participation and environmental factor. ICF categories are exhaustive, but are not practical to be used entirely and not applicable in clinical practice on their own. How is ICF used from the clinical perspective? It has to be adapted to make it usable. In Rehabilitation Medicine settings, the following are ways ICF is applied in clinical practice: research in terms of validating the use of available ICF Core Sets and development of new ICF Core Set; clinical practice based on the ICF-based sheet; and educational tools. Conclusion: The practice of Rehabilitation Medicine is in line and compatible with the concept of ICF and can serve as a new important language that can improve the practice of Rehabilitation Medicine. It can be a universal language in functioning, disability and health and can improve understanding in addressing issues on disability within the medical community, improve multi professionals’ communication among patients, healthcare providers and stakeholders.

title: Building Ontologies with Basic Formal Ontology
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive guide to building ontologies using Basic Formal Ontology (BFO) as a foundational framework. It begins by defining ontologies and distinguishing among their various types, emphasizing the importance of taxonomies in structuring domain knowledge. The work outlines best practices for designing domain ontologies, focusing on the careful selection of terms, precise definitions, and rigorous classification schemes. It introduces the core concepts of BFO, including continuants and occurrents, and explores the ontology of relations to facilitate accurate representation of complex domains. Practical aspects of implementing ontologies are addressed through discussion of relevant languages, tools, and reasoning systems. By integrating theoretical foundations with practical guidance, this paper equips researchers and practitioners with the principles and methodologies necessary for effective ontology development and reuse in diverse scientific and technical fields.

title: Superconductivity in single-layer films of FeSe with a transition temperature above 100 K
abstract: We report the observation of superconductivity above 100 K in single-layer films of FeSe grown on Nb-doped SrTiO3(001) substrates, as determined by in situ four-point probe electrical transport measurements. Our results reveal a superconducting transition temperature (Tc) as high as 109 K, significantly exceeding the Tc of bulk FeSe and previous records for Fe-based superconductors. The films were synthesized via molecular beam epitaxy with precise thickness control and characterized using reflection high-energy electron diffraction and scanning tunneling microscopy. Electrical measurements demonstrate zero resistance below Tc and a robust superconducting state persisting under magnetic fields up to 11 T. The critical current follows Ginzburg-Landau behavior, confirming the intrinsic nature of the observed superconductivity. Control experiments on bare substrates rule out substrate contributions to the superconducting signal. These findings establish single-layer FeSe/SrTiO3 as a promising platform for investigating high-Tc superconductivity and interface-driven pairing mechanisms in two-dimensional systems.

title: Personalized medicine in psychiatry: problems and promises
abstract: The central theme of personalized medicine is the premise that an individual’s unique physiologic characteristics play a significant role in both disease vulnerability and in response to specific therapies. The major goals of personalized medicine are therefore to predict an individual’s susceptibility to developing an illness, achieve accurate diagnosis, and optimize the most efficient and favorable response to treatment. The goal of achieving personalized medicine in psychiatry is a laudable one, because its attainment should be associated with a marked reduction in morbidity and mortality. In this review, we summarize an illustrative selection of studies that are laying the foundation towards personalizing medicine in major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia. In addition, we present emerging applications that are likely to advance personalized medicine in psychiatry, with an emphasis on novel biomarkers and neuroimaging.

title: The molecular biology of apoptosis.
abstract: Apoptosis, a genetically programmed form of cell death, is essential for development, homeostasis, defense, and aging in multicellular organisms. This review explores the molecular mechanisms underlying apoptosis, highlighting its evolutionary conservation from nematodes to mammals. Key regulatory genes and proteins, such as the cysteine protease Ced-3 in Caenorhabditis elegans and its mammalian homologs (including ICE and CPP32), are discussed in relation to their roles in initiating and executing cell death via proteolytic cascades. The process of apoptosis is divided into distinct phases: initiation by internal or external stimuli, signal transduction, effector activation involving proteases, and postmortem events such as DNA fragmentation and cell clearance. The interplay between pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic factors, notably the Bcl-2 family, allows for fine regulation of cell death pathways. Understanding these molecular events provides insight into the physiological roles of apoptosis and suggests potential therapeutic strategies for diseases involving aberrant cell survival or death.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Business process management - at the crossroads
abstract: PurposeBusiness process management (BPM) has attracted much focus throughout the years, yet there have been calls questioning the future of BPM. The purpose of this paper is to explore the current state of the field through a dynamic literature review and identify the main challenges for its future development.Design/methodology/approachA dynamic co-citation network analysis identifies the “evolution” of knowledge of BPM and the most influential works. The results present the developed BPM subthemes in the form of clusters.FindingsThe focus within the field has shifted from facilitating wide-ranging business performance improvements to creating introverted optimizations within a particular BPM subgroup. The BPM field has thus experienced strong fragmentation throughout the years and has accrued into self-fueling subareas of BPM research such as business process modeling and workflow management. Those subareas often neglect related disciplines in other management, process modeling and organizational improvement fields.Research limitations/implicationsThe study is limited by the initial keyword choice of the authors. The subsequent co-citation analysis ameliorates the subjectivity since it produces a data set and contributions based on references.Originality/valueA new combination of historical development and the state-of-the-art of the BPM field, by employing a co-citation and cluster analysis. This dynamic literature review presents the current state of the theoretical core and attempts to identify the crossroads that BPM has reached. The study can be replicated in the future to track the changes in the field.

title: The Weak Hydrogen Bond: In Structural Chemistry and Biology
abstract: This work provides a comprehensive examination of the weak hydrogen bond, exploring its significance and diverse roles in structural chemistry and biology. Drawing on extensive crystallographic evidence, the authors analyze the nature, energetics, and geometrical preferences of weak hydrogen bonds, distinguishing them from classical strong hydrogen bonds. The book discusses the impact of these interactions on molecular recognition, crystal engineering, and biological macromolecular structures, highlighting their importance in stabilizing protein and nucleic acid conformations as well as influencing molecular assembly in solid-state materials. By integrating theoretical insights with experimental data, this volume advances the understanding of weak hydrogen bonding as a fundamental force shaping chemical and biological systems.

title: Pretreatment data is highly predictive of liver chemistry signals in clinical trials
abstract: This study evaluated the predictive power of pretreatment (baseline) data for identifying patients at risk of developing liver chemistry signals during clinical trials. Using data from 24 late-stage clinical trials across diverse therapeutic areas, classification models were constructed based on baseline demographics, medical history, concomitant medications, and laboratory results. The models achieved an average validation accuracy of approximately 80% in predicting liver chemistry elevations, with baseline values of individual liver tests being the strongest predictors for their own subsequent elevations. Elevated baseline bilirubin was associated with increased risk of biochemical Hy’s law cases, while baseline γ-glutamyltransferase offered limited additional predictive value. These findings demonstrate that pretreatment data can effectively stratify patients by risk for liver chemistry abnormalities, supporting proactive risk management and informing the evaluation of new biomarkers in drug development.

title: Algorithms on Strings, Trees, and Sequences: Computer Science and Computational Biology
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive study of algorithms for strings, trees, and sequences, with a focus on their foundational roles in computer science and computational biology. It systematically explores exact and inexact string matching, including classical algorithms such as Boyer-Moore and Knuth-Morris-Pratt, as well as advanced preprocessing and comparison-based methods. The construction and application of suffix trees are examined in depth, highlighting their utility in problems ranging from substring search to genome-scale data analysis. Dynamic programming techniques for sequence alignment, edit distance computation, and local similarity detection are detailed alongside improvements for efficiency and space usage. The work extends to multiple sequence alignment, database search strategies using tools like FASTA and BLAST, and the algorithmic challenges posed by large-scale biological data. Additional topics include physical mapping, DNA sequencing, evolutionary tree reconstruction, gene prediction, molecular computation, and models of genome-level mutations. Through algorithmic innovations and practical applications, the paper bridges theoretical computer science with the demands of modern computational biology.

title: tRNA biology charges to the front.
abstract: tRNA biology has come of age, revealing an unprecedented level of understanding and many unexpected discoveries along the way. This review highlights new findings on the diverse pathways of tRNA maturation, and on the formation and function of a number of modifications. Topics of special focus include the regulation of tRNA biosynthesis, quality control tRNA turnover mechanisms, widespread tRNA cleavage pathways activated in response to stress and other growth conditions, emerging evidence of signaling pathways involving tRNA and cleavage fragments, and the sophisticated intracellular tRNA trafficking that occurs during and after biosynthesis.

title: Guidelines for Field Surveys of the Quality of Medicines: A Proposal
abstract: Paul Newton and colleagues propose guidelines for conducting and reporting field surveys of the quality of medicines.

title: Why people use herbal medicine: insights from a focus-group study in Germany
abstract: This qualitative study explores the motivations and factors influencing the use of herbal medicine among adults in Germany through six age-stratified focus groups comprising 46 participants. The findings reveal that treating illnesses is the primary reason for herbal medicine use across all age groups, while prevention and health promotion are particularly relevant for older adults. Herbal remedies are predominantly used for mild or moderate conditions or as initial treatments before resorting to conventional medicine, with participants recognizing their limitations for severe illnesses. Key reasons for preferring herbal medicine include dissatisfaction with conventional treatments, positive past experiences, perceived benefits, and family traditions. Information sources are mainly independent reading and family networks rather than medical professionals. The study highlights potential risks associated with self-medication and limited risk awareness, especially among elderly users who tend to consume more medicines overall. The results suggest a need for increased awareness among users regarding the limitations and risks of herbal medicine, and call on healthcare stakeholders to address dissatisfaction with conventional care as a driver of alternative medicine use.

title: Gold nanoparticles for biology and medicine.
abstract: Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) have emerged as versatile platforms in biology and medicine due to their unique size- and shape-dependent physical properties, high surface area, and facile surface functionalization. Advances in synthetic methods now enable precise control over AuNP size, morphology, and surface chemistry, allowing conjugation with a wide range of biological ligands such as nucleic acids, peptides, proteins, and antibodies. This review summarizes recent progress in the synthesis and bioconjugation of gold nanoconjugates, highlighting their cellular uptake mechanisms, biodetection applications, and burgeoning roles as therapeutic agents. Functionalized AuNPs have demonstrated utility in highly sensitive diagnostic assays, gene regulation, drug delivery, imaging, and photoresponsive therapies. Their novel physicochemical characteristics confer advantages over traditional molecular systems, including enhanced cellular internalization, stability, and multifunctionality. Despite significant advances, key challenges remain regarding cytotoxicity, targeting specificity, and in vivo behavior. Continued investigation into the design and application of gold nanoconjugates promises to expand their impact in biomedical research and clinical therapeutics.

title: B-physics anomalies: a guide to combined explanations
abstract: Motivated by additional experimental hints of Lepton Flavour Universality violation in B decays, both in charged- and in neutral-current processes, we analyse the ingredients necessary to provide a combined description of these phenomena. By means of an Effective Field Theory (EFT) approach, based on the hypothesis of New Physics coupled predominantly to the third generation of left-handed quarks and leptons, we show how this is possible. We demonstrate, in particular, how to solve the problems posed by electroweak precision tests and direct searches with a rather natural choice of model parameters, within the context of a U(2)q ×U(2)ℓ flavour symmetry. We further exemplify the general EFT findings by means of simplified models with explicit mediators in the TeV range: coloured scalar or vector leptoquarks and colour-less vectors. Among these, the case of an SU(2)L-singlet vector leptoquark emerges as a particularly simple and successful framework.

title: Transparent reporting of a multivariable prediction model for individual prognosis or diagnosis (TRIPOD): the TRIPOD Statement
abstract: Prediction models are essential tools in healthcare for estimating the probability of disease presence (diagnosis) or future outcomes (prognosis) to inform clinical decision-making. Despite their increasing development and use, the quality of reporting in prediction model studies remains suboptimal, hindering assessment of bias, reproducibility, and clinical utility. The Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis Or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) Initiative was established to address these deficiencies by providing comprehensive recommendations for reporting studies that develop, validate, or update diagnostic or prognostic prediction models. The TRIPOD Statement was developed through literature review, expert surveys, and consensus meetings involving methodologists, clinicians, and journal editors. It consists of a 22-item checklist covering essential aspects of study design, analysis, and results to ensure transparency and completeness in reporting. Adoption of the TRIPOD Statement aims to improve the reliability, interpretability, and application of prediction models in research and practice. Researchers are encouraged to use the checklist alongside the accompanying explanation and elaboration document to facilitate high-quality reporting and enhance the value of prediction model studies in medicine.

title: The iPlant Collaborative: Cyberinfrastructure for Plant Biology
abstract: The iPlant Collaborative (iPlant) is a United States National Science Foundation (NSF) funded project that aims to create an innovative, comprehensive, and foundational cyberinfrastructure in support of plant biology research (PSCIC, 2006). iPlant is developing cyberinfrastructure that uniquely enables scientists throughout the diverse fields that comprise plant biology to address Grand Challenges in new ways, to stimulate and facilitate cross-disciplinary research, to promote biology and computer science research interactions, and to train the next generation of scientists on the use of cyberinfrastructure in research and education. Meeting humanity's projected demands for agricultural and forest products and the expectation that natural ecosystems be managed sustainably will require synergies from the application of information technologies. The iPlant cyberinfrastructure design is based on an unprecedented period of research community input, and leverages developments in high-performance computing, data storage, and cyberinfrastructure for the physical sciences. iPlant is an open-source project with application programming interfaces that allow the community to extend the infrastructure to meet its needs. iPlant is sponsoring community-driven workshops addressing specific scientific questions via analysis tool integration and hypothesis testing. These workshops teach researchers how to add bioinformatics tools and/or datasets into the iPlant cyberinfrastructure enabling plant scientists to perform complex analyses on large datasets without the need to master the command-line or high-performance computational services.

title: Quantum Simulation
abstract: Quantum simulation leverages controllable quantum systems to model and study the behavior of less accessible or more complex quantum systems, addressing the exponential computational challenges inherent in simulating quantum mechanics with classical computers. This review provides a comprehensive overview of both theoretical and experimental aspects of quantum simulation, including digital and analog approaches, resource estimation, fault tolerance, and physical implementations using platforms such as neutral atoms, ions, superconducting circuits, and photons. The paper highlights the broad applicability of quantum simulators across condensed-matter physics, high-energy physics, quantum chemistry, cosmology, and related fields. Recent technological advances have enabled proof-of-principle experiments and suggest that practical quantum simulation will soon be feasible, potentially allowing quantum devices to outperform classical computers in specific tasks. The review also discusses current challenges and future prospects in this rapidly evolving area, aiming to serve as a pedagogical introduction and reference for researchers entering or working within the field of quantum simulation.

title: Design Thinking in Pedagogy
abstract: The twenty-first century has brought lots of challenges for people in all spheres, including education. In the new context, traditional approaches often seem ineffective and therefore new tools and methods have to be applied. An alternative approach that might be useful in the given context is design thinking – the approach that originated in architecture, design and art, and nowadays is applied in many fields. It is a human-centered problem-solving approach that may be used in the teaching/learning process to develop twenty-first century skills and enhance creativity and innovation. This paper introduces readers to the origin of design thinking, its attributes and processes as well as its application in pedagogy.

title: Computational Thinking, Between Papert and Wing
abstract: This paper examines the concept of computational thinking (CT) as articulated by Seymour Papert and Jeannette Wing, tracing its historical development and analyzing its significance for K-12 computer science education. Through a comparative and contextual approach, the authors clarify the distinct educational and epistemological roots of CT in both Papert’s constructionist perspective and Wing’s emphasis on computer science as a foundational discipline. The analysis highlights how Papert’s focus on social and affective engagement in learning complements Wing’s framing of CT as a scientific lens for understanding algorithmic processes. The paper also addresses the contested claim that CT skills automatically transfer to other domains, finding limited empirical support for this assertion. By disentangling misconceptions and synthesizing the core contributions of both thinkers, the authors argue that an integrated understanding of CT—grounded in computer science yet attentive to interdisciplinary and affective dimensions—is essential for effective curriculum design. The findings offer guidance for educators and researchers seeking to implement CT in schools while avoiding prevalent misunderstandings.

title: Engineering complex tissues.
abstract: This article summarizes the views expressed at the third session of the workshop 'Tissue Engineering--The Next Generation,' which was devoted to the engineering of complex tissue structures. Antonios Mikos described the engineering of complex oral and craniofacial tissues as a 'guided interplay' between biomaterial scaffolds, growth factors, and local cell populations toward the restoration of the original architecture and function of complex tissues. Susan Herring, reviewing osteogenesis and vasculogenesis, explained that the vascular arrangement precedes and dictates the architecture of the new bone, and proposed that engineering of osseous tissues might benefit from preconstruction of an appropriate vasculature. Jennifer Elisseeff explored the formation of complex tissue structures based on the example of stratified cartilage engineered using stem cells and hydrogels. Helen Lu discussed engineering of tissue interfaces, a problem critical for biological fixation of tendons and ligaments, and the development of a new generation of fixation devices. Rita Kandel discussed the challenges related to the re-creation of the cartilage-bone interface, in the context of tissue engineered joint repair. Frederick Schoen emphasized, in the context of heart valve engineering, the need for including the requirements derived from 'adult biology' of tissue remodeling and establishing reliable early predictors of success or failure of tissue engineered implants. Mehmet Toner presented a review of biopreservation techniques and stressed that a new breakthrough in this field may be necessary to meet all the needs of tissue engineering. David Mooney described systems providing temporal and spatial regulation of growth factor availability, which may find utility in virtually all tissue engineering and regeneration applications, including directed in vitro and in vivo vascularization of tissues. Anthony Atala offered a clinician's perspective for functional tissue regeneration, and discussed new biomaterials that can be used to develop new regenerative technologies.

title: The statistical physics of cities
abstract: Challenges due to the rapid urbanization of the world — especially in emerging countries — range from an increasing dependence on energy to air pollution, socio-spatial inequalities and environmental and sustainability issues. Modelling the structure and evolution of cities is therefore critical because policy makers need robust theories and new paradigms for mitigating these problems. Fortunately, the increased data available about urban systems opens the possibility of constructing a quantitative ‘science of cities’, with the aim of identifying and modelling essential phenomena. Statistical physics plays a major role in this effort by bringing tools and concepts able to bridge theory and empirical results. This Perspective illustrates this point by focusing on fundamental objects in cities: the distribution of the urban population; segregation phenomena and spin-like models; the polycentric transition of the activity organization; energy considerations about mobility and models inspired by gravity and radiation concepts; CO2 emitted by transport; and finally, scaling that describes how various socio-economical and infrastructures evolve when cities grow.This Perspective describes how statistical physics helps understand some of the key aspects of cities: their spatial structure and social organization, the distribution of their population, urban mobility and how some critical factors vary with population.

title: Click chemistry with DNA.
abstract: Click chemistry, particularly the copper-catalyzed azide–alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction, has revolutionized the field of nucleic acid chemistry by enabling efficient and selective modification of DNA. This review critically examines the application of click chemistry to DNA, highlighting its use in oligonucleotide labeling with fluorophores, carbohydrates, peptides, and other functional groups, as well as in the synthesis of cyclic DNA, DNA catenanes, and DNA–PNA conjugates. The CuAAC reaction’s high specificity, biocompatibility, and stability make it ideal for post-synthetic functionalization of DNA, facilitating the preparation of labeled probes for genetic analysis, genome screening, and high-throughput sequencing. Strategies for incorporating clickable groups into DNA include both chemical synthesis and enzymatic methods using modified nucleoside triphosphates, with careful consideration of polymerase compatibility and reaction conditions. The review summarizes pioneering studies that demonstrate the versatility and practical advantages of click chemistry in generating diverse DNA architectures and functional materials for biological and nanotechnological applications.

title: Citizen Science and Biological Invasions: A Review
abstract: Biological invasions pose significant ecological and economic challenges, necessitating effective detection and management strategies. This review synthesizes the role of citizen science in advancing research on non-indigenous species (NIS), analyzing 126 peer-reviewed articles to assess trends, effectiveness, and methodological considerations. The majority of studies focused on terrestrial environments, particularly plants, while first detections were most frequently reported for marine fish, highlighting ecosystem-specific detection biases. Citizen science initiatives demonstrated cost-effectiveness and broad geographic coverage, facilitating early detection and monitoring of NIS across diverse habitats. The review underscores the importance of adapting citizen science approaches to ecosystem characteristics, target species, and participant profiles, as well as ensuring data quality through verification and audit procedures. Outreach strategies, including the use of dedicated versus existing web platforms, are evaluated for their potential to maximize engagement and data collection. The authors propose a refined definition of citizen science that emphasizes collaboration between citizens and scientists in data collection and analysis for environmental problem-solving. Finally, a framework is presented to integrate citizen science, scientific research, and stakeholder involvement for improved management of biological invasions, with recommendations for acknowledging citizen contributions and addressing data limitations in future projects.

title: Herbal medicine use among urban residents in Lagos, Nigeria
abstract: This study investigated the prevalence, patterns, and perceptions of herbal medicine use among 388 urban residents in Surulere Local Government Area, Lagos, Nigeria, using structured interviews and questionnaires. Results showed that 66.8% of respondents reported using herbal medicines, with 'agbo jedi-jedi' being the most commonly used preparation. Family and friends significantly influenced usage decisions for 78.4% of users. Despite half of the respondents perceiving herbal medicines as safe, 20.8% reported experiencing mild to moderate adverse effects. The findings highlight widespread use and limited awareness of potential toxicities associated with herbal medicines among urban Lagos residents, underscoring the need for public education on safe use and further evaluation of the safety and efficacy of these products through clinical studies.

title: Reducing food’s environmental impacts through producers and consumers
abstract: The global impacts of food production Food is produced and processed by millions of farmers and intermediaries globally, with substantial associated environmental costs. Given the heterogeneity of producers, what is the best way to reduce food's environmental impacts? Poore and Nemecek consolidated data on the multiple environmental impacts of ∼38,000 farms producing 40 different agricultural goods around the world in a meta-analysis comparing various types of food production systems. The environmental cost of producing the same goods can be highly variable. However, this heterogeneity creates opportunities to target the small numbers of producers that have the most impact. Science, this issue p. 987 Food producer heterogeneity on a global level creates mitigation opportunities with respect to environmental damage caused by food production. Food’s environmental impacts are created by millions of diverse producers. To identify solutions that are effective under this heterogeneity, we consolidated data covering five environmental indicators; 38,700 farms; and 1600 processors, packaging types, and retailers. Impact can vary 50-fold among producers of the same product, creating substantial mitigation opportunities. However, mitigation is complicated by trade-offs, multiple ways for producers to achieve low impacts, and interactions throughout the supply chain. Producers have limits on how far they can reduce impacts. Most strikingly, impacts of the lowest-impact animal products typically exceed those of vegetable substitutes, providing new evidence for the importance of dietary change. Cumulatively, our findings support an approach where producers monitor their own impacts, flexibly meet environmental targets by choosing from multiple practices, and communicate their impacts to consumers.

title: First look at the physics case of TLEP
abstract: The discovery by the ATLAS and CMS experiments of a new boson with mass around 125 GeV and with measured properties compatible with those of a Standard-Model Higgs boson, coupled with the absence of discoveries of phenomena beyond the Standard Model at the TeV scale, has triggered interest in ideas for future Higgs factories. A new circular e+e− collider hosted in a 80 to 100 km tunnel, TLEP, is among the most attractive solutions proposed so far. It has a clean experimental environment, produces high luminosity for top-quark, Higgs boson, W and Z studies, accommodates multiple detectors, and can reach energies up to the $$ \mathrm{t}\overline{\mathrm{t}} $$ threshold and beyond. It will enable measurements of the Higgs boson properties and of Electroweak Symmetry-Breaking (EWSB) parameters with unequalled precision, offering exploration of physics beyond the Standard Model in the multi-TeV range. Moreover, being the natural precursor of the VHE-LHC, a 100 TeV hadron machine in the same tunnel, it builds up a long-term vision for particle physics. Altogether, the combination of TLEP and the VHE-LHC offers, for a great cost effectiveness, the best precision and the best search reach of all options presently on the market. This paper presents a first appraisal of the salient features of the TLEP physics potential, to serve as a baseline for a more extensive design study.

title: Instruments of Development: Randomization in the Tropics, and the Search for the Elusive Keys to Economic Development
abstract: This paper critically examines the increasing reliance on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and instrumental variable (IV) methods in development economics as tools for identifying effective policies and projects in low-income countries. While these approaches are often promoted as providing more credible or scientific evidence than traditional econometric analyses, the paper argues that both RCTs and IV strategies are subject to significant limitations, including misunderstandings about exogeneity, inadequate handling of heterogeneity, and practical challenges in implementation. Drawing on examples from the literature on aid effectiveness and project evaluation, the paper contends that neither randomization nor quasi-randomization guarantees policy-relevant or generalizable knowledge about economic development. Instead, it suggests that a narrow focus on project-level impacts is unlikely to yield cumulative scientific progress or uncover the fundamental mechanisms driving development. The author advocates for a shift in emphasis toward understanding the theoretical mechanisms underlying interventions and their contextual applicability, arguing that this approach holds greater promise for advancing knowledge and informing policy in development economics.

title: Towards quantum chemistry on a quantum computer.
abstract: Exact first-principles calculations of molecular properties are currently intractable because their computational cost grows exponentially with both the number of atoms and basis set size. A solution is to move to a radically different model of computing by building a quantum computer, which is a device that uses quantum systems themselves to store and process data. Here we report the application of the latest photonic quantum computer technology to calculate properties of the smallest molecular system: the hydrogen molecule in a minimal basis. We calculate the complete energy spectrum to 20 bits of precision and discuss how the technique can be expanded to solve large-scale chemical problems that lie beyond the reach of modern supercomputers. These results represent an early practical step toward a powerful tool with a broad range of quantum-chemical applications.

title: Theory and methods of economic evaluation of health care.
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive examination of the theoretical foundations and methodological approaches to the economic evaluation of health care interventions. It begins with an exploration of welfare economics principles, including the Pareto principle, market failure, and social welfare functions, as they relate to health care resource allocation. The analysis then addresses methods for valuing health changes, such as willingness-to-pay measures and both revealed and expressed preference techniques. Detailed attention is given to the estimation of costs, encompassing program, morbidity, and mortality costs, as well as issues like discounting and tax treatment in cost-benefit analysis. The paper further distinguishes between cost-benefit, cost-effectiveness, and cost-utility analyses, discussing their respective applications, effectiveness measures, and methodological challenges such as discounting and choice of outcome metrics like QALYs. Finally, the implications of economic evaluation for health policy are considered, including its role in treatment guidelines, organizational decision-making, technology assessment, reimbursement, and pricing. The work concludes by highlighting the critical importance of rigorous economic evaluation methods for informed policy-making in health care.
venue: Developments in health economics and public policy

title: Regional Anesthesia in the Patient Receiving Antithrombotic or Thrombolytic Therapy: American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine Evidence-Based Guidelines (Fourth Edition)
abstract: The American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine (ASRA) convened its Fourth Consensus Conference on Regional Anesthesia and Anticoagulation in conjunction with the European Society of Anesthesiology (ESA) in response to emerging patient safety issue

title: Difference Troubles: Queering Social Theory and Sexual Politics
abstract: teven Seidman examines the implications for social theory and sexual politics of taking difference seriously. He explores the troubles difference can make for the social sciences and for the very people--feminists, queer theorists, postmodernists--who champion difference. This is a wide-ranging and sophisticated discussion of contemporary social theory and sexual politics, focusing on difference, knowledge and power. It also argues persuasively for a pragmatic approach to questions of difference in theory and politics.

title: Classification, Ontology, and Precision Medicine.
abstract: Ontologies, Phenotypes, and Big Data Data-organizing methods have been in place for centuries, but very large data sets have come into being relatively recently. The authors describe terminologies,...

title: Response Rates in Business and Management Research: An Overview of Current Practice and Suggestions for Future Direction
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of response rates (RR) in business and management research, critically examining current practices and offering guidance for future studies. Drawing on a review of 1,093 survey-based articles from leading journals, the study highlights the persistent decline in RR and the lack of consensus on acceptable thresholds, noting that standards vary widely across disciplines, regions, and subfields. The analysis evaluates the effectiveness of commonly recommended strategies to enhance RR, such as Dillman’s Total Design Method, personalization, pre-notification, follow-ups, incentives, and survey design considerations. Findings indicate mixed evidence regarding the impact of these techniques and underscore inconsistent adherence to best practices in reporting and improving RR. The paper concludes by proposing informed baselines for evaluating RR adequacy rather than rigid benchmarks, aiming to assist authors, reviewers, and editors in making informed judgments about survey quality. Recommendations for future research include greater transparency in reporting RR procedures and outcomes, as well as further investigation into context-specific factors influencing participation in business and management surveys.

title: Predicted growth in plastic waste exceeds efforts to mitigate plastic pollution
abstract: A mess of plastic It is not clear what strategies will be most effective in mitigating harm from the global problem of plastic pollution. Borrelle et al. and Lau et al. discuss possible solutions and their impacts. Both groups found that substantial reductions in plastic-waste generation can be made in the coming decades with immediate, concerted, and vigorous action, but even in the best case scenario, huge quantities of plastic will still accumulate in the environment. Science, this issue p. 1515, p. 1455 Even the most optimistic scenario projects huge amounts of plastic pollution in the coming decades. Plastic pollution is a planetary threat, affecting nearly every marine and freshwater ecosystem globally. In response, multilevel mitigation strategies are being adopted but with a lack of quantitative assessment of how such strategies reduce plastic emissions. We assessed the impact of three broad management strategies, plastic waste reduction, waste management, and environmental recovery, at different levels of effort to estimate plastic emissions to 2030 for 173 countries. We estimate that 19 to 23 million metric tons, or 11%, of plastic waste generated globally in 2016 entered aquatic ecosystems. Considering the ambitious commitments currently set by governments, annual emissions may reach up to 53 million metric tons per year by 2030. To reduce emissions to a level well below this prediction, extraordinary efforts to transform the global plastics economy are needed.

title: Universally Sloppy Parameter Sensitivities in Systems Biology Models
abstract: Quantitative computational models play an increasingly important role in modern biology. Such models typically involve many free parameters, and assigning their values is often a substantial obstacle to model development. Directly measuring in vivo biochemical parameters is difficult, and collectively fitting them to other experimental data often yields large parameter uncertainties. Nevertheless, in earlier work we showed in a growth-factor-signaling model that collective fitting could yield well-constrained predictions, even when it left individual parameters very poorly constrained. We also showed that the model had a “sloppy” spectrum of parameter sensitivities, with eigenvalues roughly evenly distributed over many decades. Here we use a collection of models from the literature to test whether such sloppy spectra are common in systems biology. Strikingly, we find that every model we examine has a sloppy spectrum of sensitivities. We also test several consequences of this sloppiness for building predictive models. In particular, sloppiness suggests that collective fits to even large amounts of ideal time-series data will often leave many parameters poorly constrained. Tests over our model collection are consistent with this suggestion. This difficulty with collective fits may seem to argue for direct parameter measurements, but sloppiness also implies that such measurements must be formidably precise and complete to usefully constrain many model predictions. We confirm this implication in our growth-factor-signaling model. Our results suggest that sloppy sensitivity spectra are universal in systems biology models. The prevalence of sloppiness highlights the power of collective fits and suggests that modelers should focus on predictions rather than on parameters.

title: Evolutionary Game Theory: A Renaissance
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive survey of recent advances in evolutionary game theory, emphasizing its resurgence and expanding relevance within the social sciences. By moving beyond the traditional focus on Nash equilibrium, the review highlights how evolutionary models capture the adaptive, context-dependent behaviors of agents who may not be fully rational or farsighted. The survey organizes progress around key themes: the evolution and structure of agency, assortativity in interactions, the development of behavioral traits and cultural conventions, and applications to economic phenomena such as market selection and macroeconomic dynamics. It further examines methodological innovations in dynamic modeling, including reinforcement learning and imitation, as well as empirical studies testing evolutionary predictions. Special attention is given to contributions from emerging scholars and to open research questions that point toward future directions. The paper argues that evolutionary game theory offers a more realistic and empirically grounded framework for understanding complex social and economic systems, where simple individual rules can give rise to intricate collective outcomes.

title: Personal Knowledge: Towards a post-critical philosophy
abstract: The publication of Personal Knowledge in 1958 shook the science world, as Michael Polanyi took aim at the long-standing ideals of rigid empiricism and rule-bound logic. Today, Personal Knowledge remains one of the most significant philosophy of science books of the twentieth century, bringing the crucial concepts of “tacit knowledge” and “personal knowledge” to the forefront of inquiry.  In this remarkable treatise, Polanyi attests that our personal experiences and ways of sharing knowledge have a profound effect on scientific discovery. He argues against the idea of the wholly dispassionate researcher, pointing out that even in the strictest of sciences, knowing is still an art, and that personal commitment and passion are logically necessary parts of research. In our technological age where fact is split from value and science from humanity, Polanyi’s work continues to advocate for the innate curiosity and scientific leaps of faith that drive our most dazzling ingenuity.  For this expanded edition, Polyani scholar Mary Jo Nye set the philosopher-scientist’s work into contemporary context, offering fresh insights and providing a helpful guide to critical terms in the work. Used in fields as diverse as religious studies, chemistry, economics, and anthropology, Polanyi’s view of knowledge creation is just as relevant to intellectual endeavors today as when it first made waves more than fifty years ago

title: Gas-grain chemistry in cold interstellar cloud cores with a microscopic Monte Carlo approach to surface chemistry
abstract: We present the first integration of a microscopic continuous-time random walk (CTRW) Monte Carlo approach for surface chemistry with a standard rate-equation treatment of gas-phase chemistry to model gas-grain interactions in cold interstellar cloud cores. Our method overcomes limitations of traditional rate-equation and macroscopic stochastic approaches by explicitly tracking the diffusion, reaction, and morphology of ice mantles on olivine grain surfaces at the monolayer level, accounting for discrete populations and local fluctuations. The chemical network includes diffusive reactions among H, O, and CO leading to the formation of key mantle species such as water, carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, methanol, and molecular oxygen. Simulations iteratively couple gas-phase abundances and surface processes under conditions where only atomic hydrogen undergoes significant evaporation. We compute mantle abundances as a function of time up to 2 × 10⁵ years and resolve molecular distributions within individual monolayers. Comparison with observed ice compositions in sources W33A and Elias 16 shows strong agreement for water, carbon dioxide, and methanol, with only minor underproduction of mantle CO. This work demonstrates the efficacy of microscopic Monte Carlo methods for accurately modeling the coupled evolution of gas-phase and grain-surface chemistry in dense interstellar environments.

title: B-physics anomalies: a guide to combined explanations
abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the observed anomalies in B-meson decays that suggest violations of Lepton Flavour Universality (LFU) in both charged- and neutral-current processes. Employing an Effective Field Theory (EFT) framework with new physics predominantly coupled to third-generation left-handed quarks and leptons, the study systematically explores the minimal set of semi-leptonic operators required to explain the data. The analysis incorporates constraints from electroweak precision tests, high-pT LHC searches, and flavor observables, under the assumption of a minimally broken U(2)q × U(2)ℓ flavor symmetry. The EFT results are further illustrated through simplified models featuring explicit mediators, such as vector and scalar leptoquarks and colorless vectors at the TeV scale. Among these, the SU(2)L-singlet vector leptoquark model emerges as a particularly promising and natural candidate for a unified explanation of both sets of anomalies while remaining consistent with current experimental bounds. The findings offer a guide for constructing viable new physics scenarios addressing B-physics anomalies and highlight key directions for future theoretical and experimental investigations.

title: Quantum computing
abstract: This paper presents an accessible introduction to the principles of quantum computing using the framework of spin resonance methods. Emphasizing that quantum computing is fundamentally a reinterpretation of established concepts in quantum two-level systems, the discussion focuses on how qubits can be represented by spins and manipulated through well-known operations. The essential role of one-spin rotations and controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates is analyzed, demonstrating that any quantum computation can be decomposed into these basic operations. The challenges posed by decoherence and the practical limitations of current experimental realizations are addressed, highlighting the importance of selectivity in pulse application for accurate qubit control. The paper provides a pedagogical model for implementing quantum logic gates and offers exercises to reinforce understanding, making the subject accessible to undergraduate students and newcomers to the field.

title: Engineering optimisation by cuckoo search
abstract: A new metaheuristic optimisation algorithm, called Cuckoo Search (CS), was developed recently by Yang and Deb (2009). This paper presents a more extensive comparison study using some standard test functions and newly designed stochastic test functions. We then apply the CS algorithm to solve engineering design optimisation problems, including the design of springs and welded beam structures. The optimal solutions obtained by CS are far better than the best solutions obtained by an efficient particle swarm optimiser. We will discuss the unique search features used in CS and the implications for further research.
venue: Int. J. Math. Model. Numer. Optimisation

title: Hospital Readmission in General Medicine Patients: A Prediction Model
abstract: This study aimed to identify predictors of early hospital readmission among general medicine patients and to develop and validate a simple risk prediction model. In a prospective cohort of 10,946 patients discharged home from six academic medical centers, patients were randomly assigned to derivation (n=7,287) and validation (n=3,659) cohorts. Readmissions within 30 days were identified using administrative data and post-discharge telephone follow-up. Logistic regression analysis examined patient-level factors across sociodemographic, social support, health condition, and healthcare utilization domains. Seven variables—insurance status, marital status, having a regular physician, Charlson comorbidity index, SF12 physical component score, prior admissions in the past year, and current length of stay >2 days—were significant predictors of readmission. A cumulative risk score of ≥25 points identified 5% of patients with a 30% readmission risk in both cohorts. Model discrimination was fair (c-statistic 0.65 derivation; 0.61 validation). Easily obtainable patient characteristics shortly after admission can identify those at elevated risk for early readmission and may inform targeted interventions to reduce readmissions.

title: Information Production and Capital Allocation: Decentralized vs. Hierarchical Firms
abstract: This paper assesses different organizational forms in terms of their ability to generate information about investment projects and allocate capital to these projects efficiently. A decentralized approach with small, single-manager firms is most likely to be attractive when information about individual projects is soft' and cannot be credibly transmitted. Moreover, holding fixed firm size, soft information also favors flatter organizations with fewer layers of management. In contrast, large hierarchical firms with multiple layers of management are at a comparative advantage when information can be costlessly hardened' and passed along within the hierarchy. As a concrete application of the theory, the paper discusses the consequences of consolidation in the banking industry. It has been documented that when large banks acquire small banks, there is a pronounced decline in lending to small businesses. To the extent that small-business lending relies heavily on soft information, this is exactly what the theory would lead one to expect.

title: Opportunities and Challenges for Machine Learning in Materials Science
abstract: Advances in machine learning have impacted myriad areas of materials science, such as the discovery of novel materials and the improvement of molecular simulations, with likely many more important developments to come. Given the rapid changes in this field, it is challenging to understand both the breadth of opportunities and the best practices for their use. In this review, we address aspects of both problems by providing an overview of the areas in which machine learning has recently had significant impact in materials science, and then we provide a more detailed discussion on determining the accuracy and domain of applicability of some common types of machine learning models. Finally, we discuss some opportunities and challenges for the materials community to fully utilize the capabilities of machine learning.

title: Biology of RANK, RANKL, and osteoprotegerin
abstract: The RANK/RANKL/osteoprotegerin (OPG) system, discovered in the late 1990s, is central to the regulation of bone resorption and has expanded our understanding of bone biology and immunology. RANKL, a member of the tumor necrosis factor superfamily, expressed by osteoblasts and stromal cells, binds to its receptor RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive their differentiation, activation, and survival, processes essential for normal bone remodeling and implicated in pathological conditions such as osteoporosis and rheumatoid arthritis. OPG acts as a decoy receptor for RANKL, inhibiting its interaction with RANK and thereby protecting against excessive bone loss; thus, the RANKL/OPG ratio is a key determinant of skeletal integrity. Genetic studies have revealed that this signaling axis also plays roles beyond bone, including lymph node development, mammary gland function, and vascular calcification prevention. The identification of these molecules has provided significant insights into osteoclast biology, the interplay between bone and immune systems, and potential therapeutic targets for skeletal and systemic diseases. This review summarizes current knowledge of the RANK/RANKL/OPG system in bone remodeling and highlights emerging evidence of its broader physiological functions.

title: Molecular Weight Dependence of Polymersome Membrane Structure, Elasticity, and Stability
abstract: This study investigates how the molecular weight of diblock copolymers influences the structure, elasticity, and stability of polymersome membranes in comparison to lipid vesicles. Using a series of poly(ethylene oxide)-polybutadiene (PEO-PBD) copolymers, vesicle membranes were prepared and characterized by cryogenic transmission electron microscopy and micropipette aspiration. Results show that increasing the number-average molecular weight (Mn) leads to a significant increase in hydrophobic core thickness, reaching up to 20 nm—well beyond that of lipid membranes. The area elastic modulus (Ka) remains constant at approximately 100 pN/nm, independent of Mn but lower than values typical for zwitterionic lipid membranes. In contrast, maximal areal strain (αc) increases nearly linearly with Mn, approaching a universal limit predicted by mean-field theory and exceeding that of lipids by an order of magnitude. At higher Mn, nonlinear mechanical responses and memory effects emerge, suggesting the onset of chain entanglements. These findings reveal a molecular weight-dependent compromise between membrane stability and fluidity, highlighting fundamental interfacial constraints governing self-assembled nanoscale structures.

title: Metabolic engineering for the production of natural products.
abstract: Natural products are a vital source of bioactive compounds for pharmaceuticals and other applications, yet their structural complexity and low natural abundance often limit commercial production. Recent advances in sequencing, recombinant DNA technology, and systems biology have enabled the elucidation and manipulation of biosynthetic pathways responsible for these compounds. Metabolic engineering, which involves the rational modification of an organism’s genetic and metabolic networks, has emerged as a powerful strategy to enhance natural product titers and generate novel analogs. This review discusses key approaches in metabolic engineering for strain improvement, including increasing precursor supply, optimizing bottleneck enzymes, altering regulatory mechanisms, minimizing byproduct formation, and reconstructing pathways in heterologous hosts. The use of heterologous production platforms, particularly in well-characterized bacterial strains such as Streptomyces and Escherichia coli, has expanded access to natural products from genetically intractable or slow-growing organisms. Advances in protein engineering and genome-scale metabolic modeling further facilitate pathway optimization and the design of hybrid biosynthetic routes. Collectively, these developments have transformed metabolic engineering into a robust tool for both improving yields of existing natural products and enabling the discovery and production of new bioactive molecules.
venue: Annual Review of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering

title: Electrochemical Biosensors: Recommended Definitions and Classification
abstract: This paper presents standardized definitions and a comprehensive classification system for electrochemical biosensors, as recommended by IUPAC’s Divisions of Physical and Analytical Chemistry. An electrochemical biosensor is defined as a self-contained, integrated device that provides specific quantitative or semi-quantitative analytical information through a biological recognition element in direct contact with an electrochemical transducer. The distinction between biosensors and broader bioanalytical systems is emphasized, particularly regarding calibration and operational autonomy. The classification framework considers both the nature of the biological recognition mechanism and the mode of physicochemical signal transduction, encompassing devices based on isolated or engineered biomolecules, whole cells, or tissues. Further subdivisions are proposed based on analyte type, reaction monitored, and operational mode, including single-use biosensors. The paper addresses the proliferation and diversity of biosensors, highlighting the need for rigorous performance criteria and standardized protocols in line with IUPAC recommendations. Key performance parameters such as sensitivity, selectivity, response time, reproducibility, stability, and lifetime are outlined to guide authors, referees, and educators in the field. This work aims to promote clarity and consistency in biosensor terminology and evaluation.

title: Bone tissue engineering: state of the art and future trends.
abstract: Although several major progresses have been introduced in the field of bone regenerative medicine during the years, current therapies, such as bone grafts, still have many limitations. Moreover, and in spite of the fact that material science technology has resulted in clear improvements in the field of bone substitution medicine, no adequate bone substitute has been developed and hence large bone defects/injuries still represent a major challenge for orthopaedic and reconstructive surgeons. It is in this context that TE has been emerging as a valid approach to the current therapies for bone regeneration/substitution. In contrast to classic biomaterial approach, TE is based on the understanding of tissue formation and regeneration, and aims to induce new functional tissues, rather than just to implant new spare parts. The present review pretends to give an exhaustive overview on all components needed for making bone tissue engineering a successful therapy. It begins by giving the reader a brief background on bone biology, followed by an exhaustive description of all the relevant components on bone TE, going from materials to scaffolds and from cells to tissue engineering strategies, that will lead to 'engineered' bone. Scaffolds processed by using a methodology based on extrusion with blowing agents.

title: PYTHIA 6.4 Physics and Manual
abstract: PYTHIA 6.4 is a comprehensive event generator for high-energy physics, designed to simulate the production and evolution of multiparticle final states in collisions involving elementary particles such as e+e−, pp, and ep. The program integrates a wide range of physics models, combining analytical results with QCD-based approaches to describe hard subprocesses, initial- and final-state parton showers, beam remnants, multiple interactions, hadronization, and particle decays. This manual provides detailed documentation of the underlying physics assumptions, the structure and usage of the code, and the implementation of Monte Carlo techniques essential for event generation. It includes extensive information on subroutines, parameters, switches, and data structures, enabling users to customize simulations for diverse research applications. PYTHIA 6.4 thus serves as both a practical tool for experimental analysis and a reference for theoretical developments in multiparticle production at the forefront of particle physics research.

title: Overview of natural hydrogels for regenerative medicine applications
abstract: Hydrogels from different materials can be used in biomedical field as an innovative approach in regenerative medicine. Depending on the origin source, hydrogels can be synthetized through chemical and physical methods. Hydrogel can be characterized through several physical parameters, such as size, elastic modulus, swelling and degradation rate. Lately, research is focused on hydrogels derived from biologic materials. These hydrogels can be derived from protein polymers, such as collage, elastin, and polysaccharide polymers like glycosaminoglycans or alginate among others. Introduction of decellularized tissues into hydrogels synthesis displays several advantages compared to natural or synthetic based hydrogels. Preservation of natural molecules such as growth factors, glycans, bioactive cryptic peptides and natural proteins can promote cell growth, function, differentiation, angiogenesis, anti-angiogenesis, antimicrobial effects, and chemotactic effects. Versatility of hydrogels make possible multiple applications and combinations with several molecules on order to obtain the adequate characteristic for each scope. In this context, a lot of molecules such as cross link agents, drugs, grow factors or cells can be used. This review focuses on the recent progress of hydrogels synthesis and applications in order to classify the most recent and relevant matters in biomedical field.
venue: Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Medicine
