title: Multimodal Emotion Recognition using Deep Learning
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of recent advancements in multimodal emotion recognition using deep learning techniques, emphasizing the integration of facial expressions, speech, and physiological signals to enhance the accuracy and robustness of emotion detection systems. The study discusses the limitations of unimodal approaches and highlights the superiority of multimodal systems in capturing the complexity of human emotions. Various deep learning architectures, including convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and hybrid fusion models, are examined for their effectiveness in feature extraction and classification across different modalities. The paper also surveys recent research on combining audio, text, and visual data, detailing innovative fusion strategies such as attention mechanisms and self-supervised learning frameworks. Comparative analyses demonstrate that multimodal deep learning approaches achieve higher precision in emotion classification, with performance influenced by factors such as the number of emotion categories, feature selection methods, and dataset consistency. The review concludes by identifying current challenges and suggesting directions for future research to further improve real-time emotion recognition systems in diverse applications ranging from healthcare to human-computer interaction.
venue: Journal of Applied Science and Technology Trends

title: An efficient recombination system for chromosome engineering in Escherichia coli.
abstract: A recombination system has been developed for efficient chromosome engineering in Escherichia coli by using electroporated linear DNA. A defective lambda prophage supplies functions that protect and recombine an electroporated linear DNA substrate in the bacterial cell. The use of recombination eliminates the requirement for standard cloning as all novel joints are engineered by chemical synthesis in vitro and the linear DNA is efficiently recombined into place in vivo. The technology and manipulations required are simple and straightforward. A temperature-dependent repressor tightly controls prophage expression, and, thus, recombination functions can be transiently supplied by shifting cultures to 42 degrees C for 15 min. The efficient prophage recombination system does not require host RecA function and depends primarily on Exo, Beta, and Gam functions expressed from the defective lambda prophage. The defective prophage can be moved to other strains and can be easily removed from any strain. Gene disruptions and modifications of both the bacterial chromosome and bacterial plasmids are possible. This system will be especially useful for the engineering of large bacterial plasmids such as those from bacterial artificial chromosome libraries.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Teachers’ roles and identities in student-centered classrooms
abstract: Students and teachers in twenty-first century STEM classrooms face significant challenges in preparing for post-secondary education, career, and citizenship. Educators have advocated for student-centered instruction as a way to face these challenges, with multiple programs emerging to shape and define such contexts. However, the ways to support teachers as they transition into non-traditional teaching must be developed. The purpose of this study is to explore the impacts on educators of teaching in student-centered, peer-mediated STEM classrooms and preparing student peer leaders for their roles in these classes. Research questions examined how teachers think about themselves as they implement student-centered pedagogy, the difficulties they face as their roles and identities shift, and the ways they grow or resist growth. Qualitative research conducted at two urban secondary schools documents the diverse experiences and responses of teachers in an innovative, student-centered STEM instructional program. The experiences and perceptions of 13 STEM teachers illuminate the possibilities and challenges for teachers in student-centered classrooms.ResultsAll participating teachers described multiple benefits of teaching in a student-centered classroom and differences from traditional classrooms. Their transitions to this type of teaching fell into three major categories based upon past identities and current beliefs. Some teachers found the pedagogy consistent with preexisting identities and embraced it without radical change to their concepts of teaching. They described ways in which the model helped them become the teachers they had always wanted to be. Other teachers, who initially identified as deliverers of STEM content, had more difficult experiences adjusting to student-centered instruction. In one case, a teacher resisted change and exited the program, maintaining her identity and deciding not to become student-centered. Other participating teachers made dramatic shifts in their identities in order to implement the program. These teachers described significant learning curves as they shared responsibility for student learning with student leaders.ConclusionsThis study suggests that radically changing the learning environment can affect teachers’ identities and their approaches to teaching in predictable ways that can inform teacher education and professional development programs for STEM teachers, maximizing the success of teachers as they implement student-centered pedagogy.

title: Quantum thermodynamics
abstract: Quantum thermodynamics is an emerging research field aiming to extend standard thermodynamics and non-equilibrium statistical physics to ensembles of sizes well below the thermodynamic limit, in non-equilibrium situations and with the full inclusion of quantum effects. Fuelled by experimental advances and the potential of future nanoscale applications, this research effort is pursued by scientists with different backgrounds, including statistical physics, many-body theory, mesoscopic physics and quantum information theory, who bring various tools and methods to the field. A multitude of theoretical questions are being addressed ranging from issues of thermalisation of quantum systems and various definitions of ‘work’ to the efficiency and power of quantum engines. This overview provides a perspective on a selection of these current trends accessible to postgraduate students and researchers alike.

title: Review of collagen I hydrogels for bioengineered tissue microenvironments: characterization of mechanics, structure, and transport.
abstract: Type I collagen hydrogels have been used successfully as three-dimensional substrates for cell culture and have shown promise as scaffolds for engineered tissues and tumors. A critical step in the development of collagen hydrogels as viable tissue mimics is quantitative characterization of hydrogel properties and their correlation with fabrication parameters, which enables hydrogels to be tuned to match specific tissues or fulfill engineering requirements. A significant body of work has been devoted to characterization of collagen I hydrogels; however, due to the breadth of materials and techniques used for characterization, published data are often disjoint and hence their utility to the community is reduced. This review aims to determine the parameter space covered by existing data and identify key gaps in the literature so that future characterization and use of collagen I hydrogels for research can be most efficiently conducted. This review is divided into three sections: (1) relevant fabrication parameters are introduced and several of the most popular methods of controlling and regulating them are described, (2) hydrogel properties most relevant for tissue engineering are presented and discussed along with their characterization techniques, (3) the state of collagen I hydrogel characterization is recapitulated and future directions are proposed. Ultimately, this review can serve as a resource for selection of fabrication parameters and material characterization methodologies in order to increase the usefulness of future collagen-hydrogel-based characterization studies and tissue engineering experiments.

title: Colloquium: Atomic quantum gases in periodically driven optical lattices
abstract: Dynamics of quantum many-body systems is one of the most complex problems in physics since it involves the time evolution of a large number of particles that interact with each other under the influence of external forces. With ultracold atoms in optical atomic lattices it can be done in a controlled environment by applying a periodic force. This Colloquium covers the experimental and theoretical developments in this exciting field of physics.

title: Particle Physics and Inflationary Cosmology
abstract: This work presents a comprehensive exploration of the interplay between particle physics and inflationary cosmology, focusing on the theoretical foundations and implications of unified gauge theories, spontaneous symmetry breaking, and early universe phase transitions. It systematically examines the development of inflationary models, including new and chaotic inflation scenarios, and analyzes quantum effects, reheating, baryogenesis, and the generation of large-scale structure. The text integrates advances in scalar field theory, effective potentials, and quantum cosmology to elucidate the mechanisms driving cosmic inflation and the evolution of the universe. Emphasis is placed on the restoration of symmetry at high temperatures, the dynamics of phase transitions in both hot and cold superdense matter, and the role of quantum fluctuations in shaping cosmological perturbations. The discussion incorporates recent observational confirmations of inflationary predictions and addresses ongoing challenges such as the cosmological constant problem and the anthropic principle. This work serves as both a foundational reference for researchers and a pedagogical resource for advanced students, providing a rigorous framework for understanding the intersection of high-energy particle physics and modern cosmology.

title: Astrocytes: biology and pathology
abstract: Astrocytes, the most abundant glial cell type in the central nervous system (CNS), play critical roles in maintaining CNS homeostasis, supporting neuronal function, and modulating synaptic activity. Traditionally viewed as passive support cells, astrocytes are now recognized for their active participation in information processing and neural circuit regulation. In response to CNS injury or disease, astrocytes undergo reactive astrogliosis, a highly regulated and context-dependent process characterized by a spectrum of molecular and structural changes ranging from reversible gene expression alterations to permanent glial scar formation. Advances in molecular profiling and transgenic mouse models have elucidated the diverse mechanisms underlying reactive astrogliosis and highlighted its dual potential to be either protective or detrimental, depending on the context. Loss of normal astrocyte functions or gain of abnormal effects through reactive changes can contribute to the pathogenesis of various CNS disorders. This review synthesizes recent progress in understanding astrocyte biology in healthy tissue, the mechanisms and consequences of reactive astrogliosis and glial scar formation, and the emerging evidence for astrocyte involvement in specific neuropathological conditions.

title: Molecular Weight Dependence of Polymersome Membrane Structure, Elasticity, and Stability
abstract: This study investigates how the molecular weight of poly(ethylene oxide)-polybutadiene (PEO-PBD) diblock copolymers influences the structure, elasticity, and stability of polymersome membranes, in comparison to lipid vesicles. Using cryogenic transmission electron microscopy and micropipette aspiration, we show that increasing copolymer molecular weight leads to a significant increase in hydrophobic core thickness, reaching up to 20 nm—far exceeding typical lipid bilayers. The area elastic modulus remains constant across molecular weights but is lower than that of zwitterionic lipid membranes, while maximal areal strain increases nearly linearly with molecular weight, approaching a universal limit predicted by mean-field theory and greatly surpassing that of lipids. At higher molecular weights, nonlinear mechanical responses and memory effects emerge, indicating chain entanglement within the membrane. These findings reveal a trade-off between stability and fluidity in biomembrane mimics and highlight the interfacial constraints governing nanoscale self-assembly. Overall, this work provides new insights into how molecular architecture controls the physical properties of synthetic vesicle membranes and suggests design principles for robust biomimetic systems.

title: A Risk Society
abstract: This paper examines the transformation of rural China through the lens of Ulrich Beck’s “risk society” theory, arguing that traditional social theories centered on class and wealth distribution inadequately explain the new forms of crisis and inequality engendered by modernization. Focusing on the small peasant economy as a foundational element of China’s rural structure, the study traces its evolution from a subsistence-based, autarkic system to its integration into a dual urban-rural social structure shaped by state policies and industrialization. The analysis highlights how state-driven industrial priorities and institutional arrangements, such as the hukou system, reinforced rural-urban segregation and perpetuated the dominance of smallholder agriculture even after industrialization. With market reforms and the breakdown of spatial and institutional barriers, rural areas were exposed to new vulnerabilities as traditional economic practices collided with market mechanisms, leading to persistent disparities in welfare, security, and opportunity. The paper concludes that contemporary rural China exemplifies a risk society in which systemic hazards—rather than class-based inequalities—define social stratification and governance challenges.

title: Human organoids: model systems for human biology and medicine
abstract: Human organoids, derived from pluripotent or adult stem cells, have emerged as advanced three-dimensional in vitro culture systems that closely recapitulate the architecture and function of human organs, offering a transformative platform for studying human biology and disease. While classical cell lines and animal models have been instrumental in elucidating fundamental biological processes and guiding drug discovery, their limitations in modeling human-specific physiology and pathologies have become increasingly apparent. Organoids overcome many of these challenges by enabling the investigation of developmental processes, disease mechanisms, and drug responses in a physiologically relevant human context. This review highlights the development and applications of organoid technology, comparing its advantages and disadvantages to traditional model systems, and discusses its potential to complement or even reduce reliance on animal models. We also address current challenges in organoid research and outline emerging tools and methodologies that are expanding the utility of organoids for basic research, disease modeling, and precision medicine.

title: Parton physics on a Euclidean lattice.
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach for accessing parton physics on a Euclidean lattice by relating light-cone correlations of quarks and gluons to frame-dependent, equal-time correlators in the large momentum limit. The method enables practical calculations of parton distribution functions (PDFs) and related quantities using lattice QCD, circumventing the traditional limitations of Euclidean time and the difficulty of computing higher moments. By boosting equal-time nonlocal operators to large nucleon momenta, the leading-twist quark and gluon distributions can be reconstructed, with power-suppressed corrections systematically controlled. The approach is extended to generalized parton distributions and transverse-momentum dependent distributions, providing a unified framework for studying a wide range of hadronic structure observables on the lattice. Matching procedures are discussed to relate lattice-calculated quantities to their light-cone counterparts, accounting for ultraviolet divergences and renormalization effects. This work opens new avenues for first-principles calculations of partonic structure in hadrons, complementing and enhancing existing moment-based techniques in lattice QCD.

title: The Bioperl toolkit: Perl modules for the life sciences.
abstract: The Bioperl toolkit is an open-source collection of Perl modules designed to address the diverse computational needs of the life sciences community. Developed through international collaboration, Bioperl provides a comprehensive, user-friendly, and extensible framework for managing, analyzing, and integrating biological data. Its object-oriented architecture supports a wide range of tasks, including sequence analysis, annotation, database access, phylogenetics, protein structure, and bibliographic reference management. By offering reusable components and a consistent programming interface, Bioperl streamlines complex bioinformatics workflows and reduces redundant software development efforts. The toolkit facilitates interoperability with external applications and data formats, supports integration with Python and Java via BioCORBA, and provides extensive documentation and tutorials to lower the barrier for new users. This paper describes the design principles, module organization, and practical applications of Bioperl, highlighting how its open-source model accelerates community-driven innovation in bioinformatics software development.

title: Innovation, Dynamic Capabilities, and Leadership
abstract: The world in which today’s businesses operate has become not only riskier but also more volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA). Organizations that hew too closely to traditional ways of operating will be hampered in their ability to succeed. In contrast, those that focus on new product and process developments coupled with business model innovation will leverage their dynamic capabilities. An essential overlay is entrepreneurial leadership from top management teams. Strong dynamic capabilities are impossible without it. This article examines how business model innovations, dynamic capabilities, and strategic leadership intertwine to help organizations thrive in VUCA worlds.

title: The Past, Present, and Future of Media Literacy Education
abstract: This paper examines the evolution of media literacy education in the United States, tracing its historical roots from early 20th-century visual education movements to its current status as a cross-disciplinary field integrating constructivist learning theory, media studies, and cultural studies. The authors highlight the development of core principles that reconcile protectionist and empowerment approaches, reflecting a maturing consensus among scholars and practitioners. The analysis addresses persistent challenges, such as the fragmentation of the field and tensions between educational and commercial interests. Looking forward, the paper identifies two critical issues shaping the future of media literacy education: its relationship with educational technology integration in K-12 curricula and its connections to the humanities, arts, and sciences. By situating media literacy as both a critical citizenship practice and a transcurricular endeavor, the paper underscores its ongoing relevance in fostering communication, creativity, collaboration, and critical thinking skills in response to evolving media landscapes.

title: Pedagogic partnership in higher education: encountering emotion in learning and enhancing student wellbeing
abstract: This paper explores the role of pedagogic partnership in higher education as a means to engage with student emotion in learning and enhance student wellbeing. Recognizing that affective dimensions are often overlooked despite their fundamental importance, the authors examine how collaborative partnerships between students and faculty, as well as among students, can foster emotional awareness, resilience, and positive wellbeing outcomes. Drawing on two case studies within geography curricula, the research demonstrates that encountering and working through emotions in partnership settings supports transformative learning and academic resilience. The paper further develops an evidence-based model illustrating the mechanisms by which pedagogic partnership can enhance wellbeing, and offers practical guidance for faculty to navigate the emotional aspects of teaching. The findings highlight the need to integrate affective and cognitive domains in higher education, positioning pedagogic partnership as a key strategy for supporting student wellbeing in contemporary academic environments.
venue: Journal of Geography in Higher Education

title: Theory, General Equilibrium and Political Economy in Development Economics
abstract: This paper examines the essential role of economic theory, particularly general equilibrium and political economy considerations, in the empirical analysis of development economics. It argues that theory is crucial for ensuring the external validity of econometric estimates and for guiding counterfactual and policy analysis. The paper highlights how analyses that ignore general equilibrium effects—such as changes in factor prices or technology resulting from large-scale interventions—and political economy constraints—such as the influence of interest groups and institutional responses—can lead to misleading conclusions about policy impacts. Through illustrative examples, the paper demonstrates that partial equilibrium approaches may fail to capture important systemic responses, and stresses that robust development policy evaluation requires integrating theoretical frameworks capable of addressing these broader interactions. The discussion underscores the need for structural parameters that provide meaningful guidance beyond specific samples or contexts, and advocates for a central role for theory in both empirical estimation and policy design within development economics.

title: Economics and the Modern Economic Historian
abstract: This paper examines the evolving role of economic history within the economics profession, documenting a notable resurgence in the presence of economic history research in top economics journals over recent decades. Drawing on publication trends and job market outcomes, the analysis highlights that economic historians today enjoy professional prospects comparable to those of their peers in other fields. The study argues that historical analysis has become increasingly valued for its contributions to testing economic theories, informing policy, and addressing major economic questions. The paper also explores how advances in data availability, digitization, and computational methods are poised to further transform the field, enabling richer and more rigorous analysis of historical phenomena. Overall, the paper contends that while most economists remain primarily interested in history for its relevance to current issues, the integration of historical perspective is now recognized as essential for a deeper understanding of economic mechanisms and development.

title: Synthetic biology - putting engineering into biology
abstract: Synthetic biology is interpreted as the engineering-driven building of increasingly complex biological entities for novel applications. Encouraged by progress in the design of artificial gene networks, de novo DNA synthesis and protein engineering, we review the case for this emerging discipline. Key aspects of an engineering approach are purpose-orientation, deep insight into the underlying scientific principles, a hierarchy of abstraction including suitable interfaces between and within the levels of the hierarchy, standardization and the separation of design and fabrication. Synthetic biology investigates possibilities to implement these requirements into the process of engineering biological systems. This is illustrated on the DNA level by the implementation of engineering-inspired artificial operations such as toggle switching, oscillating or production of spatial patterns. On the protein level, the functionally self-contained domain structure of a number of proteins suggests possibilities for essentially Lego-like recombination which can be exploited for reprogramming DNA binding domain specificities or signaling pathways. Alternatively, computational design emerges to rationally reprogram enzyme function. Finally, the increasing facility of de novo DNA synthesis-synthetic biology's system fabrication process-supplies the possibility to implement novel designs for ever more complex systems. Some of these elements have merged to realize the first tangible synthetic biology applications in the area of manufacturing of pharmaceutical compounds.

title: Chemistry and biology of multicomponent reactions.
abstract: Multicomponent reactions (MCRs) represent a powerful and efficient synthetic strategy that enables the rapid assembly of structurally diverse and complex molecules from simple starting materials in a single step. This review explores the unique chemistry and biology of MCRs, highlighting their atom economy, convergence, and high bond-forming index, which make them attractive alternatives to traditional multistep synthesis. The versatility of MCRs is demonstrated through their ability to generate a wide array of scaffolds, including cyclic, acyclic, spirocyclic, macrocyclic, and polycyclic frameworks, many of which are difficult to access by other means. The scaffold diversity achievable through primary MCR products and subsequent orthogonal transformations has been instrumental in advancing combinatorial and medicinal chemistry, particularly for drug discovery. The review emphasizes the significance of MCR-derived chemical space as a synthetically feasible subset of the vast chemical universe, facilitating the design of biologically relevant compound libraries with distinct 3D shapes and physicochemical properties tailored to specific target classes. Notably, MCRs have enabled the synthesis of compounds with unique shapes and functionalities that exhibit promising biological activities, including those relevant to protein-protein interactions and challenging drug targets. This work provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in MCR chemistry with a focus on biologically active molecules, underscoring the rich opportunities MCRs offer for the discovery and optimization of new therapeutic agents.

title: A Critical Success Factors Model for ERP Implementation
abstract: This nested qualitative study explores patient and physiotherapist perspectives on Cognitive Muscular TherapyTM (CMT), a novel behavioural intervention for knee osteoarthritis that integrates muscle biofeedback and psychological strategies to target muscle overactivity. Five physiotherapists, trained in a structured CMT protocol, delivered seven individualized sessions to patients with knee osteoarthritis, who also accessed online educational materials. Semi-structured interviews conducted post-intervention revealed a process of belief change among both patients and physiotherapists, organized into three phases: identifying maladaptive pain beliefs, challenging and validating new beliefs through experience, and embedding these changes into self-management practices. Participants described developing a new understanding of their condition, recognizing the interplay between psychological factors and muscle activity, and gaining confidence in managing knee pain. The findings highlight the psychological shifts enabled by CMT and suggest its potential to facilitate reconceptualization of knee osteoarthritis, supporting improved self-management and engagement in daily activities.

title: A conceptual framework for integrated STEM education
abstract: This paper addresses the pressing global need for improved STEM education by proposing a conceptual framework for integrated STEM learning. Recognizing that traditional, siloed approaches to science, technology, engineering, and mathematics fail to engage students or prepare them for complex real-world challenges, the authors highlight the limitations of current educational reforms and the ongoing ambiguity surrounding effective STEM integration. Drawing on recent research and policy developments, the paper operationalizes key concepts in integrated STEM education and synthesizes relevant learning theories to construct a framework that emphasizes authentic contexts, cross-disciplinary connections, and the application of scientific inquiry and engineering design. The proposed framework aims to support educators and researchers in designing coherent curricula that foster student interest, enhance learning outcomes, and better equip future generations to address global economic, environmental, and societal challenges.

title: Diagnosis and treatment of diabetic foot infections.
abstract: Foot infections in persons with diabetes are a common, complex, and costly problem [1–4]. In addition to causing severe morbidities, they now account for the largest number of diabetes-related hospital bed—days [5] and are the most common proximate, nontraumatic cause of amputations [6, 7]. Diabetic foot infections require careful attention and coordinated management, preferably by a multidisciplinary foot-care team (A-II) [8–13]. The team managing these infections should preferably include, or have ready access to, an infectious diseases specialist or a medical microbiologist (B-III) [1]. Optimal management of diabetic foot infections can potentially reduce the incidence of infection-related morbidities, the need for and duration of hospitalization, and the incidence of major limb amputation [14, 15]. Unfortunately, these infections are frequently inadequately managed [16]. This may result from a lack of understanding of current diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, insufficient resources devoted to the problem, or a lack of effective multidisciplinary collaboration. The primary purpose of this guideline is to help reduce the medical morbidity, psychological distress, and financial costs associated with diabetic foot infections.

title: Recent advances in azaborine chemistry.
abstract: Azaborines, BN isosteres of arenes, have emerged as a versatile class of heterocycles with unique electronic and structural properties distinct from their all-carbon counterparts. Recent advances in azaborine chemistry have enabled the isolation of parent 1,2-dihydro-1,2-azaborine and the synthesis of a wide array of mono- and polycyclic BN-containing aromatic compounds. These developments are driven by the strategic replacement of CC units with isoelectronic BN units, allowing for fine-tuning of molecular properties such as aromaticity, stability, and reactivity. The resulting azaborines exhibit promising potential in biomedical applications and materials science due to their tunable electronic characteristics and resonance stabilization. This review highlights key synthetic methodologies, structural characterization, and functionalization strategies that have expanded the scope of azaborine chemistry, with particular emphasis on recent progress since the early pioneering work and the 50th anniversary of Dewar’s first monocyclic 1,2-dihydro-1,2-azaborine synthesis.

title: Livestock production: recent trends, future prospects
abstract: The livestock sector globally is highly dynamic. In developing countries, it is evolving in response to rapidly increasing demand for livestock products. In developed countries, demand for livestock products is stagnating, while many production systems are increasing their efficiency and environmental sustainability. Historical changes in the demand for livestock products have been largely driven by human population growth, income growth and urbanization and the production response in different livestock systems has been associated with science and technology as well as increases in animal numbers. In the future, production will increasingly be affected by competition for natural resources, particularly land and water, competition between food and feed and by the need to operate in a carbon-constrained economy. Developments in breeding, nutrition and animal health will continue to contribute to increasing potential production and further efficiency and genetic gains. Livestock production is likely to be increasingly affected by carbon constraints and environmental and animal welfare legislation. Demand for livestock products in the future could be heavily moderated by socio-economic factors such as human health concerns and changing socio-cultural values. There is considerable uncertainty as to how these factors will play out in different regions of the world in the coming decades.
venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences

title: Evolutionary Biology for the 21st Century
abstract: New theoretical and conceptual frameworks are required for evolutionary biology to capitalize on the wealth of data now becoming available from the study of genomes, phenotypes, and organisms - including humans - in their natural environments.

title: Whose Science? Whose Knowledge?: Thinking from Women's Lives
abstract: This paper critically examines the relationship between science and feminism, interrogating traditional scientific paradigms through the lens of women's lived experiences. It explores how feminist perspectives challenge the presumed objectivity and universality of scientific knowledge, advocating for an epistemology that recognizes the social situatedness of knowers. The analysis addresses the limitations of using physics as a model for all sciences and highlights the contributions of the women's movement to scientific inquiry. By engaging with issues of race, sexuality, and global context, the paper demonstrates how feminist epistemology can broaden and democratize scientific practices. Ultimately, it argues for a reimagined science that incorporates strong objectivity and values diverse standpoints, positioning feminist science as a transformative force in knowledge production.

title: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for fluid mechanics: a review
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising framework for integrating physical laws, expressed as partial differential equations, with observational data in fluid mechanics. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the principles and recent advances in PINNs, highlighting their ability to solve both forward and inverse problems without the need for mesh generation or separate data assimilation schemes. We discuss the formulation of PINNs, including the incorporation of governing equations and boundary conditions into the loss function via automatic differentiation, and review methodological developments such as domain decomposition, uncertainty quantification, and adaptive network architectures. The effectiveness of PINNs is demonstrated through applications to three-dimensional wake flows, supersonic flows, and biomedical flow problems, illustrating their flexibility and potential for addressing high-dimensional, multiphysics, and data-driven challenges in fluid mechanics. Limitations related to optimization and accuracy compared to traditional computational fluid dynamics solvers are also discussed, along with future directions for improving PINN performance and applicability.

title: Computational Modeling, Formal Analysis, and Tools for Systems Biology
abstract: The rapid expansion of publicly available biological data has driven the adoption of advanced computational modeling and formal analysis techniques in systems biology. This review examines the integration of concepts and tools from theoretical computer science—such as process algebras, rule-based systems, Petri nets, model checking, and static analysis—into the modeling and investigation of complex biological processes. We discuss how these approaches enable precise, executable representations of biological systems, facilitate hypothesis testing, and support both qualitative and quantitative analyses. Emphasizing the importance of domain-specific languages and graphical modeling frameworks, we highlight their accessibility to biologists and their capacity to bridge mathematical and computational paradigms. The review also considers the potential for cross-disciplinary feedback, where advances in systems biology can inspire new developments in computer science. By surveying key methodologies and software tools, we aim to foster a deeper understanding of formal modeling concepts among systems biologists and encourage broader adoption of rigorous computational practices in the study of biological systems.

title: Introduction to the non-asymptotic analysis of random matrices
abstract: This is a tutorial on some basic non-asymptotic methods and concepts in random matrix theory. The reader will learn several tools for the analysis of the extreme singular values of random matrices with independent rows or columns. Many of these methods sprung off from the development of geometric functional analysis since the 1970's. They have applications in several fields, most notably in theoretical computer science, statistics and signal processing. A few basic applications are covered in this text, particularly for the problem of estimating covariance matrices in statistics and for validating probabilistic constructions of measurement matrices in compressed sensing. These notes are written particularly for graduate students and beginning researchers in different areas, including functional analysts, probabilists, theoretical statisticians, electrical engineers, and theoretical computer scientists.

title: Durkheim and the Internet: On Sociolinguistics and the Sociological Imagination
abstract: This book critically examines the foundational assumptions of sociolinguistics through the lens of Durkheim’s concept of the social fact, exploring how language operates as a normative collective system that both reflects and shapes social integration, inequality, and identity. By tracing the evolution of sociolinguistic theory from Durkheim’s era to the complexities introduced by digital communication and globalization, the work proposes new theoretical frameworks—including indexical-polynomic, genre, microhegemonic, and polycentric models—to account for the dynamic, fragmented, and polycentric nature of contemporary language practices online. Ultimately, the book argues for a renewed sociological imagination that recognizes theory as an evolving tool grounded in empirical research, capable of addressing the challenges posed by rapidly changing linguistic landscapes in the digital age.

title: Recent advances and applications of machine learning in solid-state materials science
abstract: One of the most exciting tools that have entered the material science toolbox in recent years is machine learning. This collection of statistical methods has already proved to be capable of considerably speeding up both fundamental and applied research. At present, we are witnessing an explosion of works that develop and apply machine learning to solid-state systems. We provide a comprehensive overview and analysis of the most recent research in this topic. As a starting point, we introduce machine learning principles, algorithms, descriptors, and databases in materials science. We continue with the description of different machine learning approaches for the discovery of stable materials and the prediction of their crystal structure. Then we discuss research in numerous quantitative structure–property relationships and various approaches for the replacement of first-principle methods by machine learning. We review how active learning and surrogate-based optimization can be applied to improve the rational design process and related examples of applications. Two major questions are always the interpretability of and the physical understanding gained from machine learning models. We consider therefore the different facets of interpretability and their importance in materials science. Finally, we propose solutions and future research paths for various challenges in computational materials science.

title: The Weak Hydrogen Bond: In Structural Chemistry and Biology
abstract: The weak hydrogen bond, also known as non-conventional hydrogen bond, has been the subject of intense scrutiny over recent years in several fields, in particular structural chemistry, structural biology, and the pharmaceutical sciences. Today, there is a large body of experimental and theoretical evidence confirming that hydrogen bonds like C-H···O, N-H···π, C-H···π and even bonds like O-H··· metal play distinctive roles in molecular recognition, guiding molecular association, and in determining molecular and supramolecular architectures. The relevant compound classes include organometallic complexes, organic and bio-organic systems, as well as DNA and proteins.

title: Water quality remediation faces unprecedented challenges from 'legacy phosphorus'.
abstract: The past three decades have witnessed a dramatic increase in recognition of the role of diffuse phosphorus (P) pollution in eutrophication of surface waters. Agricultural conservation and nutrient management programs have been very successful at reducing P losses in runoff at the edge-of-field, but there has often been disappointingly little improvement in downstream water quality and ecology. (1) Growing evidence indicates that a major reason for this is the chronic release of P from “legacy P” stores, which have accumulated in watersheds and water bodies. (2-4) As a result, we face unprecedented challenges in meeting water quality targets, given that P legacies from past land management may continue to impair future water quality, over time scales of decades, and perhaps longer (Figure 1). Agricultural strategies across Europe and the U.S. are currently undergoing fundamental reevaluation, with reform of the Common Agricultural Policy and revising how conservation programs operate in the new Farm Bill, respectively.
